t: Phosphorylated tau (pT231)-positive cells were significantly elevated in olfactory bulb, cortex, and hippocampus of 6- and 20-month-old CoV-2-infected mice, with significantly greater increases in olfactory bulb and cortex of 20-month-old mice compared with 6-month-old mice; no p-tau was seen in mock or 3-month-old infected mice.

Tau oligomers (T22-positive cells), a toxic form of tau, were significantly increased in 6- and 20-month-old CoV-2-infected mice compared with mock, with a further significant increase in 20-month-old mice compared with 6-month-old mice across all brain regions.

p-tau was localized specifically adjacent to CD31+ endothelial cells, and increased von Willebrand factor staining was observed in infected brains, suggesting blood-brain barrier damage and a possible vascular etiology of tau pathology.
Immunohistochemistry showed elevated GFAP (astroglial activation) and IBA1 (microglial activation) expression in olfactory bulb, cortex, and hippocampus of CoV-2-infected mouse brains.

A significantly increased grade of demyelination (MBP staining) was seen in the striatum of infected aged brain tissue, along with significantly increased α-synuclein staining in 6- and 20-month-old infected mice.
The SMAD4-I500V variant retains the ability to dimerize but shows severely compromised transcriptional activity compared to wild-type SMAD4.
SMAD4-I500V acts in a dominant-negative manner on wild-type SMAD4 and on receptor-regulated SMADs, altering transcription of downstream target genes.
SMAD4-I500V impacts the transcription and functional activity of the developmental transcription regulator NKX2-5.
The dominant-negative effect of SMAD4-I500V leads to overall dysregulation of TGF-beta and BMP signaling pathways, underlying Myhre syndrome pathogenesis.
Germline variants causing Myhre syndrome localize at two positions in SMAD4, I500 and R496, with I500 V/T/M substitutions being more commonly identified in affected individuals.
Phenytoin stimulated CCN2 (connective tissue growth factor) synthesis in human gingival fibroblasts.
Phenytoin activated latent TGFβ1 in human gingival fibroblasts.
Phenytoin increased cellular ROS generation in human gingival fibroblasts.
Blocking TGFβ signaling with a TGFβ-neutralizing antibody, the TGFβ receptor kinase inhibitor SB431542, or the Smad3 inhibitor SIS3 completely inhibited phenytoin-induced CCN2 synthesis.

The general antioxidant N-acetylcysteine, the NOX inhibitor diphenylene iodonium, and the specific NOX4 inhibitor plumbagin almost completely suppressed phenytoin-induced ROS generation and latent TGFβ1 activation, indicating NOX4-derived ROS mediate this activation.
Curcumin dose-dependently decreased phenytoin-induced TGFβ1 activation and CCN2 synthesis in human gingival fibroblasts.
Higher total sedentary time was directly associated with greater depressive symptoms in women with fibromyalgia.
Time accumulated in sedentary bouts of 30 minutes or more was directly associated with greater depressive symptoms.
Time accumulated in sedentary bouts of 60 minutes or more was directly associated with greater depressive symptoms.
Associations between sedentary time and depressive symptoms generally remained significant after adjusting for moderate-to-vigorous physical activity and physical fitness.
Higher total sedentary time was directly associated with greater state anxiety in women with fibromyalgia.
Time accumulated in sedentary bouts of 30 minutes or more was directly associated with greater state anxiety.
Time accumulated in sedentary bouts of 60 minutes or more was directly associated with greater state anxiety.
The association between sedentary time and state anxiety disappeared after accounting for physical fitness, suggesting a protective/moderating role of fitness.
MVPA did not modify the associations between sedentary time and depressive symptoms or state anxiety.
The association between sedentary time (total and prolonged bouts) and state anxiety was no longer statistically significant after adjusting for physical fitness.

Physical fitness, but not moderate-to-vigorous physical activity, appeared to modify the associations of sedentary time with depressive symptoms and especially state anxiety, suggesting a protective role of fitness.
The authors suggest that reducing sedentary time and avoiding its accumulation in prolonged periods could be a rehabilitation strategy to reduce depressive symptoms and state anxiety in fibromyalgia.
Quantitative proteomics and biological validation showed elevated CCN2 protein levels in NGLY1-deficient human and mouse cell models compared to control cells.
Functional assays demonstrated over-stimulation of TGF-beta signaling in NGLY1-deficient cells, coinciding with elevated CCN2.
NGLY1-deficient cells show abnormal accumulation of endoplasmic reticulum-associated degradation (ERAD) substrates.
The authors propose that increased CCN2 and TGF-beta signaling may be linked to microscopic liver fibrosis observed in NGLY1 patients.
Mast cell infiltration in intestinal tissue was significantly increased in the IBS rat model compared to normal controls.
Abdominal massage reduced mast cell counts in IBS rat intestinal tissue, and combining massage with ketotifen further reduced mast cell counts.
IBS induction reduced mitochondrial number and caused swollen morphology with disrupted cristae in intestinal mucosal cells compared to control.
Abdominal massage protected mitochondrial integrity in intestinal mucosa of IBS rats, and this effect was enhanced when combined with the mast cell blocker ketotifen.
TRPV1 mRNA expression was reported as upregulated in the IBS group compared to control, though the difference was not statistically significant.
Abdominal massage significantly attenuated the upregulation of TRPV1 mRNA compared to the IBS group, and addition of a mast cell blocker further reduced TRPV1 expression.
TRPV1 protein, examined by immunofluorescence and localized to the plasma membrane, was highly expressed in the IBS group compared to control.
Abdominal massage suppressed TRPV1 protein expression compared to the IBS group; addition of a mast cell blocker further reduced TRPV1 but not significantly.
Tryptase granule levels in mast cells were significantly higher in the IBS group compared to normal controls.
Abdominal massage significantly reduced tryptase particle levels compared to the IBS group, but adding a mast cell blocker did not further reduce tryptase.
PAR2 protein was upregulated in the IBS group compared to control rats.
PKC (PKCepsilon) protein was upregulated in the IBS group compared to control rats.
Abdominal massage reduced PAR2 and PKCepsilon expression compared to the IBS group, and combining massage with a mast cell blocker further suppressed their expression.
Proteins of the PIP2-PLC downstream signaling axis were upregulated in the IBS group and downregulated upon abdominal massage or mast cell blocker treatment.

Histological analysis showed that abdominal massage restored normal intestinal villous morphology in IBS rats, whereas combining massage with ketotifen paradoxically resulted in swollen mucous membrane and acinar cells.
Red blood cell count differed significantly between fibromyalgia patients and healthy controls.
Hematocrit differed significantly between fibromyalgia patients and healthy controls and correlated with clinical parameters of fibromyalgia.
Mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC) differed significantly between fibromyalgia patients and healthy controls.
Platelet count differed significantly between fibromyalgia patients and healthy controls.
Serum creatinine levels differed significantly between fibromyalgia patients and healthy controls.
HbA1c levels differed significantly between fibromyalgia patients and healthy controls.
ESR values differed significantly between fibromyalgia patients and healthy controls and correlated with clinical parameters of fibromyalgia.

ROC analysis indicated that routine laboratory parameters (RBC count, hematocrit, MCHC, platelet count, creatinine, HbA1c, ESR) may assist in differentiating fibromyalgia patients from healthy controls.
Both ME/CFS patients showed approximately 20-fold higher unique CpG-site methylation variability across time points compared to the healthy control.
Fragment-level (multi-CpG) methylation variability scores were higher in both patients than in the control, with the more symptomatic patient showing the highest score.
Patients showed greater methylation variability than the control across gene bodies and CpG islands, but variability was similar across all three individuals at transcription start sites.

Hierarchical clustering of 577 common methylation fragments across all 15 samples grouped samples by individual (patient/control identity) rather than by time point, though intra-individual variation across time points was also visible.

STRING pathway enrichment of genes containing differentially methylated fragments in P1 versus control identified nicotine addiction and morphine addiction pathways, driven by GNAS, CACNA1A and GABRD.

STRING pathway enrichment of genes containing differentially methylated fragments in P2 versus control identified TGF-beta family and Immunoglobulin C-2 type domains, from genes IGSF9B, OPCML, GDF7, CERS1 and LINGO3.
In patient P1, all 17 methylation fragments that correlated strongly with self-reported health scores were hypomethylated during the relapse period compared with recovery periods.
In patient P2, of 14 relapse-correlated methylation fragments, 11 were hypomethylated and 3 were hypermethylated during the relapse period compared with recovery.

The number of genes associated with relapse-correlated methylation fragments was significantly greater in the two patients than in simulated 'relapse' analyses performed on the healthy control's data, supporting that the changes reflect true disease biology rather than random variation.

Genes associated with relapse-related methylation changes in both patients were predominantly linked to immune/inflammatory function, including NF-kappa-B activity, wound healing, cytokine release, and angiogenesis, suggesting an enhanced inflammatory state during relapse.
In patient P2, differential methylation of CXCR1 and CXCR2 during relapse suggested potential activation of the interleukin-8 (IL-8) mediated signalling pathway.

The authors cite prior work indicating IL8 is the gene most differentially expressed between ME/CFS patients and controls, and that IL-8 levels are significantly higher in severely affected ME/CFS patients than in healthy controls or moderately affected patients, supporting their own CXCR1/CXCR2 methylation findings.

In patient P1, a hypomethylated fragment during relapse overlapped the first intron of NLRP7 and an enhancer, alongside other NF-kappa-B-associated genes (COMMD5, LRRC14, TONSL), suggesting increased inflammatory gene regulation during relapse.

In patient P2, differentially methylated fragments associated with TICAM1 and IL17RA, genes involved in positive regulation of cytokine production in inflammatory responses, were identified during relapse.
Several methylation-affected genes in patient P2 during relapse (TMBIM1, SLC11A1, MOSPD2, CXCR2, CXCR1, LRG1) are involved specifically in the neutrophil degranulation pathway.

Seven mitochondrial genes, including ACOT9 (acyl-CoA hydrolysis) and HADHA/HADHB (mitochondrial beta-oxidation of long chain fatty acids), showed relapse-associated methylation changes in patient P1, potentially reflecting reduced mitochondrial function during relapse.

A relapse-associated methylation fragment in patient P2 was located within the last (17th) exon of SEMA6B, a gene involved in peripheral and central nervous system development, overlapping a promoter region and regulatory element clusters with YJU2, PLIN5, and LRG1.
Sleep-related symptoms were identified as a risk factor for suicidal ideation among people with ME/CFS.
Stigma was identified as a risk factor for suicidal ideation among people with ME/CFS.
Disability status was identified as a risk factor for suicidal ideation among people with ME/CFS.
Lower physical functioning was identified as a risk factor for suicidal ideation among people with ME/CFS.
Marital status was identified as a risk (or protective) factor for suicidal ideation among people with ME/CFS.
IKZF2 expression was significantly increased in bedridden (severe) ME/CFS patients compared to non-bedridden patients.
IKZF3 expression was significantly increased in bedridden ME/CFS patients versus non-bedridden patients and was among the genes most associated with bedridden status when controlling for age and sex.
ABCE1, an inhibitor of the antiviral OAS/RNase L pathway, was upregulated in severe (bedridden) ME/CFS cases, suggesting impairment of RNase L antiviral signaling in these patients.
BACH2 expression was significantly increased in bedridden ME/CFS patients compared to non-bedridden patients.
CD3D, a T-cell receptor/CD3 complex gene, was significantly upregulated in bedridden ME/CFS patients relative to non-bedridden patients.
HSPA8 was among the top genes associated with bedridden status in ME/CFS patients, significant even after controlling for age and sex.

In the subset of ME/CFS patients with comorbid autoimmune disease, the six bedridden-associated genes showed even greater differential expression between bedridden and non-bedridden patients than in the overall ME/CFS cohort, suggesting an additive effect of autoimmune comorbidity on fatigue-related gene expression.
Interferon-stimulated genes IFIT1, ISG15, and IFI6 were enriched (upregulated) in female ME/CFS patients compared to males within unsupervised clustering analysis.
APOL6 and SLC2A3 expression was higher in ME/CFS patients aged 55 years and older compared to younger patients.
Thirty percent of ME/CFS participants reported having one or more comorbid autoimmune diseases, compared to 10% of healthy controls.
HHV-6 was detected via qPCR in 7 of 163 CFS blood samples and 1 of 79 control samples, a difference that did not reach statistical significance.
Only one CFS blood sample tested positive for EBV DNA by qPCR, indicating that active EBV infection was rare in this cohort.
Approximately half (49%) of ME/CFS participants reported being housebound or bedridden due to their symptoms.

Seventy-six percent of ME/CFS patients reported a triggering event before disease onset, and 80% of those identified a viral or bacterial infection (e.g., EBV, mononucleosis, flu, H. pylori, pneumonia, strep throat, COVID) as the trigger.

Replicate blood samples collected 3-4 weeks apart from the same participants showed high correlation (Spearman r = 0.86) across all 51 AIP panel genes, supporting reproducibility of the fingerstick gene expression test.

Citing a prior Norwegian clinical trial, B-cell depletion with rituximab (anti-CD20) was reported to produce clinical benefit in about half of ME/CFS patients treated, with symptom improvement delayed 3-7 months after initial B-cell depletion.

A cited case series described three ME/CFS patients (7-10 years disease duration) who had substantial relief of all CFS symptoms after rituximab treatment, lasting until about 40 weeks post-treatment before gradual symptom return.

A cited 2013 study found CFS was associated with an increased risk of non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, particularly diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, marginal zone lymphoma, and B-cell NHL not otherwise specified.

Two superordinate themes, 'Lack of knowledge and understanding' and 'Holistic Impact', were identified across carers of youth, young adults, and spouses with ME/CFS, echoing themes found in prior caregiver studies.

The sub-ordinate themes 'Caring Blindly', 'Emotional and physical health cost', and 'Impact on the whole family' were more evident among carers of youth with ME/CFS than among carers of young adults or spouses.

The theme 'Worry for the future' was more prominent among carers of young adults and spouses with ME/CFS compared to carers of youth, plausibly reflecting differences in life stage and time since diagnosis.
IgG autoantibodies against the alpha-2A adrenergic receptor were significantly lower in both PCS/ME/CFS and PCS/non-ME/CFS patients compared with both healthy control groups (HC and PCHC).

Autoantibodies against the beta-2 adrenergic receptor were significantly decreased in both PCS/ME/CFS and PCS/non-ME/CFS relative to HC and PCHC, and ADRB2-Ab was the top-ranked classifier in random forest analysis.

Autoantibodies against the scavenger receptor Stabilin-1 were significantly lower in both PCS groups compared to healthy controls and ranked among the top classifiers of PCS in random forest analysis.
Autoantibodies against the chemokine receptor CXCR3 were significantly reduced in both PCS/ME/CFS and PCS/non-ME/CFS compared to healthy control groups.
Autoantibodies against the muscarinic receptor CHRM5 and nicotinic receptor CHRNA1 were specifically diminished in PCS/ME/CFS patients but not clearly in PCS/non-ME/CFS.
Autoantibodies against the protease-activated receptor F2R/PAR-1 were reduced specifically in PCS/non-ME/CFS patients compared to healthy groups.
MAS1 autoantibody levels were the only AAB found to differ between the two healthy control groups (post-COVID PCHC vs seronegative HC), unlike all other measured AABs.

Total serum IgG concentrations did not differ significantly between PCS patients and control groups, indicating that AAB differences are not explained by global hypogammaglobulinemia or hypergammaglobulinemia.

Regression modeling showed that 13 of the 20 measured autoantibodies were significantly affected by confounders, with 9 influenced by gender, 3 by disease duration, and ADRB1 by both, with a general trend toward higher AAB levels in males and decreasing levels with time since infection.

After adjusting for sex, age and time since infection, PCS/ME/CFS patients had higher levels of CHRM1 and F2R/PAR-1 autoantibodies but lower levels of ADRB1, CHRNA1 and EDNRA autoantibodies compared with PCS/non-ME/CFS patients.

Random forest classification using all 20 measured autoantibody levels distinguished healthy individuals from PCS patients with an AUC of 0.77 and an out-of-bag error rate of 20.34%, with ADRB2-Ab, STAB1-Ab, and ADRA2A-Ab as the top three classifiers.

Spearman correlation networks among the 20 autoantibodies showed altered inter-AAB relationships in PCS patients, including weakened correlation of ADRB2 with ADRB1 and CHRM4 compared with healthy groups, and stronger correlations of CHRM1 with AGTR2/CHRM2 in patients and of EDNRB with BDKRB1 mainly in PCS/ME/CFS.

In PCS/ME/CFS patients, fatigue severity correlated positively with circulating autoantibody levels against AGTR1, EDNRA, BDKRB1, ADRB1/2, and CHRM3/5, all of which were otherwise reduced in this group.

Severity of cognitive symptoms in PCS/ME/CFS patients correlated positively with autoantibody levels against F2R/PAR-1, CXCR3, and STAB1, receptors involved in inflammatory processes rather than vasoconstriction.
Immune symptom severity in PCS/ME/CFS correlated positively with autoantibody levels against EDNRB, BDKRB1, and CHRM5.
In PCS/ME/CFS patients, secretomotor autonomic symptoms (dry eyes, dry mouth) on COMPASS-31 correlated negatively with autoantibody levels against AGTR1, EDNRA, ADRA1A, ADRB1/2, and CHRM3.
ADRB2-Ab and CHRM3-Ab levels correlated with vasomotor (Raynaud) symptoms in PCS/ME/CFS patients on the COMPASS-31 questionnaire.

In PCS/non-ME/CFS patients, gastrointestinal symptoms correlated with MAS1-Ab, gastrointestinal and pupillomotor symptoms correlated with F2R/PAR-1-Ab, and bladder symptoms correlated negatively with ADRA2A- and CHRM2/5-Ab; none of the fatigue/cognitive/immune correlations seen in PCS/ME/CFS were significant in this group.

PCS/ME/CFS patients had significantly worse fatigue (Chalder Fatigue Scale), higher PEM score, greater disability (Bell Disability Scale), and worse physical functioning (SF-36) than PCS/non-ME/CFS patients, though overall symptom severity scores for fatigue, cognitive symptoms, headache, and muscle pain did not differ between groups.

The authors note that a sequence in Epstein-Barr virus with high homology to ADRA2 may induce cross-reactive IgG antibodies, potentially relevant given that EBV reactivation during COVID-19 has been identified as a risk factor for Post COVID Syndrome.
Pooled analysis of 52 studies found the global prevalence of chronic fatigue syndrome among long COVID-19 patients to be 45.2%.
Heterogeneity among the included studies was extremely high (I2=99.7%), prompting use of a random effects model.
Publication bias was found to be statistically significant, indicating the pooled prevalence estimate should be interpreted with caution.
Meta-regression showed that the prevalence of chronic fatigue syndrome among long COVID patients increased with larger sample size and later year of study.
Several cited studies report higher prevalence of post-COVID fatigue among women compared to men, with one study finding fatigue prevalence three times higher in women.
Some studies reviewed did not find a difference in fatigue prevalence between men and women.
Chronic post-COVID-19 fatigue prevalence and severity were reported to be higher among adults than younger age groups, and aging was significantly associated with fatigue in one study.

Hospitalized patients experienced greater severity of chronic post-COVID-19 fatigue than non-hospitalized patients in some studies, and length of hospital stay affected the duration of fatigue, though one study found the opposite pattern.
In a Swedish study of healthcare professionals, 8% of participants reported disturbances in their work life and 15% reported disturbances in their social life due to post-COVID-19 syndrome.
In one cited study, 49% of patients experienced long COVID symptoms and chronic fatigue, and social disability was reported in more than 30% of participants in a study by Lemhofer.
FM patients (total group) showed significantly worse levels of depression, stress, anxiety, pain, fatigue, and fibromyalgia impact compared to healthy reference women.
FM patients showed greater fear and anxiety toward COVID-19 compared to the healthy reference group.
Codiagnosis of CFS in FM patients did not significantly affect levels of depression, stress, state anxiety, or trait anxiety compared to FM-only patients.

FM patients (with or without CFS) who reported habitual physical exercise (HPE) showed significantly better levels of depression, stress, and anxiety compared to sedentary patients, approaching reference group values.
COVID-19 related anxiety did not improve significantly with HPE, although a strong trend toward improvement was observed.
FM patients (both FM-only and FM+CFS) who reported HPE had lower levels of fear of COVID-19 compared to sedentary patients, nearly reaching reference group levels.
Codiagnosis with CFS did not affect quality of life/personal control or pain levels in FM patients, although both parameters were worse than the reference group.
The complete FM+CFS group reported significantly greater fatigue than the complete FM-only group.
FM patients (both with and without CFS) who reported HPE had significantly higher quality of life and personal control scores than sedentary patients, reaching reference group values.
No improvement in fatigue and pain levels was observed in women with FM who reported performing HPE, regardless of CFS codiagnosis.
Only in the FM-only group, HPE had a positive influence on the impact of fibromyalgia on daily life.
A differential effect of CFS codiagnosis was observed only in depression response to exercise: only FM patients without CFS showed improved depression with HPE.
A higher percentage of FM+CFS patients reported performing habitual physical exercise compared to FM-only patients, at a similar rate to the healthy reference group.
Patients with CFS/FM reported significantly more symptoms on the CFS Symptom List (CSL) than healthy controls.
No significant between-group differences were found in temporal summation or conditioned pain modulation (CPM) to cold or heat stimuli.
Serum IFN-γ concentration was significantly lower in patients with CFS/FM compared to healthy controls.
DNA methylation at the third CpG region of the MB-COMT promoter (MB-COMTc) was significantly higher (roughly double) in patients with CFS/FM than in healthy controls.
Mean MB-COMT promoter DNA methylation was significantly higher overall in patients with CFS/FM compared to healthy controls.
Mean S-COMT promoter DNA methylation did not differ significantly between patients with CFS/FM and healthy controls.
Genotype frequencies for the COMT polymorphisms rs4633, rs4818, and rs4680 did not differ significantly between patients with CFS/FM and healthy controls.
COMT haplotypes associated with high enzyme activity showed significantly lower S-COMT promoter DNA methylation than the intermediate-low activity haplotype, across the whole sample.
COMT haplotype was significantly associated with TGF-β expression, with the high-activity haplotype showing lower TGF-β levels than the intermediate-low activity haplotype.

COMT haplotype was significantly associated with CSL symptom severity, with the intermediate-low activity haplotype associated with higher symptom scores than the high-activity haplotype in both patients and controls.
COMT haplotype was significantly associated with cold pain thresholds, with the intermediate-low activity haplotype showing higher cold thresholds than the high-activity haplotype.
COMT haplotype significantly affected conditioned pain modulation to cold stimuli (C-CPM), differing between high- and intermediate-low activity haplotype groups.
No significant associations were found between COMT DNA methylation and cytokine levels, nor between DNA methylation and CSL symptom scores.
Older age was significantly associated with reduced DNA methylation at the MB-COMTb CpG region.
Age and IL-6 concentration were significant predictors of IFN-γ expression, with age negatively associated and IL-6 positively associated with IFN-γ levels.
Neither disease group nor COMT haplotype significantly affected IL-6 concentration.
IFN-γ concentration was significantly positively associated with IL-6 concentration.
Serum TGF-β levels did not differ significantly between patients with CFS/FM and healthy controls.
Serum IL-6 levels showed no statistically significant difference between patients with CFS/FM and healthy controls, though patients trended higher.
TNF-α was not detectable via ELISA in serum samples, precluding analysis of this cytokine, possibly due to sample degradation.

In this cohort of 100 patients with interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome, 31% tested positive for small-fiber polyneuropathy based on skin biopsy intraepidermal nerve fiber density measurement.
Intraepidermal nerve fiber density was below the age- and sex-matched median in 81% of the IC/BPS patients studied.
Chronic fatigue syndrome co-occurrence was significantly more common among SFPN-positive IC/BPS patients (31%) than SFPN-negative patients (10.6%).
SFPN-positive IC/BPS patients reported significantly fewer allergies (37.9%) than SFPN-negative patients (60.6%).
There was no significant difference in bladder capacity or Hunner lesion status between SFPN-positive and SFPN-negative IC/BPS patients.
Pooled data from 26 RCTs showed Chinese herbal medicine (CHM), as adjuvant or monotherapy, significantly decreased FS-14 fatigue scores compared with control groups.
Meta-analysis of nine RCTs showed CHM significantly decreased FAI scores versus control, though the effect was not significant in the subgroup with intervention duration >60 days.
Pooled analysis of five RCTs showed CHM significantly lowered SCL-90 mental state scores compared to control.
Meta-analysis of seven RCTs showed CHM significantly decreased SAS anxiety scores compared to control.
Meta-analysis of six RCTs showed CHM significantly reduced SDS depression scores compared to control.
Pooled data from 24 studies showed CHM significantly decreased overall clinical symptom severity scores compared to control.
Meta-analysis of eight RCTs found CHM significantly elevated IgA levels in CFS patients compared to control.
Meta-analysis of eight RCTs found CHM significantly elevated IgG levels in CFS patients compared to control.
Meta-analysis of eight RCTs found CHM significantly elevated IgM levels in CFS patients compared to control.
Pooled analysis of three RCTs found no significant difference in NK cell levels between CHM-treated and control CFS patients overall.
In a subgroup comparing CHM to placebo, one study showed CHM significantly elevated NK cell levels, in contrast to the null overall pooled result versus WCM.
Pooled clinical effective rate across 79 RCTs was significantly higher with CHM treatment than with control interventions.
Across 14 studies reporting adverse events, CHM caused only mild adverse effects (nausea, dry mouth, indigestion, constipation, fever) with no serious adverse events or deaths reported.
A cited study found that IgA, IgG, and IgM levels are significantly lower in CFS patients compared with healthy subjects, providing rationale for the immune-modulating effect of CHM.
A cited study reported that NK cell activity, CD4+, and CD8+ T cell counts were all significantly reduced in CFS patients.
Among 16 patients diagnosed with EDS, 9 (56.3%) also carried a diagnosis of functional movement disorder (FMD).
Among 190 patients diagnosed with FMD, 16 (8.4%) were also diagnosed with EDS.
In all cases where both diagnoses were present, the diagnosis of EDS preceded the onset and diagnosis of FMD, suggesting EDS may be a prodromal subtype of FMD.
Classical EDS patients with heterozygous COL5A1 or COL5A2 mutations show abnormal corneal thinning and increased corneal steepness.
In a study of 50 classical EDS patients, Villani et al. demonstrated corneal surface irregularity and tear film dysfunction.
In a TNX-deficient EDS cohort, approximately 30% of individuals exhibited recurrent subconjunctival hemorrhages.

Cardiac-valvular EDS is defined by a COL1A2 mutation causing absence of the pro-α2 chain of type I collagen via nonsense-mediated mRNA decay, associated with severe cardiac valvular disease and variable ocular findings such as myopia, strabismus, astigmatism, and blue sclera.

A vascular EDS patient with COL3A1-related type IV EDS developed advanced glaucoma with markedly elevated intraocular pressures (46 and 42 mmHg) and glaucomatous optic atrophy, suggesting type III collagen defects predispose to open angle glaucoma via trabecular meshwork abnormalities.

A vEDS patient developed carotid-cavernous fistula presenting with vision loss, proptosis, conjunctival hyperemia, chemosis, orbital pain, and ocular bruits; embolization attempt resulted in retinal ischemia, endophthalmitis, and fatal aortic rupture.
Ghabriya et al. found hEDS patients reported more dry eye symptoms than controls, with symptom severity correlating with Schirmer test findings.
In a study of 12 hEDS patients, dry eye symptoms were present in 83%, with 46% showing objective findings including punctate epithelial erosions or decreased tear break-up time.

Ho et al. found a higher prevalence of sicca complex (dry eye) in EDS patients with comorbid POTS dysautonomia relative to the general public, hypothesized to result from autonomic dysfunction impairing exocrine/lacrimal gland function.

Gharbiya et al. found approximately 16% of hEDS patients exhibited significant retinal atrophy and choroidal thickening (associated with pathological myopia >-6.0 diopters) compared to 0% of controls.
Mishra et al. found higher rates of myopia (>3.00 diopters) in hEDS patients, with 88% of patients having refractive errors between -3 and +3 diopters.

Chiarelli et al. showed hEDS fibroblasts exhibit dysregulated gene expression of extracellular matrix glycoproteins such as elastin, suggesting matrix dysfunction as a mechanism for ocular findings like myopia.
Recent evidence indicates there is likely no increased risk of angioid streaks in hEDS patients, contradicting earlier literature concern.
Mishra et al. examined 34 hEDS patients and found 68% had abnormal eyelids, with 41% exhibiting excess lid laxity and 24% having prominent horizontal upper lid skin folds.
Gharbiya et al. found minor lens opacities were significantly more prevalent in young adult hEDS subjects compared to controls.
Convergence insufficiency was reported to be common in a case series of EDS patients, with 60% of patients manifesting symptoms affecting near vision tasks (fatigue, nausea, headache).
Migraine is reported to be more common in hEDS patients, associated with reduced vision from aura and postdromal glare sensitivity/convergence insufficiency.

hEDS patients with poor concussion recovery showed persistent visuomotor complaints (convergence insufficiency, smooth pursuit and saccadic deficiency, glare sensitivity) that in a series of 7 patients led to previously undiagnosed hEDS.
In a review of 49 patients with arthrochalasia EDS (COL1A1/COL1A2 mutations), 3 subjects had blue sclera and 3 had both hypertelorism and epicanthal folds.
Foster et al. reported decreased ADAMTS2 expression in cultured keratoconus cells, linking this dermatosparaxis EDS-causing gene to corneal abnormalities.
Flitcroft et al. implicated ADAMTS2 mutations in myopia in genome-wide association studies.

In a case series of six patients with PLOD1-related kyphoscoliotic EDS, all had microcornea with corneal diameters ranging from 9 to 10.5 mm, versus normal adult diameters of 11.04-12.50 mm (men) and 10.70-12.58 mm (women).
In a case series of eleven kEDS patients, all had corneal thinning, and seven of eleven had experienced spontaneous or minimal-trauma corneal rupture, with one having corneal hydrops.
Presence of blue sclera in Brittle Cornea Syndrome correlates with at least a 33% reduction in central corneal thickness.

Arunrut et al. observed bilateral corneal clouding with unilateral corneal scarring and bilateral inferonasal iris colobomas in a 5-year-old female with a novel missense mutation in B4GALT7, associated with spondylodysplastic EDS.
Musculocontractural EDS caused by CHST14/D4ST1 or DSE mutations, leading to dermatan sulfate deficiency, is associated with microcornea, glaucoma, and refractive error as minor diagnostic criteria.

Almost all individuals (96%) with periodontal EDS (C1R/C1S mutations) reported easy bruising from early childhood, with skin fragility involving periorbita causing dermatochalasis and visual field crowding.

Brain MRI in adults with periodontal EDS has shown white matter abnormalities consistent with underlying small-vessel disease, with patients at risk of transient monocular vision loss requiring stroke workup.
Individuals with hEDS had lower muscle mass than healthy controls.
Individuals with G-HSD had lower muscle mass than healthy controls.
Individuals with hEDS had lower muscle cross-sectional area at the tibia than healthy controls.
Individuals with G-HSD had lower muscle cross-sectional area at the tibia than healthy controls.
Individuals with hEDS had lower cortical bone mineral content at the tibia than healthy controls.
Individuals with G-HSD had lower cortical bone mineral content at the tibia than healthy controls.
Individuals with hEDS had lower cortical bone area at the tibia than healthy controls.
Individuals with G-HSD had lower cortical bone area at the tibia than healthy controls.
Individuals with hEDS had lower muscle density than healthy controls.
Individuals with hEDS had lower muscle density at the lower leg compared to healthy controls.
Individuals with hEDS had lower trabecular bone mineral content (BMC) compared to healthy controls.
Individuals with hEDS had lower trabecular bone mineral density (BMD) compared to healthy controls.
Individuals with G-HSD had a lower stress-strain index (a measure of bone bending strength) compared to healthy controls.
Individuals with G-HSD had a lower periosteal circumference of the tibia compared to healthy controls.
Individuals with G-HSD had a lower endosteal circumference of the tibia compared to healthy controls.

A heterozygous multi-exon deletion spanning exons 2-65 of COL5A1 (almost the entire gene) was identified by MLPA as the cause of classical Ehlers-Danlos syndrome in the proband after initial NGS sequencing failed to detect a causal variant.

The COL5A1 deletion was inherited from the patient's clinically unaffected father, who harbored the deletion in mosaic form (parental gonosomal mosaicism) at approximately 43% in blood and 30% in skin biopsy DNA.

The multi-exon COL5A1 deletion identified in this patient is absent from control populations in gnomAD structural variants v2.1 and has not been previously reported in ClinVar, LOVD, or HGMD professional 2021.4.
In the LOVD database, only 0.8% (4 of 487) of reported COL5A1 variants are exon-level deletions, indicating that gross deletions are a rare mutation type in classical EDS compared to small variants.
Of 168 reported COL5A2 variants in LOVD, only one (0.6%) is a gross (multi-exon) deletion, similarly indicating that large rearrangements are rare in this gene relative to point mutations.
Haploinsufficiency of collagen V (from loss-of-function COL5A1 variants such as large deletions) is described as an established disease mechanism in classical EDS.
No loss-of-function structural variants in COL5A1 are reported among controls in gnomAD structural variants v2.1, supporting intolerance of the gene to such loss-of-function changes.

A study of 75 classical EDS patients suggested milder multisystem involvement and a more favorable disease course in cEDS compared with other EDS subtypes, consistent with the proband's relatively mild presentation.
In vascular EDS (caused by COL3A1 variants), parental mosaicism has been reported to occur at a rate of 2%-3%, providing a comparator estimate for parental mosaicism prevalence in EDS subtypes.

In a Marfan syndrome cohort of 333 individuals, approximately 5% of assumed de novo cases were caused by parental gonosomal mosaicism, and within this study the first reported case of low-level parental mosaicism for a COL5A1 variant (c.3179G>A, 11% VAF in blood) causing cEDS was described.

A second previously reported case of parental gonosomal mosaicism in cEDS involved a COL5A1 c.1369G>T p.(Glu457*) nonsense variant inherited from a father with an estimated 4.8% variant allele frequency in blood.

In a large trio-based exome sequencing study of 4293 probands with developmental disorders, parental mosaicism was identified in 0.5% of trios, associated with a substantially increased sibling recurrence risk.
Classical EDS can rarely be caused by the specific COL1A1 c.934C>T p.(Arg312Cys) variant, as opposed to the more common COL5A1/COL5A2 variants.
Among 93 mutation-positive cEDS patients, two-thirds of pathogenic COL5A1/COL5A2 variants arose de novo, as reported by Symoens and colleagues.
Nearly half of the EDS cohort (47.9%) showed retinal arterial tortuosity (RAT), either possible or definite, on retinal imaging.
No statistically significant differences in age, sex, or EDS subtype were found between patients with possible/definite RAT and those without RAT.
Hypertension and diabetes mellitus prevalence did not differ significantly between patients with definite RAT and those without RAT, and neither was associated with severe RAT.
Three patients in the cohort with vascular EDS carried COL3A1 mutations confirmed by genetic testing.
One patient with classical EDS in the cohort carried a COL5A1 mutation confirmed by genetic testing.
One patient with myopathic EDS in the cohort carried a COL12A1 mutation confirmed by genetic testing.
Among eyes with definite RAT, the severity distribution was 39.2% mild, 40.2% moderate and 20.6% severe tortuosity, using ROP-like grading criteria.

In patients with definite RAT, first-order arterioles were the most commonly involved vessel type (84.9%), distinct from the macular-predominant pattern seen in familial retinal arterial tortuosity (FRAT).
Over half of patients with possible or definite RAT also showed scattered yellowish-white retinal dots of unclear clinical significance, possibly reflecting a degenerative process related to EDS.

hEDS was the most common subtype in the cohort (69.7%) and is proposed to be associated with abnormal vascular extensibility and connective tissue, which may explain retinal arteriolar tortuosity despite hEDS not being classically linked to major vascular abnormalities.

Skin extensibility has been reported as strongly and linearly associated with, and the most predictive factor for, postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) in patients with hEDS in prior literature cited by the authors.
Inter-grader agreement for the presence/absence of RAT and for RAT severity grading was substantial (Kappa = 0.78 and 0.61, respectively).
Tarlov cysts in EDS are thought to arise from weakening of the epineurium and perineurium caused by defective connective tissue.
The pediatric patient with hypermobile-type EDS was found on investigation to have both a tethered spinal cord and a Tarlov cyst in the distal spinal cord.
Surgical obliteration of Tarlov cysts is reported in the literature to be 80-88% successful with complete postoperative symptom resolution.
After surgical resection of the Tarlov cyst and S1-S2 laminectomy, the patient's urinary and bowel incontinence improved drastically and continued to improve at six months.
Approximately one year after cyst resection, the patient's urinary incontinence recurred up to five times per week, exacerbated by daily activities, along with new lower back pain and numbness.

A second surgery (microsurgical resection of the filum terminale for tethered cord) led to improved mobility, reduced pain, and reduced paresthesia/radiating leg pain, but bowel/bladder incontinence and intermittent nerve pain persisted.
The patient continues to have bowel and bladder incontinence and intermittent nerve pain, currently managed pharmacologically with Tamsulosin, Pregabalin, and Hydromorphone as needed.
A large meta-analysis found a 0.53% incidence of Tarlov cysts in the pediatric population overall, with cysts more prominent in females.
The patient had a past medical history of hypermobile-type EDS (type III) alongside a CPA1 gene mutation.
The authors conclude that this case helps recognize urinary incontinence as a symptom associated with Tarlov cyst development in pediatric EDS patients.
Neurological complications reported in EDS include musculoskeletal pain, fatigue, muscle weakness, dystonia, and paresthesia.

The electronic visual analog scale (e-VAS) showed good agreement with the paper-based VAS (p-VAS) for pain intensity measurement in children and adolescents with HSD/HEDS, with an intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.87.
Bland-Altman analysis showed a slight bias with e-VAS scoring on average 0.19 points higher than p-VAS, within acceptable limits of agreement, supporting interchangeable use of the two methods.
Median pain scores differed by only 0.20 between the two VAS platforms among children and adolescents with symptomatic hypermobility.
The study sample was predominantly female, reflecting the reported higher prevalence of hypermobility spectrum disorder/hypermobile EDS among females.

The title reports a newly discovered gene mutation in a case of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome associated with elastosis perforans serpiginosa, but no further detail on the gene, variant, or patient characteristics is available from the title alone.
Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is caused by autosomal dominant mutation of the COL3A1 gene, which encodes type III collagen.

A postpartum patient with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome presented with spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) of the left anterior descending and obtuse marginal arteries, causing cardiogenic shock.

The patient sustained ischemic rupture of both the anterolateral and posteromedial papillary muscles secondary to the coronary dissection, described as the first reported case of ischemic double papillary muscle rupture in vEDS.
The true prevalence of vEDS is estimated to be at least 1 in 100,000 people, accounting for about 4% of all Ehlers-Danlos syndrome cases.
Unlike classic EDS, vEDS is characterized by increased risk of spontaneous vascular or visceral rupture and notably lacks large-joint hyperextensibility.
Rupture of internal organs such as intestine and muscles has been reported in most vEDS patients by age 40, and peripartum mortality is higher than average in this population.

Percutaneous catheter-guided thrombectomy (Penumbra and FlowTriever devices) was used to treat severe mitral stenosis from a large organized thrombus on a prosthetic mitral valve after anticoagulation failed, reducing the mean transvalvular gradient from 13 to 5 mm Hg.

Surgical mitral valve replacement with a 27 mm porcine bioprosthesis was performed for bilateral papillary muscle rupture, and repeat surgery was avoided for subsequent valve thrombosis due to extreme tissue fragility, with the patient recovering to NYHA class I at 6 months postoperatively.

Traditional Growing Rods (TGR) surgery was used to treat early-onset scoliosis in four patients with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, with pre-operative Cobb angles of 70-104 degrees corrected via surgery preceded by Halo-gravity traction.
All four EDS patients undergoing TGR treatment for early-onset scoliosis had kyphoscoliosis, indicating a notable spinal deformity phenotype in this population.
The large majority of adult vEDS patients in this national cohort had a documented history of arterial lesions (medium-sized artery and/or aortic).
Medium-sized artery (MSA) lesions were far more common than aortic lesions in this vEDS cohort.
After adjusting for age, patients with dominant-negative COL3A1 variants had a significantly higher prevalence of medium-sized artery lesions than those with haploinsufficiency variants.
Renal artery and supra-aortic trunk lesions were more frequent in patients with dominant-negative COL3A1 variants than in those with haploinsufficiency variants, after age adjustment.

The apparently higher rate of aortic lesions in haploinsufficiency patients compared with dominant-negative patients disappeared once adjusted for age at first arterial lesion, indicating the difference was explained by older age at diagnosis in HI patients rather than genotype.
Digestive events (e.g., colonic perforation) as the first manifestation of vEDS occurred exclusively in patients with dominant-negative COL3A1 variants.

Patients with dominant-negative COL3A1 variants had an earlier onset of their first arterial event than those with haploinsufficiency variants, though this did not translate into earlier molecular diagnosis.
Among the 43 deaths recorded (all in patients with prior arterial lesions), those with dominant-negative variants died at a significantly younger age than those with haploinsufficiency variants.
Carotid intima-media thickness and distensibility were substantially lower than predicted from age-, sex-, and BP-based normative reference values in vEDS patients, similarly across genotypes.
Aortic stiffness (carotid-femoral pulse wave velocity) was higher than expected from normative reference values for age and blood pressure in vEDS patients.

Carotid incremental elastic modulus (intrinsic wall stiffness) was significantly lower (i.e., wall more elastic) in dominant-negative than haploinsufficiency patients, persisting after adjustment for age, sex and blood pressure.

In a logistic regression model for aortic lesion occurrence, older age at first arterial lesion was a significant predictor, male sex showed a non-significant trend, and COL3A1 variant type was not significantly associated.
Female sex was independently associated with a higher risk of supra-aortic trunk lesions in the logistic regression model.
Dominant-negative COL3A1 variants were independently associated with a higher risk of supra-aortic trunk lesions in the logistic regression model.

Patients with aortic lesions had higher unadjusted carotid-femoral PWV, carotid IMT, and elastic modulus than those without, but all these differences disappeared after adjustment for age, indicating age (vascular aging) rather than aortic lesion status per se drives these arterial stiffness changes.

Patients with MSA lesions had significantly higher age-adjusted carotid-femoral PWV and reduced carotid distensibility than those without MSA lesions, with the distensibility difference persisting after further adjustment for sex and blood pressure.

Patients with supra-aortic trunk lesions had a significantly smaller carotid diameter than those without, even after adjustment for age, sex, and mean blood pressure, suggesting a possible developmental anomaly.
The type (rupture/dissection/aneurysm) and anatomical location of aortic lesions were not associated with COL3A1 variant class.
Citing prior work, the authors note that celiprolol selectively reduces carotid elastic modulus and has been shown to significantly reduce cardiovascular events in vEDS patients.
Prevalence of classical cardiovascular risk factors (smoking, overweight, hypertension, dyslipidemia, diabetes) at molecular diagnosis was low and similar between DN and HI variant groups.
Aortic lesions in this vEDS cohort were characterized predominantly as dissections and aneurysms, with rupture being rare, and thoracic and abdominal aorta equally affected.
Patients with haploinsufficiency COL3A1 variants were diagnosed at a significantly older median age than those with dominant-negative variants.

Periodontal Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (pEDS), characterized mainly by early-onset periodontitis, is caused by heterozygous mutations (missense, in-frame insertion, deletion) in the C1R gene (15 families) or C1S gene (2 families).
A study identified multiple heterozygous C1S mutations (G962C, T961G, T961A) in an extended family as pathogenic variants underlying pEDS.
In cellular studies, the pEDS-associated C1s mutants Val316del and Cys294Arg were produced as truncated proteins lacking their N-terminal domain.

Structural analyses showed that C1r and C1s interact via an extensive interface encompassing the N-terminal regions of both proteins, suggesting pEDS-causing mutations may disrupt this C1r-C1s binding and/or C1r-C1s-C1q coupling, facilitating aberrant C1s activation.
pEDS-associated mutations lead to constitutive (unregulated) activation of C1r and C1s, driving development of periodontal Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
Plasma norepinephrine levels are higher in fibromyalgia patients than in the general population.
Dopamine levels are reduced in fibromyalgia patients compared with the healthy population, potentially underlying diffuse pain and discomfort.
Serotonin levels are reduced in fibromyalgia patients compared with the healthy population.
Glutamate contributes to greater central pain sensitization in fibromyalgia.
Cerebrospinal fluid substance P concentration is threefold higher in fibromyalgia patients than in healthy subjects, contributing to pain modulation.
Fibromyalgia patients have lower nighttime melatonin secretion than healthy subjects, which may contribute to poor sleep, daytime fatigue, and altered pain perception.
Low nighttime melatonin is proposed to intensify nocturnal pain sensation in fibromyalgia.
Brain MRI shows increased sensory activity in the insula during fibromyalgia pain episodes.
Fibromyalgia patients show hypofunctioning of the HPA axis, resulting in relative adrenal insufficiency that may explain fatigue and reduced exercise/muscle performance.
CoQ10 levels are reduced in fibromyalgia and contribute to mitochondrial dysfunction, decreased mitochondrial membrane potential, increased superoxide activity, and lipid peroxidation.
Excessive mitophagy and autophagy are detected in blood mononuclear cells and plasma of fibromyalgia patients, potentially promoting cell injury and oxidative stress.
Lipid peroxidation products positively correlate with fibromyalgia severity as measured by the FIQR.
Reduced functioning of superoxide dismutase, catalase, and NADPH oxidase correlates with pain and fatigue severity in fibromyalgia.
Fibromyalgia subjects show low antioxidative enzyme activity (CAT, GR, GPx) with increased NO and MDA in red blood cell lysate.
Antioxidative enzymes are negatively associated with FIQR severity (functioning, pain, distress, sleep), while lipid peroxidation levels are positively correlated with FIQR.
Elevated serum nitrite, related to NOS activation and NO elevation, is a prooxidant marker linked to pain sensation via the spinal pain pathway in fibromyalgia.
La Rubia et al. found that lower antioxidant enzyme activities may lead to oxidative stress via DNA oxidation and elevated protein carbonyl content, affecting FM patients' health status.
Total antioxidant capacity is diminished in women with fibromyalgia compared to controls.
In a rat reserpine-induced myalgia model, melatonin supplementation prevented myotube deterioration and increased mitochondrial markers and CoQ10 in gastrocnemius muscle.
Melatonin administration in fibromyalgia patients can reduce pain and improve sleep quality, improving overall quality of life.
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy deactivates caspase 3 and 9 and increases Bcl-2 expression, suggesting reduced mitochondrial-induced apoptosis.
In animal models, hyperbaric oxygen therapy reduces lipid peroxidation and prooxidative processes.
Clinical trials show hyperbaric oxygen therapy improves global functioning, reduces pain, provides psychological relief, and normalizes brain activity in fibromyalgia patients.
Combined CoQ10, vitamin D, alpha-lipoic acid, magnesium, and tryptophan supplementation significantly reduced pain after one month and improved quality of life in fibromyalgia patients.
In an RCT by Cordero et al., CoQ10 combined with pregabalin significantly reduced pain and anxiety compared to pregabalin monotherapy in fibromyalgia patients.
A case report found that CoQ10 supplementation reduced oxidative stress markers, improved mitochondrial function, and diminished clinical symptoms in a fibromyalgia patient.
A randomized controlled trial found no significant symptomatic improvement in fibromyalgia patients receiving 50,000 IU of vitamin D weekly for three months.
Wepner et al. found that daily supplementation with 1200 IU or 2400 IU vitamin D for 25 weeks decreased pain sensitization (VAS) and morning fatigue (FIQ) in fibromyalgia patients.
A case series reported that vitamin A supplementation reduced or resolved fibromyalgia symptoms including musculoskeletal pain, fatigue, and depressed mood.
A controlled trial found that daily supplementation with 200 mg vitamin C and 200 mg vitamin E for 8 weeks resulted in pain reduction in fibromyalgia patients.
Nazıroğlu et al.'s controlled clinical pilot study found no significant symptom changes after 12 weeks of daily vitamin C (500 mg) and vitamin E (150 mg) supplementation in fibromyalgia patients.
Daily consumption of 50 mL of olive oil for three weeks improved FIQ score, physical ability, and mental health in 23 fibromyalgia patients.
Olive oil consumption decreased cardiovascular risk factors including lipid profile, inflammatory markers, and thrombosis-related parameters in 15 women with fibromyalgia.
Serum zinc concentration is significantly lower in chronic fatigue syndrome patients, associated with oxidative stress.
Serum zinc levels were substantially lower in 45 female fibromyalgia patients compared to controls (p<0.001).
Zinc deficiency is positively correlated with severity of depression, a key clinical feature of fibromyalgia.
Selenium levels are reduced in fibromyalgia patients, a trace element cofactor for glutathione peroxidase involved in neuroprotection.
In an animal model of fibromyalgia-induced rats, selenium supplementation reduced pain intensity, ROS levels, and lipid peroxidation.
Selenoproteins are necessary for development of parvalbumin-positive GABAergic interneurons, whose dysfunction is implicated in central hyperalgesia in fibromyalgia.
Fibromyalgia patients have significantly reduced serum ferritin levels compared to healthy controls.
Iron deficiency anemia was associated with increased risk of fibromyalgia prevalence in females, replicated by a second study showing higher FM incidence in iron-deficient individuals.
A placebo-controlled trial of ferric carboxymaltose in 80 women with fibromyalgia found improved FIQR and brief pain inventory scores and reduced fatigue after 42 days.
Folic acid has antioxidative properties and is reported to improve immune function and pain sensation in fibromyalgia.
Prooxidative processes induce mast cell activation and systemic macrocytosis in fibromyalgia, with mast cells located near nerve fibers modulating nociception via communication with microglia.

In the reserpine-induced myalgia rat model, combined melatonin and folic acid supplementation restored superoxide dismutase activity and reduced lipid peroxidation more effectively than either agent alone, decreasing pain sensitivity and depression-like behavior.
Serum copper and ceruloplasmin levels were significantly elevated in 45 fibromyalgia patients compared to healthy controls.
Serum copper, manganese, and aluminum concentrations were significantly higher in fibromyalgia patients than controls, correlating with FIQR score, tender points, and pain sensation.
In a randomized controlled trial, dietary glutamate significantly increased fibromyalgia symptom severity as assessed by worsening FIQR score.

Vellisca and Latorre found no significant difference in pain severity among 36 female fibromyalgia patients after discontinuing dietary MSG and aspartame for three months, contrasting with earlier case studies suggesting benefit.
Serum taurine levels were increased in fibromyalgia patients but were not significantly associated with clinical severity measured by FIQR.
Larson et al. found a significant relationship between CSF taurine level and tender point index in fibromyalgia patients.
A randomized trial found 12 weeks of Tai Chi and aerobic exercise significantly reduced FIQR scores and improved anxiety, pain, and global assessment in fibromyalgia patients.
A telerehabilitation aerobic exercise program showed similar benefits for Spanish fibromyalgia patients, though oxidative stress markers were not assessed in this study.

Whole-body vibration exercise increased superoxide dismutase activity, reduced catalase activity, decreased iron reduction capacity, and diminished thiobarbituric acid reactive substances in fibromyalgia patients.

Antidepressants such as amitriptyline and SNRIs (duloxetine, mirtazapine, venlafaxine) increase serotonin and norepinephrine, improving sleep and reducing pain and fatigue in fibromyalgia, but do not affect tender point tenderness.
Pramipexole, pregabalin, and gabapentin reduce pain in fibromyalgia, but pregabalin may be less effective overall than SNRIs and may induce more somatic symptoms.
Functional MRI shows fibromyalgia patients have greater neuronal activation in brain pain-processing areas, including the insula, compared to controls.
Fibromyalgia patients show increased functional connectivity between the default mode network and the insula.
Fibromyalgia patients show decreased functional connectivity within the descending pain-modulating system.
The cerebrospinal fluid of fibromyalgia patients contains high levels of the excitatory neurotransmitter substance P.
The cerebrospinal fluid of fibromyalgia patients contains high levels of the excitatory neurotransmitter glutamate.
Nearly half of fibromyalgia patients show objective evidence of peripheral small nerve fiber damage, demonstrated via skin biopsy and corneal confocal microscopy.
In rodent models, stressors such as unpredictable noise or forced swimming induce dorsal root ganglia neuroplasticity and resultant neuropathic pain.
Severe fibromyalgia has been associated with a particular dorsal root ganglia sodium channel gene variant.
IgG passively transferred from fibromyalgia patients into mice induces painful behavior and peripheral denervation, with IgG deposition found exclusively in the dorsal root ganglia.
There is clear evidence of sympathetic autonomic nervous system malfunction in individuals with fibromyalgia.
Fibromyalgia is reported to affect 2-4% of the population.
A systematic review found signs of small fiber damage in about half of FM patients, potentially contributing to pain and autonomic symptoms, though findings were heterogeneous.
Diagnosis in the literature has relied on identifying 18 tender points, with FM defined by pain on digital pressure at 11 or more of these points.
In a study of 86 FM patients, 10 who received myofascial release therapy showed marked improvement in tender points, physical function, and clinical severity that was sustained at six months.

An observational interview study of the Fibromyalgia Self-Management Program (FSMP) found it successfully facilitated behavior change via goal-setting and other self-management techniques over a six-week period.
Multiple systematic reviews conclude that cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is an effective approach for chronic pain management in FM.
Higher mindfulness in FM patients was associated with better sleep quality and reduced sleep disturbance, pain, and depression, potentially mediated by these psychological factors.
A mindfulness-based intervention (MBI) in women with FM significantly improved satisfaction with life, positive affect, mental health, and resilience compared to controls.
Mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR) added to treatment-as-usual (TAU) achieved a significant reduction in indirect and primary healthcare costs compared to TAU alone in Spanish FM patients.
Central sensitization in FM appears to involve an imbalance of BDNF and inflammatory biomarkers, implicated in pain modulation and hyperalgesia.
In an RCT, attachment-based compassion therapy (ABCT) produced significant improvement in FIQ scores and reduced BDNF, CRP, and a pro-inflammatory composite compared to relaxation therapy (RT).

MAIR (Mindfulness plus Amygdala and Insula Retraining) plus TAU improved functional impairment, clinical severity, and quality of life compared to relaxation therapy, and significantly decreased BDNF levels, though no significant change was found in immune-inflammatory variables.
A systematic review (2007-2011) found aerobic and power training exercise improves fitness, physical function, reduces FM symptoms, and improves quality of life.

A systematic review of exercise programs (dance, water activities, body-mind work, fitness, stretching) found pain reduced 10-44.2% and negative quality-of-life impact reduced 5.3-17.9% after multidisciplinary intervention.
Aerobic exercise and Zumba dancing both significantly improved working memory, motor function, and depressive symptoms in women with FM.

Aquatic physiotherapy plus health education significantly reduced fatigue, improved functional capability, and reduced anxiety, depression, and sleep problems in FM patients, but did not significantly reduce pain.
An exercise trial in adults with FM found a 54% increase in daily step count on the 6-minute walk test, 18% improvement in overall function, and 35% reduction in pain.
Improvements achieved during an exercise-based intervention program were not maintained over time, highlighting the problem of persistent inactivity relapse in FM patients.
A three-year longitudinal study found that a six-month combined training program produced immediate health improvements in women with FM, with benefits maintained for 30 months.
The FDA has approved three drugs specifically for FM treatment: duloxetine, milnacipran, and pregabalin.
Tricyclic antidepressants, SNRIs (duloxetine, milnacipran), and alpha2-delta ligands (gabapentin, pregabalin) were found effective in reducing FM-associated pain by at least 30%.
Amitriptyline was associated with improvement in pain, fatigue, sleep, and quality of life in FM patients.
A study among FM patients found improvement within two hours in VAS scores, reduced pain and stiffness, enhanced relaxation, and increased well-being following cannabis use.
A six-month longitudinal cohort study of 367 FM patients found significant decreases in average pain intensity, sleep disturbances, and depression-associated symptoms with cannabis use.
Vestibulodynia is described as the most common cause of sexual pain, affecting 16% of reproductive-aged women in the United States.
Vestibulodynia frequently co-occurs with irritable bowel syndrome, reported in 35% of patients.
Vestibulodynia frequently co-occurs with fibromyalgia syndrome, reported in 17% of patients.

Women with the peripheral vestibulodynia subtype (VBD-p) show normal psychological profiles, balanced pro-/anti-inflammatory cytokines, and dysregulated microRNAs that regulate oestrogen-pathway gene expression, whereas women with the central subtype (VBD-c) show decreased functional status, increased somatic awareness, lack of compensatory anti-inflammatory cytokine increases, and dysregulated microRNAs relevant to muscle, nerve, and immune-cell function.
Topical 5% lidocaine applied for 7 weeks decreased dyspareunia in women with vestibulodynia, likely by blocking sodium channels on peripheral nociceptors.
Topical oestrogen applied for 3 months reduced peripheral pain and inflammation and improved sexual function in premenopausal women with vulvar pain.
Tampon-induced vaginal pain is highest during the premenstrual phase, corresponding with systemic low oestrogen levels, suggesting oestrogen deficiency contributes to vestibulodynia pain.
An open trial of nortriptyline for 2 months found that 6 of 7 women experienced complete or partial reduction in chronic pelvic pain.
In a case study, nortriptyline completely alleviated vaginal pain in a woman for whom topical lidocaine, oestrogen, and other peripheral treatments had failed.
Amitriptyline efficacy data for vulvar pain are limited, and up to 30% of women discontinue its use due to sedation and other side effects.
A randomized controlled trial found that gabapentin was ineffective in reducing pain among women with vestibulodynia.
In a prior study, mean IL-8 levels differed between VBD patients and controls by approximately 4 pg/mL.
In a prior study, mean IL-1ra levels differed between VBD patients and controls by approximately 300 pg/mL.

Vestibulodynia subtypes are operationally defined by presence of chronic overlapping pain conditions (COPCs): women with no COPCs are classified as VBD-p (peripheral) and women with one or more of nine COPCs (including fibromyalgia, IBS, TMD, migraine, chronic fatigue syndrome, endometriosis, interstitial cystitis, back pain, tension headache) are classified as VBD-c (central).
Mastocytosis is driven by clonal mast cell expansion typically caused by a somatic gain-of-function KIT D816V mutation affecting the KIT/CD117 stem cell growth factor receptor.
The estimated prevalence of mastocytosis is approximately 1 in 10,000 individuals, though the exact figure remains uncertain.

Hereditary alpha tryptasemia (HaT), caused by increased copy number of the TPSAB1 gene, shows increased prevalence among patients with systemic mastocytosis, suggesting a possible link between the two conditions.
Tryptase directly increased intestinal epithelial permeability in Caco-2 monolayers, reducing transepithelial resistance and junctional protein expression while increasing FITC-dextran permeability.
PAR-2 inhibitor, but not propofol, restored intestinal barrier integrity disrupted directly by tryptase.
In a Caco-2/LAD-2 mast cell co-culture model, mast cell degranulation disrupted epithelial integrity, and this disruption was dramatically attenuated by propofol pretreatment.
Mast cell degranulation caused significant increases in intracellular ROS and Ca2+ levels, which were blocked by propofol and by the antioxidant NAC.

Propofol pretreatment inhibits mast cell activation via a ROS/Ca2+-dependent mechanism, thereby restoring intestinal barrier integrity disrupted by mast cell activation, but not the integrity disrupted directly by tryptase.
A young female with severe, treatment-resistant mixed inflammatory and atopic skin manifestations was diagnosed with hereditary alpha tryptasemia (HaT).
The authors note that HaT has previously been linked to a broad range of dermatologic, allergic, gastrointestinal, neuropsychiatric, autonomic, and connective tissue abnormalities.
The authors recommend considering HaT in patients with refractory inflammatory dermatologic disease and signs/symptoms suggestive of mast cell activation.

A 44-year-old woman developed type I Kounis syndrome with coronary vasospasm, ventricular fibrillation, and markedly elevated troponin I (up to 14.23 ng/mL) following a wasp sting, with resolution after antihistamine/H2-blocker therapy and supportive care.

A 44-year-old woman developed type I Kounis syndrome with ST depression and serial troponin I rise from 0.32 to 6.76 ng/mL after a brown spider bite, with chest pain resolving within 24 hours of nitroglycerin and antihistamine/corticosteroid therapy.

A 66-year-old man receiving maintenance FOLFOX plus panitumumab developed anaphylactic shock with severe Kounis syndrome (troponin I rising from 1.85 to >25 ng/mL) immediately after oxaliplatin infusion, and died three days later from multiorgan failure.

A 46-year-old man developed stent thrombosis (type III Kounis syndrome) five days after bare metal stent implantation, potentially due to hypersensitivity to stent components or to drugs administered in the ICU (aspirin, clopidogrel, ampicillin-sulbactam), resulting in a second myocardial infarction and death.

Mast cell degranulation releases histamine, tryptase, chymase, cathepsin-D, platelet activating factor, thromboxane, and leukotrienes, which together drive coronary vasoconstriction, matrix metalloproteinase-mediated plaque disruption, and thrombosis formation in Kounis syndrome.
The reported incidence of Kounis syndrome among patients hospitalized with allergy, hypersensitivity, anaphylaxis, or anaphylactoid reactions is between 2% and 3.4%.

A retrospective study of 235,420 patients hospitalized for allergy, hypersensitivity, anaphylaxis, or anaphylactic reactions between 2007 and 2014 calculated a Kounis syndrome-related mortality rate of 7%.
Postmortem studies have implicated mast cell degranulation in up to 13% of sudden deaths.
Glucagon is recommended over adrenaline for treatment of anaphylactic reactions in patients presenting with Kounis syndrome, since adrenaline can aggravate coronary vasospasm.
Beta-blockers can exacerbate coronary spasm in Kounis syndrome by leaving alpha-adrenergic receptors unopposed, so their use is cautioned in this setting.

The short half-lives of major mast cell mediators (platelet activating factor <5 minutes, histamine <15 minutes, tryptase approximately 2 hours) limit the clinical utility of measuring mast cell degranulation markers for diagnosing Kounis syndrome.
Mast cell numbers and levels of tryptase, chymase, and histamine are elevated in the airways of asthmatic patients.
IgE-mediated systemic or cutaneous anaphylaxis is completely absent in mast cell-deficient mice, demonstrating mast cells are required for this response.
Three months of omalizumab therapy reduced basophil FcεRI receptor levels by 95%, an effect later shown to also occur on cutaneous mast cells and to be sustained long-term.
A 1:1 molar ratio of ligelizumab to IgE inhibited 90% of IgE-mediated human mast cell degranulation.
16 weeks of dupilumab (anti-IL-4Rα) treatment decreased IL-4/IL-13-regulated Th2 response gene expression, including CCL17, CCL18, CCL26 and DPP4, in skin and serum of atopic dermatitis patients.

Vaccinating mice with IL-4 or IL-13 conjugated to a mutant, nontoxic diphtheria toxin elicited persistent neutralizing antibodies that greatly reduced eosinophilia, mucus production, and airway hyperresponsiveness in an allergic airway disease model.
In 15 patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome, one year of rituximab treatment depleted salivary gland mast cells by 50% without an associated decrease in T cells.
A 2013 study found no change in serum IgE levels after 6 months of rituximab therapy among 47 patients.
A retrospective study of rituximab-treated eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA) patients found that among a subset with asthma, 12 of 17 achieved disease remission.
Anti-Siglec-8 antibody lirentelimab suppressed FcεRI-dependent calcium flux, β-hexosaminidase and histamine release, and cytokine/chemokine secretion in cultured human mast cells.

The anti-tryptase antibody MTPS9579A diminished IgE-mediated systemic anaphylaxis in a humanized mouse model and reduced tetrameric tryptase levels in lung tissue of allergen-challenged cynomolgus monkeys.

CDX-0159, an anti-KIT antibody, produced a near-absence of serum tryptase (suggesting mast cell depletion) and a 4-fold increase in plasma SCF in human subjects, with an extended serum half-life of 32 days.
In patients with severe refractory asthma and airway hyperresponsiveness, six months of imatinib decreased mast cell counts, serum tryptase, and airway hyperresponsiveness.
Patients on long-term (>24 months) imatinib therapy showed a 90% reduction in mast cells and serum tryptase.

Ibrutinib and acalabrutinib (BTK inhibitors) prevented IgE-mediated cytokine production and degranulation in human basophils and primary mast cells and blocked IgE-mediated bronchoconstriction in human lung tissue.
In adults with tree nut or peanut allergy, short-term ibrutinib treatment (as few as two doses) eliminated IgE-mediated basophil activation and attenuated skin prick test responses.
PI3K inhibition with the FDA-approved drug pictilisib essentially ablated granule release by skin-derived mast cells, more potently than MAPK inhibition.
Rapamycin, an mTORC1 inhibitor, reduced inflammation in an IgE-mediated food allergy mouse model and inhibited IgE-induced mast cell cytokine production without affecting degranulation.

Tacrolimus was found to be 100-fold more effective at suppressing IgE-mediated human mast cell function than cyclosporine A, though it was questioned whether this activity is due to calcineurin antagonism.
The JAK1/2 inhibitor ruxolitinib inhibited mast cell degranulation and reduced food allergy symptoms in a mouse model, and improved quality-of-life measures for a systemic mastocytosis patient.

Fluvastatin reduced IgE-mediated degranulation and cytokine production in human and mouse mast cells in vitro and suppressed passive systemic anaphylaxis in mice, with effects attributed to reduced protein isoprenylation rather than cholesterol synthesis inhibition alone.
Three large studies (n>10,000) found significant improvements in asthma outcomes associated with statin therapy, while smaller studies yielded mixed but generally positive results.
In an ovalbumin-sensitized rat model, 20 mg/kg fluoxetine treatment decreased serum IgE, IL-4 and TNF levels, and reduced airway obstruction on lung histology.
In a small study of 21 patients with severe asthma, 12 weeks of escitalopram treatment improved asthma control and decreased inhaled corticosteroid use.
MRGPRX2 is a mast cell receptor identified in 2006 that causes IgE-independent activation, producing pseudo-allergic reactions with symptoms overlapping true allergy.
17β-estradiol exposure increased FcεRI-mediated β-hexosaminidase and leukotriene C4 secretion in RBL-2H3 and HMC-1 mast cell lines, along with elevated SCF, TGF-β, and MCP-1 mRNA.

The checkpoint kinase inhibitor AZD7762, which also inhibits Lyn, Fyn and Syk, suppressed antigen-induced mast cell degranulation and cytokine production and reduced passive cutaneous anaphylaxis in mice.
WZ3146, an EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor, reduced IgE-mediated Lyn, Fyn, and Syk activity and degranulation in mast cells and inhibited IgE-dependent passive cutaneous anaphylaxis in mice.
The BCR-ABL inhibitor dasatinib antagonized Lyn, Fyn, and Syk activity, reduced antigen-induced mast cell degranulation and cytokine production, and inhibited passive cutaneous anaphylaxis in mice.
The FDA-approved PI3K inhibitor pictilisib essentially ablated granule release from skin mast cells stimulated via FcεRI or MRGPRX2, more potently than MAPK inhibition.
The selective allosteric Akt inhibitor MK2206 reduced Akt activation, inhibited airway inflammation, diminished HMGB1 levels, and attenuated histamine/H4-receptor-induced mast cell migration in mice.
The mTORC1 inhibitor rapamycin reduced inflammation in an IgE-mediated food allergy mouse model and inhibited IgE-induced mast cell cytokine production without affecting degranulation.
The flavonoid mTORC1 inhibitor methoxyluteolin inhibited expression and release of pro-inflammatory mediators from human mast cells stimulated by neuropeptides.

The mTOR activators MHY1485 and 3BDO paradoxically inhibited FcεRI-mediated mast cell degranulation and suppressed IL-6/TNFα production, coincident with decreased mTORC2-mediated AKT phosphorylation, an effect reversible by an AKT agonist.

Bortezomib, a proteasome inhibitor, inhibited calcium ionophore- or PGE2-induced human mast cell degranulation and cytokine secretion, and induced apoptosis in mast cell leukemia cells attributed to the unfolded protein response.

Vorinostat (SAHA), a histone deacetylase inhibitor, induces cell death in the transformed human mast cell line HMC-1.2, though it is unclear whether this occurs via HDAC inhibition or subsequent NFκB inhibition.
The novel NFκB inhibitor DHMQ covalently blocks NFκB nuclear translocation and diminished FcεRI-mediated IL-6 and TNF production as well as migration towards antigen in RBL-2H3 mast cells.
Pyrrolidine dithiocarbamate, an NFκB DNA-binding inhibitor, reduced HMC-1 mast cell cytokine production elicited by polychlorinated biphenyl compounds.

Tacrolimus, a calcineurin inhibitor, inhibits IgE-induced histamine and PGD2 release from human mast cells and was found to be 100-fold more effective than cyclosporine A at suppressing IgE-mediated human mast cell function.
Cyclosporine A, a calcineurin inhibitor, inhibited IgE-induced TNF secretion from mouse mast cells and ionomycin-mediated cytokine production, along with c-Kit-mediated proliferation.
Pimozide, a neuroleptic that prevents STAT5 phosphorylation, inhibited IgE-induced rodent mast cell degranulation and migration in vitro and cutaneous or systemic anaphylaxis in vivo.

The STAT3 inhibitor C188-9 reduced anaphylaxis in vivo, though its effects could be partly attributed to inhibiting histamine or platelet activating factor receptor actions on the vasculature rather than STAT3 alone.

Tofacitinib, a JAK3-selective inhibitor, decreased IgE-mediated degranulation and cytokine production in the RBL-2H3 mast cell line and suppressed allergic conjunctivitis.

Two small clinical trials (n=6 and n=69) of atopic dermatitis patients showed significant improvement in clinical scoring lasting up to 29 weeks with JAK inhibitor therapy, and three JAK inhibitors (ruxolitinib, upadacitinib, abrocitinib) have since gained FDA approval for atopic dermatitis.
