Tamoxifen inhibited outward chloride flow via a CIC-5-like channel on HMC-1 and human lung mast cells, corresponding to decreased proliferation, and reduced rat mast cell degranulation elicited by compound 48/80, substance P, or ionomycin.

Thiazolidinediones suppress mouse mast cell maturation and induce apoptosis; pioglitazone stabilized body temperature in a passive systemic anaphylaxis model and suppressed airway hyperresponsiveness, serum IgE, and cytokines in a cockroach allergen asthma model, while rosiglitazone inhibited degranulation and reduced cytokine and IgE/IgG1 levels in a food allergy model.

Perphenazine, a dopamine receptor antagonist, reduced serum IgE, histamine, and IL-4/IL-5/IL-13 transcription and secretion, and inhibited mast cell migration to lesion sites in a mouse model of Th2-type allergic dermatitis.

Berberine, a dopamine receptor antagonist used in traditional medicine, attenuated DNFB-induced allergic contact dermatitis in rats and significantly reduced ear swelling, mast cell recruitment, serum IgE, and p38 phosphorylation.

Increasing both dose and duration of statin use reduced the hazard ratio for emergency department visits and hospitalizations attributed to asthma, and a meta-analysis found statin use correlated with protective outcomes in patients who later suffered sepsis or other infections.

Simvastatin reduced the inflammatory phenotype in a mouse model of allergic airway inflammation and airway hyperreactivity, and inhibited human airway smooth muscle cell proliferation through a GGT- and Rho-dependent mechanism.
20 mg/day rosuvastatin therapy reduced Th1-related TNF and IFNγ levels in patients.

The authors' own work found that fluvastatin reduced IgE-mediated degranulation and cytokine production in human and mouse mast cells in vitro and suppressed passive systemic anaphylaxis in mice, with effects phenocopied by inhibiting geranylgeranyl transferase-1 (GGT-1) rather than cholesterol synthesis alone.

Statin effects on mast cells varied widely among mouse strains, human donors, and among different statin drugs, with some statins having no effect on IgE-mediated activation while others were potent inhibitors, suggesting genetic background and HMGCR upregulation modulate statin responsiveness.

The index patient carried the mtDNA variant m.10191T>C in MT-ND3 (p.Ser45Pro), confirmed in buccal mucosa cells by whole exome sequencing and mtDNA sequencing, consistent with a Leigh-like syndrome diagnosis.
The patient also carried the m.12770A>G variant in MT-ND5, previously associated with MELAS syndrome, which may have contributed speculatively to the phenotypic heterogeneity.
Small fiber neuropathy was diagnosed via skin biopsy at age 23 in the index patient, presenting with lancinating nerve pain from age 19 that responded to gabapentin.
The patient exhibited severe orthostatic hypotension confirmed on tilt table testing at age 23, following a history of syncope beginning at age 7 and multiple syncopes per day by age 14.

Joint hypermobility was present from age 3 with recurrent sprains, dislocations, and easy bruising, alongside impaired wound healing, consistent with connective tissue involvement in this mitochondrial disease.
Migraine without aura, presenting as unilateral throbbing pain in the right middle cerebral artery territory starting at age 7, responded to sumatriptan and indomethacin.
Recurrent central hypoventilation, documented on sleep studies at ages 19, 23, and 26, improved with aerobic training and ubiquinol supplementation.
Recurrent severe diarrhea from age 6 did not stop until ubiquinol was administered at age 26.
The patient had intermittently elevated serum lactate and a lactate/pyruvate ratio reaching 28, which decreased with aerobic training and medication.

Muscle biopsy showed >10% ragged-red fibers with corresponding ragged-blue fibers on succinate dehydrogenase staining and 2% cytochrome-C oxidase-negative fibers, a frequency much greater than expected for the patient's age, along with denervation and fiber-type grouping.

The patient had markedly elevated CD19 counts, mild hypogammaglobulinemia, borderline-low IgM, and permanent lymphocytosis, hypothesized to relate to B cells' heavy reliance on oxidative phosphorylation.

The patient developed hemolytic anemia with hypersplenism from age 25, treated with splenectomy at age 26, complicated by a 12-hour delay of awakening from general anesthesia and severe thrashing ballism.

The patient required only gabapentin (not additional anti-seizure drugs) for her seizures, possibly because fenofibrate, which she was also taking, increases ketone bodies that have an anticonvulsant effect in mitochondrial disease patients.

Cerebral MRI showed bilateral T2/FLAIR hypointense lesions in the globus pallidus and midbrain with the 'face of the giant panda' sign, alongside calcifications on CT, supporting the diagnosis of Leigh-like syndrome after other panda-sign differentials (e.g., Wilson's disease) were ruled out.

Compared to 28 previously reported m.10191T>C carriers (Li et al.) with manifestations such as anopia, myoclonic epilepsy, stroke-like episodes, hearing loss, and short stature, the index patient shared only cognitive impairment, epilepsy, delayed speech development, and migraine, indicating a distinct, expanded phenotype.
Two of the three patients with neuropathic corneal pain and confirmed small-fiber neuropathy had high anti-TS-HDS IgM autoantibody titers.
One of the three patients with neuropathic corneal pain had a high anti-FGFR-3 IgG autoantibody titer in addition to anti-TS-HDS IgM.
Skin biopsy confirmed decreased intraepidermal nerve fiber density consistent with small-fiber neuropathy in all three patients with neuropathic corneal pain.
Cardiac Col-1α mRNA was significantly increased in Npr1-/- and Npr1+/- mice compared with wild-type controls.
α-SMA mRNA and protein were markedly increased in Npr1-/- hearts compared with wild-type controls, indicating myofibroblast activation.
Baseline SMAD-1, -2, -3, and -4 protein levels were significantly increased while SMAD-6 was decreased in Npr1-/- hearts compared with wild-type mice.
Phosphorylated TAK1 and ERK1/2 (non-canonical TGF-β1 signaling mediators) were increased in Npr1-/- mouse hearts compared with wild-type mice.
ECM remodeling proteins MMP-2, MMP-9, PCNA, and CTGF were significantly increased at the protein level in Npr1-/- and Npr1+/- hearts compared with wild-type mice.
TGF-β1RI and TGF-β1RII protein expression were significantly increased in Npr1-/- and Npr1+/- mouse hearts by both Western blot and immunohistochemistry.
Phosphorylated SMAD2 and SMAD3 were significantly increased in Npr1-/- and Npr1+/- hearts compared to wild-type controls, confirmed by Western blot and immunohistochemistry.
Treatment with the TGF-β1 receptor antagonist GW788388 significantly reduced fibrotic marker mRNA and protein expression, TGF-β1 receptor levels, and SMAD phosphorylation in Npr1 mutant mouse hearts.
Systolic blood pressure was more severely elevated in male Npr1 mutant mice than in female mutants of the same genotype, indicating sex-dependent hypertension severity.
GW788388 treatment lowered systolic blood pressure in both male and female Npr1 mutant mice but had no significant effect in wild-type mice.
Cardiac hypertrophy (HW/BW ratio) was much more pronounced in male than female Npr1 mutant mice, with GW788388 only partially normalizing the hypertrophy.
Both interstitial and perivascular cardiac fibrosis were markedly increased in male Npr1-/- and Npr1+/- mice, and were substantially attenuated by GW788388 treatment.

Male Npr1-/- and Npr1+/- mice showed significantly worse left ventricular dilation, reduced fractional shortening, and compromised heart rate compared with wild-type mice, whereas female mutants showed only modest changes in these parameters.
GW788388 treatment normalized LVED-s, LVED-d, IVST, PWT, FS, and HR toward wild-type levels in male Npr1 mutant mice.
Male Npr1 mutant mice exhibited more severe hypertension, cardiac hypertrophy, fibrosis, and dysfunction than female mutants, potentially related to estrogen's protective effects.
Four patients heterozygous for the CAH-X CH-1 allele (a CYP21A2 deletion extending into TNXB) did not present clinical manifestations of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
The TNXB gene, which partially overlaps CYP21A2, encodes the matrix protein Tenascin-X, and complete Tenascin-X deficiency causes Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
95% of congenital adrenal hyperplasia cases result from mutations in CYP21A2, which encodes 21-hydroxylase and impairs cortisol biosynthesis.

The female neonate was found in compound heterozygosity for the pathogenic CYP21A2 IVS2-13A/C>G splice variant and the TNXA/TNXB CAH-X CH-1 chimera, explaining her severe salt-wasting CAH phenotype with Prader 5 virilization.
The 30-year-old mother was found to carry the pathogenic CYP21A2 IVS2-13A/C>G variant in heterozygosity.
The 28-year-old father was found to carry the TNXA/TNXB CAH-X CH-1 chimera in heterozygosity, confirmed by MLPA and a real-time PCR CNV assay showing a large CYP21A2 deletion.

The CAH-X CH-1 chimera is characterized by a 120-bp deletion in exon 35 of TNXB, causing TNXB haploinsufficiency and disrupted TGF-beta signaling, and in the homozygous state produces a contiguous CAH/Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

CAH-X syndrome, resulting from a monoallelic nonfunctional TNXB/TNXA chimeric gene combined with a CYP21A2 pathogenic mutation on the other allele, is estimated to occur in approximately 7–9% (up to 10%) of CAH patients.

CAH-X CH-1 does not alter TNX protein structure but reduces TNX expression, whereas CAH-X CH-2 and CH-3 chimeras (derived from TNXA pseudogene variants) produce altered/structurally abnormal TNX proteins.
CAH-X CH-2 is characterized by the variant c.12174C>G (p.Cys4058Trp), derived from the TNXA pseudogene.

The pathogenic IVS2-13A/C>G variant comprises 20-25% of CYP21A2 mutant alleles across European, Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, and Chinese populations and translates to the most severe salt-wasting CAH form when homozygous.

Only about 10% of CAH-X patients (carrying compound heterozygous CYP21A2/TNXB genotype) also manifest EDS features; the present neonate and her father carrying the CAH-X CH-1 chimera showed no EDS-related clinical manifestations, including normal skin.
Baxdrostat exhibited dose-proportional plasma exposure with a mean half-life of approximately 26 to 31 hours, supporting once-daily dosing.
Baxdrostat at doses ≥1.5 mg produced a dose-dependent reduction in plasma aldosterone, with levels reduced by approximately 51 to 73% by day 10 regardless of salt diet.

Baxdrostat had no meaningful effect on plasma total or free cortisol, or 11-deoxycortisol, even under ACTH challenge, indicating selectivity for aldosterone synthase over 11β-hydroxylase (cortisol synthase).

Baxdrostat caused a modest (~2- to 3-fold) increase in the aldosterone precursor 11-deoxycorticosterone under both normal- and low-salt diet conditions, a smaller increase than the up to 10-fold rise previously reported with LCI699.
18-hydroxycorticosterone, the immediate precursor to aldosterone, levels were generally comparable to or decreased from baseline, but to a lesser extent than aldosterone itself.
Corticosterone levels increased in an apparent dose-dependent manner with baxdrostat, likely reflecting increased 11β-hydroxylase activity as a downstream consequence of pathway shunting.

Under low-salt diet conditions, baxdrostat was associated with somewhat more pronounced increases in baseline plasma ACTH compared to placebo, whereas under normal-salt diet conditions baxdrostat produced a dose-dependent decrease in ACTH.

Baxdrostat treatment was associated with a slight trend toward mild decreases in orthostatic blood pressure and moderate increases in orthostatic heart rate, without clear dose-dependency, most pronounced in the 5-mg group; seated heart rate and blood pressure showed no clinically significant changes.

Baxdrostat administration resulted in mild dose-dependent decreases in plasma sodium levels and increases in plasma potassium levels, consistent with the observed reduction in aldosterone; urinary sodium increased and urinary potassium decreased correspondingly.
Baxdrostat was associated with mild increases in BUN, creatinine, and BUN:creatinine ratio, and a mild reduction (<15%) in glomerular filtration rate, suggesting a mild diuretic effect.

Baxdrostat was well tolerated with no deaths, serious adverse events, or discontinuations due to treatment-emergent adverse events; TEAEs considered drug-related occurred in 14.3% of baxdrostat subjects vs 21.4% of placebo subjects, and all baxdrostat-related TEAEs were mild.

In contrast to baxdrostat, the aldosterone synthase inhibitor LCI699 showed a time-dependent loss of selectivity for aldosterone synthase over 11β-hydroxylase with multiple dosing, evidenced by increased 11-deoxycorticosterone, dose-dependent 11-deoxycortisol accumulation, and impaired ACTH-stimulated cortisol synthesis.
Gestational treatment with Ang 1-7 reduced the elevated systolic blood pressure and proteinuria associated with preeclampsia.
Losartan (AT1 receptor antagonist) treatment during gestation reduced PE-associated elevated systolic blood pressure and proteinuria.
Pioglitazone (RAS modulator) treatment during gestation reduced PE-associated elevated systolic blood pressure and proteinuria.
Combined losartan/pioglitazone therapy was the most effective gestational treatment for reducing PE-associated hypertension and proteinuria among the tested regimens.

In weaning PE rats, LPS-induced potentiated falls in mean arterial pressure and cardiac sympathovagal balance (LF/HF ratio) were attenuated by Ang 1-7, losartan, pioglitazone, and combined losartan/pioglitazone therapies.
Pioglitazone was more effective than other treatments at reversing the LPS-induced increase in left ventricular contractility seen in endotoxic weaning preeclamptic rats.
Ang 1-7 was more effective than other treatments at reversing the LPS-induced decrease in isovolumic relaxation time constant in endotoxic weaning preeclamptic rats.
Cardiac TLR-4 expression was increased in endotoxic preeclamptic rats, and this increase was abrogated by Ang 1-7 or combined losartan/pioglitazone treatment.
Increased cardiac ACE expression seen in endotoxic preeclamptic rats was blunted by Ang 1-7 or combined losartan/pioglitazone treatment.
Cardiac ACE2 expression was not significantly altered by any of the gestational treatments tested (Ang 1-7, losartan, pioglitazone, or combined losartan/pioglitazone).
Serum TGF-β1 levels were significantly higher in patients with cervical artery dissection than in healthy controls.
Serum TGF-β2 levels were significantly higher in patients with cervical artery dissection than in healthy controls.
TGF-β1 and TGF-β2 levels peaked at 2-3 months after CeAD onset, suggested to reflect an active reparative process in the arterial wall.
TGF-β levels did not correlate with clinical presentation (stroke vs headache vs cranial nerve palsy) or angiographic parameters (artery involved, tortuosity, aneurysm) in CeAD patients.
Older age at disease onset was independently associated with recovery or significant improvement (R/I) in multivariate analysis.
A shorter diagnostic delay (time from symptom onset to ME/CFS diagnosis) was independently associated with a higher likelihood of recovery/improvement.
A non-significant trend toward a negative association between comorbid irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) and recovery/improvement was observed in multivariate analysis.
Only 8.3% (14/168) of ME/CFS patients achieved complete recovery over a median 17-month follow-up, consistent with previously reported low recovery rates.
Only 4.8% (8/168) of patients achieved significant improvement, a notably lower rate than the 17–64% previously reported in the literature.

Comorbid Hashimoto's thyroiditis differed significantly in prevalence between R/I patients and the rest of the cohort in univariate analysis, though it was not retained in the final multivariate model.
A longer follow-up duration was significantly associated with R/I in univariate analysis, but this association did not persist in multivariate analysis.
Baseline fatigue severity and its functional impact were comparable between R/I patients and the rest of the cohort, unlike some prior reports linking baseline fatigue severity to prognosis.
PEM severity did not differ significantly between R/I patients and the rest of the cohort, contrasting with prior studies linking PEM to poorer outcome.
Comorbid depression was not a significant predictor of poor outcome in this cohort.
Comorbid fibromyalgia was not associated with poor outcome in this cohort, contrary to a previous study by Ciccone et al.
In recovered patients (subgroup 1), fatigue severity scores (FSS and FS) were significantly lower at recovery than at initial assessment.
In significantly improved patients (subgroup 2), fatigue severity scores (FSS and FS) were significantly lower after improvement than at initial assessment.

More than a quarter of R/I patients experienced better prognosis after receiving financial compensation or disability recognition, suggesting stable financial support may facilitate recovery/improvement.
Recovered and improved patient subgroups were comparable for age at disease onset, diagnostic delay, and time of follow-up post R/I, suggesting these factors do not differentiate degree of recovery.
During resting-state fMRI, functional connectivity of two salience network hub connections differed from healthy controls, and this was specific to patients meeting Fukuda criteria.

During task fMRI, 10 functional connections overall differed from healthy controls, with 5 distinct connections altered in the ICC-defined class and 5 distinct connections altered in the Fukuda-defined class, and none were shared between the two diagnostic classes.
Of the 10 altered task-fMRI connections, 8 involved a salience network hub, with 6 connections weaker and 4 connections stronger in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls.
Salience network connectivity to the hippocampus and brainstem reticular activating system was stronger in ME/CFS patients than in healthy controls.

The distinct, non-overlapping patterns of functional connectivity differences between ICC- and Fukuda-defined ME/CFS patients suggest that different neuropathologies underlie these two diagnostic classes, providing objective evidence that questionnaire-based criteria distinguish separate disease states.

85% of children and young people (23/27) with moderate to severe ME/CFS showed improvement in at least one of four functional domains (mobility, sleep, education, socialising) after multidisciplinary hospital-based rehabilitation.
70% of CYP (19/27) improved their level of physical mobility/dependence during the rehabilitation programme, while 5 showed no change and 3 regressed.
Of 24 CYP with disordered sleep at baseline, 50% (12/24) improved their sleep patterns during treatment, with a third of these achieving normal sleep patterns.
Of 23 CYP able to show change in education/employment status, 65% (15/23) improved their educational attainment or engagement upon leaving the service.
16 of 27 CYP (59.2%) demonstrated improvement in their ability to socialise or take part in recreational activities after treatment.
Only 8 of 27 (30%) patients demonstrated improvement across all four measured domains (mobility, education, sleep, socialising), highlighting variable and partial treatment response.
The most common comorbidities in this pediatric moderate-severe ME/CFS cohort were anxiety, low mood, joint or muscle pain, and headaches, with most CYP having more than one diagnosis.

This cohort of severely/moderately affected CYP represented 5.2% of the service's total patient population, consistent with current prevalence estimates of ~5-10% for severe ME/CFS among affected children and young people.
The majority of ME/CFS participants (93.4%) reported neurocognitive impairment symptoms on the DePaul Symptom Questionnaire.

Orthostatic intolerance occurring without concurrent neurocognitive symptoms only allowed an additional 1.7-4.5% of participants to meet IOM ME/CFS criteria, indicating substantial overlap between the two symptom domains.

The authors conclude that neurocognitive symptoms and orthostatic intolerance overlap substantially in ME/CFS, and their data do not support treating them as interchangeable diagnostic criteria as proposed by the IOM.
The overall prevalence of HHV-6A/B genomic sequence in blood DNA was similar between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls.
HHV-6A/B infection was significantly more frequent in patients with severe ME/CFS than in those with mild disease.

A higher proportion of ME/CFS patients with high HHV-6 viral load (>1,000 copies/10^6 PBMCs) was found with increasing disease severity, and this proportion was much higher in patients than in HHV-6-positive controls.
HHV-6B was the predominant subtype detected in nearly all HHV-6-positive ME/CFS patients and all HHV-6-positive controls.

Anti-muscarinic acetylcholine receptor 3 (anti-M3) antibody levels did not significantly differ between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls, by sex, or by disease severity, and were not useful as a discriminating marker by ROC analysis.
Anti-muscarinic acetylcholine receptor 4 (anti-M4) antibody levels were significantly higher in ME/CFS patients than in healthy controls.

Anti-M4 antibody elevation reached statistical significance in male ME/CFS patients versus male controls, but not in female patients versus female controls, likely reflecting the small female control sample.
Anti-beta2-adrenergic receptor (anti-β2AdR) antibody levels were significantly elevated in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls, in both women and men.
ROC analysis identified anti-β2AdR as the best-performing diagnostic marker overall to discriminate ME/CFS patients from healthy controls, but not for disease severity.
ROC analysis showed anti-M4 antibody could serve as a good general marker for ME/CFS, unlike anti-M3, though it could not discriminate disease severity.
ME/CFS disease severity was positively correlated with HHV-6 viral load across the full cohort.
ME/CFS disease severity showed a strong positive correlation with anti-β2AdR antibody levels.
ME/CFS disease severity showed a weak positive correlation with anti-M4 antibody levels.
Anti-M3 and anti-M4 antibody levels were positively correlated with each other.

HHV-6 viral copy number was positively correlated with anti-M4 antibody levels in ME/CFS patients, and higher HHV-6 load also correlated with higher anti-β2AdR levels, suggesting anti-M4 and anti-β2AdR act as linked double markers.
Plasma SARS-CoV-2 RBD IgG seropositivity was found in 19% of ME/CFS patients versus 32% of healthy donors, with statistically similar mean antibody levels (MFI) between groups.
A higher proportion of ME/CFS patients (44%) than healthy donors (25%) had detectable saliva SARS-CoV-2 RBD IgG, indicating a more pronounced local mucosal antibody response in ME/CFS.

Total saliva IgG concentration was significantly lower in ME/CFS patients compared with healthy donors, ruling out saliva volume/dilution as the explanation for the elevated virus-specific antibody signal.
Saliva RBD IgG levels were significantly higher in ME/CFS patients than healthy donors in both the local-responder and systemic-responder subgroups.
No differences were found in saliva NP-specific IgG, IgM, or IgA antibody levels between ME/CFS patients and healthy donors.
Within the healthy donor cohort, local (saliva-only) responders had significantly higher RBD IgM and IgA responses than systemic responders, underlining a distinct mucosal antiviral defense.

Systemic SARS-CoV-2 antibody responders among ME/CFS patients showed significant upregulation of saliva anti-EBV VCA IgG and EBNA1 IgG, and HHV6A IgG/IgM, compared with SARS-CoV-2-negative ME/CFS patients, consistent with latent virus reactivation.

Anti-EBNA1 IgG elevation after SARS-CoV-2 infection was unique to ME/CFS patients and was not observed in healthy donors, highlighting EBNA1 as a distinguishing feature of the ME/CFS antiviral fingerprint.
Unlike ME/CFS, systemic SARS-CoV-2 responders among healthy donors showed no significant elevation of antiviral antibodies compared with SARS-CoV-2-negative healthy donors.

Local (saliva-only) SARS-CoV-2 responders among ME/CFS patients showed significant upregulation of EBV (VCA IgG/IgA, EBNA1 IgG), HHV6A (IgG/IgM), and HERV-K IgG compared with SARS-CoV-2-negative ME/CFS patients.

Local SARS-CoV-2 responders among healthy donors also showed upregulation of EBV (VCA IgG/IgM/IgA), HHV6A (IgM/IgA), and HERV-K (IgG/IgM/IgA) compared with SARS-CoV-2-negative healthy donors, indicating COVID-19 triggers latent virus reactivation even in healthy people.
Among systemic SARS-CoV-2 responders, ME/CFS patients had significantly higher saliva VCA IgG, HHV6A IgG, and HERV-K IgG levels than healthy donors.

HSV1 IgG and HSV2 IgG titers were significantly higher in local SARS-CoV-2 responders with ME/CFS than in local HD responders, but this difference lost significance after adjusting for age and gender.

Gender was a significant confounding factor for HERV-K IgG and HHV6A IgM antibody responses, with ME/CFS females showing a stronger elevation of HERV-K IgG than males, although the low sample size warrants caution.

Age was a significant confounder for HSV1 IgG and HSV2 IgG saliva responses; when cohorts were stratified, antibody titer differences were confined to participants under 40 years of age with no difference in those over 40.
A self-reported history of infectious mononucleosis as an ME/CFS trigger event was not associated with differences in antiviral antibody titers compared with patients without such a history.
Use of antiviral drugs (e.g., aciclovir) and/or corticosteroids, reported by 14% of ME/CFS patients versus 3% of healthy donors, was not associated with differences in antiviral antibody titers.

In a paired subgroup of 19 participants (15 HD, 4 ME/CFS) sampled before and after documented SARS-CoV-2 infection, saliva antibody levels against EBV VCA IgG, HSV1 IgG, HERV-K IgM, and CMV IgG significantly increased after infection, directly linking SARS-CoV-2 infection to latent virus reactivation.

Among SARS-CoV-2-negative participants, ME/CFS patients had significantly higher baseline saliva EBV VCA IgG than healthy donors, indicating a higher baseline level of latent EBV reactivation independent of COVID-19 infection.

Unlike SARS-CoV-2 RBD/NP antibodies, which correlated between saliva and plasma in systemic responders, EBV VCA IgG and HSV1 IgG showed no significant difference in plasma but generated a distinct antibody fingerprint in saliva consistent with local latent virus reactivation.

A cohort of 33,940 individuals with breakthrough SARS-CoV-2 infection followed up to 6 months showed a higher risk of death and incident post-acute sequelae including deteriorated mental health, musculoskeletal, and neurologic disorders.
Compared with unvaccinated individuals infected with SARS-CoV-2, those with breakthrough infection after vaccination had lower odds of mortality and post-acute incident sequelae.

In a 2-year retrospective cohort of 1,284,437 COVID-19 patients matched to controls with other respiratory infections, increases in mood/anxiety disorders were transient, but increased risk of cognitive deficit, dementia, psychotic disorder, or seizures persisted throughout, with similar outcomes across delta and omicron waves.

Brain fog was the most common neurologic symptom lasting more than 6 weeks, reported in 81% of long COVID patients with no history of acute severe illness, hypoxia, or respiratory compromise, per Northwestern University's Neuro-COVID-19 Clinic.
A systematic review of long COVID symptom prevalence found fatigue to be the most frequently reported complaint, occurring in 58% of patients.
In the same systematic review, chronic trouble concentrating and attention problems were reported in 31% and 27% of long COVID patients, respectively.
Short-term memory abnormalities (32%) and attention abnormalities (27%) were also observed among long COVID patients presenting with brain fog.

In a study of 84,285 individuals with biologically confirmed COVID-19 infection who completed the Great British Intelligence Test, significant cognitive deficits were found, comparable in magnitude to the average 10-year age-related cognitive decline observed between ages 20-70.
One post-COVID-19 follow-up study reported that 45.2% of COVID-19 patients met specific ME/CFS diagnostic criteria six months after infection.
Post-exertional malaise, a hallmark ME/CFS symptom, was reported by 56.8% of a sample of 3762 COVID-19 patients surveyed across 56 countries.
Disrupted circadian TGF-β signaling has been proposed as a key mechanism underlying ME/CFS's characteristic disturbances in sleep, activity, cognition, and autonomic function.

In a retrospective study of 110 elderly patients on a mean melatonin dose of 46 mg/day for at least 12 months prior to COVID-19 vaccine availability, none died from acute COVID-19, compared with a 10.5% lethality rate in the local elderly population.

A retrospective analysis of MCI patients treated with melatonin (3-24 mg/day) alongside usual medication showed significantly improved cognitive performance, Beck Depression Inventory scores, and sleep/wake rhythm quality compared with an untreated group.

In 40 MCI patients receiving melatonin 0.15 mg/kg daily for 6 months versus 39 placebo-treated MCI patients, melatonin was associated with less decline in hippocampal volume and lamina cribrosa thickness and lower CSF T-tau levels.

A meta-analysis of 22 randomized controlled trials found that Alzheimer's disease patients receiving melatonin (2.5-10 mg daily) for more than 12 weeks showed improved MMSE scores, particularly in mild-stage disease.

An analysis of 27 publications surveying COVID-19 drug efficacy concluded that melatonin was at least twice as effective as remdesivir or tocilizumab in reducing inflammatory markers of COVID-19 infection.
Circulating secreted phospholipase-A2 (Group IIA) levels correlate with the severity of COVID-19 disease.
Melatonin reduces proinflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8) and increases the anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10.
Melatonin activates the Nrf2 transcription factor, enhancing glutathione-synthesizing enzyme expression, and has been proposed as a candidate treatment for long COVID.
Melatonin has beneficial effects on fibromyalgia, a condition commonly associated with ME/CFS, with findings confirmed by multiple subsequent studies.
Persistent fatigue at 6 months or more after infection was reported by 17.2% of SARS-CoV-2-positive individuals compared to 8.9% of SARS-CoV-2-negative individuals.
Post-exertional malaise was reported by 8.2% of SARS-CoV-2-positive individuals compared to 3.5% of SARS-CoV-2-negative individuals at 6+ months.
Criteria for chronic fatigue syndrome were met by 1.1% of SARS-CoV-2-positive individuals versus 0.5% of SARS-CoV-2-negative individuals at 6+ months follow-up.
Among SARS-CoV-2-positive individuals reporting fatigue (n=258), 35.3% had moderate to severe functional limitations on the ECOG scale.
Among fatigued SARS-CoV-2-positive individuals, 83.0% scored ≥4 on the bimodal Chalder fatigue scale, indicating severe fatigue.
After adjusting for age and sex, 47.7% of SARS-CoV-2-positive individuals with fatigue at 6 months or more met frequency and severity criteria for post-exertional malaise.
Among fatigued SARS-CoV-2-positive individuals, 6.2% (age/sex-adjusted) met criteria for chronic fatigue syndrome at 6+ months.

SARS-CoV-2-positive individuals had a higher, age/sex-adjusted prevalence of newly developed insomnia, cognitive impairment, headache, generalized pain, functional impairment, reduced work capacity, and decreased physical activity, with prevalence increasing with fatigue severity, presence of post-exertional malaise, or chronic fatigue syndrome criteria.

Individuals with fatigue were more likely to be vaccinated, an association partially explained by older age and higher comorbidity burden in vaccinated individuals rather than a direct effect of vaccination on fatigue.
Activity pacing interventions significantly reduced fatigue compared to no treatment/usual care in people with CFS.
Activity pacing interventions significantly reduced psychological distress compared to no treatment/usual care in people with CFS.
Activity pacing interventions significantly reduced depression compared to no treatment/usual care in people with CFS.
Activity pacing interventions significantly improved physical function compared to no treatment/usual care in people with CFS.
Improvement was greater for activity pacing interventions that encouraged graded escalation of physical and cognitive activities.
Peripheral nerve stimulation was used as part of a multimodal treatment regimen for shoulder and knee pain in two hEDS patients, a use not previously reported in this population.

The paper argues that because chronic pain in hEDS is multifactorial, effective management requires a multidisciplinary approach combining physical therapy, psychotherapy, pharmacotherapy, and interventional procedures (trigger point injections, peripheral nerve block, radiofrequency ablation, peripheral nerve stimulation).

Molecular genetic testing identified a suspected de novo heterozygous C1R mutation c.890G>A (G297D) confirming the diagnosis of periodontal Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (pEDS) in the patient, with no evidence of the mutation in tested relatives.
The case describes multifocal periapical cemental dysplasia (PCD) affecting all four dental quadrants in a patient with pEDS, a manifestation not previously reported in this condition.

CBCT and technetium-99m bone scintigraphy revealed graded periapical sclerotic/mineralization changes (CBCT grades 1-4) across multiple tooth-bearing regions, correlating radiotracer uptake intensity with maturation stage of the periapical dysplasia.

Cranial MRI revealed small-spot confluent, symmetric periventricular white matter hyperintensities on T2/FLAIR sequences with slightly hypointense T1 signal, consistent with leukoencephalopathy previously reported in association with periodontal EDS.

A prior study (Kapferer-Seebacher 2018) reported C1R mutations c.926G>T and c.149_150TC>AT associated with leukoencephalopathy in eight pEDS patients from two families, with neuroradiological signs increasing with age.

Unlike classical EDS (cEDS), where pulp calcification/pulp stones are common (reported in 15 of 17 individuals per Kapferer-Seebacher et al. 2020, primarily linked to COL5A1/COL5A2), the present pEDS case showed no pulp calcification but instead drumstick-shaped molar formation and hypercementosis.

The patient displayed classic pEDS clinical features including early-onset periodontitis/gingivitis, lack of attached gingiva, pretibial hematomas with atrophic scars, easy bruising since childhood, marfanoid habitus, joint hypermobility (Beighton score 5/9), skin hyperextensibility, and uterus bicornae.

Blood investigation showed slightly reduced beta-Crosslaps (CTX) and osteocalcin, while calcium, potassium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, parathormone, 25-hydroxy-vitamin D3, and FGF-23 were normal.

Genetic testing for Anoctamin 5 (associated with gnathodiaphysial dysplasia/familial gigantiform cementoma) was negative, helping exclude alternative fibro-osseous jaw disease diagnoses (HPT-JT, GDD, FGC) in favor of pEDS-associated PCD.

Postmortem genetic panel testing identified a heterozygous pathogenic COL3A1 variant (c.1024G>A, p.Gly342Arg) in exon 15, confirming a molecular diagnosis of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome that had not been suspected preoperatively.
The patient developed a fatal retrograde Type A aortic dissection (RTAoD) with cardiac tamponade 48 hours after TEVAR for a Stanford Type B dissection, later attributed to unrecognized vEDS.
The paper states that mortality rates for both open and endovascular aortic repair in EDS patients range from 20 to 30%.
vEDS carries a poor prognosis with a median life expectancy of 40 to 50 years, with about 7% of patients experiencing a first major vascular event by age 20 and 40% by age 40.
Vascular EDS is estimated to affect approximately 1 in 50,000 to 250,000 people.
Sequencing analysis of COL3A1 has a high sensitivity (98%) for identifying the underlying pathogenic variant in suspected vEDS.
Use of endograft devices with proximal uncovered struts should be avoided in vEDS, as they can induce new entry tears leading to retrograde Type A aortic dissection in up to 25% of cases.
The authors recommend that in vEDS/AoD patients, endograft oversizing greater than 10% and use of a molding balloon are contraindicated because they may further damage the weakened aortic wall.
mcEDS is caused by biallelic mutations in CHST14 (dermatan 4-O-sulfotransferase 1 deficiency) or DSE (dermatan sulfate epimerase deficiency), both leading to systemic depletion of dermatan sulfate.
Twelve of thirteen patients (92.3%) had a history of dislocations, with ten patients (76.9%) having a history of two or more dislocations.
Shoulder dislocation was the most common dislocation site, occurring in 11 of 13 patients (84.6%), followed by patellar dislocation in 7 patients and elbow dislocation in 2 patients (15.4%).
Eight patients (61.5–66.7%) sustained extensor tendon dislocation at the metacarpophalangeal joint, attributed to relaxation of the sagittal band.
Four patients (30.8%) had swan neck deformity, possibly due to congenital laxity of the volar plate of the PIP joint.

Elbow range of motion differed by age: pediatric patients tended toward hyperextension (mean −11° flexion contracture reversed / extension ~11°... actually mean 145° flexion, 11° hyperextension), while adult patients showed limited extension (mean 143° flexion, −4° extension), indicating age-related shift from hyperextension to extension limitation.
Thumb and finger DIP/IP joints showed significantly limited range of motion, with mean thumb IP flexion of 34° and extension of −2°, and DIP extension ranging from −16° to −23° across fingers.
Adult patients had markedly reduced grip strength (mean 8.2 kg) and side pinch strength (mean 3.3 kg) compared with published healthy Japanese adult norms (42.0 kg males, 25.5 kg females).

Radiographic elbow indices in mcEDS patients (ACI 1.70±0.26, TDI 0.39±0.07, ROA 103±11) indicated a shallow trochlear notch pattern, with lower ACI/TDI and higher ROA than reported healthy subjects and values consistent with post-fracture coronoid morphology.
Six patients (46.2%) sustained radial head dislocation, all posterior, and the PUB (proximal ulnar bow) tended to be larger in patients with radial head dislocation.
Elbow osteoarthritis occurred in four of six adult patients aged 20–50 years (66.7%), a markedly higher rate than the 25% prevalence of elbow OA reported in the general population aged 50–90 years.

Three adult patients (23.1%) had distal radioulnar joint (DRUJ) osteoarthritis, possibly related to relative ulnar lengthening from radial head dislocation, with ulnar variance plus prominent in adults but not teenagers.

Two patients (15.4%) had unilateral congenital fusion (coalition) of the scaphoid and trapezium, a rare defect (general population prevalence <0.1%) suggesting it may be a common complication in mcEDS.
The ratio of medullary cavity width to metacarpal width decreased with age, particularly sharply in the late teens, suggesting a role for dermatan sulfate in bone formation/growth.
Adult phalanx and metacarpal bone width (but not length) tended to be narrower in mcEDS patients compared to the general Japanese population, evaluated by gender.

Mean QuickDASH score across patients was 34.5 (range 4.5–54.5), indicating reduced upper extremity function in the majority of mcEDS-CHST14 patients, with pain domain scores tending to increase in adults and patients with frequent shoulder dislocations.

The single patient with mcEDS-DSE had a milder phenotype than mcEDS-CHST14 patients: no history of dislocation, no severe loss of grip/pinch strength, and a better QuickDASH score of 15.9 compared to the group mean of 34.5.

Authors suggest that bracing to limit elbow extension and educating patients about fall mechanics may help prevent posterior/posterolateral elbow dislocations in mcEDS patients with elbow hyperextension.
Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS type IV) is an autosomal-dominant disorder caused by mutations in COL3A1, the gene encoding type III pro-collagen.

In a prior review of 220 VEDS patients, 103 died from arterial rupture and half of the remaining deaths were secondary to organ rupture, underscoring vascular rupture as the hallmark cause of reduced survival in VEDS.

The patient presented with markedly elevated high-sensitivity serum troponin I (initially 23 ng/mL, peaking at 29.3), consistent with acute myocardial injury during an exercise-induced myocarditis episode.
The patient developed a 10-beat run of ventricular tachycardia during ICU monitoring, temporally associated with the myocarditis episode.

Cardiac MRI demonstrated abnormal delayed myocardial enhancement in a non-ischemic pattern within the septum and lateral wall (myonecrosis/scarring) and T2 hyperintense myocardial enhancement (edema), satisfying two of the Lake Louise criteria for myocarditis.

The patient was treated with metoprolol extended-release 25 mg daily following the myocarditis episode, with a recommendation for indefinite prophylactic use to prevent future exercise-induced myocarditis events.

The patient had a recurrent history of exercise-induced myocarditis, with a prior episode in 2020 presenting similarly with crushing chest pain, V-tach, elevated troponin, and MRI evidence of myocarditis, treated with six weeks of metoprolol 25-mg ER and activity restriction.
The patient's mother also had EDS type IV and died shortly after delivery due to aortic dissection, illustrating the heritable and life-threatening vascular risk of this condition.

This case report identifies exercise-induced myocarditis as a novel/atypical manifestation of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, with no other published cases of this association found in the literature.

A two-week internet-delivered mindfulness meditation intervention produced a statistically significant and clinically important improvement in the SF-36 mental component summary score in people with hypermobile EDS.
Thematic analysis of interviews with 10 participants identified increased body awareness and reduced pain intensity as key lived-experience themes following meditation practice.
Participants identified barriers to practicing meditation and recommended the intervention be made more flexible (varying meditation type and duration) to better suit hEDS-specific needs.

Whole exome sequencing identified a heterozygous COL3A1 exon19:c.1340G>A (p.Gly447Asp) variant in the patient, classified as likely pathogenic per ACMG/AMP criteria and previously linked to vEDS in one prior case report.
Immunofluorescence of skin-derived dermal fibroblasts showed complete absence of COL3A1 protein expression in the patient compared to age-matched control fibroblasts.
Patient fibroblasts carrying the COL3A1 variant were morphologically larger than control fibroblasts.

Transmission electron microscopy of vEDS patient fibroblasts revealed lamellar vacuolar bodies (interpreted as amphisomes, autophagy pathway organelles) in the cytoplasm, absent in control fibroblasts.

The vEDS patient presented with stroke due to left internal carotid artery dissection, followed a year later by aneurysmal dilatation of the left hepatic artery, dissections of bilateral renal arteries and right common iliac artery, and hemoperitoneum from hepatic artery rupture requiring aneurysmal coiling.
The patient's serum C-reactive protein was elevated, which the authors attribute to delayed thrombus clearance and vascular insult in vEDS.
Nerve conduction study and nerve biopsy in the patient showed axonal and demyelinating neuropathy in both lower legs, consistent with prior reports of polyneuropathy in vEDS.
Two additional non-synonymous COL3A1 variants (exon30:c.2092G>A and exon50:c.4059T>G) identified on WES were classified as non-deleterious based on high minor allele frequencies.

Prior literature indicates a genotype-phenotype correlation in vEDS: missense substitution of valine or aspartic acid for glycine confers a poorer prognosis than substitution of serine, and haploinsufficient patients have ~50% penetrance and survive 10-15 years longer than those with RNA splicing or glycine substitution mutations.

The authors note that Celiprolol has been reported to improve biomechanical integrity of the aorta and may be an option for preventing complications in vEDS, though it was unavailable to this patient in India.

A cited preclinical study identified the PLC/IP3/PKC/ERK signaling pathway (phospholipase C/inositol 1,4,5-triphosphate/protein kinase C/extracellular signal-regulated kinase) as a major driver of vascular pathology in vEDS models.

The upcoming PREVEnt clinical trial will assess whether enzastaurin (AR101), an orally active PKC/ERK pathway inhibitor previously tested in over 40 human cancer trials, can prevent cardiac or arterial events in COL3A1-confirmed vEDS patients.

In younger patients without significant cardiovascular risk factors, thoracic aortic and thoracoabdominal aneurysms may have a genetic basis, including connective tissue syndromes such as Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
The patient had hypermobile joints noted on childhood physical examination, but the findings were not consistent with a diagnosable hypermobility syndrome and no further workup was pursued.

The patient presented with severe hypoxemic respiratory failure from multifocal pneumonia and bronchiectasis with a history of recurrent childhood respiratory illness, failure to thrive requiring gastrostomy tube feeding, and intermittent asthma, but a normal newborn screen and no family history of pulmonary, autoimmune, or connective tissue disease.
Antidepressant drugs including duloxetine were found effective in treating depression and pain in fibromyalgia patients across the reviewed studies.
The FDA-indicated drugs for fibromyalgia in adults include the gabapentinoid pregabalin, alongside duloxetine and milnacipran, as first-line pharmacological therapy to reduce symptoms.
Chronic stress and depression are proposed to play a crucial role in the etiology and pathophysiology of fibromyalgia, potentially dysregulating central pain, neuroendocrine, and immune mechanisms.
Non-pharmacological alternative approaches including patient education, behavioral therapy, exercise, pain management, and healthy diet are widely used interventions for fibromyalgia.
At baseline, fibromyalgia patients had significantly lower tolerance and pain thresholds than healthy controls.
Fibromyalgia patients showed significantly lower baroreflex sensitivity than healthy controls at baseline and across the epochs of both control protocols.
All baseline heart rate variability measures were significantly lower in fibromyalgia patients compared to controls.

The EP protocol (pain and pain-free electrical stimuli synchronized to systolic/diastolic cardiac phases) significantly increased pain threshold and tolerance in FM patients, with larger increases than in controls.
In fibromyalgia patients, pain threshold and tolerance after the EP protocol were significantly higher than after either control protocol (CC1 or CC2).
When only painful cardiac-gated stimuli were delivered (CC1 protocol, without pain-free stimuli), fibromyalgia patients showed smaller threshold increases than controls, unlike the EP protocol.
Pain threshold and tolerance were not increased in FM patients when stimuli were delivered independent of the cardiac cycle (sham CC2 protocol), validating central nociceptive hypersensitivity.
The EP protocol produced a statistically significant reduction in clinical pain (VAS) in fibromyalgia patients after two stimulation sessions.
The non-cardiac-gated sham protocol (CC2) significantly increased reported clinical pain in fibromyalgia patients.
After the second epoch of the EP protocol, BRS in fibromyalgia patients was no longer significantly different from that of healthy controls, indicating a reset toward normal.

In fibromyalgia patients, the EP protocol significantly increased BRS from baseline to the second stimulation epoch, and between the first and second epochs, while control protocols had no such effect.

The EP protocol produced a greater increase in high-frequency HRV (parasympathetic activity) from baseline in FM patients compared with the two control protocols, while low- and very-low-frequency (sympathetic) HRV increases were smaller.
In fibromyalgia patients, nearly all HRV variables increased significantly across stimulation epochs, whereas in controls only total power and SDNN increased, and only during the sham (CC2) protocol.
Plasma CRP levels showed no significant difference between patients with episodic migraine, chronic migraine, and healthy controls after adjusting for age and BMI.
The proportion of participants with elevated CRP (>3.0 mg/L) did not differ significantly among EM, CM, and control groups.
After excluding participants with medication overuse or fibromyalgia, CRP levels still did not differ significantly among EM, CM, and control groups.

Among overweight/obese participants (BMI ≥25 kg/m2), CRP levels were numerically higher in EM and CM groups than controls but this did not reach statistical significance after adjustment, and the subgroup analysis was underpowered.
A multivariable regression analysis found a significant positive linear relationship between CRP levels and BMI among migraine patients.
No significant linear relationship was found between CRP levels and headache frequency, anxiety severity, or depression severity in migraine patients.
CRP levels did not vary significantly according to headache intensity (mild, moderate, or severe).
CRP levels did not significantly vary with clinical characteristics and comorbidities, including fibromyalgia, among the 365 migraine participants.
CRP levels did not significantly differ according to preventive migraine medication class used.

Among the migraine participants, 42 (11.5%) had medication overuse and 85 (23.3%) had comorbid fibromyalgia; anxiety and depression were diagnosed in 126 (34.5%) and 100 (27.4%) participants respectively, while no control participants had these comorbidities.

The authors propose that discrepancies across prior CRP-migraine studies may be explained by differences in BMI distribution and geographic/ethnic population, since elevated CRP-migraine associations were mainly seen in Western/overweight cohorts, not in normal-weight or Asian/Middle Eastern cohorts.
Inhibition of GSK3 with CHIR99021 impaired reactive oxygen species (ROS) production in mast cells.
GSK3 inhibition impaired allergen-induced mast cell degranulation.
GSK3 inhibition, via modulation of MKK4-JNK, c-jun, and NF-κB signaling, reduced production and release of IL-6 from mast cells.
GSK3 inhibition reduced production/release of IL-13 from mast cells via MKK4-JNK/c-jun/NF-κB modulation.
GSK3 inhibition reduced production/release of TNF from mast cells via MKK4-JNK/c-jun/NF-κB modulation.
GSK3 inhibition reduced production/release of CCL1 from mast cells via MKK4-JNK/c-jun/NF-κB modulation.
GSK3 inhibition impaired only the release (not production) of CCL2 from mast cells.
GSK3 inhibition impaired only the release (not production) of CCL3 from mast cells.
CHIR99021-mediated GSK3 inhibition reduced c-kit receptor levels on mast cells, altering their pro-inflammatory phenotype.
GSK3 was implicated in FcεRI signaling, as its inhibition reduced release of IL-6, TNF, and CCL1 upon FcεRI stimulation.
CCL2 release was unaffected by GSK3 inhibition when mast cells were stimulated through FcεRI.
CCL3 release was unaffected by GSK3 inhibition when mast cells were stimulated through FcεRI.
CCL2 release was increased with GSK3 inhibition when mast cells were stimulated with SCF alone (independent of FcεRI).
CCL3 release was increased with GSK3 inhibition when mast cells were stimulated with SCF alone (independent of FcεRI).
The study concludes that GSK3 is a potential therapeutic target warranting further consideration in contexts of pathological mast cell activation.

Mouse peritoneal mast cells (PMCs) express ionotropic P2X1, P2X4, and P2X7 receptors and G protein-coupled P2Y1 and P2Y14 receptors, with expression profiles similar to bone marrow-derived mast cells.
BzATP, a potent P2X7 agonist, directly induced marked mast cell degranulation that was completely blocked by the P2X7 antagonist AZ10606120.
Extracellular ATP, but not αβmeATP, ADP, or UDP-glucose, selectively enhanced compound 48/80 (CP48/80)-induced MrgprB2-mediated degranulation in peritoneal mast cells.
The P2X4R antagonist NP-1815-PX inhibited ATP-induced enhancement of CP48/80-induced degranulation in a concentration-dependent manner.
In P2rx4-deficient PMCs, ATP no longer enhanced CP48/80-induced degranulation, and the P2X4R positive allosteric modulator ivermectin promoted the ATP effect only in wild-type but not P2rx4-/- PMCs.
ATP enhanced degranulation induced by the MrgprB2 agonists substance P, PAMP-12, and vancomycin in a P2X4R expression-dependent manner, with no enhancement seen in P2rx4-/- PMCs.

ATP-enhanced CP48/80-induced degranulation was inhibited by the PI3K inhibitor wortmannin but not by the p38 MAPK inhibitor SB203580, while the MEK1/2 inhibitor U0126 showed a non-significant trend toward inhibition.

Co-stimulation of PMCs with ATP and CP48/80 markedly increased sustained intracellular Ca2+ elevation compared to either agonist alone, and this synergistic Ca2+ response was absent in P2rx4-/- PMCs despite normal individual responses to ATP or CP48/80 alone.
The wortmannin (PI3K inhibitor) blocked the enhanced Ca2+ increase induced by co-stimulation with ATP and CP48/80.
CP48/80-induced Evans blue vascular extravasation in mouse ear was mast cell-dependent (absent in MC-deficient KitW-sh/W-sh mice) and significantly lower in P2rx4-/- mice than in wild-type mice.

Intravenous CP48/80 induced a rapid, marked decrease in rectal temperature in wild-type mice, whereas P2rx4-/- mice showed a much smaller, faster-recovering temperature decrease, indicating a milder systemic pseudoallergic reaction.
Pretreatment with the P2X4R antagonist NP-1815-PX (10 mg/kg, i.p.) significantly alleviated CP48/80-induced reductions in rectal temperature in wild-type mice.

Mast cell-deficient KitW-sh/W-sh mice reconstituted with P2rx4-/- bone marrow-derived mast cells showed a much milder CP48/80-induced rectal temperature decrease than mice reconstituted with wild-type BMMCs, demonstrating that mast cell-intrinsic P2X4R drives the systemic pseudoallergic reaction.
Fermentation and aging of ginseng sprouts increased compound K (CK) content 3.9-fold compared to unfermented ginseng sprouts, the largest increase among ginsenosides measured.
OVA-challenged mice showed dose-dependent increases in airway hyperresponsiveness (enhanced pause, Penh) upon methacholine challenge compared to controls, which was reduced by FAGS and CK treatment.
Total and OVA-specific plasma IgE levels, elevated by OVA sensitization, were significantly decreased by FAGS and CK treatment.

OVA-induced increases in total BALF inflammatory cells (neutrophils, lymphocytes, eosinophils, macrophages) were significantly reduced by FAGS and CK, with high-dose FAGS and CK showing roughly 2-fold greater reduction than low-dose FAGS.
Th2 cytokines (IL-4, IL-5, IL-13), which were elevated by OVA sensitization, were reduced by FAGS and CK, with CK showing the greatest reduction in IL-5.

Mast cell activation markers histamine and tryptase, elevated in BALF after OVA challenge, were significantly reduced by FAGS and CK treatment, with CK reducing tryptase approximately 2-fold more than either FAGS dose.

OVA-induced peribronchial inflammatory cell infiltration, goblet cell hyperplasia, collagen deposition, and macrophage infiltration in lung tissue were all significantly decreased by FAGS and CK treatment, with CK showing a stronger effect than FAGS on goblet cells and macrophage infiltration.
Lung tissue calcium concentration, elevated after OVA challenge, was significantly reduced by 30% and 48% with HFAGS and CK treatment, respectively.
ROS and MDA (lipid peroxidation marker), elevated in OVA-challenged lung tissue, were reduced by approximately 60% and 40% respectively with HFAGS and CK treatment.
TUNEL-positive apoptotic cells, cleaved caspase-3, and Bax/Bcl-2 ratio, all elevated after OVA exposure, were significantly decreased by HFAGS and CK treatment.
ER stress markers PERK, eIF2α, ATF4, and CHOP, upregulated by OVA exposure, were markedly decreased by HFAGS and CK treatment.

OVA exposure decreased SLC7A11 and GPX4 (ferroptosis-protective proteins) and increased 4-HNE (lipid peroxidation product), consistent with ferroptosis induction; these changes were significantly restored by HFAGS and CK treatment.
The number of iron-positive cells in lung tissue, increased after OVA exposure, was decreased by HFAGS and CK treatment.
Body weight and thymus weight did not differ significantly between experimental groups, whereas spleen weight was significantly increased by OVA and was not affected by FAGS or CK treatment.
Human cells transfected with the Lit-LAMP-DNA-vaccine expressed the intended LAMP-1-Lit v1-Lit v4-Lit v3 fusion protein, confirming the plasmid construct functions as designed.
Mice treated with the Lit-LAMP-DNA-vaccine developed anti-Lit v1, Lit v3, and Lit v4 IgG2a antibody responses along with a Th1-skewed immune response.
In a mouse model of shrimp allergy epicutaneously sensitized with shrimp protein extract, the Lit-LAMP-DNA-vaccine potently suppressed anaphylactic reactions.
Lit-LAMP-DNA-vaccine treatment suppressed mast cell activation in the murine shrimp allergy model.

The IgG1:IgG2a ratio in Lit-LAMP-DNA-vaccine-treated mice was significantly lower than in mice treated with oral immunotherapy (OIT), indicating a distinct mechanism of action favoring Th1/IgG2a responses.

Passive transfer of plasma from mice previously vaccinated with the Lit-LAMP-DNA-vaccine conferred a suppressive effect on allergic reaction in recipient mice, confirming an antibody-mediated mechanism.
Officially recorded allergic reactions after COVID-19 vaccination were about 80-fold more frequent in high-risk allergic patients (3.8%) than in the general vaccinated population (0.047%).

Among 208 high-risk allergic patients vaccinated under medical supervision, 30.3% self-reported an allergic reaction, with 8.7% occurring early (within 4 hours) and 21.6% late (>4 hours) after immunization.
Female sex was independently associated with a roughly three-fold higher risk of developing an allergic reaction after COVID-19 vaccination in multivariable analysis.
Patients with a documented history of drug allergy had a significantly lower risk of developing an allergic reaction after COVID-19 vaccination than those without such history.
Skin testing for excipients showed no PEG-positive results among 18 patients tested, whereas 1 of 3 patients tested for polysorbate 80 (PS80) was positive.
Despite being classified as high-risk for allergic reactions, none of the 208 vaccinated patients developed anaphylaxis or severe allergic reactions under extended post-vaccination monitoring.
Urticarial reactions after COVID-19 vaccination were markedly more frequent in females than males in this high-risk allergic cohort.

Patients with mast cell disorders, along with those with other high-risk allergy features, were vaccinated in a hospital setting and monitored for 1-2 hours by a dedicated allergy team including resuscitation staff.

The authors describe rapid post-vaccination allergic reactions as being mediated either by IgE antibodies against a vaccine component or by direct mast cell activation via complement activation-related pseudoallergy (CARPA), a mechanism previously described for liposomal formulations.

A cited external study (Ieven et al., 2022) reported that 13.2% of late allergic reactions to COVID-19 vaccination had mast cell activation-like symptoms, consistent with the mild self-limited late skin reactions seen in the present cohort.

This high-risk allergic Trieste cohort had higher rates of food allergy (25.6%) and drug allergy (53.5%) than a comparable Israeli high-risk allergic cohort from Sheba Medical Centre (15.9% food allergy, 32.9% multiple drug allergy).
Apigenin significantly inhibited compound 48/80-induced release of β-hexosaminidase and histamine from HMC-1 mast cells.
Apigenin blocked LPS-induced decreases in HMC-1 cell viability and increases in apoptosis and inflammatory cytokine secretion by suppressing TLR4/MyD88/NF-κB pathway activity.
Apigenin treatment reduced serum levels of OVA-specific IgE, IgG1, and IgG2a in allergic rhinitis mice.
Apigenin reduced serum β-hexosaminidase, histamine, and ECP levels in allergic rhinitis mice, indicating decreased mast cell/eosinophil mediator release.
Apigenin decreased Th2 cytokines (IL-4, IL-5, IL-13) and the Th2 transcription factor GATA-3, while increasing the Th1 cytokine IFN-γ and transcription factor T-bet in AR mice.
Apigenin promoted the ratio of Th1 (CD4+IFN-γ+) to Th2 (CD4+IL-4+) cells in peripheral blood mononuclear cells of AR mice.
Apigenin treatment reduced serum levels of β-hexosaminidase, histamine, and eosinophil cationic protein (ECP) in OVA-induced allergic rhinitis mice.
In mouse nasal mucosa tissues, apigenin suppressed activation of the TLR4/MyD88/NF-κB signaling pathway proteins.
Apigenin significantly alleviated nasal symptoms and reduced nasal eosinophil infiltration in allergic rhinitis mice.
Intraepidermal nerve fiber density was significantly lower in patients with SFN and Sjögren's syndrome than in patients with idiopathic SFN.
Anti-SSA(Ro) antibody positivity was present in nearly half of Sjögren's-associated SFN patients but in none of the idiopathic SFN patients.
Xerophthalmia (dry eyes) was significantly more frequent in patients with Sjögren's-associated SFN than in idiopathic SFN.
Xerostomia (dry mouth) was significantly more frequent in patients with Sjögren's-associated SFN than in idiopathic SFN.
Focus score on salivary gland biopsy was significantly higher in the Sjögren's-associated SFN group compared to idiopathic SFN.
Initial symptoms at disease onset (paresthesia, pain, numbness, limb distribution patterns) did not significantly differ between idiopathic SFN and Sjögren's-associated SFN.
There was no significant difference in the duration from symptom onset to skin biopsy between idiopathic SFN and Sjögren's-associated SFN groups.
The frequency of subepidermal nerve plexus rarefication on skin biopsy was similar between patients with Sjögren's-associated SFN and idiopathic SFN.
Cerebrospinal fluid parameters (cell count, total protein, Q-albumin, oligoclonal bands, lactate) showed no significant differences between idiopathic SFN and Sjögren's-associated SFN patients.

Among 97 patients with clinically and histopathologically confirmed SFN, 24 (25%) were found to have an underlying diagnosis of Sjögren's syndrome according to ACR/EULAR classification criteria, while 73 (75%) were classified as idiopathic SFN.
Patients with postherpetic itch showed increased touch-evoked itch (punctate hyperknesis) in the affected skin area compared with the contralateral unaffected site.
Skin biopsies from two patients demonstrated histopathologically reduced intraepidermal nerve fibers in the affected skin areas, indicating small C/Aδ fiber neuropathy.

In one patient, itch severity improved and touch-evoked itch became comparable between affected and contralateral sites after 6 months without medication, coinciding with restored intraepidermal nerve fibers on rebiopsy.
Among patients with small fiber neuropathy, 54.5% reported clinically significant pain relief after intravenous lidocaine infusion, one of the highest response rates among diagnosis subgroups.
Overall, 37.9% of the 282 chronic pain patients receiving 25-hour intravenous lidocaine infusion reported clinically significant benefit, while 38.3% reported no effect.
Myofascial pain syndrome patients had the highest response rate to lidocaine infusion at 55.0%.
Patients with peripheral (mono)neuropathy of other origin showed an above-average response rate of 55.6% to lidocaine infusion.
Vascular disease-related pain patients had the highest observed response rate (60%), though this subgroup was very small.
None of the patients with cancer pain reported any pain relief from lidocaine infusion, contrasting with prior positive trial evidence in opioid-refractory cancer pain.
Postherpetic neuralgia patients had a low response rate (8.3%) to lidocaine infusion, contrasting with earlier placebo-controlled studies showing significant benefit.
Chemotherapy-induced neuropathic pain patients showed a low response rate (20.0%) to lidocaine infusion.
Radicular pain patients showed a low response rate (20.0%) to lidocaine infusion.
Adverse effects from the 25-hour lidocaine infusion protocol were reported in only 4.3% of patients, all mild and transient.
There were no significant differences in treatment effect between male and female patients receiving lidocaine infusion.

One proposed pathophysiological mechanism of neuropathic pain is upregulation of sodium channels in nociceptor cell membranes, causing spontaneous firing and neuronal hyperexcitability, which systemic lidocaine is thought to counteract via selective sodium channel blockade.
Semi-automated CCM measures of corneal nerve fiber density, length and branch density all showed a significant negative correlation with age in the diabetes cohort.
Automated CCM analysis similarly showed significant negative correlations between age and CNFL, CNFD and CNBD, along with corneal total branch density.
CNFD measured by semi-automated software was on average 16.49% higher than automated software, with moderate agreement between methods.
CNFL agreement between semi-automated and automated software was moderate (ICC=0.63) with a mean difference of 5.73 mm/mm2, but confidence intervals were broad.
CNBD showed the poorest agreement between semi-automated and automated software (ICC=0.41), with the largest percentage disagreement of any parameter.
Nearly 12% of female subjects with diabetes had CNFL below the age-corrected normative cut-off, classified as abnormal (25% of type 1 and 11.39% of type 2 diabetic females).
A slightly higher proportion of male subjects (13.46%) had CNFL below the normative cut-off compared to females, with 20% of type 1 and 13.25% of type 2 diabetic males classified as abnormal.
Combining sexes, 12.88% of the whole diabetes cohort had abnormal CNFL, suggesting a similar proportion may have underlying small fiber neuropathy based on this single measure.
Among type 2 diabetes subjects diagnosed within the previous 2 years, 9.18% already had CNFL below the age-corrected normative cut-off, suggesting early corneal nerve changes.
Abnormal CNFL prevalence increased with longer diabetes duration, from 9.18% in subjects with ≤2 years duration to 15.38% in those with >20 years duration.

CNFD reduction became more pronounced with worsening diabetic retinopathy grade, with 75% of pre-proliferative (R2) and 100% of proliferative (R3) retinopathy subjects showing CNFD below normative values.
CNFD did not significantly differ between subjects with no retinopathy (R0) and background retinopathy (R1).
CNFL did not significantly differ between subjects with no retinopathy (R0) and background retinopathy (R1).
In 241 subjects with no evidence or history of retinopathy or maculopathy (R0/M0), 12.0% still had abnormal CNFL, suggesting corneal small fiber changes can precede clinically detectable retinopathy.
Among subjects with no retinopathy/maculopathy history, most (68%) scored 0 on the Diabetic Neuropathy Symptom score, but 32% reported at least one symptom suggestive of DPN.
Persistent stress causes glucocorticoid receptor (GR) resistance, maintaining high glucocorticoid levels and impairing their anti-inflammatory action.
Stress-induced glucocorticoids raise intracellular calcium, driving glutamate influx via NMDA receptors and causing excitatory toxicity, nerve cell damage, and death.
In a stressed rat model, EAAT expression and function were reduced, leading to impaired glutamate reuptake and sustained high extracellular glutamate.
Acute stress upregulates Ang II production via sympathetic β-adrenergic activation, raising circulating Ang II levels.
Elevated Ang II promotes ROS and pro-inflammatory cytokine production, which in turn increase COX-2 activity and PGE2 production.

Stress exposure increases iNOS activity and expression in brain and periphery, raising NO production, and NF-κB inhibitors administered before stress reduced both iNOS and NF-κB activation via an unclear mechanism.
COX-2 mRNA levels increased in mice subjected to forced swimming stress, mediated by glutamate and NF-κB signaling.

Administration of MK-801 (dizocilpine), a non-competitive NMDA receptor antagonist, reduced stress-induced TNF-α activity and expression despite increased TNF-α and TACE activity in stressed rat brain cortex.
PPARα agonism (e.g., omega-3 fatty acids) prevented multiple post-stress neuroinflammatory changes including iNOS induction, NF-κB activation, TNF-α release, and COX-2 expression.
Natural and synthetic PPARγ ligands administered to rats prevented stress-derived CNS inflammation and oxidative/nitrosative damage.
A clinical study found that patients prescribed ACE inhibitors and ARBs had a protective effect against stress-related disorders.

Ang(1-7) activation of the Mas receptor (ACE2/Ang(1-7)/MasR axis) counteracts Ang II-induced hypertension and weakens inflammatory responses, and Ang(1-7) treatment inhibited inflammatory markers across several disease models.
Telmisartan, an AT1R blocker, reduced microglial TNF-α and IL-1β synthesis and significantly reduced iNOS.

COX-2 inhibitors (e.g., celecoxib, rofecoxib, etoricoxib), while effective at inhibiting neuroinflammatory pathways in animal studies, significantly increased the risk of heart attack and stroke in clinical trials, leading to revocation of some drugs.
Meta-analysis and clinical studies show antidepressant treatment decreases TNF-α, IL-1, and IL-6, along with reduced TNF-α and IL-1β mRNA expression in microglia of antidepressant-treated rats.
Antidepressant therapy induces upregulation of Treg cells, which downregulate cytokine production, explaining the anti-inflammatory benefit of antidepressants.
A study reported that nuclear receptor binding factor 2 (NRBF2), involved in autophagy activation, weakened neuroinflammation.
Bone marrow stem cell therapy alleviated chronic inflammation in a stroke animal model.
Mesenchymal stem cell therapy showed anti-inflammatory properties within the CNS.

Sudo (2004) found that HPA axis reactivity to stress was over-activated in mice with unbalanced gut microbiome compared to those with normal microbiome, supporting a gut-brain axis link to neuroinflammation.
Preclinical studies report that gut-microbiome-deficient mice show increased blood-brain barrier permeability associated with altered claudin-5 and occludin expression.
In a population sample from Damascus, Syria, 11.8% of participants met the modified ACR 2010 criteria for fibromyalgia, one of the highest reported prevalence rates.
Among participants who met FM diagnostic criteria, only 8.2% had ever been formally diagnosed with fibromyalgia by a physician, indicating substantial underdiagnosis.
Female sex was associated with 1.31-fold higher odds of meeting fibromyalgia diagnostic criteria compared to males.
Being employed was associated with lower odds of meeting fibromyalgia criteria compared to being unemployed.
Having health insurance was associated with nearly double the odds of meeting fibromyalgia criteria, likely reflecting confounding with occupational/public-sector status in Syria.
A current diagnosis of major depressive disorder was associated with 2.62-fold higher odds of meeting fibromyalgia criteria.
Generalized anxiety disorder diagnosis was not significantly associated with fibromyalgia status in the adjusted model.
A current diagnosis of irritable bowel syndrome was associated with 1.8-fold higher odds of meeting fibromyalgia diagnostic criteria.
A current diagnosis of restless legs syndrome was associated with 1.72-fold higher odds of meeting fibromyalgia diagnostic criteria.
Marital status (single vs. in a relationship) was not significantly associated with fibromyalgia status.
Rural versus urban residence was not significantly associated with fibromyalgia status.
Self-reported financial status was not significantly associated with fibromyalgia status, contrary to European and Lebanese studies.
Among FM cases, the large majority (87.1%) reported widespread pain involving 7 or more body sites in the past week.
Across 154 cohort studies covering 27 subtypes of persistent somatic symptoms, biological factors such as infections and body-weight-related metrics showed strong evidence as predictors of PSS onset.
Psychological factors, particularly sleep problems and psychopathology, were identified as strong predictors of PSS onset in the general population.
Interpersonal factors, including life events and childhood/interpersonal stress, were found to have strong evidence as predictors of PSS onset.
Contextual factors, specifically employment status, showed strong evidence as a predictor of PSS onset.
Health behavioral factors, particularly health care utilization, showed strong evidence as a predictor of PSS onset, though this domain is relatively under-investigated.
There was no evidence that the identified predictors of PSS onset differ by PSS subtype (e.g., fibromyalgia vs. IBS vs. other subtypes).
Any hospital-diagnosed infection in the preceding 17 years was significantly associated with all delimitations of functional somatic disorder except pure multiple chemical sensitivity.
The association between any prior infection and functional somatic disorder was strongest for multi-organ bodily distress syndrome, with an OR of 2.74.
A dose-response relationship was found between the number of prior infections and risk of bodily distress syndrome.
Prior gastrointestinal infections were significantly associated with all functional somatic disorder delimitations except pure chronic widespread pain.
Prior respiratory infections were significantly associated with all functional somatic disorder delimitations except MCS, pure IB, pure CWP and pure MCS.
Sepsis, ear infections, skin infections and urological infections in the preceding 17 years were each significantly associated with bodily distress syndrome.
Hepatitis, genital infections, pregnancy-related infections and central nervous system infections in the preceding 17 years were not significantly associated with bodily distress syndrome.
Bacterial infections in the preceding 17 years were significantly associated with all functional somatic disorder delimitations except MCS, pure IB and pure MCS.
Viral pathogens were not significantly associated with any delimitation of functional somatic disorder at any time period assessed.
Infections with other pathogens (parasites, fungi, unspecified) in the preceding 17 years were significantly associated with all FSD delimitations except pure IB and pure CWP.

Any infection was significantly associated with BDS (oligo- and multi-organ), chronic widespread pain, chronic fatigue and pure chronic fatigue across all subdivided time periods (0-2, 2-9, 9-17 years), whereas associations with irritable bowel and MCS in the shorter periods (0-2 and 2-9 years) were not significant.

Bacterial infections were significantly associated with BDS, chronic widespread pain and chronic fatigue across nearly all subdivided time periods, supporting prior studies linking bacterial agents to fibromyalgia.
In contrast to prior studies, viral infections were not significantly associated with chronic widespread pain in this cohort.

Multiple infection types (bacterial, other pathogens, GI, respiratory) were consistently associated with chronic fatigue and pure chronic fatigue, suggesting infection in general, rather than specific pathogen type, is important for chronic fatigue.
No significant associations were found between any infection type and pure multiple chemical sensitivity in any time period, likely reflecting low case numbers.
Pressure pain threshold worsened (decreased) over the 5-year follow-up period in women with fibromyalgia.
Objectively measured sedentary time increased (worsened) over the 5-year follow-up.
Objectively measured light physical activity worsened (decreased) over the 5-year follow-up.
Objectively measured moderate-to-vigorous physical activity worsened (decreased) over the 5-year follow-up.
Self-reported FIQR (disease impact) scores improved over the 5-year follow-up despite objective worsening in activity/pain-threshold measures.
Self-reported SF-36 quality-of-life scores improved over the 5-year follow-up despite objective worsening in activity/pain-threshold measures.
Baseline sedentary time was not associated with future pain, disease impact, or HRQoL outcomes.
Baseline light physical activity was not associated with future pain, disease impact, or HRQoL outcomes.
Higher baseline moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA) predicted better bodily pain (SF-36) scores at 5-year follow-up.
A reduction in sedentary time over the follow-up period was associated with better SF-36 bodily pain scores at 5-year follow-up.
An increase in light physical activity over the follow-up period was associated with better SF-36 bodily pain scores at 5-year follow-up.
A reduction in sedentary time over the follow-up period was associated with better SF-36 physical component scores at 5-year follow-up.
An increase in light physical activity over the follow-up period was associated with better SF-36 physical component scores at 5-year follow-up.

An increase in moderate-to-vigorous physical activity over the follow-up period was associated with less pain (pressure pain threshold, VAS, FIQR-pain) and better SF-36 physical component scores at both 2- and 5-year follow-up.
Intracisternal (but not intraperitoneal) administration of the muscarinic M1 positive allosteric modulator BQCA blocked the increase in colonic permeability induced by lipopolysaccharide in rats.
Vagotomy abolished the BQCA-induced improvement of colonic hyperpermeability, indicating the effect requires an intact vagus nerve.
Intracisternal pirenzepine, a selective muscarinic M1 antagonist, prevented the improvement of intestinal barrier function induced by intravenous 2-deoxy-D-glucose, a central vagal stimulant.

An adenosine A2B receptor antagonist, but not dopamine or opioid receptor antagonists, prevented the BQCA-induced blockade of colonic hyperpermeability, implicating A2B signaling downstream of BFCN activation.
Intracisternal pirenzepine blocked orexin-induced improvement of intestinal barrier function, indicating BFCNs mediate orexin's effect on gut permeability.
