Intracisternal pirenzepine also blocked butyrate-induced improvement of intestinal barrier function, indicating BFCNs mediate butyrate's effect on gut permeability.
Mice undergoing cardiothoracic surgery (bi-atrial pericardiectomy with aortic cross-clamping) had higher rates of inducible atrial fibrillation 72 hours post-surgery compared to sham-operated mice.
Age stratification by tertiles showed that the greatest increase in postoperative AF risk after cardiothoracic surgery compared to sham occurred in mice aged 12-19 weeks.
Cardiothoracic surgery increased the risk of postoperative AF in female mice, but had no significant effect on AF risk in male mice.
Quantitative PCR of atrial tissue showed upregulation of transforming growth factor beta 1 expression in THOR mice compared to Sham mice.
Quantitative PCR of atrial tissue showed upregulation of interleukin 6 expression in THOR mice compared to Sham mice.
Quantitative PCR of atrial tissue showed upregulation of interleukin 18 expression in THOR mice compared to Sham mice.
The FBN1 gene on chromosome 15q21.1, encoding the extracellular matrix glycoprotein fibrillin-1, is the principal genetic cause of Marfan syndrome.

Defective FBN1 microfibrils fail to properly sequester the large latent TGF-beta complex, resulting in increased active TGF-beta in the extracellular compartment of the aortic wall and increased collagen deposition that reduces aortic elasticity.
Aortic root dilation is more prevalent in adults than children with MFS, approximately 90% versus 80% according to Roman et al.
Erkula et al. reported a similar age-related pattern, with aortic root dilation prevalence of 81% in adults versus 76% in children.
Males with MFS are reported to be more predisposed than females to developing both aortic aneurysm and aortic dissection.
Rybczynski et al. found that more than half of MFS patients had mitral valve regurgitation, with severe regurgitation reported in up to 12% by age 30.
In 227 adult MFS patients (Porciani et al.), mitral valve prolapse occurred in 78.9% and mitral insufficiency in 72.7%, with aortic valve regurgitation seen in up to one-third of adults overall.
Among 70 MFS patients with cardiac manifestations, Yetman et al. found 68% had a dilated left ventricle and 11% had reduced ejection fraction.

Kiotsekoglou et al. found MFS patients had defective right ventricular systolic function (reduced dp/dt ratio) compared with controls, confirmed by Alpendurada et al. showing reduced RV ejection fraction and increased end-diastolic/end-systolic volumes.
Fbn1 (C1039G/+) mice exhibited left ventricular contraction dysfunction with upregulation of the TGF-beta molecular pathway associated with microfibril abnormalities.

Fbn1mgR/mgR mice, which synthesize only around 20% of normal fibrillin-1, developed aortic root and proximal ascending aortic aneurysms with severe mitral and aortic regurgitation and died from ruptured aortic aneurysms within their first year of life.
FBN1 mutations, particularly in exons 24-32, are associated with an approximately 48% higher prevalence of ventricular arrhythmia compared to the general population.

Muiño-Mosquera et al. found that 20 of 86 MFS patients had non-sustained ventricular tachycardia, of whom 12 had prior valvular surgery or valvular dysfunction, suggesting arrhythmia is often secondary to valvular pathology.
Hoffmann et al. found NT-proBNP levels above 214.3 pg/ml were associated with sustained ventricular tachycardia and sudden cardiac death in MFS patients, independent of valvular pathology.

Jolley et al. found the mitral annular height-to-commissural width ratio (AHCWR) was reduced in MFS patients (mean ~20%) compared to normal (~24%), producing a planar rather than saddle-shaped annulus.

A randomized controlled trial by Lacro et al. reported higher prevalence of mitral valve prolapse and regurgitation in females than males (45% vs 33% for prolapse; 25% vs 13% for regurgitation), whereas Detaint et al. found equal prevalence between sexes with increased incidence with age.

Combination therapy with beta-blockers and angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) is the most commonly used pharmacologic regimen believed to delay or prevent progression of aortic root dilation in MFS.

Aortic root replacement, either total root replacement (TRR) or valve-sparing root replacement (VSRR), is described as the most effective surgical option for MFS-related aortic root disease, with VSRR preferred in younger patients to avoid lifelong anticoagulation risk.

Post-Bentall graft infection, a rare late-onset complication caused by gram-positive cocci, presents with prolonged fatigue and fever and is associated with elevated leukocytosis and raised C-reactive protein levels.

An iPSC line was generated from peripheral blood mononuclear cells of a thoracic aortic aneurysm-presenting Loeys-Dietz syndrome type V patient carrying a heterozygous causal TGFB3 variant, retaining normal karyotype, pluripotency marker expression, and tri-lineage differentiation capacity.

Low-dose acrylamide (0.5 µg/kg bw/day for 28 days) significantly increased the percentage of CART-immunoreactive neurons in the myenteric plexus of the jejunum, with no change in the submucosal plexuses.
High-dose acrylamide (5 µg/kg bw/day) markedly increased CART-positive neuron populations in both the myenteric plexus and the outer submucosal plexus of the jejunum.
Low-dose acrylamide significantly increased VAChT-positive neuron numbers only in the myenteric plexus, with no change in the submucosal plexuses.
High-dose acrylamide increased VAChT-positive neuron populations across all three tested plexuses (myenteric, outer submucosal, inner submucosal) of the jejunum.
Low-dose acrylamide decreased nNOS-positive neuron populations in the inner submucosal plexus and myenteric plexus, with no change in the outer submucosal plexus.
High-dose acrylamide caused a statistically significant drop in nNOS-positive neuron populations across all three tested jejunal plexuses.
Low-dose acrylamide significantly increased GAL-positive neuron numbers in the myenteric plexus and outer submucosal plexus, with no change in the inner submucosal plexus.
High-dose acrylamide significantly increased GAL-positive neuron numbers across all three tested jejunal plexuses, suggesting an inflammatory/neuroprotective adaptive response.
Low-dose acrylamide increased substance P-positive neuron numbers only in the myenteric plexus of the jejunum.
High-dose acrylamide increased substance P-positive neuron numbers in the myenteric plexus and both submucosal plexuses of the jejunum, indicating sensory/nociceptive changes.
Homozygous variants in SLC18A2 (encoding VMAT2) cause brain monoamine vesicular transport disease, an infantile-onset movement disorder that mimics cerebral palsy.
Affected individuals commonly exhibited autonomic nervous system involvement, including temperature dysregulation/sweating abnormalities, hypersalivation, and gastrointestinal dysmotility.
Among 58 individuals described to date with biallelic SLC18A2 variants, 16 (28%) died before age 13 years, indicating substantial early mortality in this disorder.
Genotype was strongly associated with survival: 9 of 17 patients with p.Pro237His died, whereas all 14 patients with p.Pro387Leu survived.
Individuals homozygous for the p.Pro237His SLC18A2 variant had markedly higher mortality, with 9 of 17 affected individuals dying, compared to variant subgroups with milder outcomes.
All 14 patients homozygous for the p.Pro387Leu SLC18A2 variant survived, indicating a milder disease course compared to other variants such as p.Pro237His.
Dopamine agonist treatment mildly improved disease symptoms in the majority of treated patients with biallelic SLC18A2 variants.

Some individuals with p.Ile43Phe and p.Pro387Leu variants showed milder disease phenotypes and prolonged survival even in the absence of dopamine agonist treatment, suggesting variant-specific residual transporter function.
A Caenorhabditis elegans model of SLC18A2 loss-of-function exhibited behavioral abnormalities, providing functional validation of pathogenicity.

Among 1234 women with breast cancer receiving taxane chemotherapy, patient-reported chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN) was reported in 76.9% of EORTC QLQ-CIPN20 surveys and 79.3% of FACT/GOG-Ntx surveys.
The EORTC QLQ-CIPN20 and FACT/GOG-Ntx questionnaires showed substantial agreement in detecting patient-reported CIPN.
At 6 weeks after treatment initiation, CIPN was most frequently reported in the nab-paclitaxel group compared with paclitaxel and docetaxel groups, which did not differ significantly from each other.
In multivariate proportional hazards analysis, patients treated with paclitaxel had a lower risk of patient-reported CIPN than those treated with nab-paclitaxel.
In multivariate proportional hazards analysis, patients treated with docetaxel had a lower risk of patient-reported CIPN than those treated with nab-paclitaxel.
After propensity-score overlap weighting to reduce confounding, paclitaxel and docetaxel remained associated with a lower risk of patient-reported CIPN compared with nab-paclitaxel.
On the sensory subscale, patients receiving paclitaxel or docetaxel reported less sensory discomfort than those receiving nab-paclitaxel after propensity weighting.
Risk of motor symptoms was not significantly lower with paclitaxel or docetaxel compared with nab-paclitaxel, indicating motor toxicity is not reduced with these taxanes.
Risk of autonomic symptoms (e.g., blurred vision) was essentially the same across nab-paclitaxel, paclitaxel, and docetaxel groups.
Sensory symptoms occurred earlier in the nab-paclitaxel group (median 1.1 weeks) than in the paclitaxel (4.0 weeks) or docetaxel (5.9 weeks) groups.
Patients reported motor symptoms earlier than sensory symptoms across all taxane groups, with the earliest onset in the nab-paclitaxel group.
Time to onset of autonomic symptoms did not differ significantly among the three taxane groups.

Patients receiving different taxanes reported distinct symptom profiles: nab-paclitaxel patients predominantly reported sensory numbness, while paclitaxel and docetaxel patients predominantly reported motor weakness and autonomic blurred vision.
Previous taxane treatment cycles and treatment stage (neoadjuvant, adjuvant, or palliative) were independent factors associated with patient-reported CIPN, in addition to taxane type.
Multiple prior treatments including the Lightning Process, physical therapy, psychotherapy, and diets failed to halt symptom worsening in one participant, despite providing some coping tools.

A gradual, individualized pacing and exercise program (slow yoga/Pilates, structured 4x-weekly schedule) at an outpatient exhaustion-disorder clinic was associated with subjective improvement and was described as a turning point in recovery.
Openly disclosing the extent of illness to others ("stopping pretending to be healthy") in a supportive peer setting was reported to reduce energy expenditure and support recovery.
A relaxation/cognitive technique taught by a therapist helped one participant reduce negative thoughts and stress-related setbacks over time.
Setbacks (exhaustion relapses), sometimes triggered by fear of relapse and stress, were common during the recovery process and could require weeks to months before returning to prior functioning.

Of 13 participants, 8 considered themselves completely recovered and were working/studying full-time, while the remaining 5 considered themselves much better but still experienced residual fatigue requiring adequate rest.
All participants reported a greater need for structure and routine in daily life (e.g., meals and sleep) after illness compared to before falling ill.

One participant experienced a sudden 'awakening' recovery pattern with abrupt onset of small movements after years of being bedridden and totally disconnected from her body, contrasting with another participant's gradual, structured recovery.
A pre-illness personality trait of excessive self-criticism and inability to say no to others was retrospectively linked by one participant to her experience of exhaustion prior to and during ME/CFS.
In one severely affected participant, ME/CFS progressed to inability to eat or use the toilet independently, requiring nasogastric tube feeding, illustrating extreme functional impairment.

Post-exertional "collapses" in one participant were characterized by profound fatigue, diffuse pain, memory loss and loss of appetite, followed by periods of being bedbound, isolated and severely ill for months.
One participant's ME/CFS diagnosis followed a prolonged period of pain, exhaustion, and sensitivity to light and sound (photophobia/phonophobia).
Six months after SARS-CoV-2 infection, patients continued to experience fatigue, post-exertional malaise, and cognitive dysfunction.
A survey of the Body Politic COVID-19 support group found that 91% of respondents had not recovered 40 days after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
A longitudinal prospective cohort study found 30% of patients with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection had recurring symptoms 9 months after infection.
A meta-analysis found IL-6 is related to the development of hypoxemia in COVID-19, suggesting it may be a biomarker for respiratory risk.
Increases in interleukin-8 (IL-8) have been proposed as a biomarker for post-viral fatigue, specifically in ME/CFS.
PASC patients have elevated inflammatory proteins, suggesting an unbalanced inflammatory/anti-inflammatory cytokine response.
A Th2/Th1 cytokine imbalance is suggested to be related to higher mortality in COVID-19 patients.
Six weeks of daily 20-minute meditation downregulated pro-inflammatory genes in cancer survivors.
An 8-week meditation intervention was associated with significant improvements in CD4+ T lymphocyte counts and halted CD4 decline in people with AIDS.
A meta-analysis by Sanada et al found mindfulness-based interventions had significant positive effects on cytokine blood levels related to low-grade inflammation.
In a bioinformatics study of COVID-19, a hyper-methylated status was associated with worse outcomes, and COVID-19 severity was related to seventy-seven differentially methylated positions.
Mindfulness meditation was related to increased telomerase activity.
A meta-analysis found a moderate effect size (0.46) for meditation's effect on telomere length across novice and long-term meditators.
Research on long-term meditators found telomerase changes with strong effect sizes (0.66-0.88), though based on small sample sizes (n<20).
Mindfulness and compassion meditation practitioners showed a decreased epigenetic aging rate based on CpG methylation profiling.

A smartphone-based mindfulness meditation training was associated with reduced pro-inflammatory gene expression, with 1027 gene transcripts differing by more than 50% between groups from baseline to post-intervention.

Using T1-weighted spin echo MR imaging, patients with post-viral fatigue showed decreased signal intensity in the brainstem and increased signal intensity in sensorimotor white matter compared to healthy controls.
A longitudinal imaging study found progressive atrophy in the left inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus in patients with post-viral fatigue measured 6 years apart.

A diffusion tensor imaging study found increased fractional anisotropy and decreased mean and axial diffusivity in the corona radiata, external capsule, and superior frontal-occipital fasciculus in recovered SARS-CoV-2 patients.

Patients with post-viral fatigue had reduced functional connectivity within the salience network between the anterior cingulate cortex and right insula using arterial spin labeling-based functional connectivity.
Resting-state fMRI in female patients with post-viral fatigue showed aberrant connectivity between the posterior and anterior cingulate cortex.
COVID-19 patients, even younger individuals and those with milder infections, showed an increased risk of stroke.
A meta-analysis found mind-body practices effective at reducing symptom severity (fatigue, anxiety, depression) and improving physical and mental functioning in post-viral fatigue/ME-CFS.
A review of meditation for post-viral fatigue (ME/CFS) found no significant differences at follow-up for interventions lasting less than 8 weeks.
Patients provided meditation after SARS-CoV-2 infection reported improvement in multiple sleep indicators.
After extensive diagnostic evaluations of patients with PASC, no persistent viral infection or abnormal immune activation was found.

ME/CFS patients frequently show autoantibodies against ß-adrenergic and muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, which have been linked to altered brain network structure and hypothesized to underlie vascular and neural symptoms.
ME patients show increased serum IgA and IgM against LPS of Enterobacteria and increased Bacteroides in the gut microbiota, suggesting increased gut permeability contributes to ME pathophysiology.

16S rRNA metagenomic sequencing in ME patients showed an overall reduction in microbial diversity, decreased Ruminococcaceae and other Firmicutes, and a two-fold increase in Enterobacteriaceae abundance.

Children with autism showed lower levels of Bifidobacterium spp. and higher levels of Lactobacillus spp. compared to controls, with similar levels of other bacteria and yeast.

Finegold et al. found severely autistic children had higher Bacteroidetes and lower Firmicutes than controls, with more Desulfovibrio sp. and Bacteroides vulgatus in stool of severely autistic children.
A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial found that combining a casein/gluten-free diet with the B-GOS prebiotic improved behavioral symptoms in autistic children.
Gastric and small-bowel specimens from children with autism were more likely to contain Clostridia and a higher number of Clostridia species than control specimens.
ASD children treated with oral vancomycin improved in behavioral, cognitive, and GI symptoms, with symptoms relapsing after therapy discontinuation, possibly due to persistence of Clostridium spores.
Low intestinal carbohydrate digestive enzyme activity was reported in 58.3% of autistic cases examined, with no abnormality found in pancreatic function.

The patient was diagnosed with both cleidocranial dysplasia (CCD) and hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (hEDS), representing what the authors describe as the first documented co-occurrence of these two rare syndromes.

The patient scored 5 on the Brighton criteria, consistent with generalized joint hypermobility (fifth finger dorsiflexion >90°, right thumb passively flexed to forearm, knee hyperextension >10° bilaterally, but not elbow hyperextension or trunk forward flexion).
The patient exhibited skin extensibility beyond the normal range without associated bruising, a feature supporting the hEDS diagnosis.
Three of the patient's six siblings and his father displayed an analogous phenotype, suggesting familial/hereditary transmission of the combined syndromic features.

The paper states that CCD is mainly caused by heterozygous mutations in RUNX2, located at 6p21, which is critical for osteoblast/osteoclast differentiation and dental lamina regression, though genetic testing was not reported for this specific patient.
Despite the hEDS diagnosis, TMJ examination showed no hypermobility or subluxation, although masseter muscle tenderness/atrophy and temporalis muscle enlargement were observed.

Disturbed osteoclastogenesis in the dental follicle and periodontal ligament impairs resorption of bone and roots of primary teeth, leading to delayed shedding of primary teeth, delayed eruption of permanent teeth, and multiple supernumerary teeth.
Chest radiography demonstrated aplasia of the right clavicle, hypoplasia of the left clavicle, and a narrow bell-shaped thorax with oblique ribs, consistent with cleidocranial dysplasia.
Pelvic and feet radiographs revealed a wide pubic symphysis, coxa vara, and hypoplasia of the distal phalanges.

CT imaging with 3D reconstruction showed extreme open sutures, plagiocephaly, widely open anterior/posterior/posterolateral fontanelles, wormian bones, orbital malformations, absent nasal bone, patent mandibular symphysis, cleft palate, and bilaterally discontinuous zygomatic arches.
Imaging identified 26 unerupted teeth in the maxilla and 15 in the mandible, along with multiple dentigerous cysts surrounding unerupted teeth.

The patient presented with signs atypical for CCD alone—generalized joint hypermobility, excessive skin laxity, smooth skin, prominent eyes, lobeless ears, and limb pain—prompting the diagnosis of a second, coexisting syndrome (hEDS).

A novel homozygous ADAMTS2 missense variant (11:2491238G>A) was identified by whole genome sequencing in an adult Catahoula Leopard Dog with EDS, predicted to substitute a conserved arginine with histidine at residue 966.

An identical novel homozygous ADAMTS2 frameshift deletion (11:2280117delC) was found in an EDS-affected Pit Bull Terrier and an Alapaha Blue Blood Bulldog, predicted to produce a severely truncated, non-functional protein.
Genotyping 492 Alapaha Blue Blood Bulldogs for the ADAMTS2 deletion showed 9 homozygous, 158 heterozygous, and 325 homozygous-reference, giving a variant allele frequency of 0.27 in this cohort.
Among 217 archived Pit Bull Terrier DNA samples, only 2 dogs (littermates with clinical EDS) were homozygous for the deletion allele, indicating the variant is rare in this breed.
Likely-causal homozygous ADAMTS2 variants were found in 4 of 26 whole genome sequences from dogs diagnosed with EDS, suggesting dermatosparaxis is a significant but uncommon subtype of canine EDS.

Dermatosparactic EDS results from biallelic ADAMTS2 variants causing deficiency of procollagen-I-N-proteinase, the enzyme that removes the N-terminal propeptide from fibrillar collagen α-chains, impairing normal collagen fibril assembly.
Fragile skin (atrophic scars, lacerations at various healing stages, subcutaneous hematomas/seromas) was the most consistent clinical finding across all eight dogs with dermatosparactic EDS.
Joint instability and hyperextensible skin were present in most affected dogs but do not distinguish dermatosparaxis from other more common canine EDS subtypes.

Painful swellings around appendicular joints (elbows, tarsi, carpi, paws) were common in the Pit Bull Terrier and Alapaha Blue Blood Bulldog puppies and may be a distinguishing feature of severe canine dermatosparaxis.

Bilateral narrowed palpebral fissures were a distinct feature in five of six affected puppies, possibly reflecting periocular edema linked to impaired ADAMTS2-mediated activation of VEGF-C, a lymphangiogenesis factor.

Intermittent ataxia was observed in two affected puppies (one Pit Bull Terrier, one Alapaha Blue Blood Bulldog), an unexpected finding not previously reported in ADAMTS2-related EDS, though full neurological workup was not performed.
Dermal collagen fibrils from affected dogs showed abnormal curved, linear ('hieroglyphic-like') cross-sectional ultrastructure, in contrast to the uniform circular profiles of control dermis.
Corneal collagen fibril ultrastructure and transparency were largely preserved in affected dogs, suggesting ADAMTS2 plays a relatively minor role in corneal collagen fibrillogenesis compared to skin.
Descemet's membrane was much thinner in affected puppies compared to the control dog, though this may be confounded by age difference between the animals compared.

Tendon and ligament collagen fibril ultrastructural abnormalities in affected dogs were less severe than in the dermis, possibly because ADAMTS3 and ADAMTS14 partially compensate for ADAMTS2 deficiency in these tissues.
All eight dogs with dermatosparactic EDS carried likely-causal ADAMTS2 variants in the homozygous state, consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance of dermatosparaxis reported in other species.
A previously reported Doberman Pinscher puppy (Dog 8) with EDS had a homozygous ADAMTS2 nonsense mutation in the fourth of 22 coding exons, likely causing loss of protein via nonsense-mediated decay.

The authors speculate that the missense ADAMTS2 variant in the Catahoula Leopard Dog may retain residual procollagen-I-N-proteinase activity, potentially explaining its milder clinical course and survival to adulthood compared to dogs with null variants.
The patient scored 9 out of 9 on the Beighton hypermobility scale, indicating maximal generalized joint hypermobility consistent with EDS.
Mild TBI has been previously reported to unmask undiagnosed EDS in 7 adult patients, who experienced slower and less complete recovery than typical concussion patients.

The patient displayed left-sided upper and lower extremity weakness and impaired balance/tandem gait after concussion, which the authors note is atypical for a mild concussion and may be attributable to underlying EDS.
A Lower Extremity Functional Scale (LEFS) assessment showed 95% function 3 months post-concussion, indicating near-normal but incomplete recovery of everyday task ability in the lower extremities.

Post-concussion visual assessment showed impaired oculomotor control, horizontal/vertical smooth pursuit and saccades, and a convergence measurement of 22 cm indicating convergence insufficiency, worse on the left side.

Cognitive-linguistic evaluation revealed premature cognitive fatigue, slowed processing, word-finding difficulties, mood changes, irritability, working memory difficulty, and moderate immediate/short-term memory deficits after concussion.

Six months post-concussion the patient still reported headaches, fatigue, left-sided weakness, dizziness, blurred vision, sleep difficulty, noise sensitivity, and trouble focusing, far exceeding the expected less-than-one-month recovery period for a mild concussion at her age.
Menstrual-cycling females are reported to be at higher risk for increased number, severity, and duration of symptoms secondary to TBI.

In the Fbn1C1039G/+ Marfan syndrome mouse model, the middle cerebral artery showed increased wall/lumen hypertrophy along with elevated TGF-β and MMP-9 expression and increased reactive oxygen species production.

ApoE-deficient Fbn1C1039G/+ mice showed accelerated blood-brain barrier degradation with increased inflammatory cytokine TNF-α, MMP-2/MMP-9, and TGF-β in the middle cerebral artery and choroid plexus.
Vascular EDS is caused by pathogenic variants in the COL3A1 gene, which encodes type III procollagen, a major structural protein of blood vessel walls and hollow organs.
Mutations affecting glycine residues in COL3A1 are associated with more severe and earlier-onset vascular risk in vEDS compared with other variant types.

Celiprolol treatment as part of secondary prevention is associated with a lower annual rate of arterial complications and improved survival in vEDS patients, per an observational study by Frank et al.

In this five-patient case series, endovascular or hybrid interventions for acute vascular complications of vEDS resulted in only one minor complication (at a puncture site) and no procedure-related deaths.
A cited series (Freeman et al.) reported major complications in 22% of cases and a 5.6% death rate among 18 vEDS patients undergoing angiography.
A cited series (Schievink et al.) reported that 24% of 25 angiographies resulted in severe bleeding at the arterial puncture site despite manual compression in vEDS patients.
A more recent series (Okada et al.) reported fewer complications than earlier reports, with only three minor complications occurring across seven endovascular procedures.
A literature review (Bergqvist et al.) found higher mortality with open surgical repair of arterial complications (30%) compared with endovascular procedures (24%) in vEDS.
The Mayo Clinic case series showed higher perioperative mortality for open surgical treatment of vEDS vascular complications, though most surgeries were aortic rather than visceral.
Pregnancy is suspected to promote vascular 'storms' in vEDS patients, and vEDS carries one of the highest maternal mortality rates during labor or the postpartum period.
A cited report recommends delivery by cesarean section at 32 weeks gestation to reduce vascular risk in pregnant vEDS patients.

Patient 1, with a confirmed COL3A1 glycine mutation, was successfully treated by endovascular embolization of a pulmonary arteriovenous fistula and pseudoaneurysm and remains alive after 8 years on celiprolol despite further arterial dissections and a celiac trunk rupture.

Patient 3 underwent successful mechanical thrombectomy and carotid stenting for stroke due to bilateral carotid dissection from vEDS, and after 3 years on celiprolol had no further arterial events but retained persistent left hemiparesis.

Patient 4, with a confirmed COL3A1 glycine mutation, was treated by embolization of a ruptured renal artery aneurysm and remains alive after 12 years on celiprolol and losartan despite further dissections and new asymptomatic aneurysms.

Patient 5, with a confirmed pathogenic COL3A1 glycine variant, underwent hybrid endovascular/surgical management of multiple arterial dissections and was in good health at 10-month follow-up on celiprolol, irbesartan, and activity adaptation.

The authors hypothesize that repeated embolization and hybrid intervention in Patient 2 may have increased systemic vascular stress and inflammation, contributing to a subsequent hepatic artery rupture during hospitalization.

Two vEDS patients known to the center for small ('infracentimetric') visceral aneurysms died outside the institution during follow-up—one from a cardiac complication and one from an unknown cause—raising the possibility of unwitnessed aneurysmal rupture.
Whole exome sequencing identified a heterozygous missense variant c.C7853T (p.Thr2618Met) in the COL12A1 gene in the patient, classified as likely pathogenic and known in dbSNP as rs201988277.
The patient's serum cortisol level was below the normal reference range, while serotonin, tryptophan, and catecholamines were within normal limits.

The patient scored 6 out of 9 on the Beighton Hypermobility Score and 5 on the Five-Point Questionnaire, indicating generalized joint hypermobility.
Mutations in COL5A1 and COL5A2 reduce synthesis of type V collagen, which plays a central role in the pathogenesis of classical EDS.

In a study of 126 suspected classical EDS patients, 93 of 102 patients meeting all three major Villefranche criteria had type V collagen mutations, representing 90% of that population, though this did not extend to hypermobile EDS.
Chronic pain incidence can reach 100% in patients with hypermobile EDS and up to 90% across EDS types generally.
Patients with EDS report an average diagnostic delay of 14 years, attributable to clinical and genetic heterogeneity of the disorder; the case patient was diagnosed at age 38.
A meta-analysis found that people with joint hypermobility syndrome/hEDS more often present with anxiety and depressive manifestations than the general population.

The patient scored 8 (intermediate) on the Beck Anxiety Inventory and 3 (minimum) on the Beck Depression Inventory, alongside a very low stress scale score, despite being described elsewhere as having a major depressive disorder diagnosis.
Small fiber neuropathy is described as a characteristic feature of EDS, and cognitive deficits have been reported in this type of neuropathy, likely related to pain.

Migraine can be a clinical manifestation of EDS with earlier onset and reduced quality of life; the patient had a 3-year history of migraine with head dullness, pressure, stabbing pain, and photophobia worsened by sweets.
COL12A1 mutant mice exhibited fragile bones with disorganized collagen fiber arrangement, decreased bone matrix protein expression, and decreased bone-forming activity.

COL12A1 knockout mice showed decreased grip strength, delayed fiber-type transition, and deficient passive force generation, suggesting collagen XII acts as a matrix-based passive force-transducing element in muscle.
EDS classical types affect approximately 1 in 5000 people, with estimates that hypermobile EDS (hEDS) accounts for 80-90% of diagnosed EDS cases, though sources disagree on precise figures.
Prior studies have reported cognitive impairment in visuospatial problem-solving, attention, and memory among EDS patients, along with deficits in concentration.

Gastrointestinal manifestations, including unexplained GI symptoms, abdominal emergencies, and hernias, are recurrent in EDS patients; this patient presented with an umbilical hernia and biopsy-confirmed gastroesophageal reflux disease.
Early-onset varicose veins are associated with vascular EDS, and varicose veins are more common among pregnant women with hypermobile-type EDS, suggesting a convergent pathophysiological pathway.
Hearing loss is reported as common in patients with EDS, consistent with this patient's presentation of hearing loss, vertigo, and imbalance.
Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS type IV) results from defective production of type III procollagen, causing profound vascular fragility.
Among the vEDS patients evaluated, direct cavernous carotid fistulas (DCCF) were the most common cerebrovascular lesion treated.
Modern neuroendovascular procedures achieved a 94% success rate in treating cerebrovascular disease in patients with vEDS.
Neuroendovascular procedures in vEDS patients carried a 30% complication rate.
Neuroendovascular treatment of cerebrovascular disease in vEDS patients carried a 7.5% mortality rate.

People with heritable disorders of connective tissue, including Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Marfan syndrome, Loeys-Dietz syndrome, and Stickler syndrome, are reported to have an increased risk of Chiari I malformation.
MICS treatment produced a significant reduction in pain perception during and after treatment across all three groups (MTrP, MTrP+GJH, MTrP+JHS).
MICS increased parasympathetic (vagal) autonomic nervous system activity in the general joint hypermobility (GJH) and joint hypermobility syndrome (JHS) groups.
The LF/HF ratio showed significant differences across protocol phases (rest, stimulation, recovery), but sympathetic activity predominance persisted throughout the protocol despite treatment.
Overall heart rate variability increased in joint hypermobility patients following MICS treatment, indicating improved autonomic modulation with increased vagal tone and decreased sympathetic tone.
LH3 (PLOD3) knockout in PFHR9 cells significantly reduced extracellular secretion of COL4A1/COL4A2 while intracellular COL4A1 accumulated, indicating impaired collagen IV secretion.
In wild-type PFHR9 cells, newly synthesized collagen IV took approximately 7 to 8 hours to be secreted, markedly slower than the ~2 hours reported for collagen I.
LH3 knockout severely delayed collagen IV secretion, with only about one-fourth of newly synthesized collagen IV secreted even after 48 hours in culture.

In LH3 knockout MEFs, secretion rates of fibrillar collagens I and III were comparable to wild-type, though a delay was seen at early time points for collagen I; LH3 deficiency does not impair biosynthesis of these fibrillar collagens.

Collagen IV purified from LH3 knockout cells was predominantly monomeric and lacked disulfide crosslinking and higher-order (hexamer/dodecamer) structures seen in wild-type, with a lower-molecular-weight truncated species identified as truncated COL4A1/COL4A2 by mass spectrometry.

Rotary shadow electron microscopy showed wild-type collagen IV formed >80% trimers, ~8.5% hexamers, and ~9.0% dodecamers, whereas LH3 knockout collagen IV showed no dodecamers and instead shortened, amino-terminally truncated trimers (72.8%) and hexamers (7.8%).
Circular dichroism showed that collagen IV from LH3 knockout cells did not adopt a stable triple helical conformation even at 10°C, resembling heat-denatured wild-type collagen IV.

Surface plasmon resonance showed HSP47 bound collagen IV from LH3 knockout cells with lower affinity and altered (increased dissociation constant) binding kinetics compared with wild-type collagen IV.

Amino acid analysis showed prolyl 4-hydroxylation was reduced specifically in COL4A1 (but not COL1A1, COL1A2, COL3A1, or COL4A2) upon LH3 knockout, while 3-hydroxyproline levels were largely unchanged across all chains.

LH3 knockout produced significantly fewer hydroxylysines (more unmodified lysines) on COL4A1 and COL4A2, whereas lysine/Hyl levels on COL1A1, COL1A2, and COL3A1 were largely unchanged, indicating LH3's lysyl hydroxylase function is selective for collagen IV.

Collagen IV from LH3 knockout cells had high occupancy of galactosyl Hyl but not glucosyl galactosyl Hyl, indicating LH3 is required for the glucosylation step but not the galactosylation step of hydroxylysine O-glycosylation.

GGHL was also reduced in collagen I and collagen III from LH3 knockout cells, indicating LH3 has a general glucosyltransferase role across fibrillar and network-forming collagens even though its lysyl hydroxylase activity is selective for collagen IV.

No enrichment of rare, predicted-damaging PLOD3 variants was found comparing the 113-fetus intracerebral hemorrhage cohort to gnomAD control databases, though authors attribute this to genetic heterogeneity of fetal ICH.

Two unrelated fetuses with intracerebral hemorrhage (negative for COL4A1/COL4A2 variants) carried rare, predicted-damaging PLOD3 missense variants: fetus F09 was heterozygous for p.L198P, and fetus F12 was compound heterozygous for p.R197W and p.P489L, located in the catalytic and accessory glycosyltransferase domains respectively.

Prior clinical reports show biallelic loss-of-function PLOD3 variants cause a connective tissue disorder overlapping Stickler-like syndrome and epidermolysis bullosa, with craniofacial dysmorphism, skeletal/ocular disorders, sensorineural hearing loss, variable skin manifestations, and cerebral hemorrhage in three cases.

Fibromyalgia patients showed significantly reduced local (short-distance) functional connectivity in the sensorimotor cortex across most levels of the cortical body representation, as well as in occipital visual areas, compared to matched healthy controls.

In fibromyalgia patients, a significant group-by-distance interaction was found in the inferior (opercular) somatosensory cortex, angular gyrus, and visual cortices, indicating that alterations differentially affected specific local connectivity distances.

Knee osteoarthritis patients showed significantly reduced local functional connectivity in the bilateral insula extending to the ventral-lateral frontal cortex and occipital visual areas, compared to matched healthy controls.
In osteoarthritis patients, a significant group-by-distance interaction was observed in the left posterior insula and right anterior insula, indicating distance-specific alterations.

Across both osteoarthritis and fibromyalgia, all identified alterations were in the direction of weaker local connectivity compared to controls, and effects predominantly involved short cortical distances (5-10 mm) over longer distances (25-30 mm), suggesting a primarily regional, short-distance cortical dysfunction.

In a direct comparison of new patient samples adjusting for age, fibromyalgia patients showed significantly weaker sensorimotor cortex local connectivity than knee osteoarthritis patients, mainly involving short distances.

The direct comparison of osteoarthritis and fibromyalgia patients showed a significant group-by-distance interaction in the inferior opercular somatosensory cortex, angular gyri, lateral occipito-temporal junction, and lateral frontal cortex.

Osteoarthritis patients showed weaker local connectivity than fibromyalgia patients in the left frontal operculum, inferior parietal lobe, and medial frontal pole, confirming distinct distributions of cortical dysfunction between the two conditions.
Across both osteoarthritis and fibromyalgia patients, older age was associated with weaker local functional connectivity in the auditory cortex.

In fibromyalgia patients specifically, older age correlated with weaker local connectivity in the auditory cortex, visual cortex, somatosensory cortex, and frontal operculum/anterior insula (gustatory cortex).

In osteoarthritis patients, significant age-related negative correlation with connectivity was restricted to the lateral frontal pole at whole-brain threshold, with only a marginal (sub-threshold) negative correlation in the left auditory cortex, suggesting a weaker age effect than in fibromyalgia.

The discussion cites prior evidence that a relevant proportion (34%) of severe fibromyalgia patients show low levels of insulin-like growth factors, which normally mediate collagen synthesis in tendon and muscle, potentially contributing to weak proprioceptive input.

The discussion notes that joint hypermobility is three times more frequent in fibromyalgia patients than in control groups, supporting the hypothesis of deficient proprioception contributing to sensitization in fibromyalgia.

Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) analysis showed that artemisinic acid has a binding affinity of KD = 2.64 x 10^-6 for Lyn.
Artemisinic acid attenuates substance P/MRGPRX2-mediated chronic urticaria and mast cell activation, acting as a Lyn kinase antagonist.
OVA-sensitized/challenged asthmatic mice showed increased airway hyperresponsiveness (Penh) to methacholine compared with control mice, and EB-A treatment reduced Penh to near control levels.
Serum PGD2, a mediator of bronchial smooth muscle contraction, was elevated in asthmatic mice and was reduced to control levels by EB-A treatment.
Asthmatic mice showed increased cough/wheeze frequency and shortened incubation periods, both of which were significantly reversed by EB-A treatment.
Total serum IgE was significantly elevated in OVA-sensitized mice compared to controls, and both dexamethasone and EB-A (low and high dose) significantly lowered IgE levels.
Lungs of asthmatic mice showed severe inflammatory cell infiltration and increased collagen deposition, both of which were markedly reduced by EB-A treatment based on histological scoring.
Apoptosis and ROS levels in primary lung tissue cells were significantly increased in asthmatic mice and were significantly decreased by EB-A treatment.
Th2 cytokines IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, and TNF-α were upregulated in serum/BALF of asthmatic mice while IFN-γ and IL-10 were downregulated; EB-A treatment reversed both trends.
PAR2 was activated in lung tissue of asthmatic mice with increased downstream GM-CSF, IL-33, and TSLP, and EB-A treatment inhibited PAR2 activation and reduced these downstream effectors.
Molecular docking showed hydrogen bonds and electrostatic/hydrophobic interactions between EB-A and the antagonist binding pocket of PAR2 (PDB 5NDD), suggesting EB-A acts as a PAR2 antagonist.
EB-A treatment decreased dendritic cell (DC) maturation and increased regulatory T cell (Treg) differentiation in peripheral blood and lung tissue after OVA sensitization.

Mast cell activation markers (mMCP-1, β-MCT, histamine, LTC4, TPSAB1) and toluidine-blue-positive mast cells were increased in lung tissue/serum/BALF of asthmatic mice, and EB-A treatment obviously inhibited mast cell activation.
EB-A dose-dependently inhibited compound 48/80-induced degranulation (β-hexosaminidase and histamine release) of RBL-2H3 mast cells in vitro.
PAR2-activating peptide (500 mM) significantly increased PAR2 expression in 16HBE bronchial epithelial cells, and EB-A co-administration at this concentration suppressed the increase.

In a 16HBE-BMDC co-culture system, PAR2 activation significantly increased expression of DC surface maturation markers (MHC Class II, CD40, CD80, CD86), and EB-A intervention significantly inhibited this upregulation.

Several furofuran/tetrahydrofuran lignans isolated from Magnolia biondii (compounds 7, 8, 13, 15, and 18) significantly inhibited β-hexosaminidase release from mouse bone marrow-derived mast cells, indicating suppression of mast cell degranulation.

Thirty-three lignans were isolated from Magnolia biondii flower buds, including two novel furofuran lignans, two novel tetrahydrofuran lignans, and 16 other known lignans reported for the first time from this species, suggesting furofuran/tetrahydrofuran lignans are the main constituents responsible for antiallergic activity.
IgE-sensitized and antigen-challenged KU812 mast cells showed markedly increased intracellular ROS (superoxide) levels compared to untreated control cells.

Treatment with UCMSC-derived extracellular vesicles reduced ROS fluorescence in IgE-activated KU812 mast cells by approximately 50%, without a clear dose-response relationship across 10^7–10^9 particles/mL.
IgE/antigen stimulation significantly increased mast cell degranulation (tryptase release) in KU812 cells by approximately 350% relative to control.
UCMSC-EVs (10^7–10^9 particles/mL) significantly decreased IgE-induced mast cell degranulation and tryptase release in KU812 cells.
UCMSC-EVs significantly reduced IL-1β expression in KU812 cells relative to the IgE-induced upregulation of this proinflammatory cytokine.
UCMSC-EVs significantly reduced TNF-α expression in KU812 cells relative to the IgE-induced upregulation of this proinflammatory cytokine.
UCMSC-EVs significantly reduced IL-6 expression in KU812 cells relative to the IgE-induced upregulation of this proinflammatory cytokine.
IgE stimulation induced activation (phosphorylation) of p38 MAPK in KU812 mast cells.
UCMSC-EVs suppressed IgE-stimulated phosphorylation of p38 MAPK in KU812 mast cells.
IgE stimulation induced activation (phosphorylation) of JNK in KU812 mast cells.
UCMSC-EVs suppressed IgE-stimulated phosphorylation of JNK in KU812 mast cells.
NF-κB (p65) protein levels increased following IgE-driven activation of KU812 mast cells.
UCMSC-EVs at a relatively low dose (10^7 particles/mL) reduced NF-κB (p65) protein levels in IgE-activated KU812 mast cells.
UCMSC-EVs suppressed IgE-induced STAT5 phosphorylation in activated KU812 mast cells in a concentration-dependent manner.
UCMSC-EVs at concentrations from 1 to 100 μg/mL total protein were not cytotoxic to KU812 mast cells over 24-72 hours, with no significant difference in cell viability across doses.
Lowering extracellular Na+ from 145 to 121 mmol/L caused a stable dilation of the isolated, pressurized rat middle cerebral artery beginning at 15 minutes and persisting to 180 minutes.

Normalizing osmolality with N-methyl-D-glucamine (NMDG) or Tris-HCl while lowering Na+ to 121 mmol/L did not change the magnitude of MCA dilation compared with the hypoosmotic hyponatremic condition, indicating the response depends on Na+ concentration rather than osmolality or Cl- deficit.
Removal of the endothelium abolished the MCA dilation response to 121 mmol/L Na+, indicating the dilation is endothelium-dependent.
Inhibiting NO synthase with L-NAME converted the normal dilatory response of the MCA to hyponatremia into an additional constriction, showing NO synthesis is required for the dilation.
Inhibiting cGMP synthesis with ODQ also converted the hyponatremia-induced dilation into further constriction, implicating the cGMP arm of NO signaling in the dilation.

Blocking the reverse (Ca2+ entry) mode of the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger with 10 µmol/L KB-R7943 abolished the MCA dilation induced by lowering extracellular Na+, indicating that reverse-mode NCX activity mediates this dilation.

A lower dose of KB-R7943 (1 µmol/L) that selectively blocks TRPC channels did not affect the MCA dilation response to hyponatremia, suggesting TRPC channels are not the primary Ca2+ entry route for this response.

Buffering intracellular Ca2+ in endothelial cells with BAPTA-AM did not alter the MCA dilation response to hyponatremia, supporting an extracellular (transmembrane influx) rather than intracellular-store origin of the Ca2+ signal.

Under normal sodium conditions, blocking reverse-mode NCX (and TRPC at lower dose) with KB-R7943 caused dilation of the MCA, indicating that reverse-mode NCX Ca2+ entry (and TRPC channels) contribute to maintenance of basal myogenic tone.
Under normal sodium conditions, chelating intracellular Ca2+ with BAPTA-AM caused constriction of the MCA, indicating baseline intracellular Ca2+ contributes to maintenance of basal vascular tone.
Under normal sodium conditions, NOS inhibition with L-NAME alone constricted the MCA, confirming a tonic NO-dependent dilator influence on basal vessel diameter.
Under normal sodium conditions, cGMP synthesis inhibition with ODQ alone constricted the MCA, confirming tonic cGMP-dependent dilator influence on basal vessel diameter.
Fatigue was reported by most participants (10 of 15) as a reason for limiting general activities.
All participants reported that neuropathic pain in SFN was accompanied by other complaints, mainly symptoms of autonomic dysfunction.
Most participants (13 of 15) reported negative catastrophic thoughts about worsening pain and harmful consequences of activities, leading to avoidance behavior.
Most participants (12 of 15) used structuring/planning of daily activities as a coping strategy to manage pain and avoid symptom flare-ups.
Only a minority of participants (3 of 15) reported full acceptance of SFN and pain, using strategies such as meditation.
Half of participants (9 of 15) reported using distraction, such as focusing on a hobby or daily activity, for pain relief.
More than half of participants (12 of 15) reported fear, including fear of future disability (e.g., becoming wheelchair-dependent) and fear of worsening pain.
Half of participants (8 of 15) reported experiencing stress due to their inability to perform daily or work-related activities.
Among those who reported stress, several participants (3 of 8) also reported frustration related to disability and daily limitations.
A small subset of participants (3 of 15) reported anger stemming from the lack of a cure or effective treatment for SFN.
Most participants (13 of 15) reported a lack of understanding in their social and work environment about SFN, which contributed to loneliness and loss of friendships.
Most participants (13 of 15) reported incomprehension by healthcare providers, which led to avoidance of consultations and loss of trust in physicians.
Most participants (11 of 15) were not currently employed, with more than half having quit their job because of restrictions caused by SFN.
SFN interrupted performance of daily activities in most participants (12 of 15), such as taking a bath, cooking, and cleaning, and social activities in 8 of 12 participants.
Most participants (11 of 15) made lifestyle adaptations such as changing clothing/shoes because of fabric sensitivity or moving to another house to ease physical functioning.
Participants commonly attributed worsening of SFN-related complaints to heavy workload (7 of 15) and work-related stress (6 of 15).
All 15 participants had abnormal temperature thresholds on quantitative sensory testing, while 5 (33.3%) also showed abnormal intra-epidermal nerve fiber density on skin biopsy.
Three patients developed small fiber neuropathy (SFN) following mRNA-based SARS-CoV-2 vaccination (two Pfizer, one Moderna).
Skin punch biopsy in patient 1 revealed reduced intra-epidermal nerve fiber density (IENFD), confirming SFN diagnosis.
Patient 1's SFN symptoms were refractory to initial symptomatic treatment but improved after addition of intravenous immunoglobulins (IVIG).
Patient 2 was diagnosed with SFN via skin punch biopsy after vaccination but her symptoms resolved spontaneously without treatment.
Patient 3's skin punch biopsy confirmed SFN with reduced IENFD, and most of her diverse symptoms resolved upon symptomatic treatment.
The authors propose that post-SARS-CoV-2 vaccination SFN is likely immune-mediated, based on favorable response to IVIG treatment.

A prior case report described a 57-year-old woman who developed burning dysesthesias in the feet and calves one week after her second Pfizer SARS-CoV-2 vaccine dose, consistent with post-vaccination SFN.
IVIG treatment did not produce a significantly greater improvement in intraepidermal nerve fiber density than placebo over 6 months in patients with SFN and TS-HDS/FGFR-3 autoantibodies.
Pain scores improved similarly in both IVIG and placebo groups over 24 weeks, with no significant difference between groups.
Neurologic examination scores (UENS) improved in both groups with no significant difference between IVIG and placebo.
Overall, this pilot RCT did not detect a benefit of IVIG over placebo in patients with small fiber neuropathy associated with TS-HDS and FGFR-3 autoantibodies.
The authors report that MMP3 carried within exosomes can be transferred to recipient cells, translocate into the nucleus, and transactivate the CCN2/CTGF gene.
CCN2 (CTGF) protein induction is described as occurring in response to TGFβ/Smad signaling or the transcriptional activity of MMP3.
TDT-CBT plus standard medical care was not more efficacious than standard medical care alone for the primary outcome (Work and Social Adjustment Scale) at 52-week follow-up.
TDT-CBT plus SMC showed a significant treatment effect compared with SMC alone for WSAS at the end of active treatment (20 weeks).
TDT-CBT plus SMC showed a significant treatment effect compared with SMC alone in reducing symptom severity (PHQ-15) at 52 weeks.
Reductions in catastrophising, measured mid-treatment, were found to be one of the strongest mediators of the TDT-CBT treatment effect on WSAS at the end of treatment.
Improvements (reductions) in symptom focusing, measured mid-treatment, mediated the TDT-CBT treatment effect on WSAS at the end of treatment.
Improvements in symptom focusing mediated the TDT-CBT treatment effect on symptom severity (PHQ-15).
IAA-induced ulcerative colitis caused significant body weight loss and colon edema compared to control rats.
All treatment regimens except low-dose carvedilol (CR15) restored body weight and reduced the colon edema index toward control levels.
Colonic phospho-PS1 (Ser353) protein was increased 2.9-fold in ulcerated rats compared to controls.
Colonic BACE-1 protein was increased 4.1-fold in ulcerated rats compared to controls.
Colonic Aβ(1-42) content was increased 3.2-fold in ulcerated rats compared to controls, indicating colon amyloidosis.
High-dose carvedilol, mirabegron, and the combination regimen markedly reduced PS1 and BACE-1 to non-significant levels versus control, while low-dose carvedilol only partially reduced PS1.
IAA-induced colitis activated the NOTCH1/NICD/HES1 signaling pathway, with 2.3-fold, 6.4-fold, and 3.2-fold increases respectively versus controls.
All single treatment regimens significantly reduced NOTCH1/NICD/HES1, and the combination regimen reduced NICD to a non-significant level versus control, outperforming low-dose carvedilol alone.
Ulcerated rats showed a sharp reduction in mucus-producing goblet cell count compared to controls, consistent with HES1-mediated goblet cell depletion.
Mirabegron treatment increased goblet cell count beyond control levels, with an even stronger effect in the mirabegron+low-dose carvedilol combination group.
Colonic PPAR-γ content was reduced by 32% and inactive phospho-GSK-3β (S9) was reduced by 76% in ulcerated rats, while TNF-α increased 5-fold and MDA increased 3.9-fold versus controls.
All treatments reduced TNF-α and MDA content, but only the mirabegron+carvedilol combination normalized these markers with an additive drug interaction (CDI analysis).
Colonic NF-κB immunoreactivity was strongly increased in ulcerated rats compared to controls, and was best suppressed by mirabegron and the combination regimen.
IAA-induced colitis increased colonic TGF-β1 expression 3.6-fold, driving fibrosis, while the anti-fibrotic marker SMAD-7 was reduced by 76% versus controls.
All treatments partially increased SMAD-7 content, with the combination regimen producing the highest increment (2.8-fold versus the ulcerated group).

Colonic α-SMA immunoreactivity, a downstream fibrotic marker of TGF-β1, was increased in ulcerated and low-dose carvedilol-treated rats, but reduced by high-dose carvedilol, mirabegron, and the combination regimen to a level not significantly different from control.

IAA-induced colitis caused marked collagen fiber deposition in the colon, which was reduced toward normal by mirabegron and the mirabegron+carvedilol combination, showing an additive drug interaction.
IAA-induced colitis increased colonic phospho-β-catenin (Y654) 5.6-fold and reduced E-cadherin content by 59% versus controls, indicating disrupted adherens junction integrity.
Carvedilol at both doses failed to restore colonic E-cadherin content, while mirabegron alone or combined with carvedilol restored it to near-normal levels.

The authors conclude that β-adrenergic receptor modulation via mirabegron and/or carvedilol offers anti-colitic efficacy in the IAA-induced ulcerative colitis model by simultaneously suppressing the PS1/BACE-1/Aβ axis, NOTCH1/NICD/HES1 signaling, GSK-3β/NF-κB/TNF-α inflammation, TGF-β1/α-SMA/SMAD-7 fibrosis, and restoring E-cadherin/β-catenin barrier integrity.
TGFβ treatment of ex vivo skin explants significantly induced COL1A1 (Collagen 1A1) mRNA expression compared with vehicle control at 48 hours.
TGFβ treatment strongly induced FN1 (Fibronectin1) mRNA expression in skin explants at 48 hours relative to vehicle control.
TGFβ treatment significantly induced CTGF (connective tissue growth factor) mRNA expression in skin explants at 48 hours.
ACTA2 (alpha smooth muscle actin) showed an increasing trend with TGFβ treatment at 48 hours but did not reach statistical significance.
Histological assessment showed a significant increase in dermal ECM bundle density in TGFβ-treated skin explants compared to vehicle-treated explants at 120 hours.
Baseline FN1 mRNA expression in untreated skin was significantly higher in breast skin than abdominal skin.
Baseline COL1A1 expression trended higher in abdominal skin compared with breast skin, but the difference was not statistically significant.
The TGFβ-induced fold-change in FN1 expression was significantly higher in abdominal skin than breast skin, opposite to the baseline expression pattern.
TGFβ-induced fold-change in COL1A1 expression was modestly but significantly higher in abdominal skin compared with breast skin.
TGFβ-induced fold-change in ACTA2 expression trended lower in abdominal skin than breast skin, but this did not reach significance.
TGFβ-induced fold-change in CTGF expression showed no difference between breast and abdominal skin.
The magnitude of TGFβ-induced FN1 fold-change expression showed a significant positive correlation with donor age, unlike COL1A1, CTGF, or ACTA2.
No significant correlation was found between donor age and baseline expression of FN1, COL1A1, CTGF, or ACTA2.
Baseline FN1 expression was significantly inversely correlated with the magnitude of the TGFβ-induced fibrotic response, suggesting low baseline expression predicts a stronger fibrotic response.
Baseline COL1A1 expression was significantly inversely correlated with the magnitude of the TGFβ-induced fibrotic response.
Baseline ACTA2 expression was significantly inversely correlated with the magnitude of the TGFβ-induced fibrotic response; this correlation was also significant specifically within abdominal skin.
Unlike FN1, COL1A1, and ACTA2, CTGF baseline expression did not show a significant inverse correlation with its TGFβ-induced fibrotic response.

Pooled analysis across breast and abdominal tissue showed FN1 baseline expression was significantly lower than COL1A1 and ACTA2, while its TGFβ-induced fold-change was significantly higher than that of COL1A1 or ACTA2, supporting an inverse relationship between baseline and induced expression.

The modified consistency diet with rapid-acting insulin produced a smaller postprandial rise in interstitial glucose than the standard consistency diet with insulin, with glucose returning close to baseline by 4 hours.
Patients had significantly lower Gastroparesis Cardinal Symptom Index (GCSI) scores after the modified consistency diet with insulin compared to the standard diet with insulin.
Specific GCSI symptom items — inability to finish a meal, loss of appetite, and feeling that the stomach/belly is enlarged — decreased with the modified consistency diet.
After 6 weeks, patients receiving slow, deep breathing (SDB) had significantly lower total IBS-SSS symptom severity scores than controls.
At week 3, the abdominal pain intensity subscore was significantly higher (worse) in the control group than in the SDB group.
By week 6, stool consistency (BSFS score) was significantly improved (higher/softer) in the SDB group compared with controls.
Weekly frequency of spontaneous bowel movements was significantly increased in the SDB group compared with controls at week 6.
Weekly frequency of complete spontaneous bowel movements was significantly increased in the SDB group compared with controls at week 6.
Maximum tolerable rectal balloon distension volume was significantly higher in the SDB group than controls at week 3 and week 6.
Threshold volume for first rectal sensation was significantly higher in the SDB group compared with controls at week 6.
Threshold volume for desire to defecate was significantly higher in the SDB group compared with controls at week 6.
RAIR threshold volume did not differ between SDB and control groups at either week 3 or week 6.
Threshold volume for urge to defecate did not differ significantly between the SDB and control groups at week 3 or week 6.
Corrected high-frequency HRV power, reflecting parasympathetic/vagal activity, was significantly higher in the SDB group than controls at weeks 3 and 6.
Sympathetic activity (Baevsky Index) did not differ significantly between SDB and control groups at week 3 or week 6.
SDNN, a time-domain HRV measure of overall autonomic variability, was significantly higher in the SDB group than controls at weeks 3 and 6.
RMSSD, a time-domain HRV measure of parasympathetic/vagal activity, was significantly higher in the SDB group than controls at weeks 3 and 6.

A substantial subset of IBS-C patients had rectal sensory threshold volumes (first sensation, desire to defecate, urge to defecate, maximum tolerable volume) outside normal reference ranges at baseline, indicating altered visceral sensitivity.
Synbiotic supplementation for 12 weeks significantly increased the proportion of Treg cells compared to baseline, with a significant between-group difference versus placebo.
FoxP3 gene expression significantly increased from baseline in the synbiotic group, with a significant between-group difference versus placebo.

IL-10 gene expression significantly increased from baseline in the synbiotic group, with a significant between-group difference versus placebo, though serum IL-10 protein levels did not differ significantly between groups.

TGF-β gene expression significantly increased from baseline in the synbiotic group, with a significant between-group difference, though serum TGF-β protein levels did not differ significantly between groups.
miRNA-146a gene expression significantly increased from baseline in the synbiotic group, with a significant between-group difference versus placebo.
miRNA-25 gene expression significantly decreased from baseline in the synbiotic group, with a significant between-group difference versus placebo.
Serum TGF-beta levels significantly increased from baseline after 12 weeks of synbiotic supplementation.
Gene expression of miRNA-25 significantly decreased from baseline after 12 weeks of synbiotic supplementation.
Gene expression of miRNA-106b significantly decreased from baseline after 12 weeks of synbiotic supplementation.
The proportion of Treg cells differed significantly between the synbiotic and placebo groups after the trial.
FoxP3 gene expression differed significantly between the synbiotic and placebo groups after the trial.
IL-10 gene expression differed significantly between the synbiotic and placebo groups after the trial.
TGF-beta gene expression differed significantly between the synbiotic and placebo groups after the trial.
The gene expression of miRNA-25 was significantly lower in the synbiotic group compared with the placebo group after treatment.
The gene expression of miRNA-106b was significantly lower in the synbiotic group compared with the placebo group after treatment.
The gene expression of miRNA-146a was significantly higher in the synbiotic group compared with the placebo group after treatment.
Serum IL-10 levels did not differ significantly between the synbiotic and placebo groups.
Serum TGF-β levels did not differ significantly between the synbiotic and placebo groups.
Overall, synbiotic supplementation modulated the Treg cell response in axSpA patients and is suggested as a promising adjunctive therapy, pending further investigation.
A single session of device-guided slow breathing acutely increased baroreflex sensitivity in both normotensive and hypertensive adults.
Long-term device-guided slow breathing (4 weeks to 3 months) did not produce sustained improvements in baroreflex sensitivity.
Device-guided slow breathing acutely reduced muscle sympathetic nerve activity in both normotensive and hypertensive adults.
Long-term device-guided slow breathing studies showed inconsistent effects on muscle sympathetic nerve activity.
Vagally mediated components of heart rate variability increased with slow breathing in some studies, but acute versus long-term results were incongruent overall.
Non-device-guided slow breathing reduced arterial stiffness in adults with type I diabetes.
Non-device-guided slow breathing increased microvascular endothelial function in adults with irritable bowel syndrome.
Non-device-guided slow breathing increased microvascular endothelial function in adults with irritable bowel syndrome in acute and chronic studies.
Across the reviewed trials of device-guided and non-device-guided slow breathing, no adverse effects or non-adherence to treatment were reported.

A 47-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes and severe diabetic gastroparesis (gastric pacemaker, then J-tube) presented with a seizure caused by severe hypoglycemia (glucose 27 mg/dl) related to intolerance of tube feeds.

Patients with diabetic autonomic neuropathy tend to have hypoglycemic unawareness and hypoglycemic autonomic failure, blunting the normal counter-regulatory response and increasing risk of severe hypoglycemia.

Approximately 25-29% of patients with gastroparesis have underlying diabetes mellitus as a major contributing factor, and 4.8% of type 1 diabetics carry a gastroparesis diagnosis (likely underestimated).
In individuals with gastroparesis, the prokinetic hormone motilin has been noted to be low, which is part of the rationale for using macrolides such as erythromycin as prokinetic treatment.

Patients with gastroparesis have been found to have lower stem cell factor (SCF) and interstitial cells of Cajal, causing deficits in smooth muscle 'pacemaker' cells of the stomach and resulting in antral hypomotility and atrium-duodenum-pylorus desynchrony.
In one study, 44 of 54 patients reported more difficulty controlling glucose levels after being diagnosed with gastroparesis, with the effect more pronounced in type 1 than type 2 diabetics.
Another study found hypoglycemia was reported in 25% of patients with gastroparesis compared to 11% of patients with diabetes mellitus but no gastroparesis.
Risk factors increasing the likelihood of developing gastroparesis include older age, lower socioeconomic status, longer duration of diabetes mellitus, and higher hemoglobin A1c.
Gastroparesis was found to be more prevalent in females than males (5.8% vs. 3.5%).
Insulin pumps were shown to be a protective factor against the development of gastroparesis.

Gastric pacemakers (gastric electrical stimulation) used in refractory gastroparesis have shown symptom improvement in double-blind and many open-label studies, though not all open-label studies showed benefit and surgical risks must be weighed.
One study found that only 1.2% of patients presenting with seizures were found to be hypoglycemic (glucose <60), suggesting hypoglycemia-induced seizures are relatively rare.
A study of 156 ICU patients with severe hypoglycemia (<45 mg/dl) found only one patient developed a resultant epileptic seizure.

Switching the patient's tube feed formula to a peptide-based formula (Vital) improved feed tolerance, allowing her to reach her goal of 15 hours per day of feeds with subsequent improvement in glycemic control.
Hyperglycemia may decrease the seizure threshold partially due to an increase in GABA metabolism and subsequent low GABA levels.

Using endoscopic confocal laser endomicroscopy, 24 of 85 patients (28%) with functional gastrointestinal symptoms and food intolerance showed spontaneous transfer of intravenous fluorescein into the duodenal lumen, indicating leaky gut syndrome (LGS).

The proportion of patients showing spontaneous fluorescein leakage (LGS) varied by functional GI symptom subgroup, being highest in functional abdominal bloating (50%) and lowest in IBS and FAP (~28-33%), though this was descriptive rather than a formally significant difference.

Blood markers of mast cell function, duodenal mucosal inflammation, intraepithelial lymphocyte counts, and mast cell number/distribution/morphology did not differ significantly between LGS-positive and LGS-negative patient subgroups.
Fibroblasts treated with TGF-β1-overexpressing hDPSC secretome showed increased CD44 gene and protein expression compared to control secretome-treated fibroblasts.
Proteomic and western blot analyses indicated that activation of the canonical TGF-β1/Smad pathway upregulates CD44 expression in fibroblasts.
Smad pathway-mediated CD44 upregulation was associated with increased mitotic activity, proliferation, and wound healing potential in fibroblasts treated with TGF-β1 secretome.
Proteomic comparison identified 174 proteins common to both control and TGF-β1 secretomes, with 140 proteins unique to control secretome and 66 proteins unique to TGF-β1 secretome.

A confirmatory factor analysis supported a three-factor structure of the new Long Covid Stigma Scale (LCSS) comprising enacted, internalised and anticipated stigma domains, with good model fit in the full UK sample and both diagnosis subgroups.
The three stigma domains were strongly and significantly correlated with each other, with the strongest correlation between anticipated and enacted stigma.
Internal consistency of the LCSS subscales was good, with Cronbach's alpha of 0.82 for anticipated, 0.88 for enacted, and 0.86 for internalised stigma.
Concurrent criterion validity was supported: overall LCSS score and its three subscales were consistently positively associated with depressive symptoms (PHQ-8) and disclosure concerns.
Almost all respondents reported experiencing some form of Long Covid stigma at least 'sometimes', with 95.4% overall prevalence.
Enacted stigma (overt discrimination) was reported by 62.7% of respondents at least 'sometimes', and by 25.3% 'often' or 'always', the lowest prevalence among the three domains.
Internalised stigma (self-shame/worthlessness) was reported by 86.4% of respondents at least 'sometimes' and 59.7% 'often' or 'always'.
Anticipated stigma (expectation of bias) was the most frequently reported domain, with 90.8% of respondents reporting it at least 'sometimes' and 59.0% 'often' or 'always'.
People with a clinical diagnosis of Long Covid had higher prevalence of overall and all three stigma subtypes than those without a clinical diagnosis, using both prevalence estimates.
The majority of respondents reported being careful about disclosing their Long Covid status, and a third reported regretting having disclosed it to some people, at least 'sometimes'.
Black patients with ME/CFS reported significantly higher chest pain severity than White patients with ME/CFS, the only symptom item that significantly differentiated the two ME/CFS groups.

Despite directional trends, Black patients with ME/CFS showed directionally higher symptom scores on 27 symptoms across four domains (Neurocognitive, Neuroendocrine, Pain, Orthostatic), while White patients with ME/CFS showed directionally higher scores on 21 symptoms across three domains (Sleep, PEM, Immune), though only one item reached statistical significance.
Black patients with ME/CFS scored significantly higher than Black healthy controls on 19 of 49 symptom items across five domains (Sleep, PEM, Neurocognitive, Pain, and Orthostatic).

Black patients with ME/CFS scored significantly higher than White healthy controls on 27 of 49 symptom items across six of seven domains (all except Immune), more items and domains than seen versus Black controls.
White patients with ME/CFS scored significantly higher than Black healthy controls on only 13 of 49 symptom items across three domains (Sleep, PEM, and Orthostatic).
White patients with ME/CFS scored significantly higher than White healthy controls on 21 of 49 symptom items across six of seven domains (all but Immune).

Among the two healthy control groups, Black controls had directionally worse symptom scores than White controls on 40 of 49 items and six of seven domains, whereas White controls were directionally worse on only nine items and one domain, suggesting greater baseline symptom burden in Black individuals independent of ME/CFS status.
At baseline, tissue sodium content in lower leg muscles was higher in ME/CFS patients than in healthy controls across all five muscle compartments, most strongly in the anterior extensor muscles.

After exercise, tissue sodium content increased in exercised muscles in both groups but was significantly higher in ME/CFS than controls at all 8 measured time points during the 40-minute recovery period.
The decline of sodium content after peak exercise levels was slower in ME/CFS than controls in medial gastrocnemius, indicating delayed recovery of sodium homeostasis.
No difference in tissue water content between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls was detected in any muscle compartment at any time point, before or after exercise.
ME/CFS patients showed markedly reduced maximal and mean handgrip strength compared to healthy controls, both initially and after a 60-minute recovery period.
The recovery rate of handgrip strength between the two sessions was lower in ME/CFS patients, whereas healthy controls maintained similar mean handgrip strength across sessions.
Baseline tissue sodium content in lower leg muscles was inversely correlated with initial handgrip strength across all study subjects.
Post-exercise average tissue sodium content in lower leg muscles was inversely correlated with handgrip strength measured after a 60-minute recovery period.
All patients with ME/CFS reported post-exertional malaise following the standardized exercise protocol, whereas controls experienced painful sore muscles for two days but not PEM.

The authors propose that increased NHE1 activity (sodium-proton exchanger) combined with diminished Na+/K+-ATPase activity and reversal of the sodium-calcium exchanger (NCX) to import calcium underlies elevated intramuscular sodium and subsequent calcium overload in ME/CFS.
The estimated prevalence of confirmed severe ME/CFS seen by specialist paediatric services in the UK and Ireland was 3.2 per million children aged 5-16 years.
The incidence rate of severe ME/CFS across the UK and Ireland was 0.90 per million children-years.
When including probable and possible severe ME/CFS cases alongside confirmed cases, prevalence rose to 8.9 per million children.
Incidence including possible and probable severe ME/CFS cases was 1.97 per million children-years.
Most children with severe ME/CFS were not receiving any education provision, with 20 of 33 (63%) receiving no tuition of any kind in the 6 weeks preceding assessment.
Children with severe ME/CFS had a shorter median time from first symptom onset to diagnosis (0.47 years) compared with previously reported cohorts of less severe disease.
Cognitive impairment (impaired memory or concentration), postexertional malaise, and unrefreshing sleep were near-universal symptoms in children with severe ME/CFS.

There was no significant difference in the number of female versus male children and young people confirmed with severe ME/CFS, though overall female proportion (55%) was lower than the 60-65% reported in prior adolescent ME/CFS studies.
The vast majority of confirmed severe ME/CFS cases were white (97%, 32/33), raising the possibility of diagnostic barriers for non-white patients.
Most children with severe ME/CFS required at least some help with activities of daily living, with 13% needing help with all ADLs and 81% requiring some help sometimes.
Peak age of onset for severe ME/CFS was 13-15 years, with median age at diagnosis 13 years, median age of first fatigue 12 years, and median age of becoming housebound 13 years.
Sustained attention deficits on the TP-R test were detected in 83.3% of ME/CFS patients versus 56.2% of post-COVID-19 patients, with ME/CFS patients being more affected.
ME/CFS patients had significantly lower composite attention Z-scores than post-COVID-19 patients.
ME/CFS patients had significantly lower visuospatial ability Z-scores than post-COVID-19 patients.
ME/CFS patients perceived significantly more physical limitations than post-COVID-19 patients on the SF-36.
ME/CFS patients reported significantly lower energy levels than post-COVID-19 patients on the SF-36.
ME/CFS patients had poorer mental health scores than post-COVID-19 patients on the SF-36.
ME/CFS patients reported significantly greater impact of health on social interactions than post-COVID-19 patients.
ME/CFS patients had a significantly worse general health perception than post-COVID-19 patients.
ME/CFS patients had significantly greater trait anxiety than post-COVID-19 patients.
ME/CFS patients had significantly more depressive symptoms than post-COVID-19 patients.
ME/CFS patients had significantly greater suicidal ideation than post-COVID-19 patients.

The frequency of abdominal pain, contractions, instability/balance problems, dizziness/fainting, weight change, sweaty hands, hot/cold sensations and sore throat differed significantly between groups, being more frequent in ME/CFS.

The severity of unrefreshing sleep, bloating, abdominal pain, contractions, muscle weakness, attention difficulty, depth perception problems, nausea, instability, dizziness, weight change, sweaty hands, temperature sensation, flu-like symptoms and odor discomfort differed significantly between groups, generally more severe in ME/CFS.
The proportion of women differed significantly between groups, with 92.9% of ME/CFS patients and 69.9% of post-COVID-19 patients being female.
Within the post-COVID-19 group, patients probably infected with the 20E (EU1) variant had significantly worse mental health (SF-36) than those probably infected with the SEC8 variant.
In post-COVID-19 patients, olfactory test scores (BSIT) correlated with general cognition, processing speed, verbal memory, visual memory, attention and visuospatial ability.

Post-COVID-19 patients with abnormal BSIT results performed significantly worse on general cognition, attention, verbal memory, visual memory, visuospatial perception and abstraction than those with normal BSIT results.
In post-COVID-19 patients, education level explained the highest percentage of variance in cognitive performance across several tests.
