Physical problems (SF-36) explained substantial variance in attention (Stroop, TMT-A) and visual processing speed (SPCT) in post-COVID-19 patients.
Pain (SF-36) explained variance in sustained attention errors and impulsivity control in post-COVID-19 patients.
Fatigue (MFIS) and emotional-problem limitation (SF-36) explained variance in visual recognition, visual memory, verbal fluency and visuoconstructive capacity in post-COVID-19 patients.

In post-COVID-19 patients, sleep quality explained variance in executive function, anxiety explained variance in sustained attention and general cognition, and suicidal ideation explained variance in visual perception.
In ME/CFS patients, energy/fatigue (SF-36) explained 28.6% of the variance of sustained attention errors (TP-R).
In ME/CFS patients, sleep quality (PSQI) explained 20.8% of the variance of semantic verbal fluency (animals).
In ME/CFS patients, state anxiety (STAI) explained 28.6% of variance in executive function (M-WCST perseverative errors).
At least one in ten symptomatic COVID-19 patients develop Long COVID-19.

Redox imbalance, mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress pathways are implicated in ME/CFS and are also found in Long COVID-19, suggesting shared pathophysiological features between the two conditions.

The authors propose subgrouping Long COVID-19 patients into two clinical phenotypes: post-COVID-19 fatigue syndrome (PCFS) in previously mild/outpatient cases resembling ME/CFS, and post-acute COVID-19 syndrome (PACS) in previously hospitalised (ICU or non-ICU) cases.

A multidisciplinary treatment programme combining symptom-based pharmacological treatment, education, physical exercise, and cognitive behavioural therapy, which has high-grade evidence in ME/CFS, is suggested to be potentially effective if implemented for Long COVID-19 patients.

Female sex, type A personality, and family aggregation are established predisposing factors for ME/CFS, while infectious agents (human herpesvirus family), toxicity exposure, and psychosocial experience are precipitating/trigger factors.

ICU-related post-acute COVID-19 syndrome (ICU-PACS) should be differentiated from post-intensive care syndrome (PICS), though symptoms of both may relate to immunology alterations, vasculitis involvement, adverse therapy effects, prolonged immobilisation, and mitochondrial dysfunction.
Patients diagnosed with ME/CFS reported significantly worse physical role functioning on the RAND-36 compared to patients with similar symptoms but no ME/CFS diagnosis.
The ME/CFS diagnosed group reported significantly lower vitality/energy (fatigue) scores on the RAND-36 compared to the undiagnosed group.
Social functioning scores on the RAND-36 were significantly lower in the ME/CFS diagnosed group than in the undiagnosed group.

The ME/CFS diagnosed group reported significantly worse (higher) bodily pain scores relative to the undiagnosed group, though noted RAND-36 scoring means higher = better health, so this reflects worse pain outcome (lower score on the pain subscale reflecting more pain).
General health perceptions on the RAND-36 were significantly lower in the ME/CFS diagnosed group compared to the undiagnosed group.
No significant difference in self-reported weekly physical activity minutes was found between the ME/CFS diagnosed and undiagnosed groups.
Work ability (WAI single-item score) did not significantly differ between the ME/CFS diagnosed and undiagnosed groups.
Anxiety and depression scores (HADS) did not significantly differ between the ME/CFS diagnosed and undiagnosed groups.
RAND-36 emotional role limitations and emotional well-being subscales showed no significant differences between the ME/CFS diagnosed and undiagnosed groups.
Overly elastic connective tissue phenotype (hypermobility) is reported to be overrepresented among individuals with ME/CFS and is often accompanied by decreased interoceptive ability.
The authors hypothesize that chronic physiological stress from activity-recovery imbalance may lead to secondary dysautonomia in ME/CFS.
Approximately 10% of adults who survive an initial COVID-19 episode go on to develop long-term clinical manifestations known as post-acute COVID-19 syndrome (PACS).

The authors note that the symptom constellation of PACS closely resembles that previously described for myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS), suggesting overlapping pathophysiology.
The risk of developing PACS is stated to be higher in women than in men.
The review proposes that host genetic factors may additionally contribute to susceptibility to PACS.

PACS is characterized by dysregulation across multiple body systems, including the immune system, coagulation cascade, endocrine organs, autonomic nervous system, microbiota-gut-brain axis, hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, and hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis.

The authors hypothesize that an abnormal host response to certain infectious agents (not limited to SARS-CoV-2) could trigger the development of post-infectious fatigue syndromes such as ME/CFS and PACS.
A machine learning model using 60 functional connectivity features filtered from whole-brain fMRI data significantly distinguished CFS patients from healthy controls before intervention.
After the one-month Tai Chi intervention, the same predictive model lost its ability to distinguish CFS patients from healthy controls, suggesting normalization of brain connectivity differences.
Fatigue Scale-14 (FS-14) scores decreased significantly in CFS patients after Tai Chi exercise, indicating reduced fatigue.

Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) scores (indicating better sleep quality, i.e., lower scores) improved significantly in both CFS and HC groups after Tai Chi, with a significant group-by-time interaction showing greater improvement in CFS.
SF-36 health survey scores improved significantly in both CFS and HC groups after Tai Chi, with a significantly greater improvement in the CFS group.
Before intervention, functional connectivity involving the default mode network (DMN) was significantly lower in CFS patients compared to healthy controls.
After Tai Chi exercise, DMN functional connectivity increased significantly in the CFS group, eliminating the pre-existing difference from healthy controls.
Before intervention, the left frontoparietal network (FPN) functional connectivity was significantly lower in CFS patients compared with healthy controls.
After Tai Chi exercise, left FPN connectivity increased significantly in the CFS group, eliminating the difference from healthy controls.

The functional connection ROI 363-238 (linking DMN and somatomotor network) was the most important feature for distinguishing CFS from HC, correlated positively with sleep quality impairment, and increased significantly after Tai Chi in the CFS group.
Changes in left FPN connectivity following Tai Chi were significantly positively correlated with changes in DMN connectivity in the CFS group.
Changes in left FPN connectivity showed a moderate negative correlation with changes in SF-36 health scores, though not significant after multiple-comparison correction.

Patients with overstrain, burnout, or panic disorder showed patterns suggesting an overactive respiratory system, proposed as a shared transdiagnostic mechanism across these stress-related conditions.

Patients with fibromyalgia and/or chronic fatigue syndrome exhibited a less active respiratory fight-flight response compared to the stress-related syndrome groups, consistent with these being more chronic and severe functional conditions.

Patients with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome are at increased risk for obstructive sleep apnea due to upper airway tissue laxity, nasal-maxillary cartilaginous defects, scoliosis, and other structural abnormalities.
A patient with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and obstructive sleep apnea who failed continuous positive airway pressure therapy was successfully treated using hypoglossal nerve stimulation.
Continuous positive airway pressure therapy failed in this patient with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and obstructive sleep apnea, prompting the switch to hypoglossal nerve stimulation.
Greater functional disability was associated with greater mental health challenges (anxiety and depression) in youth with hEDS.
Perceived social support was independently associated with mental health outcomes in youth with hEDS.
Social support did not moderate the relationship between functional disability and mental health in pediatric hEDS, contrary to the study's hypothesis.
Exploratory analyses examined the influence of gender on mental health outcomes in pediatric hEDS, providing groundwork for future study but without definitive conclusions reported.
The patient showed polyarticular joint hypermobility with a Beighton score of 8/9, supporting a clinical diagnosis of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

EDS was clinically diagnosed based on hypermobility, scoliosis, history of patellar dislocation and family history of joint hypermobility, without biochemical or molecular genetic confirmation because the patient declined testing.

Dislocation of the proximal tibiofibular joint (PTFJ), likely due to EDS-related connective tissue laxity, caused posterolateral dysplasia of the lateral tibial condyle because the fibula normally acts as a supporting strut for that region.

Combined posterolateral open-wedge high tibial osteotomy (PLOWHTO) and medial closed-wedge distal femoral osteotomy (MCWDFO) corrected the severe valgus deformity, restoring the weight-bearing line ratio from 130% to 51% postoperatively.
Surgical correction reduced the mechanical lateral distal femoral angle (mLDFA) and mechanical medial proximal tibial angle (mMPTA) toward normal reference ranges.
Surgery reduced the steep lateral tibial posterior slope angle from 17° preoperatively to 11° postoperatively, targeting a planned slope of around 10° to prevent further knee hyperextension.

At 2-year follow-up, the patient showed significant improvement in Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS), exceeding the minimal clinically important difference for all subscales except the symptom subscale.
Peroneal nerve neurolysis prior to fibular osteotomy is necessary in PLOWHTO to prevent mechanical stretching-related peroneal nerve palsy or ischaemia during posterolateral opening.

Fibular osteotomy for PLOWHTO must be performed just below the fibular head rather than at the midportion, because the crural interosseous membrane otherwise prevents proximal fibular migration needed to open the posterolateral gap.

In PLOWHTO, unlike medial OWHTO where the intact PTFJ or medial collateral ligament stabilises the osteotomy site after a hinge fracture, there is no medial stabilising structure, so temporary anteromedial plate fixation before posterolateral opening is necessary to prevent instability.

The authors note special surgical care is needed in EDS patients compared to other syndromic knee dysplasias (Blount disease, Turner syndrome, Ellis-van Creveld syndrome) due to the fragility of skin and blood vessels from systemic connective tissue fragility, requiring gentle retraction, careful haemostasis, separate incisions, and a non-tourniquet technique with strict blood pressure control (<100 mmHg).
Historically used medications and surgery for pain in EDS patients have shown low efficacy.
Physical/occupational therapy is described as a newer therapy showing promising effects for decreasing pain and increasing quality of life in EDS patients.
Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) units are cited as a promising newer therapy for pain and quality of life in EDS.
Trigger point injections are described as a promising treatment for decreasing pain and increasing quality of life in EDS.
Low-dose naltrexone is cited as a promising newer therapy for decreasing pain and increasing quality of life in EDS patients.
Laser therapy is cited as a promising newer therapy for decreasing pain and increasing quality of life in EDS patients.
Addressing psychosocial aspects of pain through cognitive behavioral therapy and patient education is described as vital in minimizing pain in EDS patients.
Comprehensive pain management in EDS should target not only pain reduction but also hypermobility symptoms, central sensitization, and fatigue.

All four EDS patients showed history and/or stroboscopy findings of vocal hyperfunction, suspected to result from EDS-related hypermobility of the cricoarytenoid joint or fragility of the superficial lamina propria.
Two of the four EDS patients had respiratory symptoms, one with respiratory muscle weakness and sensation loss and one with inducible laryngeal obstruction.
All four EDS patients treated with voice therapy showed subsequent improvement in their symptoms of dysphonia or dyspnea.
A novel de novo heterozygous COL5A2 variant c.3617G>A predicting p.Gly1206Glu was identified in a patient with classical EDS, located within a triple helix domain of type V collagen.

The patient exhibited severe kyphoscoliosis but lacked atrophic scarring and marked skin hyperextensibility, the classical major diagnostic criteria for cEDS, which initially led to a misdiagnosis of kyphoscoliotic EDS.
The patient presented with bilateral keratoglobus and extremely reduced corneal pachymetry along with mild myopia and astigmatism, an ocular manifestation of connective tissue fragility.
Echocardiography revealed mitral valve prolapse, and later follow-up detected mild tricuspid valve regurgitation, indicating cardiac connective tissue involvement.
The patient had generalized joint hypermobility with a Beighton score of 7/9.
A prior cohort study of 168 patients with classical EDS found a higher occurrence of mild-to-severe scoliosis among individuals carrying COL5A2 variants compared to those with COL5A1 variants.
The patient developed restrictive lung disease secondary to severe kyphoscoliosis, with forced vital capacity of 51% at age 14, ultimately requiring home ventilation for pulmonary rehabilitation.

3D modeling demonstrated that substitution of glycine for glutamic acid at position 1206 is structurally incompatible with the triple helix conformation of the collagen α2(V) chain, providing a molecular mechanism for pathogenicity.
Vascular Ehlers Danlos syndrome (vEDS) presents with a recognisable dysmorphic phenotype in both children and adults and is primarily caused by variants in the COL3A1 gene.
Variants in COL1A1 can produce a vEDS-like phenotype, suggesting overlap with other EDS subtypes and the need for gene testing to distinguish them.
Variants in COL25A1 are noted as another gene that can present with vEDS-like features, relevant to differential diagnosis via gene testing.

Genetic testing revealed a heterozygous B4GALT7 sequence variant (c.441G>A, Gly441Ala), not previously reported in databases or literature, suggested to activate a cryptic donor splice site, confirming a diagnosis of spondylodysplastic EDS.
Despite clinical and biochemical features consistent with hypophosphatasia, genetic testing did not identify an ALPL gene sequence variation in the patient.
The patient had chronically low serum alkaline phosphatase levels (27 U/L then 23 U/L, reference 31-125 U/L) consistent with hypophosphatasia.
The patient had an elevated vitamin B6 level of 24.4 ng/mL (reference 2.1-21.7 ng/mL), supporting a clinical diagnosis of hypophosphatasia.
The patient displayed piezogenic papules on the medial aspects of both heels, a rare finding described in existing literature as associated with EDS.

Dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry showed bone density within expected range for age (z-scores +0.2 to +1.5) and a low 10-year major osteoporotic fracture risk of 1.7%, despite the patient's hypophosphatasia and spEDS diagnoses.

The patient's sister and nephew are undergoing evaluation for a different EDS subtype after a confirmed ZNF423 sequence variation, indicating a broader familial burden of connective tissue disorder variants.

Multiple family members (father, sister, mother, and two daughters) shared features and/or low ALP levels consistent with HPP and/or EDS, supporting a heritable and non-coincidental co-occurrence of the two disorders in this family.

The authors suggest that asfotase alfa (enzyme replacement therapy for HPP, FDA-approved only for infantile/juvenile onset) could be considered for adult patients with clinical HPP diagnoses and may also improve comorbid spEDS musculoskeletal symptoms, though it was not administered to this patient.
Bisphosphonates and high-dose vitamin D/calcium supplementation, common mistaken treatments given HPP misdiagnosis, are noted in the literature to potentially worsen HPP symptoms.
Across included studies, the prevalence of concomitant diagnosis of hEDS/HSD and fibromyalgia syndrome ranged from 68% to 88.9%.
The prevalence of concomitant diagnosis of Generalized Joint Hypermobility (GJH) and fibromyalgia syndrome ranged from 8.0% to 64.2% across included studies.

hEDS/HSD and fibromyalgia patients showed similar prevalence and severity of joint pain, joint swelling, muscle weakness, neurological problems, multidimensional pain inventory-activity, function, and quality of life measures.

Dysautonomia and total autonomic symptom burden, including orthostatic intolerance, reflex syncope, vasomotor, gastrointestinal, diarrhea, constipation, and pupillomotor domains, were similarly prevalent and severe in hEDS/HSD and fibromyalgia syndrome patients.
Generalized joint hypermobility and fibromyalgia syndrome shared similar mean pain level, tender points count, total myalgia score, and psychological impact.
A patient with Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome Type VI developed an acute intraoperative subgaleal hematoma during vitreoretinal surgery.

The paper reports a single patient presenting with the coexistence of two distinct rare genetic disorders: spinocerebellar ataxia autosomal recessive type 21 (SCAR21) and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome spondylodysplastic type 3.
Sanger sequencing identified a novel heterozygous 18-bp in-frame duplication in COL3A1 in the patient, classified as a Variant of Unknown Significance.
Unlike most pathogenic vEDS variants that disrupt the Gly-X-Y triplet register, this 18-bp duplication preserved the common collagen [Gly-X-Y] motif.
cDNA sequencing of fibroblast mRNA from the patient showed no splicing anomaly at the exon 33-34 boundary, with normal transcription of exon 34 on both alleles.

Procollagen electrophoresis of cultured skin fibroblasts showed the patient's collagen III expression at an intermediate level between a normal control and a vEDS disease control, indicating a deficiency.
TEM of collagenous bundles from the patient's skin showed structural abnormalities compared with normal control, but the degree of size variability was less than in the vEDS disease control.
Unlike the vEDS disease control, which showed dilated ER on TEM consistent with ER stress, the patient's fibroblasts showed no noticeable ER expansion.

Real-time RT-PCR showed ATF6 and CHOP (unfolded protein response markers) were elevated in the vEDS disease control relative to normal control, but were expressed at near-normal levels in the patient's fibroblasts.
The patient exhibited mild small joint hypermobility and acrogeria but lacked classic vEDS facial features, subcutaneous vessel visibility, or skin hyperextensibility.
The patient presented at age 58 with multiple intra-abdominal aneurysms and altered consciousness, an atypically late onset for a first major vEDS vascular complication.
The patient's antihypertensive drug was switched to celiprolol, and no serious complications occurred during the subsequent 8 years of follow-up.

The authors note a previously reported patient with a 9-bp in-frame COL3A1 deletion not affecting the Gly-X-Y repeat, who similarly showed a mild vEDS phenotype, supporting a possible pattern for in-frame mutations in multiples of nine that preserve the repeat.

Prior epidemiological literature cited by the authors indicates that vEDS patients with nonsense COL3A1 mutations (causing haploinsufficiency rather than a dominant-negative effect) display a milder phenotype than those with Gly-substitution or splice-site mutations.

Whole exome sequencing identified a heterozygous missense TGFB2 variant, c.439C>T p.(Pro147Ser) in exon 3, classified as a variant of uncertain significance, consistent with Loeys-Dietz syndrome type 4.
The patient presented with recurrent lower GI bleeding caused by markedly tortuous, dilated colonic, hemorrhoidal, and mesenteric vasculature.
CT imaging revealed segmental pulmonary thromboembolism with bilateral pulmonary infarctions and multiple abdominal vascular anomalies including portal vein atresia and venous shunting.
The patient had a markedly elevated D-dimer level of 10000 μg/mL against a normal reference of less than 0.5 μg/mL.
The patient had low serum albumin at 3.1 mg/dL.
Imaging revealed portal vein atresia with hepatic arteries not readily identified, along with an anomalous mesenteric-to-colonic venous shunt.
A second angiography identified at least three additional aneurysmatic lesions in the splenic artery, requiring coil embolization to control bleeding.

Therapeutic enoxaparin anticoagulation was started for pulmonary embolism but had to be paused for ~72 hours due to worsening GI bleeding and grade 3 anemia, then heparin infusion was resumed after thrombectomy.
Angiographic embolization of the left mesenteric vein and right colonic vein immediately stopped the patient's lower GI bleeding.

TGFB2 plays a role in chondrocyte maturation and endochondral ossification, being expressed by chondrocytes during late-stage hypertrophic differentiation, and contributes to bone remodeling, osteoblast survival, and collagen interaction.
Prior reports have described a marked association between low expression of TGFB2 and hip dysplasia.

Histologic analyses showed overabundance of aortic wall collagen (including TGF-β target genes COL1A1 and COL3A1) in TGFBR2-mutant/Marfan aortas compared to age-matched controls, indicating increased rather than decreased TGF-β signaling.
Prior case series report that approximately 55%-60% of LDS patients have aneurysmal disease beyond the ascending aorta, with reported late mortality of 9% and 14%.
Individuals with LDS types 1 and 2 predominantly show vascular features leading to critical aortic dissection and large aortic aneurysms, with early death reported at a median age of 37 years.

The authors argue that suspected LDS (here LDS type 4) should still be considered part of the LDS spectrum even in patients without aortic aneurysm, as this patient's presentation lacked aortic aneurysm despite a TGFB2 variant.
The patient had recently been diagnosed with polycystic ovary syndrome and had started hormonal contraceptives five months prior to her presentation with thromboembolic and bleeding events.
The Beighton Score showed the best agreement between in-person and telehealth modes among the three scales, with fair exact agreement and good agreement within two points.
The ULHAT total score showed poor exact agreement but excellent agreement within two points between in-person and telehealth assessments.
The LLAS total score showed poor exact agreement and only fair agreement within two points between in-person and telehealth assessments.

Total scores for all three hypermobility scales showed wide limits of agreement, large smallest detectable change (25-31%), and only fair-to-good reliability (ICC = 0.54-0.61) between in-person and telehealth modes.
Classification of Generalized Joint Hypermobility using the Beighton ≥7/9 threshold showed excellent exact agreement between in-person and telehealth modes.
Classification of Generalized Joint Hypermobility using the ULHAT and LLAS ≥7/12 threshold showed only fair exact agreement between in-person and telehealth modes.
Individual test items of the Beighton Score had the highest proportion of good/excellent agreement between modes, at 78% (7/9 items).
Individual test items of the ULHAT had 58% (14/24) with good/excellent agreement between modes.
Generalized Joint Hypermobility classification agreement between telehealth and in-person modes using the ULHAT (≥7/12 threshold) was only fair.
Generalized Joint Hypermobility classification agreement between telehealth and in-person modes using the LLAS (≥7/12 threshold) was only fair.
Individual test items of the ULHAT showed good/excellent agreement between telehealth and in-person modes in 58% (14/24) of items, a moderate level of item-level reproducibility.
Individual test items of the LLAS showed the lowest reproducibility among the three scales, with only 42% (10/24) of items achieving good/excellent agreement between telehealth and in-person modes.
GJH at age 14 was present in 19% of adolescents and was significantly more common in females (28%) than males (11%).
GJH at age 14 years was significantly associated with an increased risk of depression at age 18 years across the whole group.
A significant GJH-by-sex interaction on depression was found, with the association between GJH and depression significant only in males.
GJH at age 14 years was not significantly associated with anxiety disorder at age 18 years.
Resting heart rate at age 14 was significantly higher in females than males.
After correcting for age and BMI, higher resting heart rate at age 14 was significantly associated with presence of GJH at age 14.
Higher resting heart rate at age 14 was significantly associated with depression at age 18 years.
The odds of depression at age 18 given GJH at 14 was 1.28 across both sexes combined, and 1.38 in males only, with no significant effect in females alone.
Mediation analysis in males showed that resting heart rate at age 14 significantly mediated the relationship between GJH and subsequent depression at age 18.
Joint hypermobility syndrome (GJH plus chronic widespread pain) was present in 1% of the cohort at age 18 and was significantly more common in females than males.
JHS was significantly associated with depression at age 18 years across the whole group and remained significant when adjusted for sex, and specifically in females (male subgroup underpowered).
JHS was significantly associated with any anxiety disorder at age 18 years, a relationship that remained significant after adjustment for sex.
Individuals with JHS had significantly higher CIS-R (depression severity) scores than those without JHS, including in females specifically.
Individuals with JHS had significantly higher Anxiety Sensitivity Index scores than those without JHS, including in females specifically.

Editorial commentary states that thin hip capsules, capsular redundancy, capsular defects, joint hypermobility, hip dysplasia, and female sex are associated with increased risk of hip instability following hip arthroscopy.

The authors recommend tailoring surgical planning (avoiding surgery or performing capsular repair/plication) according to gender, bony morphology, capsular volume, and tissue properties to reduce hip instability risk after arthroscopy.
Clinical and demographic variables (pain, disability, quality of life) became progressively more abnormal in a linear fashion as PSD severity group increased.
Somatic symptom scores (PHQ-15) were highly correlated with the PSD scale, supporting a shared dimensional construct.

When comparing FM-negative (PSD 8-11) with FM-positive (PSD 12-18) patients there was considerable overlap in pain, HAQ disability, patient global, and PHQ-15 scores, with no differential pain effect specific to categorical FM-positive status.

The authors conclude fibromyalgia is more accurately represented as a dimensional (continuous) disorder governed by the PSD scale rather than a strictly dichotomous categorical diagnosis, with the pain/symptom mechanism operating across the entire symptom dimension rather than only in categorically diagnosed cases.
Women carrying the CG or GG genotype of ESR1 rs2295190 had a significantly decreased risk of fibromyalgia syndrome compared to those with the CC genotype.
No significant differences were found in the genotype distribution of ESR1 rs2228480 polymorphism between FMS patients and healthy controls.
Within the FMS patient group, no significant association was found between symptoms, pain score, FIQ score, and the ESR1 polymorphisms.
A cited meta-analysis found that fibromyalgia patients show increased blood IL-6 levels compared to healthy controls.
The same cited meta-analysis reported elevated blood IL-4 levels in fibromyalgia patients relative to healthy controls.
The cited meta-analysis also reported elevated blood IL-17A levels in fibromyalgia patients compared to healthy controls.
Increased hs-CRP, another marker of inflammation, was also reported in fibromyalgia patients in the cited meta-analysis.
Plasma BDNF levels have been reported to be elevated in individuals with fibromyalgia compared to healthy controls.
DNA methylation in BDNF exon nine has been proposed as the epigenetic mechanism driving higher BDNF protein levels in fibromyalgia patients.

Higher pretreatment levels of IL-6 and TNF-α were associated with lesser improvements in pain intensity and other patient-reported outcomes following cognitive behavioral interventions in chronic pain patients.
Higher baseline CXCL8 levels were found to attenuate clinical benefits (pain, fatigue, stiffness, sleep quality) after an 8-week mindfulness program in fibromyalgia patients.
Levels of the anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10 remained higher in fibromyalgia patients assigned to mindfulness training compared to those in the treatment-as-usual arm.

An 8-week compassion-based intervention (ABCT) produced a global anti-inflammatory effect and reduced BDNF levels compared to an active control (relaxation training) in fibromyalgia, with BDNF reductions mediating improvements in functional impairment.
A systematic review of longitudinal studies found that multicomponent programs, physical exercise and dietary modification reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-6 and CXCL8 in fibromyalgia patients.

Previous RCTs of the FIBROWALK multicomponent intervention (online and outdoor formats) reported short-term effect sizes ranging from d=0.4 to d=1.83 versus treatment-as-usual for fibromyalgia outcomes.
In a prior outdoor FIBROWALK trial, adherence was very high, with 90% of patients attending 10 or more of the 12 sessions.

A meta-analysis found that multidisciplinary (multicomponent) treatments were the most beneficial non-pharmacological interventions for fibromyalgia, with statistically significant improvements across all OMERACT-10 symptom domains.

A systematic review and meta-analysis found that psychosocial interventions (psychotherapy, psychoeducation) robustly improved immune function including pro-inflammatory biomarker levels across various health conditions, with more pronounced effects after CBT and multicomponent programs.
A cited study found alterations in butyrate-metabolizing bacterial species in fibromyalgia patients, the first demonstration of gut microbiome alteration in a non-visceral chronic pain condition.
Lactobacillus acidophilus induced expression of μ-opioid and cannabinoid receptors in intestinal epithelial cells, producing analgesic effects similar to morphine.

A small open-label microbiota transfer therapy (MTT) trial in 18 children with autism spectrum disorder significantly improved gastrointestinal and behavioral ASD symptoms, with benefits maintained 8 weeks after treatment ended.
Bacteria (Staphylococcus aureus) can directly activate nociceptors to induce pain, independent of classical inflammatory mediation.
Oxaliplatin-induced mechanical hyperalgesia was reduced in germ-free mice and antibiotic-pretreated mice, an effect mediated in part by TLR4 expressed on hematopoietic cells.

A clinical trial found probiotic preparations of Lactobacillus or Bifidobacterium reduced abdominal pain in IBS patients, with symptomatic improvement associated with a normalized anti-inflammatory to pro-inflammatory cytokine ratio.

Fecal microbiota alpha- and beta-diversity did not differ between IBS patients and healthy individuals, but IBS patients were more likely to belong to the Bacteroides enterotype, and symptom severity correlated with microbial richness, presence of methanogens, and Clostridiales/Prevotella-enriched enterotypes.

Butyrate showed conflicting effects on visceral pain: one study found it induced colonic hypersensitivity in rats, while another found it significantly decreased visceral perception and pain in healthy human subjects, suggesting dose-dependent effects.
Sodium butyrate treatment attenuated pain attacks in a mouse model of nitroglycerine (NTG)-induced migraine.
GABA produced by gut Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium species activates GABAA receptors on dorsal root ganglion neurons, producing a net inhibitory effect on nociceptive transmission.

Microbially-derived 5-HT, produced by Candida, Streptococcus, Escherichia, and Enterococcus species, can either hyperpolarize or depolarize primary nociceptive neurons depending on which 5-HT receptor subfamily is activated.
Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs), a gut microbial metabolite, are endogenous TRPV4 agonists that lead to peripheral hypersensitivity.
Reports on antibiotics and neuropathic pain conflict, with some studies showing antibiotics improve neuropathic pain and others showing antibiotics induce hyperalgesia.
Inflammatory pain was reduced in germ-free mice compared with conventionally raised mice.

Lactobacillus farciminis treatment suppressed stress-induced visceral hypersensitivity, and combined Bifidobacterium longum and Lactobacillus helveticus treatment had a synergistic therapeutic effect on stress-related visceral hypersensitivity in animal models.
Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG (LGG) increased treatment success in children with abdominal pain-related functional gastrointestinal disorders.
Application of Bifidobacteria reversed colorectal distension (CRD)-induced visceral hypersensitivity in mice.
In the absence of gut microbiota, decreased SCFA production impaired adequate inflammasome assembly and IL-1β production.
Mastocytosis is a rare clonal mast cell disorder that is driven by the KIT D816V mutation in most cases.
Mast cell activation syndromes comprise a heterogeneous group of disorders that may arise from clonal or nonclonal mast cell etiologies.
OVA sensitization increased the number of jejunal mast cells and mMCP-1 expression compared to controls, indicating mast cell activation and barrier disruption.
Serum zonulin, a marker of intestinal barrier dysfunction, was significantly increased in the STZ+OVA and OVA+STZ groups compared to controls.

Jejunal mRNA expression of the tight junction proteins ZO-1, claudin-1 and occludin was increased across allergic/diabetic groups compared to controls, interpreted as a self-negative feedback response to barrier damage.
Claudin-1 and occludin expression were higher in OVA+STZ mice than OVA-only mice, indicating jejunal barrier damage was worst in the allergic-diabetic (OVA+STZ) group.
Serum GLP-1 levels were significantly reduced in all treated groups compared to controls, with the greatest reduction seen in the allergic-diabetic (OVA+STZ) group.
Serum insulin was decreased in the OVA+STZ (allergic diabetic) group compared to the OVA-only group, consistent with reduced GLP-1-driven insulin secretion.
IL-6 was significantly increased in serum but decreased in jejunal tissue after OVA/STZ treatment, suggesting IL-6-dependent regulation of GLP-1 secretion.
Serum TNF-α was significantly increased in OVA, STZ+OVA, and OVA+STZ groups compared to controls, consistent with TNF-α-induced systemic inflammation reducing GLP-1.
Jejunal SGLT1 and GLUT2 expression decreased in all treated groups compared to controls, with GLUT2 further reduced in OVA+STZ vs OVA, implicating impaired glucose-induced GLP-1 secretion.
mRNA expression of PI3K, Akt, mTOR, and NF-κB p65 was significantly increased in the jejunum of treated groups compared to controls, implicating this pathway in linking food allergy and diabetes.

At the protein level, mTOR and NF-κB p65 were upregulated in STZ+OVA and OVA+STZ mice compared to other groups, and PI3K protein was enhanced in OVA+STZ compared to STZ alone, suggesting STZ and OVA together suppress GLP-1 secretion via this pathway.
Mice sensitized to OVA before STZ injection (OVA+STZ) had a higher success rate of developing diabetes than CK and STZ-only mice, indicating food allergy increases susceptibility to diabetes.

There was no significant difference between STZ and STZ+OVA mice in fasting glucose or insulin sensitivity, indicating pre-existing diabetes with subsequent allergic sensitization did not worsen glucose dysregulation.

No significant differences in allergic immunological markers (IgE, IgG1, IgG2a, IL-4/5, IFN-γ, histamine) were found between OVA and STZ+OVA mice, indicating that STZ treatment did not further disrupt the immune balance already induced by OVA sensitization.

OVA+STZ mice showed significantly increased IL-4 and IL-5 and significantly decreased IFN-γ compared to STZ-only mice, indicating a Th2-skewed immune response when allergic sensitization precedes diabetes induction.
Peripheral blood neutrophil proportion increased and lymphocyte proportion decreased significantly in STZ and OVA+STZ groups, with the lymphocyte decrease more pronounced in OVA+STZ.
LDL-cholesterol was increased in the OVA+STZ group compared to the STZ group, indicating food allergy sensitization worsens the metabolic/lipid profile in diabetic mice.

Rectal temperature and food-allergy symptom scores were significantly increased in OVA+STZ mice after OVA challenge compared to controls, indicating more severe allergic reactions in the allergic-diabetic group.
Histopathology showed jejunal villi damage was most severe in the OVA+STZ (allergic diabetic) group compared to all other groups.

A previous population study cited in the discussion reported a positive correlation between allergic disease and diabetes with an odds ratio of 1.25, supporting allergic disease as a risk factor for diabetes.
SCN9A gene variants were discovered in 2012 to be pathogenic causes of small-fiber neuropathy.
SCN10A variants have been found to be pathogenic causes of small-fiber neuropathy.
SCN11A variants have been found to be pathogenic causes of small-fiber neuropathy.
The review identifies 80 distinct SCN gene variants described in the literature as causing small-fiber neuropathy.
Eight genes causing hereditary sensory autonomic neuropathies (HSAN) have been described presenting with a pure small-fiber neuropathy phenotype.
At least seven genes involved in genetically inherited systemic diseases have been associated with small-fiber neuropathy involvement.
The proportion of idiopathic SFN cases has decreased over time as familial and genetic causes have been increasingly discovered.

Two unrelated SFN patients carried heterozygous missense ANO3 variants (c.2656A>T, c.3100G>C), both presenting burning pain, allodynia, sheet intolerance and abnormal TTT, suggesting disrupted thermoregulation.
A heterozygous single-nucleotide deletion in KCNK18 (c.1107del) causing a frameshift and shortened C-terminus was identified in one SFN patient.

Two SFN patients carried heterozygous missense KCNQ3 variants (c.1885G>A, c.1706A>G) and shared a similar phenotype of numb sensation, burning feet, disturbed warm/cold sensation and pain worsening at rest, with expected loss-of-function effect contrasting known gain-of-function pain-resilience mutations.

Six heterozygous TRPA1 variants (four missense, two nonsense) were identified in seven SFN patients (including two siblings sharing c.3136A>G), the largest variant group in the study, associated with numb sensation, tingling, burning pain and cold hyperalgesia.
Three heterozygous missense TRPM8 variants were detected in three SFN patients with disturbed thermal sensation on TTT/QST; one variant carrier reported increased pain with warm temperature.

Three SFN patients carried heterozygous missense TRPV1 variants; two reported increased pain during rest interfering with sleep, but no temperature-related pain change, contrasting with known TRPV1 upregulation/gain-of-function link to pain amplification.
Two SFN patients had TRPV3 variants (a transmembrane-domain missense variant with itch episodes, and a splice-site donor variant of intron 9 predicted to alter splicing).
Overall, 20 of 414 SFN patients negative for SCN3A/SCN7A-11A/SCN1B-4B screening (4.8%) carried a potentially pathogenic heterozygous ion channel gene variant across seven genes.
SFN patients carrying an ICG variant had significantly more frequent abnormal skin biopsy findings than those without an ICG/VGSC variant (77.8% vs 42%).
No significant differences were found between ICG-variant carriers and non-carriers in age of neuropathy onset, neuropathy duration, positive family history, or abnormal TTT.

Patients carrying a potentially pathogenic ICG variant reported higher maximal pain VAS scores than those without such a variant (9.36±0.72 vs 7.47±2.37), with all variant carriers scoring above the non-carrier mean and TRPA1 carriers reporting the most severe pain (mean VAS 9.65±0.7, three scoring the maximum 10/10).

SFN-SIQ symptom frequencies (burning feet, restless legs, sheet intolerance) were similarly high in ICG-variant carriers and non-carriers, with no statistically significant differences reached for any feature.

The frequency of potentially pathogenic ICG variants in the SFN cohort (4.8%) was similar to, though slightly lower than, that previously found in painful diabetic neuropathy (5.4%), with TRP-gene variants being the most common in both cohorts (3.6% in SFN vs 3.3% in DN).
No potentially pathogenic variants were identified in eight of the 15 screened ion channel genes (ANO1, HCN1, KCNA2, KCNA4, KCNQ5, KCNN1, KCNS1, TRPV4) in the SFN cohort.
Follow-up MRI over a mean of 3.1 years showed virtually no progression of cerebral white matter lesions in carriers of the D313Y GLA variant.
White matter lesion burden did not correlate with lysoGb3 levels or with the severity of clinical findings in D313Y carriers.
Symptomatic carriers of the D313Y variant almost entirely lacked the internal organ manifestations and laboratory findings typically associated with classic Fabry disease.

The D313Y variant and its associated clinical/imaging signs can serve as a differential diagnosis for multiple sclerosis, or alternatively act as a co-factor alongside it, with imaging and CSF findings helping to distinguish the two entities.
Fabry disease neurological manifestations described include small fiber neuropathy, cerebral white matter lesions, megadolicho basilar artery, and stroke.
Serial skin biopsies in a single AIP patient during and after an acute attack showed reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber density that persisted despite improving muscle strength.

In a cohort of genetically unconfirmed AIP patients, heart rate response to deep breathing remained reduced between attacks while the Valsalva ratio normalized, indicating persistent cardio-vagal impairment.
A genetically confirmed Swedish AIP cohort using frequency-domain spectral analysis of heart rate variability replicated evidence of persistent cardio-vagal impairment between attacks.
A prospective natural history study of 112 AHP patients with recurrent attacks or on prophylactic hemin found chronic pain present in 40% of patients.

Among AIP patients with recurrent attacks during partial remission, 47% reported chronic neuropathic pain characterized by burning/tingling sensations, poor analgesic response, and partial sensory loss.
Sensory neuropathy signs (19%) and motor neuropathy signs (22%) frequently overlapped with chronic pain (25-40%) in AHP patients.
Urinary ALA remains elevated in approximately 62% of AIP patients between attacks, unlike PBG and ALA/PBG in HCP/VP which fall quickly after attack resolution.

Excess ALA causes mitochondrial impairment, decreased neuronal ATP production, dysfunctional fast axonal transport, and mitochondrial/nuclear DNA damage, implicating it as the neurotoxic driver of porphyric neuropathy.

Chronic peripheral sensitization in AHP is proposed to involve functional upregulation of sodium channels Nav1.7, Nav1.8, and Nav1.9 on free nerve endings, potentially triggered by liver-derived proinflammatory mediators and glutamate-mediated NMDA receptor activation.

In a 6-month randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial, monthly subcutaneous givosiran (2.5 mg/kg) reduced the mean annual attack rate by 74% and annualized days of IV hemin use by 77%, with significantly lower daily worst pain scores versus placebo.

Real-world experience showed givosiran dramatically decreased ALA levels and reduced pain severity in AIP patients, and was most effective when given early in the disease course, though many patients still experienced chronic pain.

A British audit of 22 patients with severe recurrent attacks receiving 1-8 heme arginate infusions per month found reduced pain frequency in 67% of patients, though 12 patients continued to have repeated hospital admissions due to disease worsening, tachyphylaxis, or chronic pain.

In a qualitative study of 16 AHP patients prescribed narcotics for recurrent attacks, 56% disliked regular opioid use due to side effects or abuse concerns, and 3 participants reported struggling with addiction and inadequate counseling.
Over 90-95% of AIP patients who experience acute attacks are female, with onset typically after puberty, reflecting a strong sex/hormonal influence on disease expression.
Clinical studies in the last decade reported chronic, mainly neuropathic, pain among 18% of US AIP patients, challenging the historical assumption that patients were 'healthy' between attacks.

Nerve conduction/EMG studies in acute porphyric neuropathy typically show diffuse, motor-predominant axonal neuropathy, helping exclude alternative diagnoses like Guillain-Barré syndrome when combined with normal CSF protein.
Colonic mucosal mast cell counts were significantly higher in patients classified as having mastocytic colitis compared to both healthy controls and patients with lymphocytic colitis.
Within the mastocytic colitis group, mast cell counts did not differ between younger and older patients using median age as a cutoff.
Mast cell counts in the mastocytic colitis group were comparable between male and female patients.
Mast cell counts in the mastocytic colitis group were significantly higher in biopsies from the right colon than the left colon.
There was a non-significant trend toward increased mast cell degranulation in the right colon compared to the left colon.
The prevalence of abdominal pain did not differ significantly between controls, lymphocytic colitis, and mastocytic colitis groups.
Bloating prevalence did not differ significantly between the three groups.
Patients with lymphocytic colitis had a significantly higher number of daily evacuations than controls.
Patients with mastocytic colitis had a significantly higher number of daily evacuations than controls.
Number of daily evacuations did not differ between lymphocytic colitis and mastocytic colitis patients.
The degree of mast cell degranulation was not associated with number of evacuations, abdominal pain, or bloating.
In a subset of mastocytic colitis patients whose diarrhea was not adequately controlled with budesonide, mast cell stabilizers and H1/H2 antihistamines were added to therapy.
Patients with lymphocytic colitis treated with budesonide had a favorable clinical response in 90% of cases.
Control patients with normal histology were successfully managed with the anti-diarrheal agent loperamide.
Elevated colonic mast cell counts (≥40/HPF) were found in more than 15% of patients with chronic bloodless diarrhea and normal endoscopy who would otherwise be diagnosed with IBS.
None of the patients in the mastocytic colitis, lymphocytic colitis, or control groups progressed to inflammatory bowel disease during 10-28 months of follow-up.

The authors propose that mastocytic colitis, defined by increased colonic mast cells without meeting current microscopic colitis criteria, may explain chronic diarrhea in a subset of patients currently diagnosed with IBS.
IBS patients reported significantly greater frequency and intensity of abdominal pain and greater intensity of abdominal distension compared with healthy controls.
Levels of satisfaction with defecation were significantly lower in the IBS group than in controls.
The total GSRS score, especially diarrhea and constipation subscales, was significantly higher in IBS patients than in controls.
Anxiety and depression scores (HADS) did not differ significantly between IBS patients and controls.
SF-8 role physical, social functioning, and physical component summary scores were significantly lower in IBS patients, indicating reduced health-related quality of life.
No significant differences were found in mean LF/HF or HF between IBS patients and controls during baseline (asymptomatic), awake, or sleep periods.
The duration of periods with positive abdominal symptoms (total ANS signal count) was significantly longer in IBS patients than in controls.

During symptomatic periods, sum of LF/HF, sum of ΔLF/HF, and maximum variation of ΔLF/HF were significantly higher in IBS patients than controls, indicating increased sympathetic activity specifically during symptomatic episodes.

During symptomatic periods, sum of HF, sum of ΔHF, and maximum variation of ΔHF were significantly higher in IBS patients than controls, indicating increased parasympathetic activity during symptomatic episodes.
The number of abnormal LF/HF ratio readings was significantly higher in the IBS group than in controls.
The number of abnormal HF readings did not differ statistically between IBS patients and controls.
Time-domain HRV measures (CVRR, mean inter-beat interval, SDNN) showed no significant differences between IBS patients and controls.

Sympathetic activity (sum of ΔLF/HF and LF/HF) increased significantly starting 2 minutes before defecation in IBS patients compared with controls, and remained elevated until 9 minutes after defecation.

Parasympathetic activity (sum of ΔHF) increased significantly 3–8 minutes after defecation in IBS patients, and sum of HF was significantly higher 5–6 minutes after defecation, compared with controls.
The sum of ΔLF/HF at 2 minutes before defecation correlated positively with the intensity of abdominal pain in IBS patients.
The sum of ΔLF/HF at 2 minutes before defecation correlated negatively with satisfaction levels of defecation in IBS patients.
The sum of ΔLF/HF at 2 minutes before defecation correlated positively with the GSRS diarrhea score in IBS patients.
The sum of ΔLF/HF at 2 minutes before defecation correlated positively with the GSRS constipation score in IBS patients.
The sum of ΔLF/HF at 2 minutes before defecation correlated negatively with SF-8 role physical and role emotional scores in IBS patients, linking sympathetic activation to worse QOL.
The TC genotype of the CCN2 SNP rs12526196 was independently associated with more than a two-fold increased risk of ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm compared with the TT genotype.
The association between the rs12526196 TC genotype and TAA remained significant after adjusting for the other two CCN2 polymorphisms studied.
Under a dominant inheritance model, carrying at least one C allele of rs12526196 was a significant risk factor for TAA compared with the TT genotype.
In multivariable analysis adjusting for TAA risk factors, the rs6918698 and rs9402373 CCN2 polymorphisms were not significantly associated with TAA.
Overall genotype and allele frequencies of the three studied CCN2 SNPs did not differ between the TAA patient group and controls in unadjusted comparisons.
Bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) was the main contributor to TAA risk in the multivariable model, though the rs12526196 association remained independent of BAV status.

According to prior in silico and in vitro work cited by the authors, the rs12526196 T allele has greater binding affinity for nuclear transcription factors (including FOXQ1, FOXL1, SRY, SOX9, SOX5, SOX17) than the C allele, suggesting the C allele may reduce CCN2 transcription.
Reduced SOX9 levels, associated with fibulin-5 downregulation, have been reported in human aortic aneurysms, contrasting with elevated SOX9 seen in lung and kidney fibrosis.

Loss-of-function mutations in the gene encoding CD73 cause arterial calcification due to deficiency of CD73 (ACDC), characterized by arteriomegaly, tortuosity, and vascular calcification of lower extremity arteries.
ACDC patient vessels show fragmented elastin fibers histologically, resembling aneurysmal-like vascular pathology.
CD73-deficient smooth muscle cells display elevated expression of contractile markers and elastin genes compared with wild-type control SMCs.
Ecto-5'-nucleotidase (CD73)-deficient SMCs show increased TGFβ-2 levels and activation of SMAD signaling along with elevated elastin transcript and protein.
CD73-deficient SMCs exhibit potentiated cellular contraction compared to control cells.
Activation of the A2b adenosine receptor diminished the elevated TGFβ-2/SMAD signaling, elastin expression, and enhanced contraction seen in CD73-deficient SMCs.
Activation of the A2b adenosine receptor diminished the elevated TGFβ-2/SMAD signaling, elastin expression, and contraction seen in CD73-deficient smooth muscle cells.
The authors propose that disrupted adenosine signaling underlies ACDC vessel tortuosity and may contribute more broadly to the pathogenesis of other aneurysmal diseases.
Fatigue was the most commonly reported symptom among PASC patients enrolled in the recovery program.
Sleep disturbance was reported by nearly half of PASC patients in the program.
Body aches or pains and general weakness were commonly reported symptoms.
Respiratory symptoms including shortness of breath were common among PASC patients.
Neurologic symptoms including headache, difficulty focusing, lightheadedness/dizziness, depressed mood, and impaired memory were common.
Cardiovascular symptoms including chest pain and palpitations/heart racing were reported by roughly a third of patients.
PROMIS-29 physical functioning scores were markedly reduced (worse than population norm by more than one SD) among PASC patients.
PROMIS-29 fatigue T-scores were markedly elevated (worse than population norm) in PASC patients.
Other PROMIS-29 domains (pain interference, pain intensity, depression, anxiety, social participation, sleep disturbance) were worse than normal but within one SD of the population mean.
Fatigue Severity Scale scores indicated increased fatigue compared to general population norms.
A meaningful proportion of PASC patients reported social determinants of health hardships including inability to pay rent/mortgage, food insecurity, and job difficulty.
Work productivity and activity impairment were substantial among PASC patients as measured by WPAI.
Younger patients (<50 years) reported greater anxiety than older patients (>50 years) on PROMIS-29 subgroup analysis.
Patients of Hispanic or other ethnic origin reported greater sleep disturbance than other groups.
Females reported greater pain intensity and fatigue than males in PROMIS-29 subgroup analysis.
Patients with underlying asthma had worse PROMIS scores in fatigue and ability to participate in social roles/activities than those without asthma.
Patients hospitalized for COVID-19 had greater impairment in physical functioning than those not hospitalized.
No differences in PROMIS scores were found based on presence of allergies or diabetes.
Nearly a quarter of enrollees had been hospitalized for COVID-19, a small fraction required ICU admission, indicating a predominantly milder-severity cohort.
Singers with moderate acute COVID-19 symptoms had significantly increased odds of reporting a change in singing ability compared to those with mild acute symptoms.
Singers with severe acute COVID-19 symptoms had over five times the odds of reporting a change in singing ability compared to those with mild acute symptoms.
Cough experienced at the time of initial infection was significantly associated with increased odds of reporting a change in singing voice.
Sore throat experienced at the time of initial infection was significantly associated with increased odds of reporting a change in singing voice.
Shortness of breath at the time of initial infection was associated with lower odds of reporting a change in singing voice, suggesting a possible protective relationship.
Fatigue experienced at the time of initial infection was significantly associated with increased odds of reporting a change in singing voice.
The combination of cough and sore throat at initial infection showed a protective interaction, lowering the odds of reporting a change in singing voice compared to either symptom alone.

Runny nose/congestion at initial infection was associated with lower odds of a reported change in singing ability, suggesting a possible protective effect, potentially linked to Omicron variant upper-respiratory tropism.
Cough persisting four weeks postinfection was significantly associated with increased odds of reporting a change in singing voice.
Shortness of breath persisting four weeks postinfection was strongly associated with increased odds of reporting a change in singing voice.
Chronic fatigue persisting four weeks postinfection was significantly associated with increased odds of reporting a change in singing voice.
60.3% of singer respondents reported lingering COVID-19 symptoms lasting 4 weeks or more, meeting the study's long-COVID definition.
The three most commonly reported recurring (long-COVID) symptoms among singers were fatigue, shortness of breath, and brain fog.

Vocal stamina (comfortable singing duration) was significantly reduced after COVID-19 infection compared to before infection, with far fewer respondents able to sing an hour or more and some unable to sing more than 15 minutes.
About two-thirds of respondents reported feeling at least 76% recovered and able to perform most or all of their usual singing.

In free-text responses about how COVID-19 affected singing, phonatory (voice-related) concerns were more common than pulmonary concerns, with vocal fatigue the top phonatory theme and breath support/control the top pulmonary theme.

In the second open-ended question, mental health concerns were reported more frequently than in the first, and a substantial proportion of respondents indicated their singing-related concerns were still ongoing.
Unlike prior COVID-19 severity literature, age and sex showed no significant interaction with the odds of reporting a change in singing voice in this singer cohort.
Vaccination status could not be statistically analyzed for association with change in singing voice because too few respondents were unvaccinated.
The 2021 NICE guideline removed graded exercise therapy (GET) as a recommended treatment for ME/CFS.

The NICE evidence review found no clinical difference in outcomes including quality of life, cognitive function, psychological status, pain, and sleep quality between CBT and standard medical care or passive control arms.
Post-exertional malaise (PEM) is now recognised as a core symptom that must be present for an ME/CFS diagnosis under the new guideline.
ME/CFS can now be diagnosed after 3 months of symptoms (previously 4-6 months) following careful clinical assessment and exclusion of alternative diagnoses.
Approximately 250,000 people in England and Wales are estimated to have ME/CFS, with the number potentially higher due to long COVID-related diagnoses.

Research has identified predisposing factors (genetic predisposition, female gender), triggering events (infection most commonly, also vaccinations and physical trauma) and maintaining factors (immune system dysfunction, HPA axis hypoactivity, autonomic nervous system dysfunction) involved in ME/CFS.

Viral infection is the most common trigger preceding ME/CFS onset, and post-exertional malaise in the first few months after a viral infection is usually a red flag for the condition; COVID-19 infection may also precipitate an ME/CFS-like illness.
Orthostatic intolerance and autonomic dysfunction, including dizziness, palpitations, fainting, and nausea on standing, are listed among common ME/CFS symptoms and are experienced by many patients.

There is insufficient evidence to recommend dietary, vitamin, or supplement interventions for ME/CFS over any others, though vitamin D supplementation may be considered for those at risk of deficiency per general population recommendations.

Evidence for both pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions in ME/CFS was generally of low or very low quality, with effects when present being modest and possibly attributable to bias or regression to the mean.
A nurse-led school-based active surveillance (SBAS) process using chronic absenteeism as a signal helped school nurses effectively identify undiagnosed conditions such as ME/CFS.
Establishing relationships with school leadership and focusing outreach efforts were identified as important factors for developing health policies and programs supporting the surveillance process.
The authors suggest that because Long COVID symptoms overlap with ME/CFS, the SBAS surveillance model may offer insights for tracking the educational impact of Long COVID in students.
Twelve weeks of 6-MSITC (wasabi extract) treatment significantly improved ME/CFS performance status (PS) scores compared to baseline.
6-MSITC did not significantly change CFS-11 physical fatigue, mental fatigue, or total fatigue scores after 12 weeks.
Numerical rating scale (NRS) fatigue severity did not significantly improve after 6-MSITC treatment.
Sleep quality (PSQI) did not significantly improve after 6-MSITC treatment despite most patients having poor sleep at baseline.
Headache frequency significantly decreased after 6-MSITC treatment.
Myalgia frequency significantly decreased after 6-MSITC treatment.
Frequency and severity of arthralgia and pharyngeal pain did not change significantly after treatment.
Pressure pain threshold at the right GB20 acupoint significantly increased (reduced pain sensitivity) after 6-MSITC treatment.
Subjective severity of brain fog significantly improved after 6-MSITC treatment.
Subjective difficulty finding appropriate words significantly improved after 6-MSITC treatment.
Subjective photophobia severity significantly improved after 6-MSITC treatment.
Memory loss severity did not change significantly after 6-MSITC treatment.
Time to complete the Trail Making Test-A significantly decreased after 6-MSITC treatment, indicating improved frontal lobe/cognitive function.
Distribution of orthostatic intolerance patterns (normal, POTS, orthostatic hypotension) on active standing test did not change significantly at the group level after 6-MSITC treatment.
POMS-2 vigor score significantly increased after 6-MSITC treatment, indicating improved energy/vitality.
Anxiety and depression scores (HADS) did not change significantly after 6-MSITC treatment.
SF-36 general health perception subscale score significantly improved after 6-MSITC treatment.
SF-36 vitality subscale score significantly improved after 6-MSITC treatment.
Improvements in Trail Making Test-A time and POMS-2 tension score were predictive factors for improvement in ME/CFS performance status, explaining 42% of the variance.
No serious adverse events were reported during the 12-week 6-MSITC treatment period.
Baseline fatigue severity (CFS-11 total score) in this ME/CFS cohort was higher than that reported in a Japanese community sample.
The majority of ME/CFS patients (93.3%) had poor sleep quality at baseline, consistent with prior Japanese ME/CFS cohort data.
Baseline pressure pain threshold at the posterior neck in ME/CFS patients was lower than reported values in healthy subjects, indicating increased pain sensitivity.
Most patients (14/15) subjectively reported the 6-MSITC treatment was effective, particularly for cognitive problems and brain fog; one patient reported no benefit.

Hypothesis-free combinatorial analysis of the UK Biobank Pain Questionnaire cohort identified 84 statistically validated combinations of 199 SNPs (mapping to 14 genes) strongly associated with ME/CFS diagnosis, none of which would have been detected by standard GWAS.

Standard GWAS case-control association analysis (PLINK) on the same Pain Questionnaire cohort found no SNPs reaching genome-wide significance (p<5x10-8), in contrast to the combinatorial approach which found 84 significant multi-SNP signatures.
An intronic critical SNP in GPC5 (rs16947237), previously associated with self-reported chronic fatigue syndrome in a UK Biobank GWAS, was carried by 17% of ME/CFS cases in this study.

A critical SNP combination including a variant in AKAP1, a mitochondrial scaffold protein regulating AMPK-mediated mitochondrial respiration, was found in 27% of ME/CFS cases (the highest proportion of any RF-scored genetic variant) versus no more than 1.5% of controls, providing a genetic link to mitochondrial dysfunction in ME/CFS.

Community 1 critical SNPs in ATP9A and KCNB1 co-occurred in six disease signatures and showed significant enrichment for regulation of exocytosis and negative regulation of secretion by cell, both genes being implicated in pancreatic beta-cell insulin secretion, suggesting dysregulated insulin signalling in this ME/CFS subgroup.

Community 15 critical SNPs in SLC6A11 (GABA transporter GAT3) and SULF2 co-occurred in two disease signatures with enrichment for GABA synthesis/release and synaptic vesicle cycle pathways, supporting a CNS-related mechanism in this ME/CFS subgroup.

348 (15%) ME/CFS patients (vs 4% of controls) were associated with a disease signature community containing the insulin receptor gene INSR, and these patients also showed relatively higher blood lactate levels than the rest of the ME/CFS case population.

A critical SNP mapped to SLC15A4, a lysosomal membrane transporter enriched in immune cells and previously linked to systemic lupus erythematosus risk and mitochondrial function via AMPK/mTORC1, was identified among the ME/CFS-associated genes, though no eQTL association was found for this SNP.

CDON, a cell surface receptor gene involved in muscle regeneration and previously linked to complicated bacteremia and midbrain dopamine pathway development, was identified as one of the 14 genes mapped from ME/CFS critical SNPs.

A critical SNP in CLOCK, a key circadian rhythm regulator, was identified among ME/CFS-associated genes, and patients carrying CLOCK variants showed significant enrichment for comorbid fibromyalgia diagnosis.

Of the 25 critical SNPs identified in the Pain Questionnaire cohort, 7 showed significant association with disease in at least one of three disjoint replication cohorts (CFS Verbal Interview, post-viral syndrome, fibromyalgia), with 2 replicated across multiple cohorts.

Critical SNPs rs2304725 (SLC6A11) and rs2904106 (ATP9A), among five critical SNPs replicated in the disjoint UK Biobank CFS Verbal Interview cohort, suggest particularly strong association of these genes with ME/CFS.

Three critical SNPs (rs56218501/Affx-16805420 in SULF2, rs12530627, and rs2499908 in USP6NL) from the Pain Questionnaire cohort were replicated in the fibromyalgia cohort analysis, suggesting SULF2 and USP6NL are strongly associated with fibromyalgia cases specifically.

ME/CFS cases showed a significantly higher proportion reporting mental distress and stressful events (illness, injury, bereavement) compared with the remainder of the UK Biobank population, the largest observed covariate difference.

ME/CFS patients were slightly more likely than the rest of UK Biobank to present with at least one autoimmune disease, with the greatest co-association seen with multiple sclerosis and fibromyalgia, though misdiagnosis cannot be ruled out.

Patients with SNP combinations including SLC6A11 showed increased plasma phenylalanine levels compared to other ME/CFS subgroups, though this did not remain significant after multiple-testing correction.
The ME/CFS case cohort was disproportionately female (71%, n=1695/2382) compared with the 54.4% female proportion in the overall UK Biobank population.

Patient communities carrying variants in SLC6A11, SULF2 and CDON were significantly more likely to report illness and psychosocial stress factors (injury, bereavement, stress) over the preceding 3-8 years, suggesting a stress-vulnerability ME/CFS subgroup.

The 15 SNP-based patient communities (disease architecture) identified in the Pain Questionnaire cohort had odds ratios ranging from 2.16 to 4.47 and p-values from 10-10 to 10-72, with low (<20%) overlap between communities indicating distinct genetic patient subgroups.

Across all five EU-authorized COVID-19 vaccines, the three predominant categories of suspected adverse reaction reports in EudraVigilance were general disorders/administration site conditions, nervous system disorders, and musculoskeletal/connective tissue disorders.
In the 'infections and infestations' reaction group, serious suspected adverse reaction reports were about three times more numerous than non-serious ones.

When normalized by administered doses, Vector (CHADOX1 NCOV-19, AD26.COV2.S) and Subunit (NVX-COV2373) vaccines showed higher relative frequencies of ICSRs across all reaction categories than mRNA vaccines, despite mRNA vaccines having more total reports.

The specific term 'myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS)' was not available as a searchable MedDRA term in EudraVigilance, though the related term 'chronic fatigue syndrome' was accessible for line-listing analysis.

The total number of ICSRs for chronic fatigue syndrome following COVID-19 vaccination doubled in 2022 compared to 2021, despite 2022 vaccine doses administered in the EU being only about a fifth of the 2021 total.
For the CHADOX1 NCOV-19 vaccine specifically, chronic fatigue syndrome ICSRs rose from 26 per 10 million doses administered in 2021 to 21,667 per 10 million doses administered in 2022.

In a prospective observational study cited by the authors, 19 of 42 post-COVID-19 syndrome patients with persistent moderate-to-severe fatigue and exertion intolerance at 6 months met the 2003 Canadian Consensus Criteria for ME/CFS.
The authors note prior estimates that approximately 10% of COVID-19 survivors could develop ME/CFS, based on extrapolation from other post-infectious syndromes.

In a cited German general-practice database study of 531,468 individuals receiving 908,869 SARS-CoV-2 vaccinations, 28,287 adverse drug reactions were documented (3.1% of vaccinations), with fatigue among the most common (21.0% of the 12,575 vaccinations with definite ADRs).

Vaccine-specific differences in dominant reported reaction categories were observed: TOZINAMERAN (Pfizer-BioNTech) uniquely showed 'reproductive system and breast disorders' among its seven dominant categories, and NVX-COV2373 uniquely showed 'cardiac disorders' with a relatively high proportion of serious reactions.

Two independent groups studying chronic fatigue syndrome and fibromyalgia found that patients had intracranial pressures in the high-normal range, with some meeting criteria for IIH without papilloedema (IIHWOP).

Draining cerebrospinal fluid via lumbar puncture to lower intracranial pressure improved symptoms including headache, fatigue and pain in patients with chronic fatigue syndrome and fibromyalgia, even in those with normal-range pressures.

A third group recorded dilatation of the optic nerve sheaths and descent of the cerebellar tonsils on MRI, interpreted as evidence of raised intracranial pressure, in a large majority of patients with ME/CFS.

Narrowing of the jugular veins between the styloid processes and C1 transverse processes has been described as causing otherwise idiopathic intracranial hypertension, with treatment of the venous narrowing resolving the clinical syndrome.
The authors report cases of spontaneous intracranial hypotension caused by narrowing of the jugular veins at the styloid-C1 level, with symptom resolution following treatment of the venous stenosis.

Damage to non-dominant cranial venous outflow tracts during posterior fossa surgery has been shown to cause moderately increased intracranial pressure or CSF leaks, producing chronic headache and fatigue over many years.

In a patient with marked asymmetry of cranial venous outflow and posture-related confusion/epistaxis, stenting the non-dominant transverse sinus to increase venous drainage capacity produced substantial clinical improvement, including resolution of postural symptoms.
Stenting narrowed transverse sinuses can lower intracranial pressure and ameliorate symptoms in IIH.
IL-18, a T cell/macrophage-derived pro-inflammatory cytokine, was significantly down-regulated in long COVID patients compared to other groups.
MCP-1/CCL-2, a monocyte/macrophage-derived chemokine, was significantly down-regulated in long COVID patients compared to fully recovered patients.
Soluble TNF-RII was significantly down-regulated in long COVID patients compared to fully recovered patients.
SERPINA1, a marker of M2-polarized macrophages, was significantly up-regulated in the plasma proteome of long COVID patients.
Vitamin D binding protein (GC), a precursor of macrophage-activating signal factor, was significantly up-regulated in long COVID patients.

SERPINA5, the main endogenous furin inhibitor, was significantly down-regulated in long COVID patients versus both healthy and recovered groups, suggesting reduced control of furin activity relevant to viral entry.
SERPINF2, a protease inhibitor, was found significantly down-regulated in long COVID patient plasma proteome.
Biotinidase (BTD), essential for basic macrophage function and linked to hypotonia/lethargy/cognitive impairment when deficient, was significantly down-regulated in long COVID patients.
Soluble CD14, a macrophage-specific membrane protein secreted upon inflammatory activation, was down-regulated in long COVID patients, suggesting reduced M1-like macrophage responses.
Angiogenin (ANG), an angiogenic and anti-bacterial protein secreted by macrophages, was down-regulated in long COVID patients.
Proteoglycan-4 (PRG4), a regulator of synovial macrophage polarization and inflammation, was down-regulated in long COVID patients.
Multiple acute phase proteins were slightly but consistently down-regulated in long COVID patients, further indicating absence of systemic inflammation.
Increased plasma levels of the pro-inflammatory fatty acid arachidonic acid were mainly observed in the recovered group rather than in long COVID patients.
The anti-inflammatory omega-3 fatty acids EPA and DHA were predominantly released into blood of long COVID patients compared to other groups.
DHA oxidation products 17-HDoHE and 22-HDoHE were significantly increased in long COVID patients, corroborating increased intracellular DHA release rather than dietary confounding.
Levels of trans-DHA, a marker of nitric oxide signaling rather than dietary intake, were consistently increased in long COVID patients, supporting intracellular (not dietary) release of DHA.
The overall ratio of omega-3 to omega-6 fatty acids was significantly increased in long COVID patients compared to the other groups.
13-OxoODE, a 15-LOX product of linoleic acid with anti-inflammatory properties, was increased in long COVID patients compared to recovered patients.
Branched-chain amino acids (Val, Leu, Ile), Tyr, and Arg were down-regulated in long COVID patients, indicating disturbed energy metabolism and increased amino acid catabolism.
Tryptophan levels were down-regulated in long COVID patients, potentially resulting from prolonged IDO enzyme activity as observed during acute SARS-CoV-2 infection.
C18:1-acylcarnitine was increased while C3-acylcarnitine was decreased in long COVID patients, suggesting reduced beta-oxidation with increased amino acid catabolism.
Lactate was significantly increased in long COVID patients, pointing to increased anaerobic glycolysis.

The majority of complex lipids including triacylglycerols, glycosylceramides, glycerophospholipids, and ceramides were down-regulated in long COVID patients, a pattern the authors note resembles chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS).
Hypaphorine (TrpBetaine), an anti-inflammatory, sleep-inducing alkaloid, was the most significantly up-regulated metabolite in long COVID patients.
Taurine, an anti-inflammatory/anti-oxidative osmolyte, was significantly up-regulated in long COVID patients compared to the other groups.
Hypoxanthine, a marker of tissue hypoxia/acute inflammation, was strongly increased in the recovered group but comparable to healthy levels in long COVID patients.

One week of oral omega-3 (EPA/DHA) supplementation in healthy volunteers did not increase trans-DHA levels, ruling out dietary supplementation as the source of elevated trans-DHA seen in long COVID patients.

In vitro M2-like polarized macrophages expressed proteins promoting lipolysis (PLA2G4A), altered lipid metabolism (PLIN2, FABP4), and lipid peroxidation (HMOX1), mirroring the anti-inflammatory pattern seen in long COVID plasma.
Both arachidonic acid and DHA were released to a greater extent by M2-like macrophages than by M1-like macrophages in vitro.
COX2 (PTGS2) and its downstream products PGE2, PGF2alpha, and TXB2 were exclusively detected in M1-like (pro-inflammatory) macrophages, not M2-like macrophages, in vitro.

The lipid peroxidation products HpODE and the cytochrome P450 product 12,13-DiHOME were released at higher levels by M2-like than M1-like macrophages in vitro, consistent with the anti-inflammatory lipid pattern in long COVID plasma.
In vitro M1-like polarized U937 macrophages robustly secreted pro-inflammatory cytokines and MMP9, confirming the expected M1 phenotype used as a reference for the plasma findings.

MCP-1 (CCL2) and TNFRSF1B, both found down-regulated in plasma of LCS patients, were shown to be mainly secreted by M1-like macrophages and were down-regulated in M2-like macrophages in vitro, linking the plasma signature to macrophage polarization state.

M1-like macrophages secreted the protease furin, which cleaves the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein to enable viral cell entry, suggesting a mechanistic link between M1 macrophage activity and viral entry potential.

M2-like polarized macrophages displayed a tolerogenic phenotype expressing the immune suppressor CCL18, the angiogenesis factor ANGPT4, and proteins promoting lipolysis (PLA2G4A), altered lipid metabolism (PLIN2, FABP4), and lipid peroxidation (HMOX1).
Both arachidonic acid and DHA were released to a greater extent by M2-like macrophages than by M1-like macrophages in vitro, mirroring the plasma lipidomic pattern seen in LCS patients.
COX-derived eicosanoids PGE2, PGF2alpha, and TXB2 were only detected in M1-like macrophage secretomes, consistent with specific COX2 (PTGS2) expression in M1-like cells.

The lipid peroxidation product HpODE and the cytochrome P450 product 12,13-DiHOME were found at higher levels released from M2-like macrophages compared to M1-like macrophages, matching the anti-inflammatory lipid pattern observed in LCS plasma.
