Routine laboratory parameters including total protein, albumin, lipids, lipoproteins and CRP showed no differences between healthy, recovered, and LCS groups, ruling out overt systemic inflammation or metabolic disease at the time of sampling.

In an independent cohort of 10 healthy volunteers, one week of oral Omega-3 (EPA/DHA) supplementation did not increase plasma trans-DHA levels, indicating that the elevated trans-DHA seen in LCS patients was not attributable to dietary supplementation but likely reflected intracellular release via nitric oxide signaling.

Symptom-free recovered patients showed significant molecular alterations relative to healthy vaccinated controls across proteome, lipidome, and metabolome, indicating that systemic biological processes remain active for months after resolution of acute infection symptoms even without long COVID diagnosis.

The authors propose that system-wide alternative (M2-like) macrophage polarization, potentially triggered by lipid peroxidation during acute infection, is a key mechanism underlying the anti-inflammatory and hypometabolic molecular signature and symptoms of LCS.

The authors note that biotinidase deficiency is known to cause hypotonia, lethargy, cognitive impairment and seizures, potentially linking the observed BTD down-regulation to the symptom complex seen in LCS patients.

Increased plasma fatty acids combined with decreased triacylglycerols in LCS patients are hypothesized to reflect increased endothelial lipase activity, which has separately been associated with cognitive impairment.

The authors state that their molecular data are compatible with immune dysregulation and viral persistence as proposed mechanisms of LCS, but do not support a general role of autoimmunity, which would be expected to present with a pro-inflammatory rather than anti-inflammatory pattern.

Cognitive and behavioural responses to fatigue symptoms, measured by the CBRQ, showed small to moderate differences across the four long-term condition groups (CFS/ME, MS, T1DM, Q-fever fatigue syndrome).
Patients with higher baseline scores on damage beliefs and avoidance/resting behaviour subscales of the CBRQ showed less improvement in fatigue following CBT, regardless of diagnosis.
Reductions in fear avoidance, catastrophising, and avoidance/resting behaviour following CBT mediated the treatment's positive effect on fatigue across all four diagnostic groups.

No differentially expressed genes were found between hEDS and HSD fibroblasts, and PCA showed hEDS and HSD samples clustering together but separately from controls, supporting a shared transcriptional profile.
Separate differential expression analyses identified 722 DEGs in hEDS vs. control and 1174 DEGs in HSD vs. control fibroblasts.

590 genes were common to both hEDS-vs-control and HSD-vs-control DEG lists with the same direction of change, and an additional 132 (hEDS) and 584 (HSD) genes showed matching trends but fell below strict statistical thresholds, indicating the two groups share a common dysregulated expression pattern.
Grouping hEDS and HSD together and comparing to controls identified 952 DEGs, with 826 downregulated (750 mRNAs, 70 lncRNA, 6 snoRNA) and 126 upregulated (122 mRNAs, 4 lncRNA).

GO enrichment of all 952 DEGs highlighted cell migration, GTPase activity regulation, and protein phosphorylation (Biological Process); actin binding, protein kinase activity, and chemokine activity (Molecular Function); and cytoskeleton, Golgi apparatus, and focal adhesion (Cellular Component) as the top enriched categories.

Downregulated DEGs were enriched for transcriptional regulation, protein phosphorylation, cell migration, actin binding, ATP binding, protein serine/threonine kinase activity, and cytoskeleton/Golgi/focal adhesion cellular components.

Upregulated DEGs were enriched for chemokine-mediated signaling, neutrophil chemotaxis, inflammatory response, chemokine activity, CXCR chemokine receptor binding, nucleosome, and extracellular region/exosome terms.

Network analysis of downregulated DEGs identified 16 clusters including Wnt signaling, VEGFA-VEGFR2 signaling, and RHO GTPase cycle, linked to connective tissue, skeletal, cartilage, muscle, eye, and renal system development, as well as ECM organization and cell migration/differentiation processes.

The most significant upregulated network cluster related to chemokine biology, including cellular response to chemokines, proinflammatory/profibrotic mediators, granulocyte chemotaxis, neutrophil migration, interleukin-17 signaling, and rheumatoid arthritis pathway terms.

A second upregulated network cluster related to chromatin organization and nucleosome assembly, with nodes including HDAC/HAT histone modification pathways and disease associations to systemic lupus erythematosus and HCMV infection.
qPCR validated upregulation of all considered CC and CXC motif chemokine ligand genes and of the interleukins CSF3 and IL1RN in hEDS/HSD versus control fibroblasts.

qPCR confirmed upregulation of ECM-degrading enzymes MMP1, MMP3, and CTSS and glycoproteins TNC, LAMB3, TNFAIP6, alongside downregulation of the peptidase inhibitor PI16 and glycoproteins/proteoglycan COMP, CCN2, THSD4, IGFBP5, and VCAN in hEDS/HSD fibroblasts.

qPCR validated reduced expression of cytoskeletal structural genes (DSP, DST, MYH10, CDH10) and actin-binding proteins (PLS3, PLEC, CTNNA1, ARPC1A, ARPC3, FERMT2), along with upregulation of the phosphatase/actin regulator PHACTR1.

Core histone genes (H2A-H2B and H3 families) were upregulated while heterochromatin protein CBX1 and histone acetyltransferases EP300, JADE1, and ELP1 were downregulated in hEDS/HSD fibroblasts, suggesting chromatin/epigenetic dysregulation.

qPCR confirmed downregulation of secreted growth factors (BMP4, BMP6, WNT2, WNT2B, GDF6) and receptors (TGFBR1, FZD6, FZD8, BMPR2, JAK1, TAS2R13, TAS2R50), while INHBE and TNF receptors CD40, TNFRSF1B, and TNFRSF21 were upregulated.
qPCR confirmed significant downregulation of second messengers (SMAD1, RHOJ, DOCK11) and transcription factors (NR4A1, NR4A2, HES1, SNAI1, FOSB, FOS) in hEDS/HSD fibroblasts.

Immunofluorescence confirmed that all 20 hEDS and 20 HSD fibroblast strains showed marked disorganization of collagen I/III/V, fibronectin, and tenascins, abnormal expression of α2β1, α5β1, and αvβ3 integrins, a well-organized α-SMA cytoskeleton replacing β-actin, and expression of cadherin-11 and Snail1, consistent with a myofibroblast-like phenotype not seen in controls.

The combined cumulative incidence of hEDS/HSD is estimated at 1:500, suggesting it is far more common than the presumed autosomal-dominant hEDS alone, supporting an oligogenic/polygenic model with environmental contribution.

Citing their prior work, the authors note that doxycycline-mediated MMP inhibition rescues proper ECM organization in patient cells, reduces myofibroblast-like features, and prevents phenotypic conversion of control fibroblasts exposed to patient-derived conditioned medium, and a pilot clinical trial of doxycycline in hEDS/HSD patients is planned.

The authors propose a disease model in which abnormal ECM turnover generates ECM-derived DAMPs (collagen, fibronectin, and tenascin fragments) that activate TLR-driven proinflammatory signaling, further increasing protease and cytokine production in a self-sustaining degradative-inflammatory feedback loop underlying hEDS/HSD pathology.

Patients with hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and hypermobile spectrum disorders are increasingly presenting with GI symptoms and nutritional issues that are heterogeneously investigated and managed due to lack of specific guidance.

The absence of specific clinical guidance for GI and nutritional management in hypermobility disorders raises concern that patients are at increased risk of iatrogenic harm from heterogeneous investigation and management, including polypharmacy.
GI symptoms, while common in both groups undergoing anorectal manometry for constipation, were significantly more frequent in patients with HSD/hEDS than in matched non-HSD/hEDS patients.

Resting and squeeze anal sphincter pressures, sensory thresholds, and abnormal balloon expulsion test rates measured by high-resolution anorectal manometry were comparable between HSD/hEDS and matched non-HSD/hEDS patients.
Median rectoanal pressure gradient during simulated defecation was significantly more negative in HSD/hEDS patients than in non-HSD/hEDS patients, indicating impaired defecatory dynamics.
HSD/hEDS patients showed significantly less anal sphincter relaxation (inadequate anal relaxation) during simulated defecation compared to controls.
Residual anal pressure during attempted defecation was significantly higher in HSD/hEDS patients compared to non-HSD/hEDS patients.
Rectal hyposensitivity was present in nearly 40% of HSD/hEDS patients, a rate comparable to the 36% observed in non-HSD/hEDS patients.
The rate of abnormal balloon expulsion test (~30%) was not significantly different between HSD/hEDS and non-HSD/hEDS patients.

Predictors of abnormal balloon expulsion differed by group: in HSD/hEDS higher resting sphincter pressure and higher maximum tolerated rectal volume were associated with abnormal BET, whereas in non-HSD/hEDS a more negative rectoanal gradient was the predictor.

Across all patients regardless of HSD/hEDS status, a higher rectoanal pressure gradient during simulated defecation and lower maximum tolerated rectal volume were determinants of normal (as opposed to abnormal) rectal balloon evacuation.

When stratified by group, lower resting anal pressure and lower maximum tolerated rectal volume were independent predictors of normal evacuation in HSD/hEDS patients, whereas higher rectoanal pressure gradient was the independent predictor in non-HSD/hEDS patients.

MR defecography showed no significant differences between HSD/hEDS and non-HSD/hEDS patients in resting/straining H and M lines or in degree of rectal, uterovaginal, or bladder prolapse, though numbers were small (36 studies reviewed).
Psychiatric and somatic disorders (including anxiety and depression) were significantly more prevalent among HSD/hEDS patients with pelvic floor complaints compared to non-HSD/hEDS patients.

A prior study of gastrointestinal manifestations in hEDS found that among 30 patients undergoing HR-ARM for constipation, 10 had elevated resting sphincter pressure and 18 were diagnosed with a rectal evacuation disorder.

At the specialised GoodHope EDS Clinic, fewer than 30% of patients referred for suspected EDS/generalised hypermobility spectrum disorder are ultimately diagnosed with the condition, despite wait times exceeding two years.
Based on historical clinical encounters at the study clinic, approximately 85% of patients assessed have a negative Beighton exam.

Because goniometer use is not standard practice among all clinicians, Beighton score assessment shows inaccurate measurements and higher inter-rater variability, contributing to diagnostic error in EDS/G-HSD.
EDS affects the synthesis and production of collagen cells, with documented medical implications for joints, muscles, soft tissue, and blood circulation.
EDS patients display multiple oral manifestations, including gingival recession, lack of attached gingiva, early severe periodontitis, and dental anomalies and dental caries.
The existing literature on prosthodontic, periodontal, and implant treatment of EDS patients is limited and often contradictory, precluding consensus treatment guidelines.
Two patients with Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome successfully received dental implants with prosthetic rehabilitation, one requiring bone augmentation.
EDS patients commonly display oral manifestations including gingival recession, lack of attached gingiva, early severe periodontal disease, and dental caries.
Existing literature on dental implants in EDS patients is described as limited and often contradictory.
A case of osteogenesis imperfecta/Ehlers-Danlos overlap syndrome (COL1-related disorder) is reported in a pregnant woman whose pregnancy was complicated by aortal dilatation.
Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is associated with a higher risk of pregnancy complications including organ ruptures such as uterine rupture and aortic dissection.
Among 45 baseball pitchers, the Load and Shift test classified 62.2% as having normal glenohumeral joints, 26.7% as hypermobile, and 11% as unstable.
Pitchers with normal shoulders reported significantly higher (better) function on the FAST than pitchers with hypermobile or unstable shoulders.
Pitchers with normal shoulders showed significantly higher function than pitchers with unstable shoulders on both the FAST and KJOC scales.
Pitchers with normal shoulders reported significantly less arm pain than pitchers with unstable and hypermobile shoulders on both the FAST and KJOC scales.
Pitchers with a prior history of arm injury reported significantly lower KJOC function scores than pitchers without such a history.
There was no statistically significant difference in FAST scores between pitchers with and without a history of arm injury.

Inter-rater reliability of the researchers performing the Load and Shift test compared to an experienced clinician was good (ICC .81 and .85), and the test has previously shown 84% diagnostic accuracy for labral tearing/instability versus MRI arthrogram.

Whole exome sequencing identified a novel homozygous frameshift variant in exon 17 of AEBP1, predicted to trigger nonsense-mediated decay, classified as pathogenic and confirmed by Sanger sequencing with heterozygous carrier status in both parents.
The patient showed generalized joint hypermobility with a Beighton score of 7/9, involving knees, back, and the first and fifth fingers bilaterally.
The patient exhibited markedly hyperextensible, dry, translucent skin with visible vasculature and atrophic, hemosiderotic, or cigarette-paper-like scars.

This case is the first report of multiple congenital defects (cleft palate, foot malformation, pectoral muscle agenesis/hypoplasia) occurring in a patient with AEBP1-related classical-like EDS type 2, expanding the known phenotypic spectrum.

The ACLP isoform of AEBP1 has been shown in prior functional studies to bind collagen types I, III, and V and to enhance the stiffness, toughness, and tensile strength of collagen type I fibers in vitro.

Histological and ultrastructural analyses in prior clEDS2 patients demonstrated decreased dermal collagen and variable collagen fibril diameters with abnormal (frayed/moth-eaten, collagen-flower) morphology.

ACLP positively modulates the TGF-beta pathway by binding TGF-beta receptor II, facilitating formation of the TbR-II/TbR-I receptor complex and downstream Smad2/3 phosphorylation, suggesting that ACLP deficiency in clEDS2 may perturb TGF-beta signaling important for connective tissue and craniofacial development.

Amniotic band sequence has been associated with vascular EDS (COL3A1-related), reported in 0.4% and 1.7% of vascular EDS cohorts in two studies, representing at least a six-fold increased risk compared to the general population.

The authors propose tentative clinical criteria for clEDS2 diagnosis: major classical EDS criteria (skin hyperextensibility, atrophic scarring, generalized joint hypermobility) plus at least two additional diagnostic handles (foot deformities, hair anomalies, progeroid hand/foot appearance, early-onset osteopenia/osteoporosis), supported by autosomal recessive inheritance.
Echocardiography showed only mild, hemodynamically insignificant valvular regurgitation (mitral, tricuspid, pulmonary) with systolic arching of the anterior mitral leaflet.
Unlike most other clEDS2 cases where early-onset osteopenia/osteoporosis is common, this 26-year-old patient's bone densitometry was within normal limits, possibly reflecting his younger age.

The right pectoralis muscle hypoplasia resembled the Poland anomaly (a disruptive sequence), while the left distal limb defects resembled amniotic band sequence, suggesting distinct disruptive/vascular mechanisms possibly linked to ACLP-mediated TGF-beta dysregulation rather than primary malformation.

The patient was found to carry a homozygous recurrent pathogenic FKBP14 variant (c.362dupC, p.(Glu122ArgfsTer7)), with both parents heterozygous carriers, diagnostic of kyphoscoliotic Ehlers-Danlos syndrome type 2 (FKBP14-kEDS).

A de novo 740 kb microduplication at chromosome 17p13.3 (arr[GRCh37] 17p13.3(390601_1131255)×3 dn) containing seven OMIM genes was identified via CGH array and considered pathogenic, occurring distally to the classic Miller-Dieker syndrome critical region.

At the molecular level, FKBP22 (encoded by FKBP14) is described as interacting with type III and type VI collagens, which are central to the pathophysiology of vascular EDS, supporting a plausible mechanism for vascular complications in FKBP14-kEDS.

Scoliosis, joint laxity, and hearing loss, all present in this patient, have only been reported in four prior chromosome 17p13.3 duplication syndrome patients, suggesting these features are more specifically attributable to the co-existing kEDS diagnosis than to the duplication alone.

Cardiovascular abnormalities are considered rare in 17p13.3 microduplication syndrome (only two aortic root dilations and one aortic stenosis reported in literature), in contrast to EDS where cardiovascular follow-up (aortic root/valve assessment, blood pressure monitoring) is a core management recommendation.

Among over 30 reported FKBP14-kEDS patients, vascular complications (arterial dissections in two adults and a pseudoaneurysm rupture in one child) have been described, suggesting the true incidence of vascular involvement in this subtype may be underrated given its recent discovery.
Fatigue, muscle hypotonia, (kypho)scoliosis, joint instability, and pain are described as major determinants of disability that significantly deteriorate quality of life in EDS patients.

Mutation of the zinc transporter ZIP13 causes the autosomal-recessive spondylocheiro dysplastic form of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (SCD-EDS), characterized by skin hyperplasia/weakening and small-joint hypermobility.

Zip13-knockout mice recapitulate SCD-EDS features, showing impaired cartilage development, growth retardation, kyphosis, osteopenia, craniofacial abnormalities, and reduced corneal/dermal stromal collagen.
ZIP13 dysfunction reduces zinc levels in the cytoplasm and endoplasmic reticulum, producing ER stress that contributes to dermal dysplasia.
A TGF-β–SMAD–ZIP13 signaling axis is required for normal dermal formation.

In ZIP13-knockout mice, nuclear translocation of SMAD transcription factors in the BMP/TGF-β pathway was reduced despite unchanged phosphorylation, impairing collagen-producing cell shape, cartilage size, chondrocyte differentiation, and collagen synthesis.
Restoring intracellular zinc homeostasis and clearing mutant ZIP13 protein via the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway are proposed therapeutic strategies for SCD-EDS.
Chaperone inhibitors DBeQ and 17AAG triggered buildup of pathogenic ZIP13 mutant protein and restored zinc homeostasis within cells, suggesting a possible SCD-EDS treatment approach.
Proteasome inhibitors MG-132 and lactacystin reversed pathogenic ZIP13 mutant characteristics but were toxic, activating pathways leading to cell death, limiting their therapeutic use.
ZIP7-knockout mice show reduced dermal and hypodermal thickness, indicating ZIP7 is required for connective tissue development.

Knockout of ZIP7 under a collagen-promoter Cre-Lox system produced connective tissue disorders similar to those seen in Zip13-knockout mice, indicating both transporters are equally necessary for collagen synthesis.
ZIP13-knockout cells show increased zinc levels in the Golgi apparatus alongside decreased nuclear zinc, indicating disrupted intracellular zinc homeostasis.

SCD-EDS/connective tissue disorder presents clinically with hyperplastic skin and articular hypermobility, plus wrinkled palms, short stature, tapered fingers, absent periorbital tissue, and antimongoloid slant.

Zinc concentration is higher in the upper dermis than the lower dermis, attributed to greater mast cell accumulation, which is rich in zinc needed for cytokine production and FcεRI-dependent degranulation.
Fibromyalgia prevalence in the US ranges from 6% to 15%, with women affected roughly five times more often than men.
Fibromyalgia patients require nearly 50% less stimulus intensity to elicit a pain response compared with healthy controls, reflecting central augmentation of sensory input.

A systematic review of 22 neuroimaging studies found voxel-based morphometry evidence of reduced gray matter in the anterior cingulate cortex and prefrontal cortex in FMS patients with moderate central sensitization, though global gray matter was unchanged.
Neuroimaging review found reduced functional connectivity in the descending pain-modulation system from the anterior cingulate cortex to the amygdala, hippocampus, and brainstem in FMS patients.
FMS patients show reduced blood serum serotonin levels compared with healthy controls, possibly related to altered GABA effects at the periaqueductal grey.

FMS patients showed a significant relationship between cortisol levels and pain at awakening and one hour after awakening compared with controls, and significantly higher overall, peak, and trough plasma cortisol compared with rheumatoid arthritis patients.
A 2003 study of beta-adrenergic receptor function on mononuclear cells in 8 FMS females versus 9 healthy females found diminished basal cAMP levels in FMS patients.
During static knee extension until exhaustion, FMS patients showed decreased plasma catecholamines and ACTH compared with healthy controls.
FMS patients show autonomic nervous system abnormalities including reduced microcirculatory responses to aural stimulation and attenuated vasoconstriction responses to cold pressor testing.

Transfer of IgG antibodies from patients with nociplastic pain syndromes into mice produced reduced locomotor activity, decreased strength, and loss of intraepidermal innervation, whereas IgG-depleted serum had no effect.
IgG binding to satellite glial cells correlated with fibromyalgia disease severity, suggesting potential for an anti-SGC antibody screening test.
After amitriptyline treatment, FMS patients showed increased regional cerebral blood flow in the thalamus and basal ganglia on SPECT imaging.
Kwiatek et al. observed reduced regional cerebral blood flow in the right thalamus, inferior dorsal pons, and vicinity of the right lentiform nucleus in FMS patients using SPECT.
Arterial spin labeling imaging in 23 FMS patients found significant reductions in basal ganglia perfusion.

PET imaging in 8 FMS patients versus controls showed greater resting regional cerebral blood flow bilaterally in the retrosplenial cortex but less rCBF in the left frontal, temporal, parietal, and occipital cortices.
An FDG-PET study comparing 12 FMS patients and 7 controls did not detect a change in glucose metabolism.
Walitt et al. demonstrated a link between improvement following a comprehensive treatment program and a rise in metabolic activity in limbic structures on FDG-PET.

PET imaging with radiolabeled carfentanil showed significantly lower overall mu-opioid receptor binding potential in FMS patients, most notably in the left amygdala, nucleus accumbens bilaterally, and a trend in the right dorsal ACC, suggesting receptor downregulation from endogenous opioid release.

fMRI in 9 FMS patients versus 9 controls showed significantly greater activity in insular, prefrontal, supplementary motor, and anterior cingulate cortices in response to nonpainful stimuli, and greater contralateral insular cortex activity in response to painful stimuli.
fMRI in 16 FMS patients versus 16 controls found the rostral anterior cingulate cortex, a key part of the descending pain regulating system, showed a diminished response to pain in FMS patients.

A follow-up study found reduced functional connectivity between the thalamus and orbitofrontal cortex, and among the bilateral hippocampi, amygdala, brainstem, and rostral ventromedial medulla in FMS patients compared with controls, regions involved in the pain inhibitory network.

Skin biopsies were diagnostic for small fiber polyneuropathy in 41% of FMS patients versus 3% of controls, suggesting some patients labeled as fibromyalgia have unrecognized or concurrent small fiber polyneuropathy.
Punch skin biopsies of calf and thigh in 41 FMS patients versus 47 controls showed significantly diminished epidermal nerve fiber density in both regions in the FMS group.

A case-control study of 25 FMS patients found reduced intraepidermal innervation with sparing of myelinated fibers and elevated cold and warm detection thresholds, indicating functional impairment of A-delta and C-fibers.
A 2019 meta-analysis of 8 studies (222 participants) found a pooled prevalence of small fiber pathology in fibromyalgia of 49% (95% CI 38-60%).
First-degree relatives of FMS patients are 8.5 times more likely to have the condition than first-degree relatives of rheumatoid arthritis patients, supporting familial aggregation.
Two large twin survey studies estimated the heritability of fibromyalgia at 48-54%.
A 2013 genome-wide linkage scan of 116 families from the Fibromyalgia Family Study estimated a sibling recurrence risk ratio of 13.6, further supporting FMS heritability.

A 2012 comparative genomic study of 496 FMS patients versus 348 pain-free controls found statistically significant differences in GABRB3, among other genes, with alterations to GABRB3 linked to thermal hyperalgesia, tactile allodynia, and attenuated analgesic response to GABA agonists.
The same genomic study found significant differences in TAAR1 in FMS patients versus controls; TAAR1 is thought to modulate dopaminergic activity though its role in FMS is not entirely clear.
The same genomic study found significant differences in GBP1, an interferon-inducible gene, in FMS versus controls, though its specific role in FMS remains unclear.
In a Spanish population study, the 'high pain sensitivity' ACCG haplotype of the COMT gene was associated with fibromyalgia.
In the same Spanish population study, inactivating MC1R variants were associated with increased opioid analgesia.

A large comparative genomic study using a Pain Research Panel gene array found statistically significant differences in GABRB3, TAAR1, and GBP1 gene variants between FMS patients and pain-free controls.
In a Spanish population, the 'high pain sensitivity' ACCG haplotype of the COMT gene was associated with FMS, and inactivating MC1R variants were associated with increased opioid analgesia.
Early life physical trauma and psychosocial stressors are proposed to alter gene expression and nociceptive circuitry, producing long-lasting increases in pain sensitivity in adulthood.

Altered gray and white matter morphometry in the medial orbitofrontal cortex and cerebellum has been observed in FMS patients, with gray matter volume linked to severity of both depression and hyperalgesia, consistent with a bidirectional temporal association between depression and FMS.

Loggia and colleagues found that unpleasant odors followed by heat stimulation disproportionately worsened perceived pain and discomfort in FMS patients compared to healthy controls, supporting a role for psychological/psychosocial stressors in amplifying pain.

A retrospective case-control study found that 39% of FMS patients reported significant physical trauma in the six months preceding symptom onset compared to 24% of hospital controls, supporting physical trauma as an environmental trigger for FMS.

A case series of female fibromyalgia patients given high-dose oral thiamine (600-1800 mg/day) reported significant symptomatic improvement after 20 days of therapy, though this has not been reliably replicated.

A meta-analysis of randomized trials found that meditative exercise programs may improve sleep quality in fibromyalgia patients, whose disordered sleep (nonrestorative sleep, insomnia, early morning awakenings) is linked to worsened pain symptoms.
Twenty percent (53/265) of fibromyalgia patients had reduced electrochemical skin conductance (ESC) values, suggesting small-fiber neuropathy is present in a substantial minority of FM patients.
Fibromyalgia patients with reduced ESC values (suggestive of small-fiber neuropathy) had higher Central Sensitization Inventory (CSI) scores than those with normal ESC.
Fibromyalgia patients with reduced ESC values had higher Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) scores than those without ESC abnormalities.
Fibromyalgia patients with reduced ESC values reported a larger intake of analgesic drugs than those with normal ESC.
Extreme central sensitization (CSI score ≥60) was present in 69% of the fibromyalgia patients studied.
Central sensitization was identified as one of the main determinants of ESC (small-fiber) abnormalities in fibromyalgia patients.

Central sensitization was associated with a higher Neuropathic Pain Symptom Inventory (NPSI) score in fibromyalgia patients, although central sensitization and NPSI scores were not themselves statistically correlated.

Electrochemical skin conductance abnormalities (small-fiber neuropathy) and neuropathic pain symptom scores were not directly correlated with each other, even though both were independently associated with central sensitization.

The authors conclude that central sensitization, rather than a direct link between small-fiber neuropathy and neuropathic pain, appears to underlie the association between small nerve fiber impairment and neuropathic pain features in fibromyalgia patients.
GC-MS plasma metabolomics with OPLS-DA showed clear separation between fibromyalgia/IEI-EMF patients and healthy controls, indicating a distinct systemic metabolic profile.
A combined panel of the 19 discriminant metabolites achieved good diagnostic accuracy for distinguishing IEI-EMF/fibromyalgia patients from healthy controls by ROC analysis.
Plasma 2-aminoisobutyrate was higher in IEI-EMF/fibromyalgia patients than in controls, possibly linked to gut microbiome alterations.
Plasma alanine was elevated in IEI-EMF/fibromyalgia patients compared to controls, consistent with increased gluconeogenic amino acid supply.
Plasma glucose was elevated in IEI-EMF/fibromyalgia patients compared to controls, consistent with insulin resistance previously described in FM.
Branched-chain amino acid leucine was elevated in IEI-EMF/fibromyalgia patients, part of a metabolic signature linked to insulin resistance.
Plasma lysine was elevated in IEI-EMF/fibromyalgia patients, potentially reflecting altered collagen turnover via lysine post-translational modifications.
Plasma proline was elevated in IEI-EMF/fibromyalgia patients, associated with altered collagen metabolism and prolidase activity.
Plasma serine was elevated in IEI-EMF/fibromyalgia patients, consistent with increased gluconeogenic amino acid pools.
Plasma threonine was elevated in IEI-EMF/fibromyalgia patients, a gluconeogenic amino acid and precursor of serine/glycine.
Plasma tyrosine was elevated in IEI-EMF/fibromyalgia patients, an unexpected finding contrasting with a prior study reporting reduced tyrosine in FM linked to impaired catecholamine synthesis.
Plasma urea was elevated in IEI-EMF/fibromyalgia patients, suggested to reflect increased urea cycle activity.
Branched-chain amino acid valine was elevated in IEI-EMF/fibromyalgia patients, part of the metabolic signature associated with insulin resistance.
Plasma ornithine was increased in IEI-EMF/fibromyalgia patients, interpreted as reflecting increased urea cycle activity and/or altered mitochondrial and collagen-related metabolism.

The leucine transamination metabolite 2-ketohydroxycaproic acid (2-hydroxyisocaproate) was reduced in IEI-EMF/fibromyalgia patients, consistent with prior 1H-NMR findings and possibly linked to muscle weakness.
Plasma 4-hydroxyproline (Hyp) was reduced in IEI-EMF/fibromyalgia patients, consistent with prior reports of altered collagen turnover in FM.
Plasma arabitol was reduced in IEI-EMF/fibromyalgia patients, speculatively linked to gut dysbiosis/SIBO or dietary polyol intake.
Plasma aspartic acid was reduced in IEI-EMF/fibromyalgia patients, consistent with increased urea cycle utilization and possibly altered excitatory neurotransmission.
Plasma ethanolamine was reduced in IEI-EMF/fibromyalgia patients, hypothesized to reflect increased consumption for anandamide synthesis or reduced FAAH-mediated anandamide degradation.
Plasma isoleucine was reduced in IEI-EMF/fibromyalgia patients, confirming a prior 1H-NMR finding and potentially linked to muscle weakness.
Plasma pyruvic acid was reduced in IEI-EMF/fibromyalgia patients, consistent with its consumption as a gluconeogenic substrate.

Pathway enrichment analysis of the discriminant metabolites identified tyrosine metabolism, pyruvate metabolism, amino sugar metabolism, cysteine metabolism, ammonia recycling, glycolysis, gluconeogenesis, and citric acid cycle as the most significantly perturbed pathways distinguishing IEI-EMF/fibromyalgia patients from controls.

IEI-EMF/fibromyalgia patients showed no significant differences from controls on clinical/psychological variables (depression, anxiety, anxiety-related disorders, emotional instability), with both groups under the clinical cut-off.
Adolescents with JFM reported a median Widespread Pain Index (WPI) score of 11 painful body sites out of a possible 18.
Adolescents with JFM had a median Symptom Severity (SS) score of 9 out of 12, reflecting a high burden of associated somatic symptoms.
Fatigue and nonrestorative sleep were prominent JFM features, rated as moderate to severe by 85% of adolescent participants.
Neurologic, autonomic, gastroenterologic, and psychological symptoms were frequently endorsed by adolescents with JFM.
Widespread Pain Index (WPI) scores were significantly correlated with pain intensity and pain catastrophizing among adolescents with JFM.
Symptom Severity (SS) scores were associated with pain intensity and with all domains of physical and psychological functioning in JFM.
Higher depressive symptom scores predicted greater severity of pain-related impairment in adolescents with juvenile fibromyalgia.
Fatigue severity predicted greater severity of pain-related impairment in adolescents with juvenile fibromyalgia.

Pain catastrophizing predicted greater severity of pain-related impairment in adolescents with juvenile fibromyalgia, highlighting the relative importance of psychological over pain-distribution factors.
FM patients showed a significant decrease in white matter volume in the left rostral anterior cingulate cortex and left lateral orbitofrontal cortex compared with controls.

Several studies found regional grey matter increases (orbitofrontal cortex, cerebellum, basal ganglia, cingulate cortex, insula) alongside decreases (superior temporal gyrus, thalamus, amygdala, periaqueductal grey) in FM patients.

FM patients had increased PAG connectivity with the insula, anterior cingulate cortex, and anterior prefrontal cortex, which correlated with pain severity, disease duration, and depressive personality trait, supporting endogenous pain modulatory system dysfunction.
A study analyzing subjective cognitive dysfunction (fibrofog), objective cognitive task performance, and brain activity via fMRI found no significant neurological correlates.
Model-driven fMRI analyses found no differences in pain processing between FM and healthy control datasets, whereas data-driven analyses identified significant group differences in both datasets.
fMRI studies demonstrated increased brain activity in the insula, cerebellum, amygdala and thalamus of FM patients, with cerebellar activation correlating with catastrophizing scores.
Decreased brainstem activity was found in FM patients, suggesting an altered central pain regulatory system.

FM patients with the TSPO high-affinity binding genotype showed more pronounced pain-evoked functional connectivity in the right frontoparietal network between dorsolateral prefrontal area and parietal cortex.
Resting-state fMRI in FM patients showed atypically increased frequency power during rest in pain-related brain regions.

FM patients showed significant differences in brainstem/spinal cord network connectivity compared to healthy controls, correlating with subjective pain response differences; temporal summation of second pain (TSSP) studies also showed altered brainstem BOLD activity possibly due to deficient pain modulation.

Proton MRS showed increased glutamate levels in the posterior cingulate cortex of FM patients, suggesting a molecular role for glutamate in disease processes; pharmacological reduction of glutamatergic levels was reported to improve symptomatology.

18F-FDG PET showed a hypometabolic pattern in cortical and subcortical areas in FM patients with pain-related non-dermatomal somatosensory deficits, though not directly correlated with pain or depression indexes.
In 18 treatment-naive FM subjects, metabolism in the thalamus, lentiform nucleus, and parahippocampal gyrus was associated with prognosis.
One study found no significant differences in 18F-FDG uptake between FM patients and controls across all measured brain structures.

After cold exposure (19°C), blood pressure and BAT activity increased in healthy controls but not in FM patients, and circulating glucose was lower in FM subjects, indicating impaired sympathetic responses to stress in FM.
18F-FDG PET monitoring of FM patients after multidisciplinary rehabilitation showed an increase in limbic metabolism with concomitant symptomatic improvement.

A double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled study found that repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) improved quality of life in FM patients with a concomitant increase in right limbic glucose metabolism on 18F-FDG PET.
Semiquantitative PET analysis revealed reductions in 18F-DOPA uptake in several brain regions of FM patients, indicating disrupted presynaptic dopamine activity relevant to natural analgesia.

A positive correlation was demonstrated between an index of ventral tegmental area dopamine metabolism and grey matter density in bilateral parahippocampal gyri and left pregenual cortex in FM patients.
The MORE intervention was reported to restore dopamine function, reduce pain, and improve mood symptoms in FM patients as measured by 18F-DOPA biodistribution.

A comparative study between FM patients with and without comorbid depression found differences in D2/D3 receptor availability in striatal regions (left ventral striatum, left caudate nucleus, left nucleus accumbens) and in clinical indices between the groups.

During a painful hypertonic saline task, control subjects released dopamine in the basal ganglia correlating with perceived pain, but this dopamine release was not observed in FM patients, who found the stimulus more painful.

Self-reported spontaneous pain negatively correlated with 18F-fallypride distribution at baseline in the left orbitofrontal cortex and parahippocampal gyrus in FM patients, and imaging correlated with experimental pain sensitivity/tolerance in both groups.

18F-flumazenil PET found decreased grey matter in FM associated with T1 relaxation times (water content) but not GABA receptor concentration, while regional grey matter increases were partly explained by GABA receptor concentration, suggesting neuronal plasticity.

A flumazenil PET study in post-menopausal FM women reported increased pain sensitivity, impaired immediate memory, and increased cortical GABAA receptor concentration in attention and default-mode networks, positively correlated with functional scores and current pain.

Abnormal 11C-(R)-PK11195 uptake, a marker of neuroinflammation via TSPO binding on activated microglia/astrocytes, was described in the brains of FM patients relative to patients with complex regional pain syndrome.

In an exploratory, uncorrected analysis, higher subjective fatigue ratings in FM patients were associated with higher 11C-PBR28 SUVRs in the anterior and posterior middle cingulate cortices, suggesting glial modulation in FM pathophysiology.

In a small group of 5 FM patients, NK cell activity was negatively correlated with right hemisphere activity in somatosensory/motor cortices and thalamus, and bilaterally with posterior cingulate cortex activity, suggesting a link between immune parameters and pain/emotion/attention brain regions.

PET with 11C-carfentanil revealed decreased central mu-opioid receptor availability in FM patients within regions involved in pain modulation, including the nucleus accumbens, amygdala, and dorsal cingulate.
A study using the opioid receptor ligand 18F-FEDPN found reduced cortical opioid receptor availability in FM patients, supporting a central nervous system contribution to pain.

PET imaging of cerebral blood flow during occipital nerve field stimulation ON vs OFF conditions showed activation of the descending pain inhibitory and lateral pain pathways, with EEG showing activation of related cortical areas.
Pain catastrophising scores were weakly negatively correlated with soft tissue elasticity (strain elastography) at the non-dominant lateral epicondyle in women with fibromyalgia.
Kinesiophobia (fear of movement) scores were positively correlated with soft tissue elasticity at the dominant lateral epicondyle in women with fibromyalgia.
Kinesiophobia scores were negatively correlated with soft tissue elasticity at the non-dominant knee in women with fibromyalgia.
Kinesiophobia scores were positively correlated with soft tissue elasticity at the dominant forearm in women with fibromyalgia.
Self-efficacy scores were negatively correlated with soft tissue elasticity at the non-dominant supraspinatus origin in women with fibromyalgia.
Self-efficacy scores were negatively correlated with soft tissue elasticity at the non-dominant medial epicondyle in women with fibromyalgia.

Beyond the six significant point-specific correlations, no significant associations were found between pain catastrophising, kinesiophobia, self-efficacy and elastography values at the remaining measured myofascial trigger points.
A case is reported of fosfomycin triggering confirmed mast cell activation resulting in anaphylaxis.
The review states that MCAS is observed more frequently in people with POTS and hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
SIBO was observed to often coexist with MCAS according to the review.
MCAS is classified into primary, secondary and idiopathic subtypes based on detection of the D816V mutation in the KIT gene.
Hereditary alpha-tryptasemia, caused by replications of the TPSAB1 gene, leads to higher baseline serum tryptase (usually >8 ng/mL) and a symptom spectrum overlapping MCAS.

Per Valent et al.'s criteria cited in the review, MCAS diagnosis requires a rise in serum tryptase above baseline according to the formula baseline x1.2 + 2, measured once asymptomatically and once after an anaphylactic episode.
Eosinophilic esophagitis is reported to be more prevalent among patients with connective tissue disorders featuring hypermobility, such as hEDS or hypermobile spectrum disorder.
IL-5, along with eotaxin-1 and α4β7 integrin, is described as the most important cytokine attracting eosinophils in eosinophilic gastrointestinal inflammation.

A proposed 'local food allergy' concept suggests increased mast cell accumulation and mediator release in colonic tissue drives visceral hypersensitivity as the main mechanism in IBS, with IgE detectable only locally rather than in blood or skin tests.

Confocal laser endomicroscopy of duodenal tissue from IBS patients exposed to food components showed increased eosinophil activation and disrupted intestinal barrier integrity, indicating a nonclassical food allergy mechanism.
The review notes that MCAS and histamine intolerance may co-exist or be mutually misdiagnosed due to a lack of good diagnostic tools for either condition.

A meta-analysis of trials (25 oral, 5 sublingual, 1 epicutaneous immunotherapy) found significant desensitization effect (RR=0.16, 95% CI 0.10-0.26) and suggested sustained unresponsiveness (RR=0.29, 95% CI 0.08-1.13).
In the Canadian Healthy Infant Longitudinal Development cohort, higher gut microbial richness at 3 months was associated with a 55% reduced risk of food sensitization by age 1 year.
In food-sensitized infants, Bacteroidaceae was under-represented and Enterobacteria over-represented in gut composition compared to healthy controls.
Sampson et al. found SPT and RAST had good negative predictive accuracy (82-100%) but poor positive predictive value (25-75% for SPT, 0-57% for RAST) in a DBPCFC study of children with skin allergy.
Eosinophilic esophagitis is present in up to 8% of patients with PPI-refractory gastroesophageal reflux disease.
Per Prasad et al., approximately 10% of patients with EE-related dysphagia show no visible endoscopic mucosal changes, underscoring the need for biopsy even in normal-appearing mucosa.
The empiric six-food elimination diet produces histological remission in 70-80% of eosinophilic esophagitis patients.
Among biologics studied for EE, dupilumab (anti-IL-4Rα) showed sufficient clinical efficacy, whereas omalizumab and mepolizumab reduced mucosal eosinophil counts but did not alleviate symptoms.
α-Gal syndrome is a tick-bite-induced IgE-mediated allergy causing delayed (3-6 hour) reactions to red meat/innards, and patients may also react to cetuximab or rarely infliximab.
Secondary Staphylococcus aureus infection significantly increased mast cell activation during initial influenza A H1N1 infection, both in vivo and in vitro.
Secondary S. aureus infection suppressed autophagy in mast cells while promoting release of inflammatory mediators.
The PI3K/Akt signaling pathway was activated in mast cells during secondary bacterial infection, driving autophagy suppression and inflammatory mediator release.
Blocking the PI3K/Akt pathway with the inhibitor LY294002 rescued autophagy and inhibited inflammatory mediator release from mast cells.

In a mouse model of influenza A viral and secondary bacterial co-infection, combined treatment with LY294002 and oseltamivir reduced inflammatory lung damage and pro-inflammatory cytokine release, and improved body weight recovery and survival.
Serum PTX3 concentrations were significantly higher in shrimp extract-challenged (allergic) mice than in control mice on day 30 of hypersensitization.
Total serum IgE was substantially increased in shrimp-allergic mice compared with control mice.
PTX3 immunoreactivity was elevated in the upper region of small intestinal villi and lumen of shrimp-allergic mice after challenge compared with controls.
PTX3 pretreatment enhanced histamine release and β-hexosaminidase activity (degranulation markers) in IgE/DNP-stimulated RBL-2H3 mast cells.
PTX3 significantly enhanced mRNA levels of TNF-α, IL-4, IL-6, and IL-13, and marginally activated COX-2, in IgE/DNP-stimulated RBL-2H3 cells.
PTX3 treatment had no effect on the proliferation of RBL-2H3 mast cells.
PTX3 had no effect on increasing de novo-synthesized FcεRI mRNA in RBL-2H3 cells.
PTX3 enhanced phosphorylation/activation of Akt, ERK1/2, p38, and JNK1/2 in IgE-stimulated RBL-2H3 cells.
PTX3 serum levels positively correlated with IgE levels in shrimp extract-sensitized mice (Spearman r=0.8601, p=0.0003).
PTX3 serum levels positively correlated with IgE levels in tropomyosin peptide-sensitized mice (Spearman r=0.7972, p=0.0019).
Sensitization with short hypoallergenic tropomyosin peptide fragments attenuated shrimp extract-induced hypersensitization in mice.
Loss of Cebpd in knockout mice suppressed shrimp extract-induced total IgE in serum compared to wild-type.
PTX3 concentration remained significantly elevated during hypersensitization in Cebpd-/- mice, suggesting PTX3 is not regulated by CEBPD in this allergy model.
PTX3 treatment significantly increased CEBPD mRNA and protein levels in RBL-2H3 mast cells, and CEBPD induction was further enhanced by IgE/DNP stimulation plus PTX3, or by allergic serum.
CEBPD knockdown (shCEBPD) attenuated PTX3-induced production of proinflammatory mediators and β-hexosaminidase release, indicating CEBPD mediates PTX3-driven mast cell degranulation.
The PTX3 inhibitor RI37 peptide significantly attenuated PTX3-induced degranulation (histamine and β-hexosaminidase) in IgE/Ag-activated RBL-2H3 cells without cytotoxicity.
RI37 suppressed PTX3-increased mRNA levels of TNF-α, IL-4, IL-6, IL-13, and COX-2, and inhibited PTX3- or allergic serum-induced Akt/MAPK signaling and CEBPD expression in RBL-2H3 cells.
In vivo, RI37 co-treatment significantly attenuated IgE abundance in shrimp-allergic mice compared to shrimp extract alone, but had no effect on IgE in non-allergic control mice.
IL-6 and COX-2 mRNA expression showed no significant change in RBL-2H3 cells treated with serum from shrimp extract- or tropomyosin peptide-sensitized mice, unlike TNF-α, IL-4, and IL-13.
The REMAs scoring model showed higher diagnostic accuracy and rate of correctly classified patients for mast cell clonality than the NICAS model.
REMAs performed better than NICAS particularly among male patients.
REMAs outperformed NICAS particularly among patients with systemic mastocytosis.
REMAs was more accurate than NICAS for patients presenting anaphylaxis with urticaria.
REMAs was more accurate than NICAS for patients presenting cardiovascular symptoms during anaphylaxis.
REMAs was more accurate than NICAS for patients presenting presyncope during anaphylaxis.
REMAs performed better than NICAS in patients with a blood-negative but bone-marrow-positive KIT mutational profile.
REMAs advantage over NICAS was not observed in patients with hereditary alpha-tryptasemia-associated genotypes.
The REMAs did not show superior performance over the NICAS specifically among patients with hereditary alpha-tryptasemia-associated genotypes.
Combining the REMAs score with blood detection of KIT D816V improved overall classification efficiency for mast cell clonality to 86%, compared with 84% for REMAs alone.
The authors conclude that combined use of the REMAs and blood detection of KIT D816V is recommended, but more sensitive blood-based molecular assays for KIT D816V are still needed.
Metformin treatment reduced mast cell activation and airway resistance in rats with concomitant type 2 diabetes and asthma.
Metformin downregulated IR and IGF-1R expression through DNMT1-dependent promoter methylation, thereby repressing mast cell activation and airway resistance.
DNMT1 was identified as a direct target gene of miR-152-3p, validated by luciferase reporter and RNA immunoprecipitation assays.
Metformin blocked miR-152-3p-induced silencing of DNMT1, thereby restraining mast cell activation and airway resistance.
Chromatin immunoprecipitation showed DNMT1 binds to the promoters of IR and IGF-1R, indicating direct epigenetic regulation of these receptors.
Infliximab treatment significantly reduced sarcoidosis inflammatory activity as measured by FDG-PET SUVmax.
Overall, infliximab treatment did not significantly change small fiber neuropathy-related symptom scores (SFNSL) from start to end of treatment.
Change in FDG-PET SUVmax (inflammatory activity) did not correlate with change in SFNSL symptom score during infliximab treatment.
Despite no overall group effect, half of the patients showed a clinically relevant improvement (>3.5 points) in SFNSL score during infliximab treatment.
The time elapsed did not correlate with the magnitude of SFNSL score change during treatment.
Small fiber neuropathy is highly prevalent among sarcoidosis patients and contributes to poor health-related quality of life.
SFN patients showed a global reduction of resting-state functional connectivity compared with matched controls, primarily involving limbic and somatosensory brain systems.
Lower functional connectivity was associated with greater skin nerve degeneration, as measured by reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber density, in SFN patients.
Structural connectivity (diffusion-weighted MRI) was robustly reduced among limbic, somatosensory, and cognition-integration areas including the inferior parietal lobule in SFN patients.
Both structural and functional connectivity were reduced between the middle cingulate cortex and the inferior parietal lobule in SFN patients.
Both structural and functional connectivity were reduced between the thalamus and putamen in SFN patients, indicating shared striatal-limbic dysconnectivity.

Both structural and functional connectivity between the thalamus and putamen were reduced in SFN patients, indicating shared involvement of striatal-thalamic circuitry alongside limbic and somatosensory dysconnectivity.
Patients with small-fiber neuropathy had significantly lower intraepidermal nerve fiber density compared with healthy controls.
Patients with small-fiber neuropathy had significantly lower heart rate variability in both time and frequency domains compared with control subjects.
SFN patients showed lower cold detection thresholds and higher warm detection thresholds compared with controls, consistent with small sensory fiber impairment.
The proportion of patients with abnormal QSART results did not differ significantly between SFN patients and control subjects.
SFN patients showed a drop in diastolic BP upon standing whereas controls showed a minor rise, a significant between-group difference.
SFN patients and controls had comparable drops in systolic BP upon standing, and an equal number in each group (n=4) met orthostatic hypotension criteria.
Patients with SFN scored significantly higher on the COMPASS-31 questionnaire across all autonomic domains compared with controls.
No significant differences in vascular skin response (reduction in microvascular skin blood flow and latency) were seen between SFN patients and controls as measured by laser Doppler flowmetry.
SFN patients and controls did not differ in neural length density, vessel length density, or number of neurovascular contacts in skin biopsies.
There were no significant correlations between neurovascular, vascular, and intraepidermal nerve fiber density parameters across subjects.
Patients with SFN had higher body mass index, higher resting heart rate, and higher Utah Early Neuropathy Scale scores than controls.
Diabetic neuropathy, the most frequently described neuropathy in the reviewed literature, involves mitochondrial dysfunction including oxidative stress and inflammation.
Microvascular changes seen in diabetes and vasculitis lead to ischemia with secondary oxidative stress and inflammation contributing to peripheral neuropathy.
Structural changes in neurons and glial cells with abnormalities in neurotrophic factors were observed in the reviewed peripheral neuropathy literature.
Neuropathy induced by autoantibodies or immunological mechanisms is described in infectious and systemic inflammatory diseases.
Several ion channels may be involved in painful neuropathy, suggesting a channelopathy mechanism.
No study identified in the review explained why some patients develop predominantly large fiber neuropathy while others develop small fiber neuropathy.
Bloating and visceral sensitivity, which distinguished IBS from healthy controls, were negatively associated with abundance of beneficial gut microbes and with orbitofrontal cortex connectivity.
IBS symptom duration was linked to specific key microbes and caudate connectivity, suggesting a mechanistic contribution to pain chronicity in IBS.
IBS-D subjects showed higher fecal/metabolomic levels of tryptophan compared to IBS-C and healthy controls.
IBS-D subjects showed higher levels of phenylalanine compared to IBS-C and healthy controls.

IBS-D subjects had increased functional connectivity between the sensorimotor and default mode networks compared to IBS-C and healthy controls, suggested to reflect a 'bottom-up' brain-gut mechanism influencing diarrhea, self-related thoughts, and pain perception.
IBS-C subjects' microbiome and metabolome profiles resembled those of healthy controls, unlike IBS-D.

Compared to IBS-D, IBS-C had increased connectivity in the default mode and salience networks, interpreted as reflecting a more 'top-down' brain-gut-microbiome pathophysiology involving visceral signal processing.
Unbiased CellChat signaling analysis of soft palate scRNAseq data found TGF-β signaling activity to be the highest among tested pathways in perimysial cells.

Tgfbi, a known TGF-β downstream target, was identified as one of the top 10 conserved marker genes of perimysial cells across developmental stages, linking TGF-β signaling to perimysial cell identity.
In vivo, TGF-β signaling readout pSmad2 was present in palatal shelf mesenchyme from E12.5 and was most active specifically in perimysial cells surrounding LVP myogenic cells at E13.5 and E14.5.
Conditional loss of TGF-β type 1 receptor Tgfbr1 in palatal mesenchyme (Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl) caused deformed, cleft palatal shelves and complete absence of detectable LVP muscle fibers at E18.5.
In Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl mice, myogenic cell defects appeared as early as E13.5, preceding any detectable morphological defect in the palatal mesenchyme itself.
In E14.5 Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl soft palates, perimysial fibroblast markers Tbx15 and Smoc2 were reduced relative to controls, while the Aldh1a2+ perimysial progenitor subpopulation was unaffected.

Among perimysial-fibroblast-enriched ligands, Fgf18 and Lama4 expression were reduced in Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl perimysial cells, whereas Dlk1 expression was unaffected, implicating TGF-β signaling as a regulator of Fgf18/Lama4.
Fgf18 expression was reduced in Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl mice as early as E13.5, before palatal mesenchymal defects appeared, and its loss correlated with reduced Myod1+ myogenic cells through E16.5.

Fgfr4 expression is enriched specifically in Myf5+/Pax7+ myogenic progenitor cells, but not in more differentiated Myog+/Myl1+ myogenic cells, positioning Fgfr4 as the likely receptor for perimysial Fgf18.

Cut and Run assay confirmed significantly greater Smad2/3 binding at a predicted transcription factor binding site in the Fgf18 promoter compared to IgG control, demonstrating direct Smad2/3-Fgf18 promoter interaction.
TGF-β1 treatment (5 ng/ml) of E14.5 soft palatal mesenchymal cell cultures significantly increased Fgf18 expression at 4 hours, with a smaller increase remaining at 18 hours.

CRISPRi-mediated blocking of the Smad2/3 binding site in the Fgf18 promoter significantly attenuated the TGF-β1-induced increase in Fgf18 expression compared with control CRISPRi plasmid, confirming functional requirement of this site.

SCENIC gene regulatory network analysis and in vivo expression showed Creb5 is a perimysial-fibroblast-enriched transcription factor, expressed similarly to Fgf18 and TGF-β signaling activity from E13.5 onward.

siRNA knockdown of Creb5 in soft palatal mesenchymal cell cultures reduced Fgf18 expression and significantly attenuated the TGF-β1-induced increase in Fgf18, indicating Creb5 cooperates with TGF-β signaling to activate Fgf18.

Osr2Cre;Fgf18fl/fl mice showed no palatal shelf formation defect at birth, but had significantly smaller soft palatal (LVP) muscles, with reduced cross-sectional area and muscle volume compared to controls.

Loss of Fgf18 (Osr2Cre;Fgf18fl/fl) significantly reduced the proliferation rate of Myf5+ myogenic progenitor cells in the LVP region at E14.5, without increasing apoptosis, leading to progressively fewer myogenic cells by E16.5.

Direct FGF18 treatment (500 ng/ml) of C2C12 myoblasts significantly increased proliferation rate within 1 day and total cell number by 3 days, confirming a direct pro-proliferative effect of FGF18 on myogenic cells.

Implanting FGF18-soaked beads (versus BSA beads) into cultured Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl LVP tissue slices increased the number of MyoD+ myogenic cells, partially rescuing the TGF-β-signaling-deficient myogenic defect.
Honokiol and hexafluoro-honokiol significantly increased neuronal fiber density (differentiation) in primary myenteric neurons compared to vehicle.
Honokiol and hexafluoro-honokiol increased the number of nNOS-positive neurons in primary myenteric cultures.
Honokiol and hexafluoro-honokiol increased nNOS mRNA expression in primary myenteric neurons relative to vehicle.
Honokiol and hexafluoro-honokiol increased choline acetyltransferase (ChAT) mRNA expression in primary myenteric neurons.
Palmitate (PA) plus LPS non-significantly reduced nNOS-positive neuron numbers, and this reduction was reversed by hexafluoro-honokiol co-treatment in primary myenteric neurons.
In IM-FEN cells, PA+LPS alone increased nNOS protein, and this was further increased when hexafluoro-honokiol was combined with PA and LPS.
Honokiol and hexafluoro-honokiol increased SIRT3 protein expression in IM-FEN cells compared with vehicle.
Honokiol and hexafluoro-honokiol increased SIRT3 mRNA levels in primary myenteric neurons relative to vehicle control.
SIRT3 expression was significantly decreased in both male and female mice fed a 12-week high-fat diet compared to regular diet.

SIRT3 knockdown via siRNA abolished hexafluoro-honokiol's ability to suppress PA+LPS-induced mitochondrial superoxide (MitoSOX) release in IM-FEN cells, whereas hexafluoro-honokiol was protective in control siRNA-transfected cells.
Hexafluoro-honokiol significantly decreased cleaved caspase-1 expression, suppressing pyroptosis induced by palmitate plus LPS in IM-FEN cells.

A prior DNBS-colitis mouse model study found that SIRT3 deletion or inhibition did not increase oxidative damage in myenteric neurons compared to wildtype, contrasting with the present study's finding that SIRT3 is necessary for antioxidant protection under PA/LPS stress.

Endothelial cell proliferation (Ki-67 positivity) was significantly higher in both clinically unaffected (DUF) and affected (DAF) palmar fascia of Dupuytren's disease patients compared to control palmar fascia, with the highest proliferation in DAF.
Vascular smooth muscle and connective tissue cell proliferation in the flexor retinaculum of carpal tunnel syndrome patients did not differ significantly from control palmar fascia.
FGFR1 protein expression in blood vessel walls and connective tissue cells was significantly higher in both DUF and DAF Dupuytren's disease samples compared to control palmar fascia.
No significant difference in FGFR1 expression in blood vessels or connective tissue was found between carpal tunnel syndrome flexor retinaculum and control palmar fascia.
FGFR2 expression in blood vessels and connective tissue was significantly lower in carpal tunnel syndrome flexor retinaculum compared to control palmar fascia.
FGFR2 expression in blood vessels and connective tissue was significantly higher in DUF and DAF Dupuytren's disease samples than in controls, with no difference between DUF and DAF.

CTGF expression in blood vessels was significantly increased across CTS, DUF, and DAF samples compared to control, and was higher in connective tissue of DUF and DAF than control, with DUF showing higher levels than DAF.

Syndecan-1 expression was significantly higher in the secretory portions of eccrine sweat glands in DAF Dupuytren's disease samples compared to healthy control skin, while duct expression did not differ significantly between groups.

Proliferation of luminal and myoepithelial cells in the secretory portions of eccrine sweat glands was significantly increased in DAF Dupuytren's disease samples compared to healthy control skin, while duct proliferation did not differ significantly.
FGFR1 expression was significantly higher in both secretory portions and ducts of eccrine sweat glands in DAF Dupuytren's disease samples compared to healthy controls.
FGFR2 expression was significantly higher in both secretory portions and ducts of eccrine sweat glands in DAF Dupuytren's disease samples compared to healthy controls.
CTGF expression was significantly higher in both secretory portions and ducts of eccrine sweat glands in DAF Dupuytren's disease samples compared to healthy controls.

TGF-β1 expression was significantly higher in both secretory portions and ducts of eccrine sweat glands in DAF Dupuytren's disease samples compared to healthy controls, with the largest increase seen in ducts.
The authors note that increased FGFR1 mRNA in Dupuytren's disease tissue had been previously reported, but the current study is the first to describe the protein-level distribution.

The authors propose that profibrotic signaling molecules (FGFR1, FGFR2, CTGF) are elevated in clinically unaffected fascia adjacent to fibrotic cords, sometimes at higher levels than in the fibrotic cords themselves, suggesting these molecules prime tissue for future fibrosis and may explain high relapse rates after surgery.
Inactivating mutations in RET are described as the most common known cause of Hirschsprung disease, a condition defined by loss of enteric neurons in the distal gut.

The authors generated and validated a new zebrafish BAC transgenic line, TgBAC(ret:EGFP)b1331, expressing GFP under the ret promoter, which follows Mendelian transmission consistent with a single genomic integration.
In situ hybridization comparison of ret and gfp mRNA expression at 48, 72, and 96 hpf showed comparable expression patterns, indicating gfp expression reflects endogenous ret expression in the ENS.
At 60 hpf, GFP+ enteric progenitor cells (EPCs) were observed migrating along the developing gut in two parallel streams, confirming ret expression in migrating EPCs.
At 5 dpf, 73.2 ± 3.2% of GFP+ cells colocalized with the pan-neuronal marker Elavl, showing that the majority of ret:GFP-expressing cells in the larval ENS are neurons.
In the posterior gut region at 5 dpf, there were significantly fewer GFP+ ENS neurons compared to the anterior-mid region.
At 7 dpf, GFP+ ENS neurons were evenly distributed along the gut with no significant regional differences, suggesting the anterior-posterior differentiation gradient evens out by this stage.

The majority of nitrergic (nNOS+) and serotonergic (5-HT+) enteric neurons are GFP+ in the ret:GFP line, evenly distributed along the gut, confirming a broad role of Ret in regulating diverse neuronal subtypes.
GFP colocalizes with EdU (a marker of S-phase proliferation) across the length of the gut at 5 dpf, indicating that ret:GFP+ cells include proliferating enteric progenitor cells at larval stages.
In adult zebrafish, a smaller percentage of ENS neurons are GFP+ compared to larval stages, ranging from an average of 12.3% to 47.5% depending on gut region.
No significant sex difference was found in the proportion of GFP+ ENS neurons between adult male and female zebrafish across three gut regions.

In homozygous ret (hu2846) or sox10 (t3) mutant zebrafish, GFP+ ENS neurons were completely absent, though GFP+ enteroendocrine cells remained, confirming that ret:GFP ENS expression depends on ret and sox10 gene function.
Myrrh resin extract at 100 µg/mL reduced the metabolic activity (viability) of RBL-2H3 cells, indicating cytotoxicity at this concentration.
None of the three plant extracts affected β-hexosaminidase or histamine release from RBL-2H3 cells stimulated with the chemical agents PMA plus calcium ionophore (CI).
Myrrh resin extract reduced IgE-stimulated β-hexosaminidase release from RBL-2H3 cells to 64.3% of stimulated control.
Chamomile flower extract reduced IgE-stimulated β-hexosaminidase release from RBL-2H3 cells to 80.4% of stimulated control, an effect attributed to its flavonoid content (e.g., apigenin).
Myrrh resin extract showed a concentration-dependent inhibition of IgE-induced β-hexosaminidase release, reaching 64.3% of control at 50 µg/mL with an IC50 of 12.12 µg/mL.
Coffee charcoal extract had no effect on IgE-stimulated mediator release (β-hexosaminidase or histamine) from RBL-2H3 cells.
Chamomile flower extract at 100 µg/mL reduced histamine release from IgE-stimulated RBL-2H3 cells, likely via its flavonoid content (apigenin, luteolin).

Unlike its effect on β-hexosaminidase, myrrh resin extract did not significantly reduce histamine release from IgE-stimulated RBL-2H3 cells, suggesting mediator-specific (granule-heterogeneity-dependent) inhibition.

A cited randomized, placebo-controlled trial found that ketotifen significantly improved IBS symptoms (diarrhea, discomfort, pain) and quality of life in diarrhea-predominant IBS patients, and decreased spontaneous mast-cell mediator release.
A cited study in HMC-1 human mast cells found Commiphora myrrha extract reduced histamine release and IL-31 production, supporting the mast-cell-inhibitory mechanism proposed for myrrh.
Two months after acute SARS-CoV-2 infection, PCS patients had lymphocyte counts below reference healthy values.
Total leukocyte and neutrophil counts in PCS patients two months post-infection did not differ from reference healthy values.
Neutrophil oxygen-independent phagocytic efficiency was reduced in PCS patients, with a 20% decrease in the endocytosis completion index versus reference values.
Spontaneous (unstimulated) ROS-producing oxygen-dependent phagocytosis was elevated 3.7-fold in PCS patients versus reference values, with no further increase upon zymosan stimulation.
A high incidence of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs), absent in healthy donors, was observed in PCS patients and is proposed to drive additional DAMP production.
CRP was elevated 8-fold in PCS patients compared to reference values, consistent with prolonged inflammation.
Serum complement component C3 was doubled in PCS patients relative to reference values.
Serum complement component C4 was elevated 1.5-fold in PCS patients relative to reference values.
Serum TNF-alpha was elevated 3-fold in PCS patients versus reference values, contrasting with reports that TNF-alpha did not exceed reference levels in acute infection.
Serum IL-6 was 15-fold higher in PCS patients (30.2 pg/ml) than the reference level (2.0 pg/ml).
Anti-inflammatory IL-10 was elevated 2-fold in PCS patients versus reference values.
IL-18 was significantly and highly variably elevated (400-2500 pg/ml) compared to reference values (261.0-360.3 pg/ml) in patients with comorbid abdominal pathology and PCS.

Spectrophotometric analysis of PCS patient serum showed reduced oligopeptide absorbance (238 nm, -23%) but increased peptide (254 nm, +33%), nucleotide (260 nm, +30%), and aromatic amino acid (280 nm, +55%) fractions versus reference values, suggesting mitochondrial dysfunction.
PCS patient serum showed 2.4-fold higher complement-dependent lymphocytotoxicity against autologous lymphocytes than reference serum in the Terasaki test.

PCS patient serum showed a 5.8-fold higher integral cytotoxicity coefficient in a cross-kingdom Dunaliella viridis microalgae assay compared to healthy serum, indicating non-species-specific cytotoxic DAMPs.
All 16 PCS patients had detectable autoantibodies against a broad range of nuclear, cytoskeletal, and aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase antigens, indicating autoimmune activation as part of PCS.
Injecting rats with serum from PCS patients induced a rise in body temperature (1.5-2.5°C), body weight loss, and mild diarrhea, reproducing PCS-like physiological manifestations.
Rats injected with PCS patient serum showed increased leukocytes (+59%), lymphocytes (+51%), granulocytes (+76%), and monocytes (~2-fold) compared to saline-injected controls.
In rats, MF alone (without PCS serum) did not alter leukocyte/lymphocyte counts but increased granulocytes by 59% and monocytes by 120% versus control, indicating an immunotropic effect.
Rats injected with PCS patient serum showed 2.8-fold higher lymphocytotoxicity than controls; preventive MF administration reduced this by 20% (though still 2-fold above control).

Serum from rats injected with PCS patient serum showed a 30-35% higher integral cytotoxicity coefficient on D. viridis than control rat serum, confirming non-species-specific transfer of cytotoxic DAMPs, with preventive MF administration further increasing this effect.

MF administration alone increased complement C3 by 50% and C4 by 75% in rats compared to control; PCS serum alone raised C3/C4 to a lesser extent, and preventive MF before PCS serum inhibited C3 activation while further increasing C4.

MF alone increased CIC 2.4-fold in rats; PCS serum alone increased CIC by only 50%; MF pretreatment before PCS serum resulted in no significant change in CIC versus control, suggesting enhanced clearance.

Rats injected with PCS patient serum showed impaired phagocytic function: phagocytic number decreased 50%, digestion index reduced 2.5-fold, and active phagocyte count 2.2-fold lower than controls, despite increased neutrophil numbers available for phagocytosis.

Preventive MF administration before PCS serum injection restored phagocytic index and phagocytic number to control levels and increased antigen digestion capacity compared with PCS-serum-only animals.

Preventive MF administration reduced spontaneous NADP-H oxidase (ROS) reactions by 60% versus PCS-serum-only animals and restored the oxygen-dependent phagocytosis stimulation index to near-control values.

Nearly half of all respondents (regardless of infection status) reported at least one long-term symptom, and having had moderate/severe acute COVID-19 was associated with significantly higher odds of long-term symptoms than not being infected.
Individuals with moderate/severe acute COVID-19 reported a higher average number of long-term symptoms than those with mild infection or no infection.
Fatigue as a persistent symptom was substantially more prevalent among those with moderate/severe acute COVID-19 than uninfected individuals.
Muscle aches and joint pains as a persistent symptom were more prevalent among those with moderate/severe acute COVID-19 than uninfected individuals.
Persistent loss of taste/smell was markedly more common among those infected with COVID-19 (regardless of severity) than among the uninfected.
Among individuals with no history of COVID-19 infection, lower household income was associated with a higher prevalence of long-term (background) symptom reporting.

Both low- and high-income respondents who had moderate/severe COVID-19 showed higher long-term symptom prevalence than same-income uninfected respondents, but the increase and absolute count were largest among low-income respondents.
In the low-income group, long-term fatigue and muscle aches/joint pains rose sharply with moderate/severe acute COVID-19 severity.
In the high-income group, long-term fatigue and loss of taste/smell were significantly elevated with acute COVID-19 severity.
Ultra-Orthodox Jews showed a large and statistically significant increase in long-term symptom prevalence when they had moderate/severe acute COVID-19 versus being uninfected.
Non-Ultra-Orthodox Jews showed a non-significant increase in overall long-term symptom probability with moderate/severe acute COVID-19.

Arab Israelis showed a significant increase in the number of long-term symptoms when they had moderate/severe acute COVID-19 compared to no infection, although the change in overall symptom probability was not significant.
Among uninfected respondents, Arab Israelis reported more long-term (background) symptoms on average than non-Ultra-Orthodox Jews or Ultra-Orthodox Jews.
Among non-Ultra-Orthodox Jews, fatigue, loss of taste/smell, and muscle/joint pain each rose significantly (or near-significantly) with moderate/severe acute COVID-19 severity.
HHV-6B U94 (latency marker) and OHV-3 (active infection marker) antigens were detected in choroid plexus tissue from one of three ME/CFS patients.
U94 protein was detected in Iba1-positive microglial cells within the anterior hippocampus and left amygdala, but not the right amygdala, of the same ME/CFS patient.
FISH analysis detected viral miR-aU14 within GFAP-positive astrocytes in the same hippocampus/amygdala tissues, confirming active HHV-6 reactivation.
A second ME/CFS patient showed positive staining for HHV-6 p41 antigen (active infection marker) in cervical, lumbar, and sacral nerve roots.
The third ME/CFS patient was negative for all HHV-6 proteins, resembling the control group.
Overall, HHV-6 reactivation (viral protein and/or miRNA) was observed in selected tissue sections of two of three ME/CFS patients, but not in non-ME/CFS controls.
HHV-6 p41 protein and miR-aU14 were both detected in the dorsal root ganglia of one ME/CFS patient, with miR-aU14 found in one of two DRG samples analyzed.
HHV-6 p41 protein was detected in lumbosacral, lumbar, and cervical nerve roots but not in the general nerve tissue of another ME/CFS patient.

HHV-6 U94 protein was absent from cerebellum/Purkinje cell tissue in all three ME/CFS patients, whereas non-ME/CFS control biopsies showed signs of HHV-6 U94, suggesting viral latency in that region only in controls.
EBV dUTPase protein was detected in multiple tissue biopsies (midbrain, hippocampus, left brain, kidney) from ME/CFS patients, while all non-ME/CFS control samples were negative.
No tissue biopsy was found to be dual positive for both HHV-6 and EBV, though co-infection with each virus in different tissues within the same ME/CFS patient was possible.
miR-aU14 was detected in the axons of the spinal cord in ME/CFS patients but not in controls, suggesting HHV-6 may undergo retrograde axonal transport similar to HSV-1.

HHV-6 miR-aU14, expressed only during lytic HHV-6 infection/reactivation, has previously been linked to disrupted mitochondrial function, and its stability makes it a useful marker of viral reactivation.
At 3 months, upper respiratory/HEENT symptoms were more common in the COVID+ group than the COVID- group (37.3% vs 20.9%).
At 3 months, constitutional symptoms were more prevalent in the COVID+ group than the COVID- group (28.8% vs 19.4%).
At 3 months, musculoskeletal symptoms were more prevalent in the COVID+ group than the COVID- group (19.5% vs 14.7%).
At 3 months, pulmonary symptoms were more prevalent in the COVID+ group than the COVID- group (17.6% vs 12.2%).
At 3 months, cardiovascular symptoms were more prevalent in the COVID+ group than the COVID- group (10.0% vs 7.2%).
At 3 months, gastrointestinal symptom prevalence was nearly identical between the COVID+ and COVID- groups (8.7% vs 8.3%).

At 3 months, symptoms consistent with post-infectious syndromes (fatigue, poor sleep quality, muscle/joint pains, unrefreshing sleep, dizziness/fainting) were similarly prevalent among COVID-positive and COVID-negative participants.
At 3 months, roughly half of COVID-positive participants (49.8%) reported at least one SARS-CoV-2-related symptom compared to about one-quarter (26.7%) of COVID-negative participants.

Standard tonal air and bone audiometry showed normal hearing at nearly all frequencies, with only a mild 25 dB threshold elevation at 8 kHz bilaterally, suggesting an early degenerative process in the organ of Corti.
Luscher's suprathreshold test at 6 and 8 kHz was negative, indicating an intact cochlear compression mechanism and no recruitment phenomenon despite the mild high-frequency threshold shift.
The binaural fusion (alternate binaural speech) test, sensitive to brainstem and higher auditory processing lesions, was performed normally with 100% monaural and 95% binaural word recognition.
PASAT auditory working-memory testing showed 83% correct responses, consistent with average healthy control performance, indicating preserved auditory memory and divided attention.
