The dichotic word listening test showed a marked right-ear advantage (66% correct left ear vs 81% correct right ear), well below the >90% expected with normal interhemispheric/central auditory function, suggesting dysfunction in interhemispheric connections or right-hemisphere auditory processing.

The patient failed the gap detection test in all five test series (tone pulses and clicks), both at initial assessment and on re-examination four months later, indicating impaired temporal auditory resolution likely localized to the left primary auditory cortex.
Sound localization/movement direction testing was performed correctly in up to 80% of cases in both directions, indicating preserved brainstem-level auditory motion analysis.
Skin biopsy showed intraepidermal small fiber density of 9.4 fibers/mm, above the age-adjusted 5th percentile normal cutoff of 5.7 fibers/mm, indicating no evidence of distal small fiber neuropathy.

Corneal confocal microscopy showed normal corneal nerve fiber density and length, but corneal nerve branch density (CNBD) and corneal nerve fiber length (CNFL) were lower than gender- and age-corrected medians, a mixed/subtle small fiber finding.

Serologic testing showed positive CMV-IgG, EBV VCA IgG, and EBV EBNA IgG, consistent with past/reactivated herpesvirus infection, corroborating the patient's history of recurring herpesvirus episodes.

Ultrasonography of brachiocephalic vessels showed signs of vertebrogenic influence at the extracranial level of the vertebral arteries, a vascular finding possibly relevant to the patient's orthostatic and dizziness symptoms.

The DePaul Symptom Questionnaire (DSQ-2) supported a diagnosis of CFS/ME in the patient, alongside her clinical presentation of chronic fatigue, stress-induced pyrexia, orthostatic intolerance, and cognitive complaints.

The authors cite prior resting-state fMRI work showing that CFS patients have weaker functional connectivity between the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) and the right planum temporale (rPT) and right Heschl's gyrus (rHG) compared to healthy volunteers, proposed as a mechanism for the patient's central auditory processing deficits.

Despite prominent cognitive, vestibular, and autonomic complaints following SARS-CoV-2 infection, comprehensive testing revealed no peripheral auditory, vestibular, or peripheral nerve pathology, suggesting the deficits localize instead to the primary auditory cortex — a post-viral central complication not previously described in the literature.
Following a dog-bite-related renal abscess and sepsis caused by Capnocytophaga canimorsus, the patient developed fatigue symptoms consistent with post-infection chronic fatigue syndrome.
Confirmatory factor analysis confirmed a single-factor structure for the pSFQ, indicating it captures subjective fatigue as a unidimensional construct.
The pSFQ demonstrated good to excellent internal consistency across the study population.
The pSFQ showed strong construct validity, correlating highly (negatively) with two other established fatigue measurements.
ROC analysis established a pSFQ cut-off score of 21 or higher for identifying severe fatigue, with high sensitivity and specificity.
Normative pSFQ data for children with and without a chronic disease showed patterns similar to those seen with other established fatigue questionnaires.
Genetic screening of 100 hEDS patients with prior negative connective tissue disorder NGS panels identified 14 single structural changes in the MIA3 gene.

A single truncating variant in MIA3 (c.567dup, p.Leu1880ThrfsTer6), predicted to truncate the TANGO1 protein, was identified in one hEDS patient and proposed as a possible pathogenic mechanism underlying disrupted collagen secretion.
Thirteen of the 14 detected MIA3 variants were classified as missense benign or likely benign, indicating no established pathogenic significance for these changes.
Among adolescents seen in a multidisciplinary EDS clinic, 17% self-reported gender dysphoria or transgender identity, far exceeding the ~1.3% national prevalence in adolescents.
Among TGD adolescents with EDS, 89% were assigned female at birth and 11% assigned male at birth, showing a marked sex skew.
Of the TGD adolescents with EDS, 82% had a diagnosis of hypermobile EDS (hEDS) and 18% had hypermobility spectrum disorder (HSD).
Among the TGD/EDS cohort, gender identity breakdown was 61% transgender, 14% nonbinary, 11% fluid gender, and 7% agender.

TGD adolescents with EDS commonly reported multisystem symptoms including musculoskeletal issues (96%), neurologic issues (79%), fatigue (75%), skin issues (78%), cardiac issues (71%), and gastrointestinal issues (68%).
Dysautonomia was reported in 61% of TGD adolescents with EDS, comprising the majority of the 71% reporting cardiac issues.

Prior subspecialty evaluations among TGD adolescents with EDS included cardiology (68%), physical therapy (50%), rheumatology (43%), orthopedics (32%), neurology (32%), gastrointestinal (25%), endocrine/gender specialty (18%), gynecology (11%), sleep medicine (11%), and sports medicine (4%).
Among TGD adolescents with EDS, 36% were receiving gender-affirming hormone therapy at the time of chart review.
Psychotropic medication use was common in the TGD/EDS cohort, with 57% on antidepressants and 21% on anxiolytics.
Symptom-management medication use was common, with 61% on antihistamines, 39% on NSAIDs, and 25% on sleep aid medications.
The majority of TGD adolescents with EDS reported psychiatric issues (86%), including anxiety (75%) and depression (57%).

Sixty-four percent of the TGD/EDS cohort had a prior psychology or psychiatry evaluation; two patients reported self-harm, three reported sexual abuse, and four reported suicidal ideation in the past.
Anxiety prevalence in this TGD/EDS cohort (75%) was similar to previously reported anxiety rates in EDS patients generally (70%).
Depression prevalence in this TGD/EDS cohort (57%) was substantially higher than previously reported depression rates in EDS patients generally (25%).
89% of this TGD/EDS cohort identified as transmasculine (assigned female at birth), a higher proportion than the 55%-61% reported in general TGD adolescent populations.
A prior study found that 2.6% of adults undergoing gender-affirming surgery had a diagnosis of EDS, far exceeding both estimated TGD prevalence and general population EDS prevalence.
Every survey respondent with hEDS had trialed at least one complementary and alternative medicine (CAM) modality, with an average of nine different modalities tried per person.
Dietary supplements and massage therapy were the most commonly trialed CAM modalities among hEDS patients, each used by 81% of survey respondents.
Acupuncture and chiropractic therapy were each trialed by 65% of survey respondents, and mindfulness/meditation by 61%.
Magnesium was the most commonly used dietary supplement among hEDS patients, used by nearly a third of respondents, followed by B, C, and D vitamins and fish oil.
Overall, 58% of trialed CAM modalities were rated helpful by respondents, with massage therapy, medical cannabis, and mindfulness rated among the most useful for hEDS symptoms.

Nearly one-third of trialed CAM modalities were rated unhelpful or harmful, with acupuncture most frequently rated as the least helpful, and chiropractic therapy and acupuncture identified qualitatively as least useful.
Nearly half of participants had trialed cannabis for symptom relief, with a majority reporting benefit, particularly topical formulations for muscle spasms and deep pain.

A subset of interviewees (N=12) reported injuries from CAM treatments, which they attributed to practitioners' unfamiliarity with hypermobility-related physical vulnerabilities, including severe bruising from cupping and worsened symptoms after chiropractic care.
The Alexander Technique, a CAM modality focused on head/neck posture, was described by a participant as risky for hEDS patients with craniocervical instability, potentially causing subluxations.
Lack of insurance coverage and high out-of-pocket costs were identified as major barriers limiting hEDS patients' use of CAM therapies.

Participants generally trusted CAM practitioners as much as or more than conventional providers, largely because CAM practitioners were perceived as more attentive and less skeptical of their hEDS diagnosis, though some (N=8) expressed distrust centered on financial exploitation.

A majority of interviewees who addressed the topic (9 of 12) reported being comfortable disclosing CAM use to their conventional medical providers, a higher disclosure rate than previously reported in the literature.
One participant reported that prolotherapy injections at the neck/base of the brain greatly improved her quality of life, describing it as life-saving.

Whole-exome sequencing identified a homozygous nonsense variant (c.1894C>T:p.Arg632*) in AEBP1 in a Japanese woman previously diagnosed with classical EDS, confirming AEBP1-related classical-like EDS type 2.
During pregnancy the patient experienced painful urinary retention, migraines, and threatened premature labor, necessitating inpatient management from 20 weeks of gestation.
The patient delivered a healthy female infant via elective caesarean section at 32 weeks of gestation.
Postoperatively, the patient developed severe paralytic ileus requiring intensive care unit treatment, which resolved with conservative therapy.

Two thirds of adults with LDS or vEDS of working age (30/50) were receiving disability benefits (full-time/part-time disability pension or retraining) rather than being in full-time employment or study.
The median age at which participants began receiving full-time disability pension (early retirement) was 41 years.
Persons who were full-time employed or students were significantly younger than those who received disability benefits.
Fewer people who were full-time employed or studying reported fatigue symptoms above the FSS threshold compared with those receiving disability benefits.
Sleep problems were less common among those full-time employed or studying compared with those receiving disability benefits.
Those who were full-time employed or studying reported significantly higher satisfaction with life (SWLS) than those receiving disability benefits.
Disease burden was high overall in the LDS/vEDS study group, with 60% having high cardiovascular burden and 34% high multi-organ symptom burden.
Chronic musculoskeletal pain lasting more than three months was reported by 80% of the LDS/vEDS study group.
A very high proportion of the study group scored above threshold for anxiety and depression symptoms on the HADS.
No statistically significant differences were found in disease burden or musculoskeletal pain between full-time employed/student participants and those receiving disability benefits.
Two thirds of all participants had ever been in physically demanding (non-sedentary) work, including 23% requiring much standing/walking, 34% much walking/lifting, and 11% heavy manual work.

A markedly higher proportion of currently full-time employed/student participants had informed their employer about their HTAD diagnosis and felt met with understanding, compared with those on disability benefits recalling their prior employment.
Pain problems as an obstacle to work ability were reported more frequently among those on disability benefits than among the full-time employed/student group.
About half of participants receiving disability benefits reported that their decision to retire was influenced by their health situation related to the HTAD diagnosis.
About 37-40% of those receiving disability benefits believed they could have continued working if the workplace had been better adjusted to their health situation.

Many participants were not diagnosed with LDS or vEDS until years after graduation or after being in working life, with a median age at diagnosis of 33.5 years, meaning few had used vocational guidance when making career decisions.

Whole exome sequencing identified two novel missense variants in B3GALT6 (c.942G>C/p.W314C from the mother and c.808G>A/p.G270S from the father) forming a compound heterozygous genotype, which was determined to be the pathogenic cause of the child's EDS-like SEMDJL1 phenotype.
Laboratory testing showed a low concentration of vitamin D in the child, considered a possible contributing factor to insufficient bone calcification and the observed skeletal dysplasia.
Ultrasonography revealed cardiovascular abnormalities (atrial septal defect and patent foramen ovale) and left hydrocele testis as comorbid features in the patient.

The patient exhibited joint laxity and an increased range of motion in the hand joints, with dorsal extension of approximately 110 degrees, consistent with the connective tissue phenotype of EDS/SEMDJL1.

Genetic testing found no mutation in CHST14, a gene associated with a newer class of EDS involving vascular abnormalities, indicating it was not the cause of this patient's phenotype despite overlapping vascular features.
A hip brace was applied to correct the widened/dislocated hip joint, and after treatment the hip joint was maintained in a good reduced position.

The same B3GALT6 mutation mechanism has been reported to produce differing clinical phenotypes by population, with South African sporadic cases typically manifesting SEMDJL1 and Japanese cases typically manifesting EDS, while this Chinese case showed an overlapping EDS-like SEMDJL1 phenotype.
The patient had normal hearing, which supported a diagnosis of SEMDJL1 (not associated with hearing loss) rather than EDS, which can involve hearing loss.
The neonate carried a homozygous pathogenic SLC2A10 c.243C>G (p.Ser81Arg) variant in exon 2, confirming the clinical diagnosis of arterial tortuosity syndrome.

The neonate presented with hypotonia, bilateral upper-limb hypermobility, pectus excavatum, blepharophimosis with down-slanting palpebral fissures, high-arched palate, deviated nose, and hyperextensible skin (cutis laxa).

Echocardiogram showed mild left ventricular hypertrophy, patent foramen ovale, patent ductus arteriosus, and double aortic arch with abnormal pulmonary artery course; CT angiography confirmed an elongated, tortuous, laterally displaced left-sided aortic arch consistent with ATS.

The patient's father, paternal grandmother, and paternal aunt showed mild dysmorphic features suggestive of heterozygous SLC2A10 carrier status but no severe cardiovascular complications, consistent with reports that heterozygous carriers lack severe vascular anomalies.
A mortality rate of 40% has been reported in ATS patients under five years of age.
A retrospective cohort of 50 ATS patients reported a male-to-female ratio of 27:22, indicating no substantial sex predilection for the disease.
Analysis of 50 new and 52 previously reported ATS patients found a mean age at diagnosis of 4.84 years and a median of 2 years, though adult and prenatal cases have also been described.

Loss-of-function SLC2A10 mutations inactivate the GLUT10 ascorbate transporter, reducing prolyl/lysyl hydroxylation of collagen and elastin and upregulating TGF-β signaling, which weakens large and medium arteries.

Skin and vascular biopsies from ATS patients show elastic fiber fragmentation, increased collagen deposition, disorganized collagen bundles, and irregular internal elastic lamina with disordered medial smooth muscle cells.

A total of 114 SLC2A10 variants have been reported in the Global Variome shared LOVD database, including 16 pathogenic variants listed in ClinVar, with most missense mutations clustering in exons 2 and 3.
Takahashi et al. reported an association between ATS and early-onset pulmonary emphysema, suggesting need for COPD monitoring in some ATS patients.
A case of ATS with severe cerebral artery tortuosity presenting with migraine headaches has been reported, indicating a need to investigate intracranial blood flow changes in ATS.
A single case of ATS presenting with epilepsy has been reported, indicating some ATS patients presenting with seizures may need cerebrovascular evaluation.
Naunheim et al. observed persistent pulmonary hypertension together with venous tortuosity in a rare ATS case.
A rare ATS case was previously misdiagnosed as Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, illustrating phenotypic overlap between the two connective tissue disorders.

Among heritable connective tissue disorders, only certain rare EDS subtypes (e.g., vascular EDS) predispose to severe cardiovascular complications, whereas arterial tortuosity is more broadly prevalent across Loeys-Dietz syndrome, Marfan syndrome, and ATS.
In a screen of 53 adults with eating disorders (mostly anorexia nervosa), 41% were positive for generalized joint hypermobility compared with an estimated 20% in the general population.

Within the eating disorder plus GJH subgroup, patients showed less cognitive rigidity/control and fewer restricting behaviors compared with eating disorder patients without GJH, suggesting a distinct clinical subtype possibly mediated by connective tissue-related gastrointestinal and sensory problems.

In adults with neurodevelopmental conditions, the odds of joint hypermobility were 4.51 times higher than in the general population, and this group also reported more symptoms of orthostatic intolerance and musculoskeletal pain than a comparison group.
The severity of generalized joint hypermobility was found to mediate the relationship between neurodivergence and symptoms of both dysautonomia and pain.

A case-control study of 105 participants found no differences in generalized joint hypermobility between children with pediatric acute-onset neuropsychiatric syndrome (PANS), individuals with other mental disorders, and healthy controls.

In 199 individuals with autism spectrum disorder compared to 419 non-ASD community controls, the association between ASD and GJH appeared primarily driven by comorbid ADHD, while a stronger association was found between ASD and symptomatic GJH specifically.

In an observational, cross-sectional study of 482 medical records, severity of joint hypermobility was associated with functional limitations of movement affecting daily, instrumental, recreational, sports, and occupational activities, and pain and fatigue since childhood were identified as unrecognized features contributing to suboptimal management.
A systematic review of 14 studies found that the prevalence of IBS among FM patients is 32.5%, ranging from 28-59%.

Estimates of FM prevalence among IBS patients are discordant between studies, ranging from 48% (range 32-77%) in one systematic review to 12.9% (95% CI 12.7-13.1%) in a larger meta-analysis, likely due to differing study designs.

Among FM patients, bowel symptoms are common: bloating (65.4%), abdominal pain (57.1%), fecal incontinence (56%), constipation (52.9%), alternating diarrhea/constipation (21.3%), and diarrhea alone (6%), with FM predominating in IBS-C patients.
Anxiety and depression are highly prevalent in IBS (39.1% and 23.8% respectively), affecting the IBS-C subtype most, with 38% of IBS patients reporting suicidal ideation.
FM has a high prevalence of psychiatric comorbidity, with mood disorders in 32%, depression in 63%, and suicidal ideation in 32.5% of patients.

Central sensitization, characterized by hyperalgesia and allodynia via enhanced ascending excitatory and dampened descending inhibitory pain pathways, is proposed as a shared mechanism underlying both FM and IBS.
Patients with co-diagnosed IBS and FM show somatic hyperalgesia (lower pain thresholds, higher pain frequency/severity), whereas patients with IBS alone show somatic hypoalgesia.

IBS is associated with a high Firmicutes to Bacteroidetes ratio in gut microbiome studies, while a study of 54 FM patients versus 36 healthy controls found a low Firmicutes to Bacteroidetes ratio in FM.
Sleep disorders are highly prevalent in both conditions, estimated at 33% in IBS and 92.9% in FM, with more than 50% of FM patients meeting insomnia criteria.
Chronic fatigue syndrome shows a median comorbidity of 51% in IBS and 76% in FM, with comorbid chronic fatigue patients experiencing 57% loss of productivity and 37% decline in household income.
Patients with co-diagnosed FM and IBS experience increased fatigue and symptom severity compared to patients with FM or IBS alone.
A meta-analysis found that mindfulness and acceptance-based interventions result in moderate improvements in pain, sleep, quality of life, anxiety, and depression in fibromyalgia patients.

An online mindfulness trial for IBS demonstrated significant improvement in IBS quality of life and GI-specific anxiety, with 42% of intervention participants reporting decreased IBS symptoms compared to a 12% increase in controls.
A web-based mindful socioemotional regulation intervention (MSER) for FM improved pain, stress coping, social engagement, and loneliness compared to a health education control group.

In IBS, four CBT trials reported benefits on symptom severity, with a 24-month follow-up study finding the greatest reduction of symptom severity in a telephone-delivered CBT group compared to web-CBT and treatment-as-usual.
IBS patients who achieved a positive CBT response by week 4 of a 10-week course (rapid responders) experienced symptomatic reduction maintained at 3-month follow-up.
A trial of CBT in female IBS patients found reduced pain catastrophizing and improved quality of life compared to waitlist controls.
Yoga was shown to be safe and feasible for IBS, improving symptom severity, quality of life, physical functioning, and anxiety (Schumann et al.), though more high-quality trials are needed.

In a comparative trial, yoga was superior to mindfulness-based stress reduction, a low-FODMAP diet, and physical exercise (but not CBT) in improving quality of life, GI symptom severity, and reducing stress and anxiety in IBS.

A trial comparing a Yoga Awareness program to wait-list control in female FM patients showed decreased anxiety (42.2%), depression (41.5%), emotional distress (30%), and fatigue (29.9%) in the intervention group, with sustained improvement at 3-month follow-up.
A gentle Hatha Yoga program improved FM physical symptoms as assessed with the Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire.
Yoga combined with Tui Na massage (targeting acupuncture meridians) showed promising results in pain reduction for fibromyalgia patients.
Ara h 2-specific IgE levels were higher in peanut-allergic children compared with peanut-sensitized but tolerant children.
Ara h 6-specific IgE levels were higher in peanut-allergic children compared with peanut-sensitized tolerant children.
The Ara h 2/total IgE ratio was higher in peanut-allergic children than in peanut-sensitized tolerant children.
The diversity of IgE binding to Ara h 2 epitopes was greater in peanut-allergic children than in peanut-sensitized tolerant children.
Levels of IgE to whole peanut, Ara h 1, and Ara h 3 did not significantly differ between peanut-allergic and peanut-sensitized tolerant children.
Mast cell activation test results to Ara h 2 strongly correlated with Ara h 2-specific IgE levels.
Mast cell activation test results to Ara h 2 strongly correlated with Ara h 2/total IgE ratios.
Mast cell activation test results to Ara h 2 moderately correlated with Ara h 2-specific IgE epitope diversity.
Mast cell activation test results to Ara h 2 correlated moderately with the diversity of IgE epitope recognition for Ara h 2.
Linear regression modeling identified Arah2-sIgE levels as a significant independent determinant of mast cell response to Ara h 2.
The Ara h 2/total IgE ratio was the strongest independent determinant of mast cell response to Ara h 2 in the regression model.

The study concludes that most children sensitized to Ara h 2 are clinically peanut-allergic, and Ara h 2-specific IgE titers and specific activity are the major determinants of the mast cell response.
Among the six mouse Arf isoforms, Arf1 was found to be predominantly expressed in bone marrow-derived mast cells (BMMCs).
qPCR confirmed Arf1 mRNA was virtually absent in Arf1-KO BMMCs after 4-OHT treatment, with a slight compensatory increase in Arf4 expression.
Arf1-KO BMMCs expressed similar surface levels of FcεRI and c-Kit and showed similar maturation kinetics to control BMMCs.
Mast cell numbers were markedly decreased in Arf1-deficient BMMCs compared with controls, indicating a critical role for Arf1 in mast cell expansion.
Arf1-deficient BMMCs showed a slight but statistically significant decrease in forward scatter (FSC), indicating reduced cell size compared with control BMMCs.
No difference was found in IL-3 receptor (CD123/CD131) expression levels between control and Arf1-KO BMMCs, and both reached similar proliferation plateau at ~1 ng/mL IL-3.
Arf1-deficient BMMCs showed markedly abrogated proliferation (Ki67+ cells) upon IL-3 stimulation, while apoptosis (Annexin V+ cells) was not significantly affected.
Treatment with rapamycin, an mTORC1 inhibitor, suppressed proliferation of BMMCs, albeit requiring a relatively high dose.
IL-3 signal-induced phosphorylation of S6 (a mTORC1-p70 S6K target) was significantly decreased in Arf1-KO BMMCs compared with control, while phosphorylation of ERK was unaffected.
There was little or no difference in ERK phosphorylation between control and Arf1-KO BMMCs upon IL-3 stimulation, suggesting Arf1 specifically affects mTORC1 rather than ERK signaling.
Rapamycin had no impact on mast cell survival, whereas U0126 (ERK inhibitor) robustly induced apoptosis, phenocopying the effect of Arf1-deficiency on mTORC1 signaling but not on apoptosis.
PLD inhibition with FIPI had no impact on IL-3-induced S6 phosphorylation or mast cell proliferation, suggesting PLD is not the mediator of the Arf1-mTORC1 axis in this context.

BFA, an inhibitor of ArfGEF1, failed to suppress S6 phosphorylation or proliferation upon IL-3 stimulation, suggesting IL-3-induced Arf1 activation is mediated by BFA-insensitive GEFs such as cytohesins.

FcεRI-induced S6 phosphorylation was attenuated in Arf1-KO BMMCs (with ERK activation intact), and Akt activation upon FcεRI stimulation was also partly attenuated, suggesting Arf1 regulates the PI3K/mTORC1 pathway downstream of FcεRI.

SCF (c-Kit ligand)-induced S6 phosphorylation was also attenuated in Arf1-KO BMMCs, similar to IL-3R and FcεRI signaling, indicating Arf1 is generally involved in mTORC1 activation irrespective of upstream receptor input.

No significant difference in CD107a surface expression (granule exocytosis marker) was detected between control and Arf1-KO BMMCs upon FcεRI stimulation, contradicting a prior report that Arf1 is required for degranulation via inhibitory peptide/siRNA approaches.

Arf1-KO BMMCs secreted IL-6 upon FcεRI stimulation at levels comparable to control BMMCs, indicating Arf1 is dispensable for FcεRI-induced cytokine secretion, whereas FIPI or BFA attenuated IL-6 secretion under the same conditions.
The systems-biology model confirmed that mast cell activation via the IgE:FcεRI axis is a central pathophysiological process in chronic spontaneous urticaria.
The model indicated that anti-IgE therapy and BTK inhibitors act directly on mast cell biology by abrogating FcεRI signaling activity.
Anti-IgE therapy (omalizumab) was modeled as acting directly on mast cell FcεRI signaling, distinct from adaptive immune-targeted therapies.
Anti-interleukin therapies and anti-Siglec-8 were modeled as acting through modulation of adaptive immunity rather than direct FcεRI signaling.

A CSU-specific molecular interactome was constructed using systems biology/machine learning and validated against gene expression data from CSU patients, then used to evaluate disease pathophysiology and drug mechanisms.
Carnosic acid treatment significantly inhibited allergen-induced Ca2+ mobilization in IgE-sensitized mast cells.
Carnosic acid significantly reduced allergen-induced ROS production in mast cells.
Carnosic acid treatment reduced mast cell degranulation following IgE/allergen stimulation.
Carnosic acid treatment reduced release of all cytokines and chemokines examined following IgE-mediated mast cell stimulation.
Unlike other cytokines/chemokines, CCL2 gene expression was not reduced by carnosic acid treatment.
Carnosic acid mediates its inhibitory effects on mast cells through direct regulation of Syk tyrosine kinase activation.
Carnosic acid modulated phosphorylation of the downstream effector TAK1 at Ser412 in activated mast cells.
Carnosic acid modulated phosphorylation of Akt at Ser473 downstream of Syk in activated mast cells.
Carnosic acid reduced phosphorylation of TAK1 at Ser412 downstream of Syk in IgE-activated mast cells.
Carnosic acid reduced phosphorylation of Akt at Ser473 downstream of Syk in IgE-activated mast cells.
Carnosic acid modulated NFκB signaling downstream of Syk in IgE-activated mast cells, contributing to its anti-inflammatory effects.
Unlike previously reported effects of rosemary extract, carnosic acid alone did not alter MAPK protein phosphorylation in IgE-activated mast cells.
Novel computationally designed small molecules showed high binding affinity for the MRGPRX2 receptor in docking studies.
The small molecule antagonists inhibited MRGPRX2 signaling with half-maximal inhibitory concentrations in the low micromolar range across functional bioassays.
The small molecules inhibited the early phase of mast cell activation as measured by β-hexosaminidase release and calcium flux assays in human LAD-2 mast cells.
The small molecules also inhibited the late phase of mast cell activation, including chemokine synthesis and prostaglandin release.
Western blot analysis showed that the small molecule antagonists inhibited downstream MRGPRX2 signaling components including phospholipase C-γ, ERK1/2, and Akt.
In a mouse model of acute allergy and systemic anaphylaxis, administration of the small molecule MRGPRX2 antagonists effectively blocked acute systemic allergic reactions and inflammation.

Skin mast cell activation in chronic spontaneous urticaria can occur via the IgE-FcεRI axis as well as via autoallergy, autoimmunity, neuroimmune dysregulation, coagulation pathway activation, and microbial infection.
Recent reports suggest basophils and eosinophils, in addition to mast cells, are actively and directly involved in chronic spontaneous urticaria pathogenesis.
Hereditary or acquired C1-inhibitor deficiency is described as the primary cause of bradykinin-mediated angioedema due to increased plasma bradykinin concentration.
Angioedema pathogenesis centers on increased vascular permeability and plasma leakage into deeper dermis and subcutis, mediated by either histamine or bradykinin.
Biologic therapy introduced for chronic spontaneous urticaria over the last decade is described as a major treatment advance.
Multiple hereditary-angioedema-specific therapies for prevention and acute attacks have been approved, described as revolutionizing treatment of this disease.

Incubation of human LAD2 mast cells with PEG/Macrogol (molecular weights 2,000, 3,350, 4,000, 6,000) at concentrations up to 10 mg/ml produced no significant increase in beta-hexosaminidase release compared to unstimulated basal degranulation.
Incubation of human LAD2 mast cells with trometamol at concentrations up to 10 mg/ml did not induce significant beta-hexosaminidase release compared to basal degranulation.
LAD2 mast cell viability, measured by WST-1 assay, was preserved at 1 and 10 mg/ml but significantly reduced at 50 mg/ml for all reagents tested except Macrogol 3350.

Because neither PEG/Macrogol nor trometamol induced initial mast cell degranulation, the authors did not proceed to test MRGPRX2-silenced LAD2 cells, as the receptor-silencing step depended on finding direct activation in the first step.

Intradermal injection of autologous IL-2/IL-4/LPS-pretreated Th2/Tc2 T cells into non-atopic human skin xenotransplants was sufficient to induce a full phenocopy of human atopic dermatitis lesions without skin barrier disruption.
The induced AD lesions showed skin barrier defects despite no mechanical barrier disruption at the time of T-cell injection.
Intraepidermal eosinophils appeared as part of the immunopathology in the Th2/Tc2-induced AD lesions.
Mast cell activation was induced in the humanized AD skin lesions following Th2/Tc2 lymphocyte injection.
Thymic stromal lymphopoietin (TSLP) was increased in the Th2/Tc2-induced AD lesions.
Eotaxin-1 levels were increased in the Th2/Tc2-induced AD lesions.
The induced AD lesions showed downregulation of ß2-adrenergic receptor, a neuroimmunological abnormality characteristic of human AD.
The experimentally induced AD lesions showed downregulation of the ß2-adrenergic receptor, a neuroimmunological abnormality characteristic of human AD.
The induced human AD lesions in the xenotransplants responded to topical dexamethasone treatment.
The induced human AD lesions in the xenotransplants responded to topical tacrolimus treatment.
Systemic anti-IL-4Rα antibody (dupilumab) treatment led to resolution of the experimentally induced human AD lesions, confirming IL-4Rα signaling as central to the phenotype.
Perceived psychoemotional stress exposure in mice induced neurogenic skin inflammation and caused relapse of the resolved, experimentally induced AD lesions.

Th2-polarized lymphocytes with excessive IL-4Rα-mediated signaling were sufficient to induce human AD skin lesions even in the absence of atopy and without prior epidermal barrier disruption, indicating these factors are dispensable for AD lesion induction.
Gene expression of IL-2 in white blood cells was significantly higher in SFN patients compared to healthy controls.
Gene expression of IL-8 in white blood cells was significantly higher in SFN patients compared to healthy controls.
Gene expression of TNF in white blood cells was significantly higher in SFN patients compared to healthy controls.
Gene expression of IL-1ß in white blood cells did not differ between SFN patients and healthy controls.
Gene expression of IL-6 in white blood cells did not differ between SFN patients and healthy controls, in contrast to prior local skin findings.
Gene expression of the anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-4 in white blood cells did not differ between SFN patients and healthy controls.
Gene expression of the anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10 in white blood cells did not differ overall between SFN patients and healthy controls, though it differed by prior blood analysis.
Gene expression of TGF-beta-1 in white blood cells did not differ between SFN patients and healthy controls.

A combined panel of IL-2, IL-8, and TNF gene expression achieved the highest diagnostic accuracy (AUC=0.81) for distinguishing SFN patients from healthy controls, with 70% sensitivity and 86% specificity.
Gene expression of IL-8 and TNF was higher in female SFN patients compared to female controls, but no difference was found in male patients versus male controls.
Gene expression of IL-2 was higher in SFN patients with moderate pain (NRS<4) compared to patients with severe pain (NRS≥4).
Gene expression of IL-10 was higher in SFN patients with acral pain compared to those with generalized pain.
IL-2 gene expression correlated negatively with current pain intensity in SFN patients.
Gene expression of IL-8 and TNF did not correlate with pain intensity in SFN patients.
Serum protein levels of IL-8 and TNF measured by ELISA did not differ between SFN patients and healthy controls, in contrast to the elevated gene expression findings.
Long-term oral l-serine supplementation suppressed toxic 1-deoxySL levels in plasma and tissues, including the sciatic nerve, in a db/db mouse model of diabetic neuropathy.
l-serine supplementation significantly improved functional neuropathy and sensory nerve modalities in db/db mice, even at advanced disease stages.

Despite functional improvements, structural analyses showed ongoing axonal degeneration, apoptosis, and Schwann cell pathology in l-serine-treated db/db mice, indicating persistent structural neuropathy.
Hyperglycemia and dyslipidemia persisted in db/db mice throughout the study despite long-term l-serine supplementation.
High levels of glutathione were observed in the spinal cord of l-serine-treated db/db mice, suggesting ongoing oxidative stress responses.

Across nauseagenic stimuli, the inferior frontal gyrus, anterior cingulate cortex, and anterior insula were commonly activated on brain imaging, with lateralization toward left IFG, right AIns, and right ACC.
Basal ganglia structures, particularly the putamen, were consistently activated during nausea across studies.
Deactivation (inactivation) during nausea was rarely reported but, when present, occurred mainly in the cerebellum and occipital lobe.
Functional connectivity increased during nausea, mainly between the posterior and mid-cingulate cortex.
ADM, total nNOS, and phosphorylated-nNOS protein levels in the PVN were reduced in obesity-related hypertensive rats compared to normal-diet control rats.

PVN application of the NO donor SNP attenuated the enhanced adipose afferent reflex in OH rats, whereas nNOS inhibition, guanylyl cyclase inhibition (ODQ), or GABAA blockade (Bicuculline) strengthened it.

PVN microinjection of ADM decreased basal sympathetic nerve activity and attenuated the enhanced adipose afferent reflex in OH rats, effects blocked by an ADM receptor antagonist, nNOS inhibitor, ODQ, or Bicuculline.
Bilateral PVN microinjection of ADM increased NO and cGMP levels and nNOS phosphorylation.

PVN transfection with AAV-ADM decreased the elevated adipose afferent reflex, basal sympathetic nerve activity, and blood pressure, increased nNOS expression/activation, and improved vascular remodeling in obesity-related hypertensive rats.

Two siblings presented with a profound connective tissue disease phenotype caused by biallelic (compound heterozygous, in trans) variants in TGFBR1, representing the first reported cases of biallelic TGFBR1-related Loeys-Dietz syndrome.
Both siblings carried a paternally inherited TGFBR1 variant, c.239G>A (p.Arg80Gln) in exon 2, classified as a variant of uncertain clinical significance and not previously reported.
Both siblings also carried a maternally inherited TGFBR1 variant, c.313C>G (p.His105Asp) in exon 2, likewise a novel variant of uncertain clinical significance.
Cultured fibroblasts from Patient 2 showed decreased TGF-beta responsiveness compared to control fibroblasts, a cellular phenotype consistent with prior observations in autosomal dominant LDS.

Each parent, carrying only one of the two TGFBR1 variants in heterozygous state, had no apparent medical issues and specifically no features of Loeys-Dietz syndrome, unlike their compound heterozygous children.
Most dermal fibroblast clones derived from systemic sclerosis patients showed constitutively high expression of SOX11.
TGF-β1 significantly induces SOX11 expression in SSc dermal fibroblasts.
SOX11 forms a positive feedback loop with periostin that activates TGF-β signaling in SSc dermal fibroblasts.
Genetic deletion of Sox11 specifically in Postn-expressing fibroblasts impairs bleomycin-induced dermal fibrosis in mice.
DNA microarray analysis identified several fibrotic factors dependent on the TGF-β/SOX11/periostin pathway in SSc dermal fibroblasts.
The anti-Hu (ANNA-1) autoantibody, typically associated with small cell lung carcinoma, can directly activate enteric neurons and visceral sensory nerve fibers and exerts a cytotoxic effect.
Anti-enteric neuronal antibodies have been found to be more abundant in patients with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) than in controls.
Mast cell products such as histamine and tryptase excite visceral afferents and enteric neurons, contributing to IBS symptoms like abdominal pain and disturbed motility.
Elevated serine-protease activity in the stool of IBS-D patients may contribute to leaky gut and visceral hypersensitivity.
Elevated cysteine-protease activity in the stool of IBS-C patients may be a factor contributing to leaky gut and visceral hypersensitivity.
Autoimmune processes targeting enteric neurons may also play a role in more common disorders such as esophageal achalasia, celiac disease, or multiple sclerosis.

In mouse ileum, VNUT-immunoreactive nerve fibers were found in myenteric ganglia and circular muscle, surrounding ChAT-, nNOS-, and calretinin-immunoreactive neurons, but no VNUT-ir nerve cell bodies were detected.
TH-immunoreactive (sympathetic/catecholaminergic) nerves were detected in myenteric ganglia and the tertiary plexus of mouse ileum.

In guinea pig ileum, VNUT-ir nerve fibers did not overlap with NOS-ir nerve fibers in myenteric ganglia or circular muscle, indicating ATP and NO are likely released from distinct inhibitory motorneuron populations.

In guinea pig circular muscle, VNUT-ir and ChAT-ir were detected in separate nerve fibers, and VNUT-ir nerve fibers surrounded some ChAT-ir and calretinin-ir neurons, suggesting VNUT-ir and ChAT-ir interneurons mediate distinct cholinergic and purinergic synaptic transmission in the myenteric plexus.
Irritable bowel syndrome among healthcare administration employees was significantly associated with job absenteeism.
Chronic heartburn was significantly associated with job absenteeism among healthcare administration employees.
Severe anemia was significantly associated with job absenteeism among healthcare administration employees.
Chronic fatigue was significantly associated with job absenteeism among healthcare administration employees.
High blood pressure or hypertension was significantly associated with job absenteeism among healthcare administration employees.
Overall, employees' chronic conditions had a significant impact on absenteeism, supporting recommendations for workplace health and wellness interventions.
Serum prolidase levels were significantly higher in fibromyalgia patients compared with healthy controls.
ROC analysis showed prolidase was a statistically significant predictor of fibromyalgia with an AUC of 0.795.
Serum histone H3 protein levels did not significantly differ between fibromyalgia patients and healthy controls.
ROC analysis showed histone H3 protein was not a statistically significant predictor of fibromyalgia.
Vitamin D deficiency, defined as serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D below 20 ng/ml, is proposed as a cause, precipitating factor, or contributor to fibromyalgia syndrome.
The literature reviewed indicates that vitamin D supplementation improves pain caused by fibromyalgia syndrome, although specific dosing recommendations have not yet been established.
Vitamin D is described as playing a role in irritable bowel syndrome, alongside multiple sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, and insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus.

Across 3 studies (n=620), having at least one functional somatic syndrome (fibromyalgia, IBS, chronic headaches, or chronic low back pain) predicted significantly greater postoperative pain scores after shoulder and elbow surgery.

Patients with at least one functional somatic syndrome had lower quality of recovery and lower DASH, ASES, and SANE functional outcome scores after shoulder and elbow surgery compared with those without an FSS.

Despite worse baseline/postoperative PROM scores in patients with functional somatic syndromes, 2 of the 3 PROM-reporting studies still showed improvement in PROMs from preoperative baseline in this group.

Of 7 studies reporting postoperative opioid use (n=56,909), 5 found that having at least one functional somatic syndrome was a strong risk factor for long-term opioid use after shoulder and elbow surgery.
One study (n=480) found that time-driven activity-based hospitalization costs were significantly greater in patients with functional somatic syndromes undergoing shoulder and elbow surgery.
Serum creatinine levels increased significantly at 6-month follow-up compared with levels during hospitalization in Omicron COVID-19 patients.
Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) decreased significantly at 6-month follow-up compared with in-hospital values, suggesting a trend toward chronic kidney disease.
Serum IL-2 levels were significantly decreased at 6 months in the kidney-involvement group of Omicron COVID-19 patients.
Serum IL-4 levels were significantly decreased at 6 months in the kidney-involvement group of Omicron COVID-19 patients.
Serum IL-5 levels were significantly decreased at 6 months in the kidney-involvement group of Omicron COVID-19 patients.
Serum IL-6 levels were significantly decreased at 6 months in the kidney-involvement group of Omicron COVID-19 patients.
Serum IL-10 levels were significantly decreased at 6 months in the kidney-involvement group of Omicron COVID-19 patients.
Serum IL-2 levels were positively correlated with patient age at the 6-month follow-up.
Serum IL-5 levels were positively correlated with patient age at the 6-month follow-up.
Serum TGF-beta levels showed a negative correlation with patient age at the 6-month follow-up.
Younger age was identified as an independent risk factor for higher serum TGF-beta levels.
The authors conclude that the observed decline in renal function trending toward chronic kidney disease (CKD) is one manifestation of long COVID that deserves clinical attention.

The authors note that neopterin, an inflammatory marker generated by activated M1 macrophages via iNOS, is elevated in DMD patients and is also reported to be robustly elevated in COVID-19 patients, suggesting a shared inflammatory mechanism relevant to long-COVID pulmonary dysfunction.

The authors propose that a hyperinflammatory host response (cytokine storm) rather than direct SARS-CoV-2 toxicity underlies the multisystem/multi-organ dysfunction, hypercoagulability, and prothrombotic complications seen in COVID-19 survivors, including long-haulers.

The authors hypothesize that M1 macrophage-driven inflammasome formation via the NPT/TNF-α/TLR4/NLRP3 axis and GSDMD-mediated pyroptosis increases CD4+/CD8+ immune responses, contributing to diaphragm dysfunction and alveolar leakage in both DMD and COVID-19 infection.
DCA administration reduced time spent in the central zone of the open-field test compared to Non-IBS rats, indicating anxiety-like behavior.
Treatment with L. fermentum, rifaximin, or gabapentin significantly increased time spent in the central zone compared to untreated IBS rats, improving anxiety-like behavior.
IBS rats showed higher visceral hypersensitivity (colorectal distension scores) than Non-IBS rats at both 7 and 14 days after DCA administration.
L. fermentum treatment significantly lowered colorectal distension scores compared to untreated IBS rats, with efficacy similar to gabapentin and rifaximin.
IBS rats had a significantly lower von Frey pressure response threshold (more referred hyperalgesia) than Non-IBS rats at both time points.
L. fermentum or rifaximin treatment significantly reduced the nociceptive score compared to untreated IBS rats at one and two weeks post-DCA.
Gabapentin treatment did not significantly change the nociceptive score compared to untreated IBS rats, though a non-significant trend was noted at 2 weeks.
Colonic gene expression of Vegf-α, Cox-2, and Trpv1 was significantly increased in the IBS group compared to Non-IBS controls.
Probiotic and rifaximin treatments significantly reduced the elevated Vegf-α, Cox-2 and Trpv1 gene expression seen in the IBS group.
Intestinal mucosal mast cell numbers (toluidine blue staining) were significantly elevated in the IBS group compared to Non-IBS rats, and reduced by all treatments.
None of L. fermentum, gabapentin, or rifaximin significantly altered viability/proliferation of RBL-2H3 or HMC1.2 cells at tested concentrations, indicating no cytotoxicity.
L. fermentum significantly decreased β-hexosaminidase release (mast cell degranulation marker) in both RBL-2H3 and HMC1.2 cells compared to non-treated cells.
In Compound 48/80-stimulated RBL-2H3 cells, only L. fermentum (not gabapentin or rifaximin) significantly inhibited β-hexosaminidase production.
In HMC1.2 human mast cells, all three treatments (L. fermentum, gabapentin, rifaximin) significantly reduced Compound 48/80-induced β-hexosaminidase release.

IBS rats displayed increased colonic histological damage (villus disruption, edema, inflammatory infiltration) compared to intact Non-IBS mucosa, which was improved by all treatments including the probiotic.
Colonic Muc-3 gene expression was significantly lower in untreated IBS rats compared to Non-IBS controls, and was ameliorated by L. fermentum, gabapentin, and rifaximin.
L. fermentum, gabapentin, and rifaximin all ameliorated the reduced Muc-3 expression seen in IBS rats, contributing to gut barrier restoration.
Plasma FITC-dextran concentrations, a marker of intestinal permeability, were higher in untreated IBS rats than Non-IBS rats, and all treatments significantly lowered these levels.
Colonic occludin protein expression was diminished in IBS rats compared to Non-IBS rats, and increased by all treatments.
L. fermentum treatment significantly increased fecal microbial alpha diversity (Observed species, Shannon, Simpson, ACE, PD_whole indices) compared to untreated IBS rats.
PCoA of weighted UniFrac beta diversity showed clear separation between Non-IBS and IBS rats; L. fermentum and gabapentin groups clustered closer to Non-IBS than to IBS.

At the phylum level, Bacillota, Verrucomicrobiota, and Cyanobacteria were increased in IBS rats while Bacteroidota and Pseudomonadota were reduced, compared to Non-IBS controls; probiotic and gabapentin ameliorated these shifts.

The Bacillota/Bacteroidota (F/B) ratio was significantly greater in the IBS group than controls, consistent with reports in human IBS patients, and was significantly reduced by probiotic administration.
Genus-level abundance of Prevotellaceae_UCG_001, Prevotella, and Collinsella was increased in IBS rats compared to Non-IBS rats and was restored by probiotic treatment.

Butyrate-producing bacterial taxa Oscillibacter, Bacteroides, Butyricicoccus, and Lachnospiraceae were diminished in IBS rats compared to Non-IBS rats, being partially restored by L. fermentum or gabapentin treatment.

In the IBS group, Trpv1 gene expression positively correlated with abundance of Bacteroides, Butyricicoccus, Prevotellaceae_UCG_001, and Collinsella, a relationship not seen (or altered) in Non-IBS/treated rats.
Among 20 subjects with autonomic neuropathy and unexplained GI symptoms, 85% had abnormal QSART testing results.
Cardiovagal impairment, determined by abnormal HRDB or Valsalva ratio, was present in 20% of the AN cohort.
Cardiovascular adrenergic impairment, based on abnormal Valsalva and/or BP response to head-up tilt, was present in 65% of the AN cohort.
85% of AN subjects had objectively abnormal segmental GI transit times on wireless motility capsule testing, averaging 1.8 affected segments per subject.
Delayed transit times were the predominant abnormality, present in 60% of subjects, compared to 30% with abnormally rapid transit in one or more segments.
Delayed gastric emptying was the single most common segmental abnormality, occurring in 50% of subjects.
Delayed small bowel transit time (SBTT) and rapid gastric emptying time (GET) each occurred in 30% of subjects.
Delayed colonic transit time (CTT) and delayed whole gut transit time (WGTT) each occurred in 15% of subjects.
90% of AN subjects had objectively abnormal GI contractility recordings, averaging one affected segment per subject.
Increased colonic (hindgut) contractility was the predominant contractility abnormality, occurring in 85% of subjects, in contrast to only 5% with increased gastric (foregut) contractions.
Decreased small bowel (midgut) contractility was rare, occurring in only 5% of subjects, and this individual did not report symptomatic constipation.
The AN cohort had a markedly elevated median COMPASS-31 summary score (55.4) compared to a previously published healthy control median of 12.6.

The AN cohort's median COMPASS-31 GI domain score (16.3) was somewhat higher than a previously published AN GI domain score (12.0), potentially reflecting the cohort's selection for unexplained GI symptoms.
Among the AN cohort, 11 reported frequent/constant constipation, 12 reported frequent/constant diarrhea, and 6 reported both.
Half of individuals with one or more quantifiable segmental transit delay reported symptoms of constipation.
Two-thirds of individuals with at least one abnormally rapid segment transit time reported symptoms of diarrhea.
Most individuals with increased colonic contractility on WMC testing reported diarrhea symptoms.
Most subjects with an abnormal QSART site had abnormal WMC transit times or contractility in the neuroanatomically corresponding GI segment.
Among subjects with abnormal QSART in the proximal leg, distal leg, or foot (corresponding to midgut/hindgut innervation), most also had abnormal colonic transit or contractility.
Most subjects with abnormal forearm QSART (corresponding to foregut innervation) had abnormal gastric emptying time.
All subjects with cardiovagal impairment and most with cardiovascular adrenergic impairment had corresponding abnormal gastric emptying time.
Combining forearm QSART, cardiovagal, and cardiovascular adrenergic abnormalities, 88% of affected subjects had corresponding foregut-level autonomic reflex abnormalities on WMC testing.
Among 504 patients who recovered from confirmed COVID-19, 227 (45.0%) developed post-COVID-19 syndrome (PCS), defined as symptoms persisting beyond 12 weeks.
Female sex was an independent risk factor for developing post-COVID-19 syndrome after adjustment for other variables.
A history of asthma was associated with a higher incidence of post-COVID-19 syndrome.
A history of COPD was associated with a higher incidence of post-COVID-19 syndrome.
Having three or more co-morbid conditions was an independent risk factor for post-COVID-19 syndrome.
Receiving steroids during acute COVID-19 was independently associated with a higher risk of post-COVID-19 syndrome, a novel finding not previously reported.
Use of other chronic disease medications (e.g., for diabetes and hypertension) was associated with a higher incidence of post-COVID-19 syndrome.
ICU admission during acute COVID-19 was significantly associated with development of post-COVID-19 syndrome.
Experiencing nasal congestion during initial COVID-19 infection was an independent predictor of post-COVID-19 syndrome.
Experiencing depression during initial COVID-19 infection was an independent predictor of post-COVID-19 syndrome.
None of the collected laboratory parameters (blood workup, liver enzymes, urea, electrolytes, CPK, CRP) were associated with development of post-COVID-19 syndrome.
Fatigue was the most commonly reported persistent symptom beyond 12 weeks after COVID-19.
Joint pain was the second most commonly reported persistent symptom of post-COVID-19 syndrome.
Decreased exercise tolerance was the third most commonly reported persistent symptom of post-COVID-19 syndrome.
Nearly all acute-phase COVID-19 symptoms (except fever) were significantly associated with development and persistence of post-COVID-19 syndrome.
In a 25-year follow-up, 20 of 25 initially diagnosed ME/CFS patients no longer met Fukuda diagnostic criteria, and 15 of those 20 remitted patients were able to return to work.

POTS is diagnostically defined as a heart rate increase of over 30 bpm without accompanying hypotension during a 10-minute standing test, accompanied by symptoms such as dizziness, brain fog, palpitations, tremor, generalized weakness, blurred vision, exercise intolerance, or fatigue.
In a small study of POTS patients, 64% met clinical criteria for CFS, and 93% reported fatigue, orthostatic intolerance, palpitations, dizziness, daytime tiredness, and gastrointestinal disturbances.

A recent small study (n=28) suggested POTS may have a psychogenic/functional origin, showing that patients had a greater anticipatory heart-rate rise before tilt-table positioning, with somatic vigilance and catecholamine increases predicting heart-rate rise and hyperventilation.
An older study using a lower-body negative pressure device followed by a Stroop mental stress test found no differences between POTS patients and healthy controls, though the sample was even smaller.

ME/CFS patients had significantly higher serum levels of GPCR autoantibodies (M3, M4 muscarinic and β2 adrenergic) compared with healthy controls, implicated in dysregulated anticholinergic/adrenergic signaling, but overlap with healthy controls precluded diagnostic use.
Some studies reported reduced NK cell cytotoxic activity in ME/CFS patients, but these immunological findings were not replicated in subsequent studies.
Some studies reported elevated IL-10 levels in ME/CFS patients, but this finding was not replicated in subsequent studies.
An app-based study of 4182 SARS-CoV-2-infected individuals found that only 13.3% reported persistent fatigue, headache, dyspnea, and anosmia at 28 days post-infection, dropping to 2.3% at 12 weeks.
A separate study of 938 participants found 46% still reported fatigue between 1.5 and 6 months (mean 117.5 days) after SARS-CoV-2 infection.

In a prospective study of 40 patients with neurological symptoms during/after SARS-CoV-2 infection who underwent lumbar puncture, CSF showed no evidence of active CNS infection, though 5 patients had detectable viral PCR at very low levels.
A prospective cohort study found that the majority (85.5%) of patients with long-COVID complaints had no objectifiable neurological findings when systematically evaluated.
The Fleischer et al. prospective cohort study found a significant association between fatigue/concentration difficulties in long-COVID patients and pre-existing psychiatric illness.
A German general-population study found a 72% overlap between chronic fatigue (operationalized similarly to but not identical with ME/CFS criteria) and somatoform disorders.

Two studies from Leuven and Antwerp universities found personality disorder rates in ME/CFS patients (~13-16%) comparable to healthy controls, whereas psychiatric patients had significantly higher rates (>50%).

A UK birth-cohort study found ME/CFS patients had elevated rates of psychiatric illness before symptom onset, with depression and anxiety preceding fatigue symptoms and psychiatric severity predicting later ME/CFS diagnosis.
Psychiatric comorbidity in ME/CFS patients is reported to range from approximately 45% to 70% across studies.

A US Phase III trial in 234 ME/CFS patients showed significant improvement in objective treadmill physical performance after 40 weeks of twice-weekly intravenous rintatolimod (400 mg), a selective TLR3 agonist, compared to control.
A first double-blind study with 30 participants showed a significant improvement in a self-report fatigue-symptom questionnaire 25 weeks after treatment, as stated in text.
A subsequent open-label study of 29 ME/CFS patients found clinical response in 18 patients on a self-report questionnaire.

A long-term follow-up study found that 25 years after initial diagnosis, 20 of 25 originally diagnosed ME/CFS patients no longer met the Fukuda diagnostic criteria, and 15 of those 20 remitted patients had returned to work.
Neuropsychological testing has shown objective deficits in attention, memory, and reaction time in ME/CFS patients, despite unclear guideline criteria for testing cognitive impairment.
In a small study of POTS patients, 64% fulfilled clinical CFS criteria and 93% reported fatigue, orthostatic intolerance, palpitations, dizziness, daytime tiredness and gastrointestinal disturbances.

A study proposing an anxiety-conditioning model of POTS found that POTS patients showed a greater anticipatory heart-rate rise before tilt, with somatic vigilance and catecholamine rise during upright posture predicting the heart-rate increase and hyperventilation, interpreted as evidence of a psychogenic/functional origin.
An older study using lower body negative pressure followed by a Stroop test to induce mental stress found no differences between POTS patients and healthy controls, in an even smaller sample.
A Cochrane review found that CBT and graded exercise therapy (GET) improved fatigue in ME/CFS.

Some studies reported immunological abnormalities such as reduced cytotoxic NK cell activity and elevated interleukin-10 levels in ME/CFS, but these findings could not be replicated in subsequent studies.

Other explanatory models propose metabolic, mitochondrial, hemodynamic, and neuroimaging differences between ME/CFS patients and healthy individuals, but evidence remains limited by poor sensitivity/specificity and lack of a validated biological test.
An app-based study of 4182 SARS-CoV-2-infected individuals found only 13.3% reported persistent fatigue, headache, dyspnea and anosmia at 28 days post-infection, dropping to 2.3% at 12 weeks.
Another study of 938 participants found that 46% still reported fatigue 1.5-6 months (mean 117.5 days) after SARS-CoV-2 infection, a much higher rate than the app-based study.

Isolated histological case reports have detected SARS-CoV-2 in neuronal endothelial cells, raising the possibility of a neurotropic virus, but no actively replicating virus has ever been demonstrated.

In a prospective study, 40 patients with neurological symptoms during and after SARS-CoV-2 infection underwent lumbar puncture; CSF showed no evidence of active CNS infection, though 5 patients had detectable viral PCR at very low levels.

Neuropsychological studies show a discrepancy between perceived cognitive impairment and results on standardized neuropsychological tests in post-COVID patients, but associations were found between high anxiety/depression scores and borderline-low cognitive test results.

In a prospective cohort study by Fleischer et al., 85.5% of patients with post-COVID complaints had no objectively verifiable neurological symptoms, and a significant association was found between fatigue/concentration difficulties and pre-existing psychiatric illness.
A German study found a 72% overlap between chronic fatigue (operationalized by a fatigue cut-off score lasting >6 months) and somatoform disorders in the general population.
Good data exist on psychiatric comorbidity in ME/CFS patients, with rates reported between approximately 45% and 70%.

A UK birth-cohort registry study found that ME/CFS patients had elevated rates of psychiatric illness before symptom onset, with depression and anxiety preceding fatigue symptoms, and psychiatric severity predicting later ME/CFS diagnosis.

Two studies from Leuven and Antwerp universities found personality disorder rates in ME/CFS patients comparable to healthy controls (~13-16%), significantly lower than the rate (>50%) among psychiatric patients.

A US Phase III trial in 234 ME/CFS patients showed significant improvement in objective treadmill physical performance versus control after 40 weeks of twice-weekly intravenous 400mg Rintatolimod, a selective TLR3 agonist.
A first double-blind study of 30 ME/CFS participants reported a significant improvement in a self-report fatigue-associated symptom questionnaire 25 weeks after treatment.
A subsequent open-label study of 29 ME/CFS patients found clinical response in a self-report questionnaire in 18 of 29 patients treated with Rituximab.

The final, largest study by the same authors (n=151) found no significant difference in response (fatigue self-report, SF-36 physical form, step counts, Fatigue Severity Scale) between Rituximab and placebo over 12 months of treatment.
In a US phase III trial of 234 ME/CFS patients, twice-weekly intravenous rintatolimod (400 mg) over 40 weeks significantly improved objective treadmill exercise performance versus control.
In an initial double-blind study of 30 ME/CFS participants, a significant improvement in a self-report fatigue questionnaire was seen 25 weeks after treatment in the comparison group.
An open-label follow-up study of 29 ME/CFS patients found clinical response in 18 patients based on a self-assessment questionnaire.

The largest rituximab trial (151 patients, six infusions of 500 mg/m2 then 500 mg fixed dose over 12 months) showed no significant difference in fatigue response versus placebo across multiple outcome measures.
The first double-blind placebo-controlled IVIg trial from 1990 found a positive response in patients receiving 2 g/kg IVIg.
A contemporaneous placebo-controlled trial of monthly IVIg (1 g/kg) in 28 patients found no clinical improvement after 6 months.

A third placebo-controlled IVIg trial testing multiple doses (0.5, 1, 2 g/kg) in 73 patients versus 26 placebo patients found no significant differences in Karnofsky index or quality-of-life/activity/mood questionnaires.

A trial of valganciclovir (900 mg twice daily for 21 days, then 90 mg daily for 6 months) in 30 ME/CFS patients with positive EBV and HHV-6 IgG titers showed subjective improvements in fatigue and cognitive performance ratings over 9 months.
A Spanish trial of 50 ME/CFS patients given 1 mg melatonin plus 10 mg zinc versus placebo for up to 16 weeks showed no significant improvement in the primary fatigue-score endpoint.

A trial of oral coenzyme Q10 (200 mg) plus NADH (10 mg) versus placebo for 8 weeks showed no significant difference in fatigue or sleep questionnaires, though subjective sleep efficiency improved only in the control group.

A Japanese double-blind trial of ubiquinol-10 over 12 weeks showed significant improvement in objective endpoints (arithmetic task accuracy, nocturnal awakening, heart rate variability) but not subjective fatigue or depression scores.

An open-label Dutch study found that acetylcarnitine improved concentration and propionylcarnitine improved physical performance individually after 24 weeks, but the hypothesized combined benefit of both agents together was not confirmed.
A small crossover study using acute tryptophan depletion versus placebo found no significant difference in fatigue, mood, or concentration.

A double-blind placebo-controlled trial in 63 patients with postviral fatigue syndrome showed a significant benefit of essential fatty acid supplementation at 1 and 3 months on fatigue, dizziness, and concentration measured with a 3-point scale.
A replication of the essential fatty acid trial nine years later, using the same 3-point scale, dosing and formulation, failed to replicate the earlier positive results.

The PACE trial (n=641, up to 8 years follow-up) found that, versus standard care, CBT and graded exercise therapy (GET) produced significant improvements after one year on the Chalder Fatigue Score and SF-36 physical function questionnaire.

A mediator analysis of the PACE trial found that fear-avoidance beliefs mediated treatment response, such that patients who changed their exercise-avoidance beliefs were more likely to respond to GET and CBT.
Rintatolimod is approved only in Argentina for moderate-to-severe ME/CFS, while the US FDA rejected approval in 2009 and again in 2012 citing insufficient efficacy and safety data.

A non-placebo-controlled phase II trial of the immunosuppressant cyclophosphamide from the University of Bergen group showed response in more than half of patients, measured by questionnaires and step counts.
The first study using quantitative EMG in long-COVID patients with musculoskeletal symptoms showed myopathic changes.

In 16 patients with fatigue, myalgia, and/or weakness persisting up to 14 months after mild-to-moderate COVID-19, myopathic qEMG features and histopathological changes (muscle fiber atrophy, mitochondrial changes, subsarcolemmal accumulation, inflammation, capillary alteration) were found in skeletal muscle biopsies.

A TMS study in 12 patients with long-term fatigue and brain fog after severe COVID-19 showed disruption of post-contraction depression, i.e., loss of the normal transient decrease in motor evoked potential amplitude and prolongation of the cortical silent period after a fatiguing motor task.

In 67 patients with fatigue and cognitive difficulties after mild COVID-19, impaired intracortical GABAergic activity (disrupted long-interval intracortical inhibition) and reduced excitability of the primary motor cortex were demonstrated, alongside selective deficits in executive functions.

Increased production of autoantibodies against CNS and autonomic nervous system targets, including the β2 adrenergic receptor, has been documented in ME/CFS, potentially causing vasoconstriction and chronic muscular/cerebral hypoperfusion via disturbed vasodilator function.
Among 1,792 valid questionnaires from university students in Wuhan, 112 met CDC/Fukuda criteria for ME/CFS, giving a prevalence of 6.25%.
Prevalence of ME/CFS did not differ significantly by gender, age, grade, or academic major.
Men reported significantly higher mental fatigue scores than women on the Fatigue Scale (FS-14).
Regular exercise, sugar control, weight maintenance, and avoiding staying up all night were associated with lower fatigue scores.
Alcohol consumption was associated with increased fatigue scores among students.

Dietary patterns including overeating, frequent snacking, pickled food, and milk tea consumption were associated with higher fatigue scores, while regular eating and combining meat with vegetables were associated with lower fatigue scores.
Greater use of social support (seeking help, group activities, freely expressing emotion) was associated with lower fatigue scores.
Subjects with high fatigue scores commonly reported headache, dizziness, nausea, dyspnea, numbness and tingling, and heavy hands and feet.

Fatigue scores were significantly higher in students with anxiety than those without anxiety, and in students with depression than those without depression, with independent (non-interacting) effects of the two factors.
Anxiety and depression scores were each strongly correlated with fatigue score, with correlations increasing after adjustment for the other factor.

Staying up all night (overnights), overeating, anxiety, and poor sleep quality were identified as independent risk factors for ME/CFS in multivariate logistic regression, while appropriate study time was a protective factor.
Differences in ME/CFS prevalence by exercise habits and alcohol consumption were not statistically significant in the multivariate model.
Study time had a protective (U-shaped) association with ME/CFS, with the lowest odds at 2-4 hours of study per day, but the protective effect weakened with longer study durations.

The 6.25% ME/CFS prevalence found in this Wuhan cohort was lower than the 12.54% pooled prevalence reported in a prior Chinese meta-analysis and lower than the 20.2% and 17.55% rates reported in university students in Zhejiang and among medical students in Jiangxi/Hunan, respectively.
Among 465 Long COVID patients, 58% (272) met the Canadian Consensus Criteria case definition for ME/CFS while 42% (193) did not.

Long COVID patients meeting CCC criteria for ME/CFS had directionally higher symptom burden scores on every DSQ-COVID symptom compared to those not meeting criteria, with significant differences in 36 of 38 symptoms.
Those meeting CCC criteria had significantly higher mean scores across all symptoms on the DSQ-Short Form compared to those not meeting criteria.
Those meeting CCC criteria had significantly higher mean scores across all PEM questionnaire items compared to those not meeting criteria.
Long COVID patients meeting ME/CFS criteria had significantly worse (lower) functional impairment scores than those not meeting criteria.

There was substantial discordance between patient self-report of having ME/CFS and objectively meeting the CCC ME/CFS case definition: only 71.37% of self-reported ME/CFS cases met criteria, while 40% of those who denied having ME/CFS nonetheless met criteria.

Among Long COVID patients meeting ME/CFS criteria, the highest-scoring symptoms on the DSQ-SF were minimal exercise causing physical tiredness, fatigue/extreme tiredness, unrefreshing sleep, next-day soreness/fatigue after non-strenuous activities, difficulty sustaining attention, and problems remembering things — i.e., PEM, cognitive impairment, and unrefreshing sleep symptoms.

Some Long COVID-specific symptoms not typically part of the ME/CFS case definition, such as loss of or change in smell/taste, were also more frequent and severe in those meeting ME/CFS diagnostic criteria.
ME/CFS is estimated to affect approximately 70 million people worldwide with a prevalence of 0.89% (CDC 1994 case definition), with women 1.5 to 2 times more affected than men.
An updated US estimate reported a doubling of ME/CFS prevalence to 1.5 million people (0.45%) with an annual economic impact of 36-51 billion dollars.
The global pooled prevalence of PASC (long-COVID) is estimated at 0.43, with women approximately 1.3 times more likely than men to be affected.
Symptom scores across 62 items for the PASC group correlated strongly between two timepoints (r=0.839), indicating a stable within-person symptom profile over time.
Symptom scores at PASC timepoint one correlated moderately-strongly with ME/CFS symptom scores across 62 items (r=0.729), suggesting overlapping symptom profiles between the two conditions.

Symptom scores at PASC timepoint two correlated very strongly with ME/CFS symptom scores across 62 items (r=0.902), described as the maximum correlation obtainable within the instrument's reliability, supporting high similarity between the two conditions.
Over time, the PASC group showed an overall reduction in most symptoms including unrefreshing sleep and post-exertional malaise, but an intensification of neurocognitive symptoms.

The ME/CFS group had significantly higher (more severe) scores than the PASC/COVID-19 sample on the majority of DSQ symptom items, with the exception of the orthostatic domain where scores did not differ.
A review of HPA axis function in chronic fatigue syndrome found that patients with CFS normally suffer from HPA axis dysfunction.
A systematic review concluded that cytokines in blood and cerebrospinal fluid are closely associated with the progression and severity of CFS.

Dysregulated TGFB (transforming growth factor beta) signaling, previously associated with ME/CFS especially in peripheral cells, is hypothesized to disrupt circadian physiological rhythms in sleep, activity, and cognition in ME/CFS and PASC.

In a study of 36 female subjects (19 ME/CFS, 17 healthy controls), abnormal resting-state functional connectivity in parahippocampal and occipital seed regions correlated with the level of self-reported fatigue.
A study of cortical autonomic network connectivity observed reduced higher-order homeostatic regulation and adaptability in ME/CFS.

The Energy Envelope theory found that ME/CFS patients who expended energy beyond their perceived available energy level ('energy quotient') experienced more severe fatigue and other symptoms and lower physical and mental functioning.

A tractography analysis in six healthy adults identified structural connections between six brainstem nuclei and seven forebrain regions, with the strongest connectivity between the brainstem midline raphe and the medial temporal lobe, supporting an integrated Central Homeostasis Network in the human brain.
A patient survey of 5822 ME patients in Norway found that large fluctuations, or fluctuations with gradual deterioration, are the two most typical courses of the illness.

Increased cortisol has immunosuppressive effects on specific immune cells, such as neutrophils and natural killer cells, and is hypothesized to contribute to ME/CFS via stress-related immune suppression.
Overall HHV-6A/B specific antibody seropositivity was significantly higher in ME/CFS patients than in healthy individuals.
Anti-HHV-6A/B IgG class antibodies were significantly more prevalent in ME/CFS patients than in healthy individuals.
Anti-HHV-6A/B IgM class antibodies were slightly more frequent in ME/CFS patients but the difference was not statistically significant.
HHV-7 specific IgG antibody prevalence did not differ significantly between ME/CFS patients and healthy individuals.
B19V-specific IgG antibody seroprevalence was similar between ME/CFS patients and healthy individuals.
B19V-specific IgM antibodies, indicating recent/active infection, were found only in ME/CFS patients and not in healthy controls.
Overall markers of persistent viral infection/co-infection (by nested PCR) were significantly more prevalent in ME/CFS patients than healthy individuals.
Markers of latent (blood-leukocyte DNA) infection/co-infection were less frequent in ME/CFS patients than in healthy individuals.
Markers of active infection/co-infection (blood-plasma cell-free viral DNA) were markedly more frequent in ME/CFS patients than healthy individuals.
Absence of detectable HHV-6A/B, HHV-7, and B19V genomic sequences was less common in patients than in healthy individuals.
Among HHV-6 positive ME/CFS patients, HHV-6B was overwhelmingly predominant over HHV-6A.
A significantly higher proportion of ME/CFS patients had elevated HHV-6A/B viral load during active-phase infection compared with latent-phase infection.
Median HHV-6A/B viral load was significantly higher in patients with active-phase infection compared to latent-phase infection.
A significantly higher proportion of ME/CFS patients had elevated HHV-7 viral load during active-phase infection compared with latent-phase infection.
Median HHV-7 viral load did not differ significantly between latent- and active-phase infection.
The proportion of patients with elevated B19V viral load did not differ significantly between latent and active phase.
Median B19V viral load was significantly higher during active-phase compared to latent-phase infection.
Active-phase double HHV-6A/B + HHV-7 co-infection, and active-phase triple HHV-6A/B+HHV-7+B19V co-infection, were found exclusively in ME/CFS patients and not in healthy controls.
Active-phase double HHV-7 + B19V co-infection was significantly more common in ME/CFS patients than healthy individuals.

Plasma TNF-α, IL-12 and IL-10 levels differed significantly across ME/CFS subgroups defined by infection status (no infection, latent, active single/double/triple co-infection), while IL-6 did not differ.
TNF-α, IL-12, and IL-10 plasma levels were significantly higher in patients with severe ME/CFS course compared to those with moderate course.
IL-6 levels showed a non-significant trend toward being higher in patients with moderate rather than severe ME/CFS.
HHV-7 viral load was significantly higher in patients with severe ME/CFS compared to those with moderate course, suggesting a link to disease severity.
HHV-6A/B viral load did not differ significantly between patients with severe versus moderate ME/CFS course.
B19V viral load did not differ significantly between patients with severe versus moderate ME/CFS course.

Impaired memory, decreased concentration, and sleep disturbances were the most frequently reported symptoms among the 200 ME/CFS patients, occurring significantly more often than muscle pain, lymphadenopathy, multi-joint pain, and new-type headache.
Most ME/CFS patients experienced a moderate disease course, while a minority had a severe course.
HHV-6B was the predominant variant detected in ME/CFS patients, with HHV-6A found in only one patient.
Active double co-infection with HHV-6A/B and HHV-7 was found exclusively in ME/CFS patients and never in healthy individuals.
Active triple co-infection (HHV-6A/B + HHV-7 + B19V) was found exclusively in ME/CFS patients.
