Active double co-infection with HHV-7 and B19V was significantly more frequent in ME/CFS patients than in healthy individuals.
IL-6 level was significantly higher in ME/CFS patients with active double co-infection compared to those with latent infection/co-infection or without infection.
TNF-α level was significantly higher in patients with active triple co-infection compared to those with latent infection/co-infection or active double co-infection.
IL-12 level was significantly more elevated in patients with active triple co-infection compared to latent infection/co-infection, active single infection, and active double infection.
IL-10 level was significantly higher in patients with active double co-infection compared to patients without infection and with latent infection/co-infection.
IL-10 level was higher in patients with active triple co-infection compared to those without infection, with latent infection/co-infection, and with active single infection.
TNF-α, IL-12, and IL-10 levels were significantly higher in ME/CFS patients with a severe clinical course compared to those with a moderate course.
IL-6 level showed a non-significant trend toward being higher in patients with moderate versus severe ME/CFS course.

Impaired memory, decreased concentration, and sleep disturbances were the most frequently reported symptoms among ME/CFS patients, occurring significantly more often than muscle pain, lymphadenopathy, multi-joint pain, or new-type headache.
ME/CFS was significantly more prevalent among females than males in this cohort, consistent with prior literature reporting female predominance.
Estimated prevalence of CFS among US adolescents ranges from 0.1% to 1.9%, depending on the case definition applied.
Multiple studies found that 11–13% of adolescents experienced a prolonged recovery following common illnesses such as EBV infection.
A similar rate of prolonged post-infective fatigue was observed following Q fever (Coxiella burnetii) and Ross River virus infection as with EBV.
Between 10% and 30% of individuals developed prolonged post-viral (ME/CFS-like) symptoms following COVID-19.
Some studies have found low-grade systemic inflammation in ME/CFS, though findings are not consistent across studies.
Attenuated natural killer (NK) cell function has been reported in ME/CFS, though this finding is not consistent across studies.
Recent research reports higher levels of immunosuppressive cytokines, especially TGF-β, in ME/CFS as a promising biomarker lead.
An altered gut microbiome has been identified as a potential contributing factor/biomarker in ME/CFS.
Nanoelectric markers have been proposed as potential biomarkers for ME/CFS.
Autonomic dysfunction with clinical orthostatic intolerance is commonly present in adolescents with ME/CFS.
Neuropsychological studies show impairment of executive function and concentration along with alterations in brain blood flow in ME/CFS.
ME/CFS patients experience more sleep difficulties than healthy individuals.

In a large Australian adolescent ME/CFS cohort, depression was only mildly increased compared with age-matched population levels and generally did not precede the illness; its presence was linked to diagnostic delay, illness severity, disbelief by others, and social isolation.
Reported anxiety in adolescents with ME/CFS was higher than age-matched population norms.
A UK adolescent ME/CFS cohort reported a similar proportion with anxiety, though this cohort lacked a control group for comparison.
Long-term follow-up studies suggest that by 10 years most young people report improvement or recovery, but about 20–25% still have significant morbidity and reduced function.
In the Australian cohort, the average duration for clinically diagnosed ME/CFS among those reporting recovery was 5 years (range 1–16 years).
A double-blind study of intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) in adolescents showed promising results, but subsequent adult studies were inconclusive, and the adolescent study has not been replicated.
Numerous interventions, including antivirals and the monoclonal antibody rituximab, have not shown promising results for ME/CFS.

The PACE trial suggested graded exercise therapy and cognitive behavior therapy were useful and initially recommended as effective, but these findings were subsequently criticized by patients and scientists over methodological concerns.

In a large follow-up study, severity of initial illness, nature of infectious trigger, presence of depression at initial visit, or duration of illness prior to being seen were not predictive of recovery.
Remaining engaged in education was identified as the best predictor of a good functional outcome at follow-up in adolescents with ME/CFS.
Orthostatic intolerance has been shown to be associated with reduced cerebral blood flow, providing a mechanistic basis for cognitive symptoms and rationale for orthostatic management.
IQWiG's benefit assessment found only a low-certainty 'hint of an indication' of short- and medium-term benefit of CBT and GET over standard medical care, with no benefit found at longer follow-up.
A study by Davis et al. found that 89% of long COVID patients experienced post-exertional malaise and 88% experienced cognitive problems, overlapping heavily with ME/CFS symptomatology.
Lack of blinding in trials is associated with an average 13% exaggeration of intervention effect estimates, per the BRANDO project analysis.

In Moss-Morris et al. 2005, subjective physical functioning improved 30% after GET while objectively measured physical functioning (CPET) deteriorated 15%, illustrating divergence between subjective and objective outcomes.

Released individual participant data from the PACE trial showed that 20% of participants who reported subjective improvement in physical functioning had actually deteriorated on the objective six-minute walk test.

The GETSET trial's own therapist manual states that the treatment tested (Guided graded Exercise Self-help, GES) is explicitly not the same as graded exercise therapy (GET), undermining its use as evidence for GET efficacy.

Recalculating PEM prevalence using the ratio observed in Janse et al. (92%) suggests only 61-68% of PACE and GETSET participants actually had PEM, below the 80% threshold IQWiG itself required for study inclusion.

The Chalder Fatigue Scale shows a ceiling effect: in the PACE trial, 44% of participants had a Likert score of 30-33 (near maximum) at baseline, meaning deterioration could not be reflected in the score.

The FINE trial (sister trial of PACE) reported a null effect using bimodal scoring in its original 2010 publication, but reported a small statistically significant improvement after switching to Likert scoring in a later mediation analysis.

In a lupus GET trial involving PACE's principal investigator, GET improved Chalder Fatigue scores similarly to PACE but showed no improvement on two other fatigue scales (FSS, VAS) nor on objective VO2 peak.

In the PACE trial, quality-of-life (EQ-5D) improvement from GET and CBT over APT was minimal (2.3% and 0.5% respectively), with post-treatment scores still worse than those for stroke, MS, or ischemic heart disease.
The PACE trial showed no statistically significant improvement in the chronic fatigue syndrome symptom count at 52 weeks between GET and SMC, GET and APT, or CBT and APT.
IQWiG's own analysis of the six-minute walk test in the PACE trial found no objective short-, medium-, or long-term benefit or harm from CBT or GET compared to standard medical care.
The PACE trial showed GET had a negative effect and CBT had no effect on employment/occupational status, with more patients reliant on illness/disability benefits after treatment than before.
Adherence to internet-based CBT in Janse et al. was very low, with only 16-19% of participants fully adhering to the intervention.
Pooled patient surveys found that CBT worsened health in 20% of respondents, while GET worsened health in at least 50% of respondents.
The Oxford Brookes University survey of 2274 ME/CFS patients commissioned for NICE found high rates of symptom worsening and increased severe disability after CBT and GET.

Exercise studies (Black and McCully; Lien et al.) provided objective evidence that ME/CFS patients develop exercise intolerance and worsened physical performance/lactate response after exertion, unlike healthy controls.

Núñez et al. found that multidisciplinary treatment combining CBT, GET, and pharmacological treatment did not improve health-related quality of life at 12 months and led to worse physical function and bodily pain scores.

NICE's 2021 updated ME/CFS guideline review found that all reviewed CBT and GET trials were of low or very low quality, concluded neither treatment leads to recovery, and stated GET is harmful and should not be used.
Real-world implementation of GET in a Dutch hospital sports medicine department found very high dropout rates of 55%, 73%, and 80% at 6, 9, and 12 months respectively.
A medical statistics professor's critique noted that performing a meta-analysis on only two poor-quality studies each for CBT and GET risks giving unreliable data a false impression of objectivity.
General fatigue was the most prevalent complaint among PASC patients, reported by 94% of the cohort.
Sleep problems were reported by 74% of PASC patients, similar to ME/CFS.
Neurocognitive symptoms including memory problems (74%) and attention difficulties (62%) were common among PASC patients.
ME/CFS patients were significantly more likely than PASC patients to report unrefreshing sleep at baseline.
ME/CFS patients were significantly more likely than PASC patients to report flu-like symptoms at baseline.
Aside from unrefreshing sleep and flu-like symptoms, no other significant differences in the remaining 12 DSQ-SF composite symptom scores were found between PASC and ME/CFS at baseline.

Adaptive LASSO regression with 10-fold cross-validation confirmed that the same two symptoms (flu-like symptoms and unrefreshed in the morning) were the most predictive features distinguishing ME/CFS from PASC.
Mean composite DSQ-SF symptom scores did not significantly change over 1-year follow-up in the ME/CFS cohort.

PASC patients showed a significantly greater reduction in symptom severity across 5 of the 14 DSQ-SF items over a 1-year follow-up compared to the ME/CFS cohort, based on difference-in-differences analysis.
Nearly all patients with PASC met the Institute of Medicine clinical diagnostic criteria for ME/CFS, indicating substantial diagnostic overlap between the two conditions.
In the CFS group, heart rate changed significantly across the four EAT phases (resting, endoscopy, nasal abrasion, oral abrasion).
CVRR, an aggregate index of total autonomic nervous activity, changed significantly across EAT phases in the CFS group.
ccvHF, an index of parasympathetic function, showed a near-significant change across EAT phases in the CFS group but did not reach significance.

The L/H ratio, an index of sympathetic function, showed no significant difference across EAT phases but showed a decreasing trend in phase 3 (nasal abrasion) and increasing trend in phase 4 (oral abrasion).
In the CFS group, multiple comparisons showed HR differed significantly between phase 2 (endoscopy) and phase 4 (oral abrasion), and between phase 3 (nasal abrasion) and phase 4.
In the control (non-CFS chronic epipharyngitis) group, HR also changed significantly across EAT phases, with a significant difference between phase 2 and phase 4.
At resting baseline (phase 1) before EAT, mean HR in the CFS group was 5.3% higher than in the control group.

During nasal abrasion (phase 3), the variability/increase in ccvHF was greater in the CFS group (22.6%) than in the control group (11.1%), indicating heightened parasympathetic reactivity to EAT stimulation in CFS.
During oral abrasion (phase 4), CVRR increased more in the CFS group (35.6%) than in the control group (17.4%), indicating greater overall autonomic reactivity in CFS.
Among 288 patients evaluated for chronic epipharyngitis, chronic fatigue syndrome was the chief complaint in 11 cases (3.8%).

Nasal abrasion stimulation during EAT increased parasympathetic activity and decreased heart rate, with a greater HR decrease observed in the CFS group than the control group, suggesting an easily-triggered vagal reflex in CFS.

The CFS group showed greater fluctuation across all measured HR variability endpoints than the control group, interpreted as impaired autonomic homeostasis (autonomic ataxia) with heightened risk of pathological vagal reflex or the Reilly phenomenon.
Citing prior literature, the paper notes that CFS patients have been reported to exhibit both sympathetically dominant and parasympathetically depressed autonomic states.
Among 30 patients with chronic widespread pain/fibromyalgia, mean lumbar opening CSF pressure was 19.7 cm H2O, with over half exhibiting pressures at or above 19 cm H2O.
In 20 CFS patients, mean lumbar CSF pressure was 19 cm H2O and half exhibited pressures above 19 cm H2O.
Removal of cerebrospinal fluid via lumbar puncture temporarily improved bodily pain in 70% of fibromyalgia/chronic widespread pain patients.
Removal of cerebrospinal fluid temporarily improved headaches in 85% of CFS patients.
Brain MRI in 205 CFS patients showed an increased optic nerve sheath diameter, a radiographic sign of intracranial hypertension, in 55% of patients.
A meta-analysis of 85 studies found significantly reduced basal cortisol levels in male and female CFS patients and in female fibromyalgia patients compared to healthy controls.
A CRH stimulation test in fibromyalgia patients demonstrated a blunted ACTH response compared to controls.
A significant 30% reduction in ACTH response to hypoglycemia was observed in women with fibromyalgia compared to controls.
A CRH or naloxone challenge test found no difference in ACTH and cortisol responses between CFS patients and healthy individuals, contrasting with other blunted-response findings.
Two studies found significantly lower aldosterone levels in CFS patients than in controls.
Approximately 30-34% of fibromyalgia patients present lower basal GH or IGF-1 levels than healthy individuals across multiple studies.
CFS patients show lower nocturnal GH levels or lower IGF-1 levels than controls in several studies.
GH response to insulin-induced hypoglycemia was reduced in 73 nonobese CFS patients compared to 21 nonobese controls, indicating obesity did not account for the effect.
Among women with hyperprolactinemia, 71% were diagnosed with fibromyalgia, compared to only 4.5% of women with normal prolactin levels.

Challenging the pituitary with hypothalamic releasing hormones or buspirone elicited a higher prolactin response in fibromyalgia patients than in controls, suggested to reflect reduced dopamine inhibition.
Stimulating the pituitary gland with buspirone significantly increased the prolactin response in male CFS patients compared to controls.
Challenge with LHRH in fibromyalgia patients produced a significantly blunted LH response compared to controls, while FSH response did not differ.
No significant differences in FSH, LH, estradiol, or progesterone levels were found between CFS patients and controls in cited studies.
A TRH challenge test in fibromyalgia patients elicited a lower TSH and thyroid hormone secretion response, similar to the pattern seen in primary empty sella patients.
In a case-control study, free T3 was below the reference range in 16% of CFS patients versus 7% of controls, an odds ratio of 2.56, while TSH remained normal.
Obesity prevalence in fibromyalgia patients ranged from 22-43% across regions, and fibromyalgia prevalence in obese individuals (37-51%) was much higher than in the general population (4%).
An observational study of over 15,000 16-year-old CFS patients found they were four times more likely to be obese than healthy adolescents (OR 4.15).
The female-to-male sex ratio is estimated at 9:1 in both fibromyalgia and CFS, markedly higher than the general 5:1-6:1 ratio reported in primary empty sella syndrome.
Among fibromyalgia patients reporting headaches, migraine was diagnosed in 63%, with only 8% having probable analgesic overuse headache.
In a cross-sectional study, migraine headache prevalence in CFS patients was 84% and tension-type headache 81%, compared to only 5% and 45% respectively in healthy controls.

Fibromyalgia patients show retinal nerve fiber layer thinning and decreased optic disc perfusion, similar to findings in empty sella syndrome, hypothesized to result from ischemic/mechanical effects of increased intracranial pressure.
Fibromyalgia patients have a significantly higher likelihood of reporting hearing loss than controls (odds ratio 4.6).

A nationwide population-based retrospective cohort study found a 1.5-fold higher overall hearing loss risk in fibromyalgia patients versus non-FM patients, with significantly greater sensorineural hearing loss, after adjustment for sex, age and comorbidities.
A meta-analysis of 20 skin biopsy studies including 903 fibromyalgia patients found small-fiber neuropathy in up to 49% of patients.
A study of CFS patients with low cardiac filling pressures during exercise indirectly suggested probable small-fiber neuropathy in 31% of patients.
Vestibular function testing showed CFS patients performed below average in dynamic posturography, especially in tests requiring reliance on the vestibular system.

In 30 patients with fibromyalgia/chronic widespread pain, mean CSF opening pressure was 19.7 cm H2O and 53% had pressure ≥19 cm H2O; spinal fluid evacuation temporarily improved bodily pain in 70% of patients.

The patient was homozygous for a mutation in the PLOD1 gene (procollagen-lysine, 2-oxoglutarate 5-dioxygenase 1), confirming the diagnosis of EDS type VI.

The patient with EDS type VI developed a spontaneous retroperitoneal hematoma that caused external venous compression leading to extensive iliofemoral deep vein thrombosis and subsequent bilateral segmental pulmonary thromboembolism.

Extensive workup excluded common thrombosis risk factors (autoimmune screen, celiac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, prothrombotic study, nutritional deficiencies), supporting that the thromboembolic event was secondary to the hematoma-induced venous compression rather than an independent prothrombotic state.

Despite high bleeding risk from the retroperitoneal hematoma, the patient was safely anticoagulated first with unfractionated heparin then transitioned to low-molecular-weight heparin and warfarin without bleeding complications, based on absence of active bleeding on CT and hemodynamic stability.
Six months after the initial event, following a fall causing unilateral amaurosis (high fall risk), the decision was made in shared discussion with the patient to discontinue anticoagulation.
The patient's older sister died at age 38 from spontaneous rupture of an abdominal aortic aneurysm, prompting the family genetic study that identified the PLOD1 mutation and EDS type VI diagnosis.

Patients with EDS type VI have a high risk of catastrophic vascular events, typically occurring before the end of the fifth decade of life, due to a defect in lysyl hydroxylase relative to prolyl hydroxylase activity causing vessel and eyeball rupture susceptibility.
Despite bilateral segmental pulmonary thromboembolism, the Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index (PESI) score indicated very low risk, with 30-day mortality equal to or less than 1.6%.
Patients with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome undergoing cesarean delivery are at particular risk of hemorrhage, with little existing evidence to guide prevention or management.

Genomic testing confirmed a heterozygous COL3A1 missense variant (c.1852G>C, exon 26), classified as likely pathogenic and causative of the patient's vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
The patient's right forearm compartment pressure was markedly elevated at 62 mmHg, consistent with acute compartment syndrome.
CT angiogram of the right forearm revealed multiple pseudoaneurysms along the radial and ulnar arteries, an atypical vascular complication of vEDS presenting as compartment syndrome.

Microscopic examination of the ruptured radial artery showed variable smooth muscle thickness, partial loss of muscle wall, aneurysmal dilatation, fibrinoid necrosis, absent internal elastic lamina, and decreased elastic fibers/smooth muscle cells in the tunica media.

Adjacent small to medium-sized veins also showed focal deficient or fragmented elastic fibers in the tunica media, indicating venous tissue is also structurally affected in vEDS, which is relevant for graft durability.

Urgent fasciotomy with excision of the friable radial artery segment and reconstruction using an autologous saphenous vein graft restored circulation; at four-year follow-up the patient had good hand function with no graft rupture or complications.
On admission the patient had leukocytosis and markedly elevated CRP, which initially led to a misdiagnosis of cellulitis before compartment syndrome and pseudoaneurysms were identified.

General vEDS population data cited show the risk of a first major vascular/organ complication is about 25% by age 20, rising to over 80% by age 40, with average age of first complication 23.5 years and a median life expectancy of 48 years.

A different nucleotide change at the same codon (c.1853G>T) has previously been reported as disease-causing for vEDS phenotypes, supporting the pathogenic relevance of this codon region distinct from the novel variant found in this patient.

A prior Australian survey cited in the introduction found that women with chronic conditions wait an average of 4 years for a definitive diagnosis and nearly half are rediagnosed at least once, with 32% of rediagnosed women originally given a psychological or medically-unexplained-symptom diagnosis before later being rediagnosed with an organic condition.

A recurrent theme was that women with EDS were initially given a psychological diagnosis (e.g., anxiety) before physical/organic findings were investigated, despite objective abnormalities such as abnormal liver function.

A participant described overlapping/comorbid diagnoses of EDS and POTS with ongoing difficulty obtaining concrete diagnoses for suspected mast cell activation syndrome and gastroparesis.

Discussion of prior literature notes that medical gaslighting (invalidation, dismissal, inadequate care) is felt particularly by female patients with medically ambiguous conditions such as ME/CFS and POTS.

19 of 20 women reported having one or more secondary diagnoses, commonly including POTS, depression, complex PTSD, endometriosis, dysautonomia, supraventricular tachycardia, and fibromyalgia, alongside their primary diagnosis.

Despite widespread reports of dismissal, every woman interviewed was able to describe at least one positive health care experience, most often associated with a clinician who listened, believed them, and took their symptoms seriously.

At 3 weeks after surgery, both the patellar hypermobility group and patellar dislocation group showed a significantly larger bony sulcus angle (indicating a flatter/shallower trochlear groove) compared with sham-operated rats.
At 3 weeks postoperatively, the cartilaginous sulcus angle was significantly larger (shallower cartilage groove) in both the patellar hypermobility and dislocation groups than in sham controls.
At 3 weeks postoperatively, trochlear sulcus depth was significantly shallower in both the patellar hypermobility and dislocation groups compared with sham controls.
At 3 weeks postoperatively, all measured cartilage thicknesses of the trochlear groove (lateral, medial, central) were significantly thinner in the patellar hypermobility group than in sham controls.

At 3 weeks postoperatively, medial and central cartilage thickness were significantly thinner in the patellar dislocation group versus sham, while lateral cartilage thickness was not significantly different.
At 6 weeks postoperatively, bony sulcus angle remained significantly larger in both the patellar hypermobility and dislocation groups compared with sham controls.
At 6 weeks postoperatively, trochlear sulcus depth remained significantly shallower in both experimental groups compared with sham controls.

At 6 weeks postoperatively, lateral cartilage thickness was significantly thinner in the patellar dislocation group versus sham, but did not significantly differ between the hypermobility group and sham.

In normally developing (sham) rats, both bony and cartilaginous sulcus angles decreased significantly from 3 to 6 weeks postoperatively, indicating normal deepening of the trochlear groove with growth.

Unlike sham rats, the patellar hypermobility and dislocation groups showed no significant change in bony or cartilaginous sulcus angle between 3 and 6 weeks, suggesting a fixed, abnormally molded trochlear shape persisted despite growth.

The authors conclude that patellar hypermobility and patellar dislocation both cause femoral trochlear dysplasia that worsens with age, and that loading between the patella and trochlea is a key determinant of trochlear development, with both excessive and insufficient loading producing dysplasia.

Mitocur-3 treatment caused a dramatic increase in TMRM fluorescence indicating elevated mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm), while Mitocur-1 showed a non-significant increase.
Mitocur-1 increased mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) but this change was not statistically significant.
Both Mitocur-1 and Mitocur-3 increased mitochondrial ROS levels in RBL-2H3 cells as measured by MitoTracker Orange CM-H2TMRos flow cytometry.
Both Mitocur-1 and Mitocur-3 increased cardiolipin peroxidation, a marker of mitochondrial oxidative stress, as measured by the MitoCLox probe.
Mitocur-3 decreased Drp1 serine 637 phosphorylation, indicating Drp1 activation, while Mitocur-1 had no effect on Drp1 activity.
Mitocur-3 but not Mitocur-1 activated AMPK, shown by increased phosphorylation at threonine 172.
Neither Mitocur-1 nor Mitocur-3 increased cleaved caspase 3 levels in RBL-2H3 cells, indicating no induction of apoptosis at the tested conditions.
Mitocur-3 slightly decreased relative mitochondrial DNA content, though not significantly, and Mitocur-1 had no effect, indicating mitocurcuminoids do not reduce mitochondrial number.

All studies reviewed that measured corneal nerve fiber density in fibromyalgia patients found a significant reduction compared to healthy controls, and one report additionally found reduced CNFL and CNBD.
In fibromyalgia, reduced CNFD correlated with increasing severity of neuropathy, small fiber neuropathy symptom burden, dysautonomia symptoms, and one domain of the Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire.
No correlation was found between corneal nerve measurements and disease duration in Parkinson's disease or fibromyalgia.
Two studies found significantly reduced CNFL in Sjogren syndrome patients compared to healthy controls.
Among six studies of Sjogren syndrome, four found significantly reduced CNFD, one found increased CNFD, and one found no difference versus healthy controls.
Three studies reported a significant increase in corneal nerve fiber tortuosity in Sjogren syndrome patients.
Across six studies in Parkinson's disease, CNFL was significantly reduced in three, unchanged in two, and increased in one relative to controls.
CNFD was reduced in six of eight studies analyzing Parkinson's disease patients, with two showing no change.
CNFD and intraepidermal nerve fiber density (IENFD) were both significantly lower in Parkinson's disease patients compared to controls and correlated with each other.
CNFL and CNBD were associated with the duration of L-dopa therapy in Parkinson's disease patients.
Two studies in multiple sclerosis found significant reductions in CNFL, CNFD, and CNBD, and a third study found reduced CNFD only.

In transthyretin familial amyloid polyneuropathy (TTR-FAP), all corneal confocal microscopy parameters were significantly reduced with disease progression, with IWL, CNFL, CNBD, and CNFD all significantly lower in early-phase patients.
CNFL correlated with the severity of both sensorimotor and autonomic neuropathy in TTR-FAP patients.

In sarcoid-associated small fiber neuropathy, treatment with Cibinetide (4 mg group) increased corneal nerve fiber area (CNFA) compared to placebo, and changes in CNFA correlated with regenerating intraepidermal fibers (GAP-43+) and 6-minute walk test performance.
No correlation was found between corneal nerve fiber parameters and the duration of antiretroviral treatment in HIV patients.
In a pediatric celiac disease population, corneal nerve fiber parameters (CNFL, CNFD, CNBD) were unchanged, in contrast to the reductions seen in adult small fiber neuropathies.

Across skin biopsy comparison studies, IVCM-detected corneal nerve alterations showed a statistically significant positive correlation with skin biopsy findings of small fiber neuropathy, supporting IVCM as a comparably sensitive diagnostic tool.
Combining IVCM with pain-related evoked potentials (PREP) increased identification of patients with small fiber impairment to 85%, higher than QST, QSART, or proximal IENFD alone.
An epidemiological study in the southern Netherlands (2006–2011) found a small fiber neuropathy prevalence of 53 per 100,000 population with an incidence of 11.7 per 100,000 in 2010–2011.

A subtype of vagal preganglionic efferent axons (~24% of dextran-labeled efferents) selectively contacted and linked nitric oxide synthase-positive (nNOS+) myenteric neurons into presumptive motor modules within and between ganglia.
A second, larger subtype of vagal efferents (~62%) appeared to selectively contact and link non-nitrergic enteric neurons into a distinct effector ensemble, separate from the nitrergic pool.
A third candidate type of vagal efferent (~14% of labeled preganglionics) lacked nitrergic selectivity, contacting both nNOS-positive and nNOS-negative myenteric neurons.
Qualitative observations in the proximal duodenum showed similar selective vagal efferent projection patterns, in proportions comparable to those quantified in the stomach.
Nebivolol, but not placebo, significantly increased DLCO (diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide) by 8.5%.
Nebivolol significantly increased pulmonary capillary blood volume (Vc) by 17.7%, whereas placebo had no effect.
The DLNO/DLCO ratio was lowered after nebivolol but the change did not reach statistical significance.
Nebivolol significantly increased exhaled NO (eNO) by 17.6%, confirming its NO-stimulating action at the pulmonary vascular level.
Nebivolol reduced the dyspnoea score (DS) by 76% from baseline, while placebo had no effect.
Placebo produced no significant change in dyspnoea score compared to baseline.
Nebivolol significantly lowered systolic blood pressure by 7.5% and diastolic blood pressure by 5.1%, both mild changes.
Nebivolol significantly lowered heart frequency (HF) by 16.8%, a more pronounced change than the BP effects.
At baseline, mean pulmonary capillary blood volume (Vc) was highly reduced compared to predicted, despite normal lung volumes.
Baseline DLCO and DLNO mean values were lower than predicted in these post-COVID patients, while DLNO/DLCO ratio was slightly elevated.
At baseline, heart frequency was elevated compared to usual resting conditions despite all other parameters being normal.
The efficacy of nebivolol on pulmonary capillary blood volume was strictly correlated with the reduction in patients' dyspnoea score.

Nebivolol acts as a selective β1 adrenoceptor antagonist that also induces nitric oxide-mediated vasodilation by stimulating endothelial nitric oxide synthase via β3 agonism, distinguishing it from other vasodilatory β-blockers.
Six of fifteen included GERD studies found overall lower heart rate variability (both PNS and SNS parameters) in patients compared to healthy controls.
Four GERD studies reported decreased parasympathetic activity with enhanced sympathetic tone, shifting autonomic balance toward SNS dominance in patients versus controls.
One study found no HRV difference between alcoholic non-cardiac chest pain patients with versus without depression and alexithymia.
Nowak et al. found no significant differences in autonomic activity between children with IBS and healthy controls.
Djeddi et al. found that parasympathetic activity was significantly suppressed prior to a gastroesophageal reflux event.
Jones et al. indicated that autonomic neuropathy believed to cause gastroesophageal reflux could be reversed with treatment.
Two of three studies found that transcutaneous electric acustimulation decreased sympathetic and increased parasympathetic activity in GERD patients.
Electrical esophageal stimulation decreased sympathetic outflow (LF power) and increased cardiovagal activity (HF power) in GERD patients but not in healthy controls.
Kumar et al. did not find any autonomic nervous system abnormality in patients with delayed gastric emptying.
Most human studies of functional dyspepsia and gastroparesis found decreased vagal tone and/or increased sympathetic activity compared to healthy controls.
One functional dyspepsia study found a high parasympathetic tone and lowered LF/HF ratio, with symptoms more severe in patients with impaired PNS activity.

Gastric electrical stimulation, transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation, and epalrestat administration each enhanced suppressed vagal activity and decreased sympathetic tone in FD/gastroparesis patients.

In rodent models, delayed gastric emptying with low HF power and high LF/HF ratio was improved by sacral nerve stimulation, electroacupuncture at ST36, or auricular electroacupuncture; similar improvement was shown with electroacupuncture at ST36 in dogs.
Eight of nineteen IBS studies demonstrated high sympathetic tone (increased LF power and/or LF/HF ratio) and low parasympathetic tone (lower HF power) in IBS patients versus adult healthy controls.
Jarrett et al. found no difference in HRV parameters between children with functional abdominal pain related to IBS and healthy children.
Orr et al. found that autonomic activity differences in IBS patients were only abnormal during REM sleep and during walking.
Kano et al. and Adeyemi et al. reported a low ln(LF/HF) ratio and higher ln(HF power) in IBS patients compared to controls, opposite to the majority pattern of sympathetic dominance.
No HRV differences were found between IBS-D and IBS-C subtypes, nor between IBS patients with versus without depressive symptoms.

Jarrett et al. found IBS patients with high sympathetic tone benefited less from cognitive therapies, while Jung et al. found HRV parameters could be used to track the effect of cognitive therapy for IBS.
Cai et al. found that only IBS patients with severe gut pain had high sympathetic tone and low parasympathetic tone.
Tanaka et al. found a strong correlation between adrenaline and HRV upon corticotropin release in healthy controls that was absent in IBS patients.
In healthy controls, higher HFnu correlated with lower evening salivary cortisol, whereas this correlation was absent in IBS patients (Pellissier et al.).

Lijun, Miyagi, and J. Liu et al. concluded constipation is associated with high sympathetic tone (high sympathetic index) and low parasympathetic tone (decreased HF or RSA), with autonomic balance shifted toward SNS activity.
Enevoldsen et al. found no correlation between GI transit time and HRV parameters in constipated patients.
Ding et al. tested biofeedback to improve autonomic nervous system activity in constipated patients but could not establish it as an effective ANS-modulating treatment.

Low level laser therapy neuromodulation of lumbar and sacral autonomic nerves enhanced parasympathetic activity and decreased sympathetic activity in patients with GI disorders predominantly involving constipation.
Z. Liu et al. modulated the ANS via TEA, successfully increasing HF power and decreasing LF power and LF/HF ratio in constipation.
J. Liu et al. found ANS modulation occurred with both actual and sham TEA when combined with Macrogol 4000 powder and adaptive biofeedback, whereas MAC alone did not modulate the ANS.
Electroacupuncture treated loperamide-induced constipation in rats by increasing HF power and decreasing LF/HF ratio.

Multiple studies (Lijun et al., Miyagi et al., J. Liu et al.) found that constipated patients had high sympathetic tone (elevated sympathetic index) and low parasympathetic tone (decreased HF power/RSA), with autonomic balance shifted toward sympathetic dominance (low LF/HF).
Gondim et al. reported only a higher sympathetic nervous system tone in constipated patients compared to controls, without reporting a parasympathetic difference.
Enevoldsen et al. attempted to correlate gastrointestinal transit time with HRV parameters in constipated patients and found no correlation.
Ding et al. tested biofeedback as a method to modulate autonomic nervous system activity in constipated patients but could not establish it as an effective treatment via ANS modulation.

Low level laser therapy neuromodulation of lumbar and sacral autonomic nerves enhanced parasympathetic activity and decreased sympathetic activity in patients with GI disorders predominantly constipation.

Z. Liu et al. modulated the autonomic nervous system via transcutaneous electric acustimulation (TEA), successfully increasing HF power and decreasing LF power and LF/HF ratio in constipation patients.
J. Liu et al. found that both actual and sham TEA combined with Macrogol 4000 Powder (MAC) and adaptive biofeedback modulated the ANS, whereas MAC alone did not modulate the ANS.
Zhang et al., Wu et al., and Chen et al. successfully modulated autonomic nervous system activity using neuromodulation as a treatment effort for chronic constipation.
Wang et al. showed that Loperamide-induced constipation in rats could be treated by electroacupuncture, which increased HF power and decreased the LF/HF ratio.
Sacral nerve stimulation produced similar autonomic modulation findings (improved HRV parameters) in the same rodent model of Loperamide-induced constipation.
Jin et al. found that impaired colonic motility induced by rectal distension in dogs was associated with a significant decrease in HF power, which was reinstated by electroacupuncture at ST36.
JM25-1 at concentrations up to 250 μM did not significantly affect proliferation of HMC-1 or RBL-2H3 mast cell lines.
JM25-1 reduced β-hexosaminidase release from C48/80- and CRH-induced degranulation in HMC-1 and RBL-2H3 mast cells.
JM25-1 suppressed both protein and mRNA levels of CRHR1 in CRH-activated HMC-1 cells compared to untreated CRH-exposed cells.
JM25-1 elevated CRHR2 protein and mRNA levels in CRH-activated HMC-1 cells compared to untreated CRH-exposed cells.
JM25-1 suppressed TNFα production in CRH-activated HMC-1 cells.
JM25-1 decreased mRNA expression of IL-1β, IL-18 and IL-6 in CRH-induced HMC-1 cells.
JM25-1 restored ZO-1 tight junction protein expression in Caco2 cells that had been damaged by conditioned medium from CRH-pretreated HMC-1 cells.
TEER value of Caco2 monolayers, which dropped after co-culture with medium from CRH-pretreated HMC-1 cells, rebounded close to control levels with JM25-1 treatment.
JM25-1 prevented FITC-dextran (FD4) leakage across Caco2 monolayers induced by medium from CRH-pretreated HMC-1 cells.
Psychological stress-induced rats treated with JM25-1 showed significant weight gain compared to non-treated stressed rats.
Blood markers of intestinal barrier damage (diamine oxidase, D-lactate, bacterial endotoxin), which were elevated in psychologically stressed rats, decreased after JM25-1 treatment.
Both protein and mRNA levels of ZO-1 were decreased in the small intestine of chronic stress-induced rats, and this damage was reversed by JM25-1 treatment.
In psychologically stressed rats, JM25-1 substantially inhibited CRHR1, TNFα, IL-18, IL-1β and IL-6 while promoting CRHR2 in intestinal tissue.
The amount of CRHR1-positive mast cells, increased in small intestine after stress stimulation, was significantly repressed after JM25-1 treatment; intestinal TNFα production was also suppressed.

Network pharmacology analysis identified 71 shared targets between JM25-1 and IBS from 110 drug targets and 3170 disease targets, with eight hub targets (AKT1, SLC6A3, SRC, SLC6A4, SLC6A2, CHRNA4, DRD2, GRIN2B) identified by PPI topology analysis.
Molecular docking simulation showed AKT1 has strong binding affinity for JM25-1 with a docking score of 6.06.
JM25-1 induced phosphorylation of PI3K, AKT and mTOR in HMC-1 cells in a concentration-dependent manner, indicating activation of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway.

The mTOR inhibitor Rapamycin attenuated JM25-1's inhibitory effect on mast cell degranulation and cytokine secretion (tryptase, TNFα, IL-1β), and prevented JM25-1's effects on CRHR1 and CRHR2 expression, indicating JM25-1's action depends on PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling.
JM25-1 treatment lowered intestinal permeability (blood D-lactate) induced by transplantation of colonic mucus from IBS patients into rat colon.
Tight junction and microvilli ultrastructure destroyed by IBS colonic mucus transplantation were refreshed/restored with JM25-1 treatment, and ZO-1 epithelial integrity was recuperated.
JM25-1 significantly reduced the amount of mast cells and CRHR1 expression on mast cells in the colon of rats transplanted with IBS colonic mucus.
The paper cites prior clinical research showing diarrhea-predominant IBS (IBS-D) patients displayed jejunal up-regulation of CRHR2 and down-regulation of CRHR1 compared to healthy patients.
Across 40 pediatric patients, serum or CSF CASPR2 antibodies were detected in nearly all cases, with titers ranging widely from 1:10 to 1:5,120 and 95% of patients seropositive.

Psychiatric symptoms were the most common presenting feature in pediatric CASPR2 antibody-associated encephalitis, occurring in 72.5% of patients, including mood changes, behavior changes, and hallucinations.
Sleep disorders (short/long sleep, fragmented sleep, altered sleep timing, insomnia) were reported in 62.5% of pediatric patients, a notably higher proportion than in adult cohorts.
Movement disorders (limb shaking, dystonia, dyskinesia, hyperkinetic movements) occurred in 60% of pediatric patients, a higher rate than in adults.

Autonomic dysfunction symptoms were frequent, with cardiovascular symptoms in 15 patients, sweating in 14, gastrointestinal symptoms in 9, and genitourinary symptoms in 2 of the 40 pediatric patients.
Peripheral nervous system involvement was documented in a subset of pediatric patients, with sensory dysfunction in 12, nerve pain in 8, and visual disturbance in 1 patient.

Unlike adults with CASPR2 antibody-associated encephalitis (where thymoma occurs in 10-30%), no tumors were identified in any of the 40 pediatric patients, though 2 of 19 tested positive for tumor markers.
Three of 40 pediatric CASPR2-AE patients (8.8%) had co-existent Hashimoto thyroiditis with positive anti-thyroid peroxidase and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies.

Eleven of 40 patients (27.5%) had co-existent CASPR2 and LGI1 antibodies with high serum CASPR2 titers (1:160 to 1:5,120), presenting with variable neurological/autonomic phenotypes but no tumors identified.

CSF pleocytosis (>5 WBC) was found in 37.5% and elevated CSF protein in 31.7% of pediatric CASPR2-AE patients, while abnormal EEG (slow waves or epileptic discharge) was seen in 73.1% of tested patients.

Nearly all pediatric CASPR2-AE patients (95%) received first-line immunotherapy (steroids, IVIG, plasmapheresis), and outcomes were favorable, with 37.5% complete and 62.5% partial recovery, no deaths or relapses.
Modified Rankin Scale scores improved markedly with immunotherapy, from a mean of 3.4 at onset to 0.88 at last follow-up in 16 patients with recorded scores.

The authors note that mutations in the CASPR2 gene have been linked to focal epilepsy, mental retardation, schizophrenia, and other neuropsychiatric problems, suggesting a mechanistic link relevant to the atypical psychiatric/neurological symptoms seen in pediatric CASPR2 antibody-associated encephalitis.

In case 1, a 10-year-old boy with CASPR2 antibody-associated encephalitis and low-titer serum CASPR2 antibody (1:10), thyroid function tests showed low FT3, low TSH, and markedly elevated anti-TPO (176 IU/mL) and anti-thyroglobulin (175 IU/L) antibodies, consistent with concurrent Hashimoto thyroiditis; all normalized after immunotherapy.

In case 2, an 11-year-old boy presented with limb numbness, involuntary movements, headache, seizures, hyperhidrosis, palpitations, and insomnia, with autonomic and peripheral neuropathy signs on exam, and serum CASPR2 antibody titer of 1:32 (negative in CSF); he improved with IVIG and steroids but retained residual numbness, insomnia, and palpitations at 6 months.

Pediatric CASPR2 antibody-associated encephalitis differs from adult disease in onset age (mean 9.26 vs ~50 years), predominant symptom type (psychiatric vs cognitive), and rarity of associated tumors.

The Your COVID Recovery website, a digital health platform providing self-management information for COVID-19 recovery, was accessed by over 2 million users from 187 countries in its first year, with 61.30% of users from the UK.

Among the website's pages, those on cough, fatigue, musculoskeletal pain, taste/smell loss, and breathlessness received the highest number of page views after the homepage, reflecting the most sought-after COVID-19 recovery symptom information.

Citing the PHOSP-COVID study, the paper notes that 92.8% of patients had a persistent symptom 5 months after COVID-19-related hospitalization, most commonly muscle pain, fatigue, and physical slowing down.
The PHOSP-COVID study reported that only 29% of individuals felt fully recovered approximately 6 months after hospital discharge for COVID-19.
The paper cites literature reporting that symptoms persist for months in up to 92% of hospitalized and 36% of nonhospitalized individuals with COVID-19.
The paper notes that increasing age, higher BMI, and female sex are associated with an increased likelihood of developing post-COVID-19 condition.
Most users of the Your COVID Recovery website engaged only briefly: 78.29% visited only once, with an average of 1.71 page views per session and a mean session duration of 1 minute 13 seconds.

Page views for the Cough page unexpectedly increased between March and May 2021 without an identifiable external referral source, which the authors speculate may reflect an increase in individuals experiencing COVID-19-related cough during that period.
A separate cited cohort found that 4 months after COVID-19 infection (hospitalized and nonhospitalized), the most common persistent symptoms were fatigue, breathlessness, and muscle ache.
In the acute phase (within 21 days of diagnosis), COVID-19 patients had a markedly higher risk of cardiovascular disease compared to contemporary and historical controls.
In the acute phase, COVID-19 patients had a very large increase in all-cause mortality risk compared to contemporary and historical controls.
In the post-acute phase (beyond 21 days), COVID-19 patients continued to show significantly elevated long-term risk of cardiovascular disease compared to controls.
In the post-acute phase, COVID-19 patients had a significantly higher long-term risk of all-cause mortality compared to contemporary and historical controls.
The patient with post-COVID-19 ME/CFS was found to have decreased serum acylcarnitine levels, which supported the diagnosis.

Post-exertional malaise (PEM), a hallmark diagnostic criterion of ME/CFS, was identified through detailed history-taking as a key symptom in this patient, despite the patient having previously been advised by another physician to exercise.
Approximately 25% of patients recovering from COVID-19 reportedly meet diagnostic criteria for ME/CFS, and about 50% experience sleep disturbance and chronic fatigue after recovery.
As many as 80% of ME/CFS patients struggle to receive a diagnosis, often needing to consult multiple specialists and facilities.
Prolonged undiagnosed long COVID/ME-CFS symptoms may contribute to depression, with about 30% of long-COVID patients developing depression or other psychiatric complications.

The literature indicates that strenuous/generic exercise should be avoided in ME/CFS as it may worsen symptoms, whereas graded exercise therapy and cognitive behavioral therapy have been reported as safe and effective interventions.
The patient was referred to a specialized facility to pursue epipharyngeal abrasive therapy for its anti-inflammatory effects as management for the diagnosed ME/CFS.

Published literature agrees that ME/CFS is associated with changes in acylcarnitine and L-carnitine homeostasis, and viral infections are known to disrupt the mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation cascade, potentially decreasing serum acylcarnitine.
Older age was strongly associated with increased risk of developing Severe Fatigue, with more than a four-fold increase in risk for those over 55 compared to those 40 and younger.
Unlike Severe Fatigue, the risk of ME/CFS did not increase with increasing age.
Higher adult BMI in 1989 was strongly associated with increased risk of Severe Fatigue.
Higher adult BMI in 1989 was only marginally associated with ME/CFS risk, with a non-significant hazard ratio at the highest BMI category.
BMI at age 18 (recalled retrospectively) was not associated with risk of either ME/CFS or Severe Fatigue.
Current and past smoking were significantly associated with increased risk of Severe Fatigue but not with ME/CFS.
Higher caffeine intake was associated with a reduced risk of Severe Fatigue, and a non-significant reduced risk of ME/CFS.
Alcohol intake was unrelated to ME/CFS risk but inversely related to Severe Fatigue risk, with heavy drinkers having much lower risk of Severe Fatigue.
Use of hormone therapy and postmenopausal status were each positively associated with risk of Severe Fatigue but not with risk of ME/CFS.
Physical activity, both in adolescence (ages 18-22) and adulthood, was generally not associated with risk of ME/CFS or Severe Fatigue.
Time spent sitting at home showed a marginal trend toward elevated risk of ME/CFS, likely reflecting the disease causing inactivity rather than inactivity causing the disease.
A self-reported history of infectious mononucleosis was associated with a substantially, though not statistically significant, elevated risk of subsequent ME/CFS over 20 years of follow-up.
A self-reported history of infectious mononucleosis was associated with a slightly elevated risk of Severe Fatigue.

Citing prior work, the paper notes that the EBV protein dUTPase induces neuroinflammation and lethargy in female mice, and that people with ME/CFS have elevated anti-dUTPase antibodies correlating with symptom severity and distinguishing them from healthy controls.
Citing prior work, the paper notes that lower ACTH levels measured 6 months after mononucleosis are found in those who go on to develop ME/CFS compared to those who fully recover.
Citing prior work, the paper notes that higher interleukin-12 and lower interleukin-5 and interleukin-13 levels during acute mononucleosis are risk factors for subsequent ME/CFS.
A significantly higher proportion of ME/CFS(+)FM (54.5%) and ME/CFS(-)FM (45.5%) patients had abnormal autoantibody reactivity against GABA receptors compared to none of the healthy controls.

Anti-β2-glycoprotein I autoantibodies showed markedly more correlations with other autoantibodies in the ME/CFS(-)FM group than in healthy controls, consistent with a prior report of elevated anti-β2-GP AAb in ME/CFS.
The ME/CFS(+)FM group showed an increase in the number of correlational associations of anti-collagen and anti-TrM-03 autoantibodies with other autoantibodies compared to controls.
In the ME/CFS(+)FM group, the normal intragroup correlations between anti-neural autoantibodies observed in healthy controls were abolished.

Changes in immunoreactivity to β-endorphin were associated with more pronounced fatigue in both ME/CFS(-)FM and ME/CFS(+)FM groups, but not in healthy controls, suggesting endogenous opioid system dysfunction.

Patients in both ME/CFS groups showed loss of the normal correlation between anti-μ-opioid receptor autoantibodies and bodily pain intensity that was present in the reference relationship, consistent with dysregulated endogenous opioid signaling in pain processing.
Changes in anti-GFAP autoantibody levels were positively associated with worse mental component score (SF-36 MCS) in the ME/CFS(+)FM group.
Changes in anti-GFAP autoantibody levels were positively associated with illness duration in the ME/CFS(-)FM group.
All SF-36 and MFI subscales were significantly worse in both ME/CFS(+)FM and ME/CFS(-)FM patients compared with healthy controls, including lower physical and mental component scores.
Depression and anxiety levels (HADS) were significantly higher in both ME/CFS(-)FM and ME/CFS(+)FM groups than controls, with probable comorbid depression seen only in the ME/CFS(+)FM group.
BMI was significantly lower in the ME/CFS(+)FM group compared to healthy controls, whereas BMI in ME/CFS(-)FM group was similar to controls.

The relationship between anti-GABA-Re autoantibody deviation and mental health differed by group: in healthy controls it was associated with lower (worse) mental component score, while in the ME/CFS(-)FM group it was inversely correlated with depression score.

In healthy controls, autoantibodies correlating with neuropsychological symptom scores mostly targeted neural antigens, but this pattern was disturbed in both ME/CFS patient groups, where organ-specific and non-tissue-specific antibodies instead correlated with symptom severity, suggesting a multisystem rather than purely psychological disease process.
Infection-triggered disease onset was reported by 33% of ME/CFS+FM patients versus 73% of ME/CFS-FM patients.
A woman who developed long COVID after SARS-CoV-2 infection subsequently met diagnostic criteria for ME/CFS, illustrating that post-COVID sequelae can progress into ME/CFS.
On active standing testing, the patient showed orthostatic hypertension and slight orthostatic tachycardia (without orthostatic hypotension), with heart rate rising to 120 bpm after a short walk.
After the multi-perspective treatment protocol, the average heart rate 2-5 minutes after standing significantly decreased.
The heart rate increase upon standing (change from baseline) significantly decreased after treatment.
The patient's self-rated fatigue on the numerical rating scale dropped from 5 to 0 after completing the treatment protocol.
The patient's Brief Fatigue Inventory score decreased from a severe-fatigue level of 7.0 to 0.5 after treatment.
At baseline, the patient's Trail Making Test-A completion time was longer than the age-matched healthy mean, indicating impaired cognitive processing speed.
The patient's cognitive function as measured by TMT-A improved after completion of the treatment protocol.
The patient's score on the CES-D depression scale (9) indicated she was not clinically depressed, helping distinguish her presentation from primary depression.
The patient adopted a vegetable-based diet and daily ascorbic acid supplementation as part of her ME/CFS treatment to minimize oxidative stress.
Cognitive and behavioral modification focused on adaptive coping, self-pacing, and reducing 'idling' (rumination) was used to help manage fatigue and PEM.
Gradual, threshold-aware exercise ('reverse deconditioning') was introduced after resting dyspnea and fatigue improved, to address physical deconditioning without triggering PEM.
Low-dose amitriptyline (10 mg at night) was prescribed for its anxiolytic, sleep-inducing, analgesic, and antihistaminergic properties.
The Kampo herbal medicine hochuekkito was prescribed, reported in prior literature to ameliorate fatigue, improve hypocortisolemia and heart rate variability, and inhibit neuroinflammation.
After 21 weeks of multi-perspective treatment, the patient recovered to near-baseline physical and mental function and planned to return to work.
Oxidative stress has been proposed in prior literature to be involved in both long COVID and ME/CFS pathophysiology.
Intravenous high-dose ascorbic acid (>7.5 g) has been reported in prior literature to alleviate fatigue, concentration difficulty, and pain in long COVID patients.
Prior literature reports that gut microbiota is associated with ME/CFS pathophysiology, including neuroinflammation and symptom expression.
Prior literature suggests autonomic dysfunction in long COVID and ME/CFS is associated with autoantibodies against β-adrenergic and muscarinic cholinergic receptors.
Orthostatic intolerance and dysautonomia, particularly postural orthostatic tachycardia (POTS), are described in prior literature as common comorbidities of long COVID and ME/CFS.

Prior studies cited show that deconditioning and diaphragmatic muscle fiber atrophy can occur within days of bed rest or mechanical ventilation inactivity, relevant to the patient's post-hospitalization weakness and dyspnea.
At baseline, no urine metabolites differed significantly between ME/CFS patients and healthy sedentary controls.
Four urinary compounds—three acyl glycines and one unknown—were significantly lower in ME/CFS patients than controls 24 hours after maximal exercise.
Healthy sedentary controls showed large-scale increases in 255 urinary metabolites 24 hours after maximal exercise, with all but 5 compounds increasing.

In stark contrast to controls, ME/CFS patients showed no urinary metabolites with significant concentration changes from baseline to 24 hours post-exercise, indicating a failure of normal metabolic recovery.

110 urinary metabolites showed a significant disease-status-by-time interaction, with 102 of these 110 also significantly increasing in controls post-exercise but not changing in ME/CFS patients, evidencing exercise-recovery metabolic dysregulation.
At baseline, xanthine metabolism compounds (e.g., caffeine, theophylline) were significantly lower in ME/CFS patients' urine than in controls, though this cluster is diet-sensitive.

Twelve Metabolon subpathways, predominantly lipid (fatty acid metabolism subpathways: acyl glutamine, acyl glycine, acyl carnitine) plus tyrosine metabolism and uracil-containing pyrimidine metabolism, were significantly altered 24h post-exercise between ME/CFS and controls, with predominantly lower concentrations in ME/CFS.

Corticosteroid and androgenic steroid subpathways showed the strongest exercise-recovery signal, with 8/13 compounds significantly lower in ME/CFS patients' post-exercise/baseline ratios and 11/13 significantly increased in controls after exercise.

Two acyl carnitine subpathways (medium chain and dicarboxylate), androgenic steroids, and secondary bile acid metabolism were significantly altered in all three comparisons (post-exercise ME/CFS vs control, ratio comparison, and control pre/post), indicating robust lipid pathway dysregulation.

Polyamine metabolism showed the strongest disease-vs-control signal, with 6/9 metabolites significantly increased in controls post-exercise and 5/9 significantly decreased in the ME/CFS post-exercise/baseline ratio compared to controls.

In the urea-cycle arginine/proline subpathway, methylurea was the only metabolite with a higher post-exercise/baseline ratio in ME/CFS than controls, while carboxy-methyl-arginine, proline, SDMA, and ADMA changed differently over time between groups; SDMA/ADMA increases seen in controls but not ME/CFS suggest impaired clearance of nitric oxide synthase inhibitors during exercise recovery.

Six branched-chain amino acid (BCAA: leucine, isoleucine, valine) catabolism metabolites changed differently over time between ME/CFS patients and controls, all among compounds significantly increased in controls post-exercise but not in patients.

Pathway topology analysis found eight pathways significantly altered at 24h post-exercise between ME/CFS and controls, five involved in sugar/energy metabolism (key compound fructose) with the highest-impact pathways being catecholamine biosynthesis and tyrosine metabolism (key compounds dehydroascorbate and ascorbate), though these key compounds did not survive multiple-comparison correction individually.

Ten KEGG pathways had significantly different post-exercise/baseline ratios between ME/CFS and controls; the highest-impact were amino acid pathways (arginine/proline, cysteine/methionine, lysine degradation, aminoacyl-tRNA biosynthesis), while ether lipid metabolism (glycerophosphoethanolamine, GPC) and purine metabolism (cAMP) were also significant with individually FDR-significant key compounds.

Kynurenate showed strongly inverted urine-plasma correlations during exercise recovery, with a strong positive correlation in ME/CFS patients (R=0.74) but a strong negative correlation in controls (R=-0.77), indicating profound tryptophan/kynurenine pathway dysregulation in ME/CFS.

Pregnanediol-3-glucuronide (a progestin steroid) showed a strong positive urine-plasma correlation in ME/CFS patients (R=0.78) but a strong negative correlation in controls (R=-0.8) for post-exercise/baseline ratios, indicating altered progestin excretion dynamics during exercise recovery in ME/CFS.

Beta-hydroxyisovalerate showed a strong significant positive urine-plasma correlation in ME/CFS patients between post-exercise ratios but a weak, non-significant negative correlation in controls, consistent with dysfunctional BCAA catabolism recovery in ME/CFS.
Alanine was found at a higher mean normalized concentration in ME/CFS patients than controls at baseline, contradicting a prior study that reported lower alanine in female ME/CFS patients.

ME/CFS patients scored significantly lower than controls on the Bell Disability Scale (median 30 vs 90) and the SF-36 physical component, reflecting substantial functional impairment consistent with ME/CFS diagnosis.

In the larger cohort's plasma metabolome (of which this urine study subjects are a subset), the carnitine chemical cluster was also significantly altered during exercise recovery in controls (mostly increasing) but was not significantly altered in ME/CFS patients, mirroring the urine acyl carnitine findings.

The authors hypothesize that urea cycle dysregulation in ME/CFS during exercise recovery may cause ammonia buildup linked to neurotoxicity and exercise-induced fatigue, though ammonia itself was below the detection limit and not directly measured.
ME/CFS patients scored significantly lower than controls on the Bell disability scale and the SF-36 physical component, indicating much greater functional impairment.

Kynurenate showed inverted correlations between plasma and urine post-exercise/baseline ratios in ME/CFS patients (strong positive) versus controls (strong negative), indicating dysregulated tryptophan pathway handling during exercise recovery.

Quinolinate, which links tryptophan metabolism to nicotinate and nicotinamide (NAD+/NADP+) metabolism, was among the metabolites with differing plasma-urine correlations between ME/CFS patients and controls.

Beta-hydroxyisovalerate (a valine catabolism product) showed a strong significant positive correlation between urine and plasma post-exercise ratios in ME/CFS patients but a weak non-significant negative correlation in controls, consistent with dysfunctional BCAA catabolism recovery.

Pregnanediol-3-glucuronide (progestin steroid) showed a strong positive plasma-urine correlation post-exercise in ME/CFS patients but a strong negative correlation in controls, suggesting opposite excretion/replacement dynamics during recovery.

The unknown compound X-25524 consistently showed a strong positive urine-plasma correlation in ME/CFS patients but no correlation in controls regardless of exercise, suggesting potential as a novel diagnostic marker.
This study found alanine at higher mean normalized concentration in ME/CFS patients than controls at baseline, directly contradicting a prior study that found alanine lower in female ME/CFS patients.

Phenylalanine and valine, previously reported lower in ME/CFS patients at baseline in other studies, were both significantly increased in urine of sedentary controls following exercise in this study, suggesting prior control groups may have been more physically active.

Of eight urine metabolites previously reported lower in ME/CFS patients with PEM by McGregor et al., only serine showed a significant change in this study, increasing after exercise in the control group.

Prior findings by Armstrong et al. of differing urine-plasma correlations for acetate, lactate, and phenylalanine at baseline were not replicated in this study (acetate not detected; no correlation differences found for lactate or phenylalanine).

While methylhistidine levels were not significantly different in the LMM, differences were found in plasma-urine correlations of 1-methylhistidine and N-acetyl-3-methylhistidine between ME/CFS patients and controls.

Unlike a prior study of male cyclists showing high fold-change post-exercise increases in lactate, acetate, and hypoxanthine, this study found neither lactate nor hypoxanthine significantly changed from baseline to 24h post-exercise in female sedentary controls (acetate not measured).

Glycine levels increased post-exercise in urine of healthy controls in this study, contrary to some prior reviewed studies showing decreases, but consistent with the Kistner et al. study which included a large female cohort.

Urinary excretion of acyl glycines is known to be altered in mitochondrial fatty acid beta-oxidation disorders such as MCAD deficiency, providing mechanistic context for the reduced acyl glycine levels observed in ME/CFS patients post-exercise.
Deoxycarnitine, in the carnitine metabolism subpathway, showed differing plasma-urine correlations between ME/CFS patients and controls after exercise.

Hierarchical clustering of subjects using the four significantly altered post-exercise urine metabolites separated subjects into three groups: predominantly controls with higher concentrations, predominantly ME/CFS patients with lower concentrations, and a small mixed intermediate group.

Across all urine-plasma time point and ratio correlations, ME/CFS patients had a higher number of strong positive correlations than controls, while controls showed more strong negative correlations in the ratio comparisons.

Urine-plasma correlation analysis revealed significant differences between ME/CFS patients and controls in cystine (oxidized cysteine dimer) and cystathione, intermediates in cysteine/methionine metabolism.

Study limitations include uncontrolled diet, lack of BMI matching between groups, female-only sample restricting generalizability, and only two urine collection time points which cannot capture delayed metabolic excretion changes.
The mean time from disease onset to a confirmed ME/CFS diagnosis by physicians was 6.7 years.
Patients visited an average of 11.1 physicians before receiving an ME/CFS diagnosis, more than reported in comparable studies from other countries.
90.5% of patients were told at least once before their final ME/CFS diagnosis that their symptoms were psychosomatic.
Among 138 patients diagnosed by specialists, the top diagnosing specialties were general medicine (34%), psychiatry (32.6%) and neurology (25.4%), with only 10.1% diagnosed by immunologists.

Children were rarely diagnosed within their pediatric age category, with only one-third of pediatric-onset patients diagnosed before age 18, and only two of 24 pediatric patients diagnosed by a pediatrician.
13.5% of patients sought and obtained an ME/CFS diagnosis abroad after no Swiss physician was able to diagnose them.
Patients rated the overall medical service for ME/CFS very poorly, with only 2 of 168 rating it good and 76.8% rating it very bad, and only 16% believed physicians had sufficient ME/CFS knowledge.

Patients left medical appointments with negative feelings (not taken seriously, hopeless, desperate, humiliated, ignored) about three times more often than with positive feelings across the entire disease course.

Before diagnosis, treatment for depression was the most frequently prescribed intervention (N=93), regardless of gender, which was perceived by patients and authors as inappropriate given differing underlying pathophysiology.
After proper ME/CFS diagnosis, energy conservation strategies were the most common physician recommendation (N=78), consistent with patients' own prioritization of pacing.
Patients tried a broad range of therapies during their illness, with an average of 6.5 different therapies tried (range 1-11), and 82% trying multiple therapies.

Graded exercise therapy (GET) was the only reported therapy with a negative average efficacy score, described by patients as harmful and sometimes causing severe worsening (months-long crashes, becoming wheelchair-bound).
Pacing, symptom-alleviating medication, alternative medicine and dietary supplements were rated as helpful on average by patients.

Antiviral agents (valaciclovir, valganciclovir) were recommended to a small number of patients and were described in the literature as eliciting some improvement in patients with suspected EBV or HHV-6 as disease triggers.
Rintatolimod, a TLR3 agonist that increases natural killer cell function, is the only drug specifically assessed for ME/CFS to date but remains unapproved except in Argentina.

The authors note that post-exertional malaise in ME/CFS involves downregulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis and impairment of the central and autonomic nervous systems, distinguishing its pathology from that of depression.

The authors highlight that psychotropic medications prescribed for mood disorders/depression may worsen pre-existing mitochondrial impairment in ME/CFS via decreased carnitine availability and impaired respiratory chain/ATP production.

Al-Hakeim et al. examined effects of peripheral oxygen saturation and peak body temperature on immune, oxidative and nitrosative stress pathways in long COVID, suggesting a neuroimmune/neuro-oxidative origin for post-viral symptoms.

In a cohort of 34 ICU patients with severe COVID-19, EBV DNA was detected in 82.4% of patients, with quantifiable viral load in most, and EBV-reactivated patients had longer ICU stays than non-reactivated patients.

In a 104-patient cohort, EBV DNA was detected in 95.2% of ICU patients versus 83.6% of sub-ICU patients, with significantly higher median viral load in ICU patients, and NK cell/CD8+ T-cell reductions were seen only in patients with EBV reactivation.

In a case study of 185 patients, EBV reactivation (EBV EA-D positivity) was significantly more common in long-COVID patients than in controls, and was associated with fatigue, insomnia, headaches, myalgia and confusion.

Among 88 COVID-19 patients, 72.3% showed herpesvirus (EBV/HHV-6/CMV) reactivation, which was associated with longer hospital stay and elevated ESR, CRP, D-dimer, lymphopenia, monocytosis, and liver enzymes compared to non-reactivated patients.
EBV lytic replication was shown to induce ACE2 expression on epithelial cells, via a Zta transcriptional activator effect on the ACE2 promoter, potentially facilitating SARS-CoV-2 cell entry.

Approximately 20% of ME/CFS patients co-expressed antibodies against both EBV and HHV-6 dUTPases, and 28.41% produced antibodies against EBV, HHV-6, and human dUTPases, attributed to protein homology between viral dUTPases.

EBV-dUTPase engagement of TLR2 homodimers activates NF-κB, a strong proinflammatory mediator, and viral dUTPases from EBV, HHV-6 and other herpesviruses induce Th1/Th17 activation and inflammatory cytokine production (IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, TNF-α).

SARS-CoV-2 spike protein contains a unique superantigen-like motif near the S1-S2 cleavage site with homology to Staphylococcal enterotoxin B, capable of high-affinity TCR binding potentially triggering cytotoxic responses seen in MIS-C and cytokine storm.

Compared with healthy controls, feces of COVID-19 patients had reduced anti-inflammatory bacteria (Roseburia, Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, Eubacterium, Lachnospiraceae) and were enriched for bacteremia-associated organisms (Enterococcus, Enterobacteriaceae, Clostridium hathewayi, Bacteroides nordii, Actinomyces viscosus).

In a shotgun metagenomic study of 258 fecal samples, long COVID at 6 months was positively correlated with higher levels of Bacteroides vulgatus, Ruminococcus gnavus, Erysipelatoclostridium ramosum, Actinomyces johnsonii, Atopobium parvulum and Clostridium innocuum, while Blautia wexlerae and Bifidobacterium longum (among 13 species) were negatively associated with long COVID.
Long COVID and COVID-19 patients share certain autoantibodies with postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS), including autoantibodies known to attack G-protein-coupled receptors on neurons.
Rojas et al. found latent autoimmunity in 83% and polyautoimmunity in 62% of patients with post-COVID syndrome.

In a mouse model, neonatal infection with murine roseolovirus (analogous to HHV-6/HHV-7) led to autoimmune gastritis in adulthood via CD4+ T-cell- and IL-17-dependent breakdown of central tolerance, with production of broad autoantibodies (anti-H+/K+ ATPase, thyroglobulin, thyroid peroxidase, insulin, dsDNA, topoisomerase 1, glomerular basement membrane, myeloperoxidase).

Patients with COVID-19-induced ARDS had substantially lower serum BHB concentrations than patients with ARDS from influenza or bacterial infections, indicating dysregulated ketogenesis, and BHB supplementation enhanced Th1 cell IFN-γ production and improved antiviral T-cell function and viral clearance.
Treatment with the anti-herpesvirus drug ganciclovir, which blocks EBV replication, reduced the risk of death in patients with severe COVID-19.
In a small pilot study, the CCR5-binding monoclonal antibody leronlimab improved symptoms in some individuals with long COVID, apparently by boosting immunity.
A preclinical study found that molnupiravir attenuated chronic long COVID symptoms.
KB109, a synthetic glycan that modulates the microbiome, reduced medically attended acute care visits and shortened symptom duration in COVID-19 patients with comorbidities.

Risk factors reported for progression to long COVID include type 2 diabetes, SARS-CoV-2 viremia, EBV viremia, certain autoantibodies, age over 50, female sex, more severe acute infection, more than five symptoms in the first week, immunosuppression, underlying conditions, and incomplete/no vaccination.
Studies cited indicate that antihistamines appear to provide symptom relief for long COVID sufferers.
Among the 586 eligible respondents with severe or very severe ME/CFS, 88% were female, consistent with a strong female predominance previously reported in severe ME/CFS.

Earlier age of disease onset (before 15 years) was more common among the most severely affected patients, with 43% of very severe, 32% of severe, and 22% of severe-moderate patients having onset before age 15.
Among 577 patients reporting on disease course, 44% described a worsening and 32% a fluctuating course over time, with worsening most common among the very severely ill.

Gastrointestinal impairment and feeding difficulty were markedly more severe among very severe than severe ME/CFS patients, including much higher rates of gastrostomy, tube feeding, and swallowing problems.
Very severe ME/CFS patients were almost entirely housebound and isolated, with only one of 46 able to leave the house even once or twice a year and 76% never receiving or making visits.
Very severe ME/CFS patients reported very low tolerance for sensory stimuli, with 77% seldom or never tolerating indoor lighting, 60% sound of normal speech, and 40% touch.

Fatigue was the most debilitating symptom reported across severity groups, with a mean severity index of 3.4, followed by muscular/joint pain (2.1), cognitive problems (1.7), sleep disorder (1.6), and sensory intolerance (1.6).
The majority of severe and very severe ME/CFS patients reported not receiving adequate healthcare, with 68% of very severe and 72% of severe patients stating this.

Occupational therapy home visits were reported as helpful by a large majority of patients and carers, more so than most other healthcare professional contacts, among both severe and very severe ME/CFS patients.
Adequate care from general practitioners was reported more often among very severe patients (51%) than severe patients (29%), suggesting GP continuity of care was valued.
Only about a third of severe and very severe ME/CFS patients felt they received adequate symptom relief for pain, sleep disturbance, gastrointestinal symptoms, or nausea.
Family carers of very severe ME/CFS patients bore an extreme burden, with nearly all patients requiring around-the-clock care and 71% of carers providing more than 40 hours of care per week.

The authors developed a novel Activities of Daily Living Score (ADLS), based on weighted frequency of energy-intensive activities, to objectively reclassify patients' self-reported severity (moderate/severe/very severe) using ICC-based severity boundaries.

A substantial proportion of severe and very severe ME/CFS patients lived alone (up to about a quarter), despite the devastating symptom burden, though very severe patients living alone had daily supportive contact.
More than a third of all severe and very severe ME/CFS patients in the study had disease onset before 20 years of age.
Adults with hEDS/HSD reported significantly lower satisfaction with healthcare than population norm groups.
Adults with hEDS/HSD scored worse on most health-related quality of life domains compared to the U.S. population norm groups.
Adults with hEDS/HSD reported lower symptom management self-efficacy compared to norm groups.
Lower satisfaction with healthcare was significantly associated with lower health-related quality of life among participants.
Lower satisfaction with healthcare was significantly associated with lower symptom management self-efficacy among participants.
The most commonly desired change to improve healthcare among participants was greater knowledge about hEDS and HSD among healthcare professionals.

Maximum inter-fascial tissue displacement between the deep and superficial layers of the iliotibial tract was lowest in hEDS subjects compared to those with knee pain without hEDS and healthy controls.
Shear strain between the superficial and deep layers of the iliotibial tract was markedly lower in hEDS subjects compared with non-hEDS subjects with lower limb pain and non-hEDS pain-free controls.

The authors hypothesize that reduced inter-fascial gliding in hEDS may arise from pathologic alterations in matrix metalloproteinases and other ECM components, increasing viscosity and reducing lubrication, alongside changes in αvβ3 integrin-ILK focal adhesion complexes from fibroblast-to-myofibroblast transition.

A homozygous p.Ser268Leu mutation in DSE causes musculocontractural Ehlers-Danlos syndrome type 2, with joint hypermobility, atrophic scars, contractures of thumbs/feet, and characteristic facial features.
Recombinant p.Ser268Leu-DSE enzyme and patient-derived skin fibroblasts showed markedly reduced DSE (epimerase) activity compared with controls.
Nine reported cases of musculocontractural EDS type 2 have been attributed to a range of pathogenic DSE variants.
