Sanger sequencing of the SERPINH1 gene in 100 hEDS patients identified four different heterozygous missense variants, all of which were classified as benign according to ACMG guidelines, with no pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants detected.

A next-generation sequencing connective tissue disorder gene panel (COL5A1, COL5A2, COL3A1, COL1A1, COL1A2, TNXB, and 24 other genes) plus copy number variant analysis found no pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants and no CNVs in any of the 100 hEDS patients.

All four SERPINH1 missense variants detected in the hEDS patients were located within the N-terminal domain of the protein, with none found in the C-terminal domain, and no clear correlation was observed between variant location and patients' clinical severity, sex, age of onset, or family history.

A prior study cited in this paper found that ECM proteins (collagen types I, III, V, fibrillin, and fibronectin) were detectable only in the cytoplasm of hEDS patient fibroblasts and were largely absent from the extracellular space, unlike healthy control cells where these proteins were visible both intracellularly and extracellularly.

A cited mouse study found that HSP47 knockout (HSP47-/-) cells showed reduced secretion of type I collagen from the rough endoplasmic reticulum to the Golgi apparatus, with collagen accumulating in the rER, compared to HSP47+/+ cells.
Lightheadedness was the most common cardiovascular complaint, reported in 80.6% of the hEDS cohort.
Palpitations were reported by 77.6% of hEDS patients as a cardiovascular complaint.
Fainting (syncope) was reported by 44.8% of hEDS patients in the cohort.
Chest pain was reported by 32.8% of hEDS patients as a cardiovascular complaint.
The vast majority of echocardiograms (91.9%) showed only trace/trivial to mild valvular insufficiency, indicating minor rather than clinically significant valvular disease in hEDS patients.
21% of echocardiograms showed additional abnormalities including grade I diastolic dysfunction, mild aortic sclerosis, and trivial or small pericardial effusion.
Electrocardiograms were normal in 65% of hEDS patients, with the remainder showing only minor abnormalities or normal variants.

Despite high rates of cardiac symptoms, the overall prevalence of significant/clinically meaningful cardiac abnormalities on echocardiogram and ECG was very low in this hEDS cohort, suggesting a disconnect between symptom burden and structural cardiac findings.
Patients with vascular EDS/Loeys-Dietz syndrome (HDCTv) reported significantly higher usual fatigue than healthy subjects.
HDCTv patients had significantly more usual sleep problems than healthy subjects.
HDCTv patients scored significantly lower on SF-36 physical functioning, vitality, and general health than healthy subjects.
HDCTv patients showed higher anxiety and depression symptomatology (HADS continuous scores) than healthy subjects.
The proportion of patients exceeding the clinically significant anxiety cutoff did not differ significantly between HDCTv (25%) and healthy subjects (5.6%).
No significant difference in usual pain intensity was observed between HDCTv patients and healthy controls, both reporting low usual pain.
A greater proportion of HDCTv patients had a partner compared with hEDS patients (81.3% vs 43.8%).
Controlling for marital status, HDCTv patients scored significantly lower than hEDS patients on usual pain, fatigue, sleep problems, and depression.
HDCTv patients had significantly better scores than hEDS patients in all three QoL dimensions (physical functioning, vitality, general health) and all dimensions of psychosocial adjustment.
The vast majority of HDCTv patients (93.8%) showed optimal psychosocial adjustment to disease, compared to only 25% of hEDS patients.
None of the HDCTv patients but 31.3% of hEDS patients exceeded the clinical cutoff for depression on HADS.
No significant difference in categorical clinically significant anxiety was found between HDCTv (25%) and hEDS (50%) patients.

Qualitative interviews revealed that most HDCTv patients (n=11/16) perceive themselves as leading a normal life outside of acute vascular episodes, while taking precautions such as avoiding certain sports and stress.
The majority of HDCTv patients (n=12/16) expressed persistent fear and uncertainty about unpredictable vascular health events.
For eight of sixteen HDCTv patients, receiving a formal diagnosis enabled preventive action, sense-making of earlier symptoms, and social legitimization of their condition.
Four HDCTv patients reported frustration with health professionals' lack of knowledge and unpreparedness in managing vEDS/LDS.
Most HDCTv patients (n=10/16) reported making behavioral/lifestyle changes (diet, exercise, stress reduction, job changes) to minimize disease complications.
Twelve of sixteen HDCTv patients used positive reappraisal as a coping strategy, focusing on personal growth and reprioritization in response to their illness.
PoTS was identified as an independent predictive factor for gastrointestinal dysmotility in individuals with hEDS.

One study found dysautonomia prevalence of 70% among a hEDS/HSD sample, with affected individuals significantly more likely to have impaired QoL and exercise avoidance leading to a sedentary lifestyle.
Across included studies, PoTS prevalence in individuals with EDS/JHS ranged widely from 8% to 64%.
Individuals with both JHS and PoTS had a significantly increased risk of gastrointestinal symptomatology, including higher reflux, regurgitation and dysphagia scores.
Fibromyalgia was identified as a comorbid diagnosis in a subset of studies, with prevalence ranging from 5% in a BJHS sample up to 41% in an EDS sample.
Individuals with hEDS who also had gastrointestinal manifestations and chronic pain were significantly more likely to report a comorbid fibromyalgia diagnosis.
Women with EDS/HSD were found to have clinically significant rates of pelvic organ prolapse and related urogynaecological symptoms compared with controls.
Urinary incontinence was a clinically significant and highly prevalent symptom in a BJHS sample, causing significant embarrassment to women.
Individuals with hEDS and migraine had significantly earlier migraine onset, more frequent migraine days per month, and more photophobia than those without hEDS.
Obstructive sleep apnoea was found to be significantly more prevalent and under-recognised in HSD compared to controls, with hypopnoeas being the most common respiratory event.

Mood and anxiety disorders, particularly depression and anxiety, were significantly more frequent in EDS/HSD individuals than in the general population, with depression prevalence ranging 22%–69% and anxiety up to 75%.
HSD individuals with muscle/body pain and gastrointestinal symptoms had a significantly increased risk of depression, while GI symptoms alone were significant for anxiety.

Using the Tampa Scale for Kinesiophobia, a statistically significant difference in fear of movement was found between individuals with EDS/HSD and those without, including in activity avoidance and somatic focus subscales.
hEDS individuals with high levels of anxiety scored significantly higher on the Pain Catastrophizing Scale.
hEDS individuals with GI symptoms were significantly more likely to use GI medications (anti-secretory agents, antacids, laxatives) than controls.

In women with HSD, 31% had previously attempted suicide and 60% presented with mild suicidal risk; those with a history of suicide attempt were significantly more likely to have personality disturbances, major depression, and anxiety disorders.
ADHD was more frequent in EDS/HSD individuals than in the general population, and this difference was statistically significant specifically within the HSD subgroup.
Individuals with EDS/HSD frequently face a long and difficult diagnostic journey, sometimes waiting as long as 10 years, often being misdiagnosed, which can worsen their health.

The review found gastroenterology, mood disorders and anxiety disorders to be the most commonly reported physical and psychological manifestations of EDS/HSD, with clear implications for quality of life across over half of the included studies.
The study reports on clinical features of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome observed among biobank participants who carry predicted high-risk COL3A1 genotypes.

A cohort of 34 individuals with likely pathogenic or pathogenic COL1A1/COL1A2 variants was assembled, of whom 15 had potential OI-EDS overlap syndrome (OIEDS1, n=5 from COL1A1; OIEDS2, n=10 from COL1A2).
Among cases with potential OIEDS1 (COL1A1-related), 4 of 5 showed a predominant osteogenesis imperfecta phenotype associated with COL1A1 frameshift variants.
Among cases with potential OIEDS2 (COL1A2-related), 9 of 10 showed a predominant EDS phenotype, and four of these had been initially diagnosed with hypermobile EDS (hEDS).

An individual with a predominant EDS phenotype carried a COL1A1 arginine-to-cysteine substitution that had been originally misclassified as a variant of uncertain significance, despite this variant class being known to cause classical EDS with vascular fragility.

Vascular or arterial fragility was observed in 4 of the 15 OIEDS individuals, including one who had an original diagnosis of hEDS, highlighting a need for specific vascular surveillance in this group.

The findings suggest COL1A2 pathogenic variants may represent a genetic explanation for some individuals clinically diagnosed with hypermobile EDS, an EDS subtype currently without a known molecular basis.
EDS affects approximately 1 in 5000 individuals and is a hereditary disorder of connective tissue and collagen synthesis with twelve subtypes.
Hypermobile EDS (type III) is the most common EDS subtype, presumed autosomal dominant, with no known causative genetic mutation identified.
A 19-year-old with EDS type III and POTS underwent robotic sacrohysteropexy for uterine prolapse and had improved vaginal bulge and pelvic pain at 3- and 6-month follow-up.
Four days after sacrohysteropexy, the patient developed a suspected small bowel obstruction/ileus requiring reoperation, which confirmed diffuse ileus without true obstruction.

A 38-year-old with EDS type III and BRCA1-positive status underwent risk-reducing hysterectomy/BSO with sacrocolpopexy, retropubic sling, and posterior repair, reporting no leakage and improved bowel function at one-month follow-up.
A 52-year-old with EDS type III and prior pessary failure underwent robotic sacrocolpopexy with posterior repair and sling, remaining satisfied without bulge complaints at 22-month follow-up.
Connective tissue disorders show a much higher prevalence in women (73-89%) than men and predispose to pelvic floor disorders.

Reported pelvic floor symptom prevalence in connective tissue disorder patients ranges widely: urinary incontinence 38-60%, POP 13-75%, pelvic pain 13-75%, dyspareunia 30-77%, fecal incontinence 2-19%, and rectal prolapse 2-16%.
In a survey of 1303 women with EDS, 60% reported SUI, 54% urgency urinary incontinence, 24% fecal incontinence, 21% POP, 50% sexual dysfunction (36% dyspareunia), and 71% pelvic pain.
After adjusting for age, one study found no significant difference in complication rates after POP/SUI surgery between patients with hereditary connective tissue disorders and controls.

Neuropathic pain modulators (TCAs, anticonvulsants, SNRIs), though traditionally useful for centralized pain, have limited use in EDS due to 47% of patients experiencing adverse effects including worsening dysautonomia.
A randomized controlled trial found that a six-week generalized strength and fitness program significantly improved pain scores and self-esteem in this patient population.
A survey found that 75.5% of EDS patients who trialed supportive appliances such as pessaries reported no improvement in prolapse symptoms.
The same survey found that 80.5% of EDS patients who underwent surgery for prolapse reported symptomatic improvement.
Anatomic recurrence of pelvic organ prolapse after surgery did not differ between patients with EDS and those without.
The rate of postoperative complications did not differ between patients with connective tissue disorders and controls.

Dysautonomia in the form of POTS is common in EDS, causing orthostatic hypotension via abnormal aortic baroreceptor function, with symptoms of dizziness, nausea, palpitations, fatigue, and tachycardia, which can be worsened by anesthesia-induced vasodilation.
Defecatory problems, including straining, incomplete defecation, and need for digitation, are significantly greater in EDS groups than comparators.
Periodontal Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (pEDS) is caused by heterozygous gain-of-function mutations in the C1R and C1S genes, which trigger periodontal inflammation and alveolar bone breakdown.
The periodontal subtype of EDS (pEDS) is reported in the literature to have a 98.4% prevalence of severe periodontitis.
EDS overall is estimated to affect 1 in 5000 to 1 in 10,000 individuals across all ethnic groups, with similar proportions between males and females.
A 3-year-old girl presented with generalized tooth mobility, spontaneous gingival bleeding, and early exfoliation of several deciduous teeth beginning at age 2, attributed to periodontal EDS.

Detailed family history revealed periodontal disease, skin fragility, and poor wound healing across multiple maternal-line relatives, consistent with an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern for pEDS.

Pretibial hyperpigmentation (leg stains), observed in the patient's uncle, is described as the defining extraoral feature of pEDS, alongside easy bruising, skin fragility, and mild skin hyperextensibility.

Diagnosis of pEDS in the index child was established using clinical diagnostic criteria: early and severe periodontitis and lack of attached gingiva (major criteria) plus easy bruising (minor criterion).
The patient received scaling and root planing (SRP) on the superior teeth to treat active periodontitis once behavioral cooperation allowed clinical examination.
A 0.12% chlorhexidine gel was prescribed for 2 months to achieve supragingival biofilm control in the child with pEDS-related periodontitis.
Blood tests requested to investigate systemic causes of the child's condition were all considered adequate, supporting a clinical (rather than systemic metabolic) diagnosis of pEDS.
Exome analysis identified compound heterozygous missense and frameshift variants in exon 6 of DSE causing musculocontractural Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (mcEDS-DSE) in the patient.

A unilateral rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (RRD) in a mcEDS-DSE patient was successfully treated with scleral buckling surgery, with the atrophic hole repositioned beneath the buckle and subretinal fluid reduced postoperatively.

Retinal detachment had not previously been reported in any of 8 mcEDS-DSE patients described in the literature, in contrast to 6 of 41 mcEDS-CHST14 patients who had RD, suggesting a lower ocular complication burden in mcEDS-DSE.

Review of 66 mcEDS-CHST14 patients found retinal detachment in 6 patients (median age 15.5 years, range 9-20), retinal angioid streaks in 2 patients, and blindness in 6 patients associated with glaucoma, macular bleeding, lacquer crack in Bruch's membrane, and RRD.

During placement of tractional sutures on extraocular muscles, the patient developed prominent intraoperative bradycardia, attributed to the oculocardiac reflex, requiring reduced traction and continuous cardiac monitoring.
Previous studies have reported autonomic failure with cardiovascular dysfunction in EDS, warranting careful intraoperative systemic management.

Intraoperatively, the sclera was found to be very thin at the sclerotomy site, and postoperatively an otherwise unexplained peripapillary subretinal hemorrhage occurred, suggested to result from scleral and peripapillary vascular fragility rather than Bruch's membrane rupture.

High myopia (spherical equivalent -9.0 D, axial length 27.7 mm) was identified as the likely primary risk factor for the RRD in this mcEDS-DSE patient, rather than the mcEDS-DSE itself, since blue sclera and vitreous degeneration typical of EDS were absent.
A heterozygous COL5A1 variant c.3939G>T of uncertain clinical significance was identified in a patient presenting with musculoskeletal and vascular manifestations consistent with classical EDS.
A pathogenic FLCN mutation c.1285delC was identified in the patient, confirming a diagnosis of Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome.
The patient's echocardiogram showed mild aortic root dilation (4.6 cm) with bicuspid aortic valve, consistent with an EDS-related aortopathy.
The patient reported multiple fractures (patella, wrist, elbow, ankle) resulting from minor/low-velocity traumas, consistent with decreased bone density seen in classical EDS.
Physical examination revealed multiple fibrofolliculomas scattered around the cheeks and neck, a characteristic cutaneous manifestation of Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome.
Exposure to pepper spray triggered a spontaneous pneumothorax leading to subcutaneous emphysema, consistent with the pulmonary phenotype of Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome.
The patient had chronic neck pain with bilateral upper extremity paresthesia, and CT myelogram showed multiple bulging discs from C3-C7.
The patient was started on nebivolol 2.5 mg orally daily to manage progression of ascending aortic dilation.

The patient's mother had a positive history of Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome with pneumothoraces, pleural blebs, facial folliculomas, and cysts on kidneys, sinuses, ovaries, and breasts, indicating familial inheritance and variable expressivity.
Renal ultrasound in the patient was normal, showing no renal cysts despite confirmed BHD diagnosis and positive family history of renal cysts.
In about 50% of patients with classical EDS, there is a mutation in COL5A1 or COL5A2, the genes encoding type V collagen.
Aortic root dilation in patients with classical EDS has been documented to occur in up to 6% of cases.
Renal tumors have been reported in 27% of individuals with Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome, with a mean age of 50.5 years.
Spontaneous pneumothorax has been reported in 24% of patients with Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome at a median age of 38 years.
A 34-year-old male with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome presented with acute intraperitoneal hemorrhage due to rupture of a splenic artery aneurysm.
The ruptured splenic artery aneurysm was managed emergently with coil embolization and splenectomy.
CT imaging revealed concomitant right renal artery (RRA) and common hepatic artery (CHA) aneurysms in addition to the splenic artery aneurysm.
Under conservative management, the RRA and CHA aneurysms rapidly regressed and completely disappeared within 3 months, with resolution confirmed on imaging at 24 months.
Two pseudoaneurysms developed at other transarterial access sites during the follow-up period, requiring two secondary interventions.

The authors conclude that conservative management of complex visceral artery aneurysms was the best strategy in this vEDS case, avoiding risks of surgery on fragile tissue, while emphasizing that operative indications must be carefully weighed given unpredictable disease evolution.
Sudden aortic death (dissection and rupture) is found at autopsy with an estimated incidence between 0.6% and 7.7%.
Recent studies show that 20% of patients with thoracic aortic aneurysm or dissection (TAAD) have an identifiable genetic syndrome.
19% of patients with thoracic aortic aneurysm or dissection have an affected first-degree relative, suggesting hereditary contribution.
Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is reviewed as one of the common hereditary subtypes underlying thoracic aortic aneurysm and dissection.

No statistically significant correlation was found between total first ray sagittal plane motion (a continuous measure of hypermobility) and the first intermetatarsal angle in feet with hallux valgus deformity.
No statistically significant correlation was found between total first ray sagittal plane motion and the hallux valgus angle.
No statistically significant correlation was found between total first ray sagittal plane motion and sesamoid position.

The authors argue that hypermobility, traditionally treated as a dichotomous present/absent trait linked to hallux valgus, is more likely a continuous, normally-distributed variable, and their lack of correlation with radiographic parameters suggests the traditional link may reflect historical confirmation bias rather than a true biomechanical relationship.
Patients with benign joint hypermobility syndrome undergoing rectal prolapse surgery were significantly younger than those without the condition.
Patients with benign joint hypermobility syndrome were significantly more likely to require revisional surgery after ventral rectopexy for rectal prolapse than patients without the syndrome.
The BJHS group presenting with rectal prolapse was exclusively female, contrasting with a more male-inclusive sex ratio in the non-BJHS group.
Among 1,418 patients with genetic or non-genetic arteriopathies, an aberrant subclavian artery (ASA) was found in 34 cases (2.4%).
The prevalence of aberrant subclavian artery was similar between gene-positive (2.5%) and gene-negative (2.3%) arteriopathy patients, and ASA did not segregate with any specific genetic defect.
Among the 21 gene-positive patients with ASA, 14 had Marfan syndrome, 5 had Loeys-Dietz syndrome, 1 had vascular (type-IV) Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and 1 had periventricular heterotopia type 1.

Aortic/arterial dissection occurred in 5 of the 21 patients with genetic arteriopathies and ASA (23.8%; 2 with Marfan syndrome, 3 with Loeys-Dietz syndrome), all of whom also had an associated Kommerell's diverticulum.
No dissections occurred in gene-negative patients with ASA, contrasting with the 23.8% dissection rate seen in gene-positive patients.
None of the 5 patients who experienced ASA-related dissection had met existing guideline criteria for elective surgical repair at their baseline evaluation.
Overall treatment success (no further dislocation episodes) was achieved in 86.6% (13/15) of patients at the end of three months following polidocanol sclerotherapy.
At the four-week follow-up, 46.6% (7/15) of patients had already achieved success with a single polidocanol injection.
Pain scores measured by VAS decreased significantly after polidocanol sclerotherapy, with a statistically significant reduction reported (P = 0.016).
Masticatory efficiency scores improved significantly (i.e., chewing difficulty decreased) by the end of three months post-injection.
Maximal interincisal mouth opening (MMO) decreased significantly from baseline (40.1 ± 2.93 mm) to 36.43 ± 2.80 mm at three months post-injection, consistent with tightening of the joint ligaments.
TMJ clicking/joint sounds were significantly reduced at the end of three months after polidocanol sclerotherapy (P = 0.008).

Radiographically, the condyle shifted from an anterior-to-eminence or sub-eminence position preoperatively to a posterior-to-eminence position postoperatively in nearly all cases, except two which remained anterior.

No significant adverse effects were reported from polidocanol injections except transient oedema of the cheek and eyelid in two patients, which resolved within 24-48 hours after intravenous dexamethasone.
Prior literature (French Polidocanol Study) reported polidocanol as a safe sclerosing agent with mild urticaria as the most common complication, supporting its overall favorable safety profile.
Overall symptomatic relief (in pain, masticatory efficiency, joint sounds, regional tenderness, and mouth opening) was reported in 100% (15/15) of patients following polidocanol treatment.
Compared with a prior study reporting 100% success with ethanolamine oleate for TMJ hypermobility, the present study achieved a slightly lower success rate of 86.6% using polidocanol.
A maximum of three polidocanol injections were required across the cohort; one injection sufficed for 7/15 patients and two injections were needed for 8/15 patients to achieve the desired outcome.

FM patients showed a greater increase in perceived pain when viewing unpleasant images compared with patients with musculoskeletal pain from organic lesions, suggesting heightened sensitivity to unpleasant emotional stimuli.
A prior observational study by the authors' group found a correlation between a history of depressive symptoms and poorer quality of life in FM patients.
FM patients showed lower heart rate reactivity to stressful situations compared with pain-free individuals.
FM patients showed higher skin conductance level reactivity to stressful situations compared with pain-free individuals.
FM patients displayed higher electrodermal activity during an experimental empathic communication situation, indicating they perceive affective processing as stressful.
Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) improved pain acceptance and reduced pain catastrophizing compared with drug therapy alone.
Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) has been shown to significantly reduce painful symptoms in patients with chronic pain.

FM patients scored significantly higher on the Traumatic Experiences Checklist (more frequent childhood trauma, greater cumulative trauma impact) than pain-free healthy controls, with worse somatoform dissociation associated with more severe FM symptoms.

FM patients show difficulties adjusting and understanding their emotional states, with emotional interference in interpreting inner states contributing to greater pain impact on daily activities and increased disability burden.

FM patients show a psychological profile distinct from other chronic disease patients (rheumatoid arthritis, cancer), differentiated into 'maladaptive' (higher pain/anxiety/depression, unfavorable social comparison) and 'adaptive' (moderate pain/anxiety/depression, favorable social comparison) subgroups.

Not all FM patients have sufficient cognitive resources to engage well with mindfulness-based techniques, which some may find overly demanding, suggesting less cognitively engaging approaches (relaxation, biofeedback, acupuncture, yoga) may better help some patients reduce stress, anxiety and pain.

The overall correlation index of skin conductance concordance during psychotherapy sessions was positively and significantly correlated with the patient's empathic perception of the therapist, with high-concordance phases showing more positive socio-emotional interactions.

In fibromyalgia patients, peripheral nerve stimulation at the C2 vertebral level is thought to act on the autonomic nervous system, and C2-C3 neurons may also influence lateral spinothalamic pathways.
The review notes that dopamine has been implicated in the underlying pathophysiology of fibromyalgia.
Soreness symptoms were highly prevalent in FM patients (92.2%) alongside pain (100%), whereas only 12.2% of healthy controls reported either symptom.
Soreness intensity (NRS-S) was moderately correlated with soreness diffuseness (WSI) in FM patients.
Unlike soreness, pain intensity (NRS-P) was not correlated with pain diffuseness (WPI) in FM patients.
Pain intensity and soreness intensity were modestly correlated in FM patients, but pain and soreness diffuseness were not.
Pain intensity correlated with overall disease severity (FIQR), but soreness intensity did not.
High soreness intensity was correlated with intolerance to static activity (sitting for 45 minutes) and higher stiffness levels.
Conventional pharmacotherapy (imipramine ± pregabalin) significantly reduced pain scores over 4 weeks.
Soreness scores did not significantly improve with conventional pharmacotherapy after Bonferroni correction, unlike pain.

K-means cluster analysis and PCA identified two distinct FM phenotypes based on symptom severity: a pain-dominant group (FM-P) and a mixed pain-and-soreness group (FM-PS, 52.9% of patients) with significantly higher soreness intensity and diffuseness.
Treatment reduced soreness intensity within 2 weeks in FM-P, but FM-PS showed no therapeutic response in soreness until 4 weeks, and remained higher than FM-P after 4 weeks of treatment.
Treatment improved overall symptom severity and disease impact (FIQR domain 2) for FM-P patients but not for FM-PS patients.

Untargeted plasma metabolomics showed that upregulated metabolites (except N6-acetyl-L-lysine) were prominently higher in FM-PS but not FM-P compared with healthy controls, with incremental expression gradients across HC, FM-P and FM-PS.
Downregulated metabolites showed significantly lower peak intensity in FM-PS than healthy controls, with decreasing expression gradients across HC, FM-P and FM-PS.
FM patients with prominent soreness (FM-PS) showed decreased plasma lactate levels compared with healthy controls, unlike the lactate accumulation typical of exercise-induced soreness.
No correlation was found between plasma lactate expression and pain or soreness intensity in either FM-P or FM-PS groups.
Plasma malondialdehyde (MDA), a marker of lipid peroxidation/oxidative stress, was significantly higher in FM patients than healthy controls.

MDA level was significantly higher in the FM-PS (mixed pain/soreness) subgroup than healthy controls, but not significantly different between FM-P and healthy controls, suggesting oxidative stress specifically accompanies the soreness-prominent phenotype.

Pathway analysis identified taurine metabolism, purine metabolism and arginine biosynthesis as biologically significant pathways altered in FM, involving taurine, L-arginine, 2-oxoglutarate, hypoxanthine and AMP.
A non-significant correlative trend was observed between plasma MDA levels and soreness intensity in FM-PS compared with FM-P, suggesting oxidative stress may modulate the soreness phenotype.
The FM-PS subgroup was significantly younger on average than the FM-P subgroup, with no difference in sex ratio between the two phenotypes.

Restless leg syndrome (RLS), a comorbidity reported in up to one-third of FM patients, shares soreness as a common symptom descriptor (reported by 40.4% of RLS patients), suggesting a possible undetermined link between soreness, RLS and FM.
During MCAS episodes, serum tryptase rose on average nearly 5-fold above baseline levels.
Urinary leukotriene E4 showed the largest average increase of the metabolites measured during MCAS episodes, rising roughly 36-fold above baseline.
Urinary 2,3-dinor-11beta-prostaglandin F2alpha (a prostaglandin D2 metabolite) increased on average about 7-fold during MCAS episodes.
Urinary N-methylhistamine increased on average about 3.2-fold during MCAS episodes, the smallest average rise among the three metabolites studied.

An acute/baseline increase of 1.3-fold or greater in leukotriene E4, prostaglandin D2 metabolite, or N-methylhistamine consistently accompanied the diagnostic tryptase rise, suggesting this threshold could help corroborate MCAS diagnosis.
Formononetin dose-dependently reduced beta-hexosaminidase release, histamine release, and inflammatory cytokine mRNA expression in FcεRI-activated mast cells.
Formononetin suppressed IgE-induced NF-κB and MAPK signaling activity in mast cells.
Oral administration of formononetin attenuated passive cutaneous anaphylaxis and ovalbumin-induced active systemic anaphylaxis reactions in mice.
Formononetin reduced FcεRIγ chain expression via increased proteasome-mediated degradation and induced its ubiquitination.
Formononetin inhibited USP5 and/or USP13 activity, thereby promoting FcεRIγ ubiquitination and degradation.
A cited study found pruritus occurred in the majority of patients with small fiber neuropathy.
SFN is linked to metabolic, toxic, inflammatory, and autoimmune diseases but remains idiopathic in roughly 40% of cases.
In autoimmune-associated SFN, damage to thin Aδ and C-fibers is proposed to be mediated by TNF-α, IL-2, IL-6, and IL-8.
TNF-α expression is upregulated in patients with rosacea, promoting mast cell degranulation, vasodilation, and release of IL-6 and IL-8.
Neurogenic inflammation in rosacea is mediated by release of neuropeptides such as substance P and calcitonin gene-related peptide.

Compared with healthy controls, rosacea patients report higher subjective burning sensations but show significantly decreased heat-pain thresholds on QST, suggesting C-fiber neurovascular dysfunction.
A positive correlation between heat-pain thresholds and clinical severity of rosacea supports linking rosacea to the SFN spectrum.
SFN has been reported to be associated with voltage-gated sodium channel gene variants.
Nav1.8 sodium channel expression is significantly upregulated in the epidermis of patients with rosacea, potentially contributing to skin hyperpathia and representing a therapeutic target.
In a pathoetiological study, the number of PGP9.5-immunoreactive nerve fibers in rosacea epidermis decreased after laser therapy, suggesting a contributing neurogenic component to stinging.
A Danish nationwide cohort study found rosacea significantly associated with gastrointestinal disorders including celiac disease, irritable bowel syndrome, and inflammatory bowel disease.
Patients with SFN experience gastroparesis, diarrhea, constipation, and intestinal pseudo-obstruction attributed to C-fiber involvement in gastrointestinal smooth muscle.
Cardiac arrhythmias, photophobia, and other dysautonomia symptoms are observed in the context of neurogenic rosacea/SFN and warrant further attention.
Drugs used to treat SFN, including TCAs, pregabalin, gabapentin, and duloxetine, are reported effective for treating neurogenic rosacea that is otherwise recalcitrant to traditional therapy.
Pulsed dye lasers and endoscopic thoracic sympathectomy have been used to control facial flushing in neurogenic rosacea.
Small fiber neuropathy, assessed via sympathetic skin response and stimulated skin wrinkling, was present in 47 of 154 (30.5%) patients with idiopathic Parkinson's disease.
Large fiber neuropathy, defined by nerve conduction study abnormalities, was found in 28 of 154 (18.2%) patients with idiopathic Parkinson's disease.
Overall peripheral neuropathy (large and/or small fiber) was present in 49 of 154 (31.8%) patients with idiopathic Parkinson's disease, with overlap of both types in 16.9%.
Sympathetic skin response abnormality, a measure of small fiber autonomic dysfunction, was detected in 38.9% of the PD cohort.

Stimulated skin wrinkling abnormality after EMLA cream application, used as a marker of small fiber (postganglionic sympathetic) dysfunction, was found in 28.5% of PD patients and correlated better with clinical symptoms/signs than sympathetic skin response.
Serum homocysteine levels were positively correlated with cumulative levodopa dose, supporting a levodopa-driven hyperhomocysteinemia mechanism.
On multivariate logistic regression, only disease duration, cumulative levodopa dose, and Hoehn and Yahr severity score remained independently associated with both large and small fiber neuropathy.
About one-third of the PD cohort had elevated serum homocysteine levels above 20 mg/dl, consistent with a levodopa-related hyperhomocysteinemia mechanism of neuropathy.
Pain, numbness, burning sensation, and tingling were the most prevalent sensory symptoms reported by PD patients evaluated for neuropathy.
Temperature, pinprick, light touch, and vibration sensory impairments were the predominant clinical signs found on examination, at lower frequency than symptoms.

Phosphorylated alpha-synuclein aggregates, demonstrable in skin biopsy, are proposed to accumulate in peripheral axons of idiopathic Parkinson's disease patients (versus unphosphorylated synuclein in controls), impairing axonal transport and causing length-dependent peripheral neuropathy.
None of the levodopa-naive patients (all with disease duration <1 year) had peripheral neuropathy, supporting a role for levodopa exposure/disease duration in neuropathy development.

Rigidity-predominant PD presentation was associated with large fiber neuropathy on univariate analysis but not with small fiber neuropathy, and this association was not retained in multivariate analysis.

Among patients with large fiber neuropathy, axonal sensory neuropathy predominated (mild in 53%, severe in 29%) with sensory-motor involvement in 18%, and no demyelinating neuropathy was observed in the cohort.
Proximal leg skin biopsies showed significantly reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber density in MS patients compared with healthy controls.
Distal leg skin biopsies showed no significant difference in intraepidermal nerve fiber density between MS patients and healthy controls.
Although proximal and distal IENFD tended to be lower in MS patients with neuropathic pain, no statistically significant difference was found compared with MS patients without neuropathic pain.
The pattern of greater proximal than distal small fiber loss suggests a non-length dependent small fiber neuropathy in MS patients, distinct from typical distal-predominant SFN.
The authors describe nociplastic pain syndromes as including fibromyalgia, irritable bowel syndrome, headache, complex regional pain syndrome, and idiopathic orofacial pain.
The paper proposes that nociplastic pain may also occur in cancer patients, particularly those with pain arising from complications of cancer treatment.
Fluorescently labeled mast cell exosomes taken up by human lung fibroblasts localize to the cytosol/endoplasmic reticulum and are excluded from the nucleus.
Exposure of human lung fibroblasts to MC-EXO significantly increased hydroxyproline (proline hydroxylation) content compared to untreated fibroblasts, similar in magnitude to TGF-β stimulation.
MC-EXO exposure significantly increased secreted collagen in human lung fibroblast supernatants compared to untreated cells, at a magnitude similar to TGF-β.
Unlike MC-EXO, bronchial epithelial cell-derived exosomes (BEPI-EXO) did not induce collagen secretion by lung fibroblasts, showing the pro-fibrotic effect is specific to mast cell exosome cargo.
The stimulatory effect of MC-EXO on fibroblast collagen secretion requires continuous exosome presence; removing MC-EXO from the media after 48h abolishes the effect by 72h.
The effect of MC-EXO on fibroblast collagen secretion is dose-dependent, with doubling of MC-EXO concentration yielding a significant increase in collagen secretion.

MC-EXO and TGF-β stimulate fibroblast collagen production with distinct kinetics: MC-EXO effects are significant within 24h and continue increasing, whereas TGF-β requires 72h to produce measurable collagen secretion.
MC-EXO exposure did not induce phosphorylated Smad2/3 in fibroblasts, whereas TGF-β did, indicating MC-EXO acts via a Smad-independent pathway.
Unlike TGF-β, MC-EXO uptake did not upregulate collagen I or collagen III mRNA expression in fibroblasts, suggesting a post-translational rather than transcriptional mechanism.

Combining MC-EXO with TGF-β produced an additive increase in collagen synthesis, and TGF-βR1 inhibition blocked the TGF-β component but not the MC-EXO component, indicating two independent pro-collagen pathways.
Mast cell numbers were significantly increased in the lung parenchyma (but not airways) of COVID-19 autopsy/biopsy samples compared to control donor lungs.
Preliminary data show mast cells are present in the lung parenchyma of patients who died from COVID-19, a novel observation not previously documented alongside fibrotic histopathology.
Prior literature cited by the authors indicates mast cell abundance correlates with disease severity in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.

Prior work cited indicates histamine directly increases fibroblast proliferation and tryptase stimulates synthesis of type-I collagen by fibroblasts, representing classic mast cell degranulation-mediated fibrogenic mechanisms.
Tryptase stimulation caused enteric glial cells (EGCs) to proliferate 1.8-fold with cytoplasmic expansion and process elongation.
Tryptase stimulation made intercellular connections between enteric glial cells more complex.
Tryptase stimulation induced a 2.5-fold increase in NGF mRNA expression and also increased NGF protein expression in enteric glial cells.
Netrin-1 mRNA expression increased 3-fold at 30 minutes after tryptase stimulation and remained elevated up to 6 hours.
GDNF mRNA expression increased 3-fold at 30 minutes after tryptase stimulation but decreased by 3 hours.

Conditioned medium from tryptase-stimulated EGCs caused PC12 neuronal cytoplasmic expansion (round or ramified shapes) and neurite outgrowth with cytoskeletal filament elongation in a time- and dose-dependent manner.
Neuronal morphological changes induced by EGC conditioned medium after tryptase stimulation were similar to those induced by direct NGF stimulation.
Growth cone proteins in neurons were increased following exposure to conditioned medium from tryptase-stimulated EGCs.
A significantly higher percentage of people with ME/CFS reported hypersensitivities to noise and lights compared to people with MS.
Participants with both noise and light hypersensitivities reported greater overall symptomology than those without either hypersensitivity, regardless of whether they had ME/CFS or MS.
Pons volume was significantly larger in ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls after correction for multiple comparisons.
Whole brainstem volume was significantly larger in ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls after correction for multiple comparisons.
Pons volume was significantly larger in long COVID patients compared with healthy controls after correction for multiple comparisons.
Superior cerebellar peduncle (SCP) volume was significantly larger in long COVID patients compared with healthy controls after correction for multiple comparisons.
Whole brainstem volume was significantly larger in long COVID patients compared with healthy controls after correction for multiple comparisons.
Medulla volume was larger in long COVID patients than HC but did not reach statistical significance after correction for multiple comparisons.
Midbrain volume was larger in long COVID patients than HC but did not reach statistical significance after correction for multiple comparisons.
No brainstem subregion or whole brainstem volumes differed significantly between ME/CFS and long COVID patients, despite ME/CFS volumes trending smaller.
Pons volume showed a strong positive correlation with self-reported pain severity in ME/CFS patients, indicating larger pons volumes associated with greater pain.
Whole brainstem volume showed a strong positive correlation with self-reported pain severity in ME/CFS patients.
Midbrain volume showed a strong negative correlation with breathing difficulty severity in ME/CFS patients, indicating smaller midbrain volumes associated with worse breathing difficulty.
Whole brainstem volume showed a strong negative correlation with breathing difficulty severity in ME/CFS patients.
Midbrain volume showed a very strong negative correlation with breathing difficulty severity in long COVID patients.

The discussion notes that high ACE2 receptor expression in the brainstem is consistent with reported high SARS-CoV-2 concentrations detected there in COVID-19 autopsy studies, proposed as a mechanism for brainstem involvement in long COVID.

The discussion cites a prior study showing TRPM3 ion channel dysfunction as a biological overlap between ME/CFS and long COVID, noting TRPM3 is highly expressed in the brainstem, potentially explaining shared brainstem pathology.
A significant association was found between participants' fatigue illness (ME/CFS or Long COVID) and having a family member with similar symptoms.
A strong association was found between participants' fatigue illness and having a family member who developed Long COVID after an initial COVID-19 infection.
A combinatorial genomic analysis of GWAS data identified clusters of 199 SNPs connected to 14 genes that could identify 91% of ME/CFS patients in a UK Biobank sample.
A large multi-cohort GWAS (Norwegian, Danish, UK Biobank; >2500 patients) did not identify ME/CFS risk loci reaching genome-wide significance.
In a study of pregnancy in ME/CFS women, symptom trajectories diverged: 41% had no change, 30% improved into near remission, and 29% relapsed.

In a Stanford trial of the dopamine D2 agonist aripiprazole in 101 ME/CFS patients, 74% showed improvement in fatigue, brain fog, sleep and post-exertional malaise, 12% showed no change, and 14% worsened.
A retrospective review of 218 patient records found about 75% of patients reported a positive response in some neurological symptoms with LDN.
LDN was found to restore functional activity of TRPM3 in Ca2+-dependent Natural Killer cells of ME/CFS patients.
A safety and efficacy trial of LDN in 53 Long COVID patients concluded the drug was safe and may reduce symptoms.
Rituximab, which depletes B cells and looked promising in early trials, was not associated with clinical improvement in a phase 3 trial for ME/CFS.
Antivirals reduced fatigue and increased CD4+ T cells and natural killer cells, but only in a subgroup of ME/CFS patients.
Gene expression profiling by Kerr et al. found differential expression of 88 human genes and qPCR clustering revealed seven distinct ME/CFS subtypes with different clinical phenotypes and severity.
A Spanish cluster analysis identified five ME/CFS subtypes based on clinical phenotype and multi-domain questionnaire data including dysautonomia and cognitive function.

Longitudinal Seahorse stress-test analysis of PBMC mitochondrial oxygen consumption after exercise showed markedly different individual response patterns among ME/CFS patients despite similar clinical phenotype, while the control showed no change.

Protein carbonylation (oxidative stress marker) after exercise varied individually among ME/CFS patients within the same phenotype: one showed a decrease like controls, one a significant increase, and two showed no change.
A year-long DNA methylome study of two ME/CFS patients found site-specific methylation changes during relapse that reverted to baseline levels upon recovery.

A national ME/CFS patient survey (ANZMES) found 1 in 4 New Zealand ME/CFS patients had ongoing severe adverse reactions (major relapse) to the COVID-19 RNA vaccine, while about 1 in 20 reported improvement.

PET/MRS imaging with a TSPO radioligand showed 50-200% higher tracer binding (neuroinflammation marker) in ME/CFS patients versus healthy controls, correlating with symptom severity, mainly in the limbic system.

Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy found increased inflammation-linked metabolite ratios in 7 of 47 brain regions and elevated brain temperature in ME/CFS patients compared with matched controls, correlating with fatigue.

ME/CFS patients showed reduced white matter volume in the pons, with correlation patterns in autonomic centre nuclei reflecting dysfunction such as POTS, orthostatic intolerance, arrhythmia and abnormal breathing.

In an HHV-6 latency cell-culture model, early-stage viral transactivation induced mitochondrial fragmentation and strong dUTPase induction, and this fragmentation was reproduced by transferring serum from ME/CFS patients.
Postmortem brain and spinal cord tissue from a small cohort of ME/CFS patients showed abundant HHV-6 viral miRNA by fluorescence in situ hybridisation, absent in matched controls.

EBV-encoded dUTPase induces secretion of multiple proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines (TNF-α, TGF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, IL-12p40, IL-23, CCL5, CCL20, IFN-γ) in PBMCs, potentially disrupting blood-brain barrier integrity.
Reduced abundance of health-promoting butyrate-producing gut bacteria was linked to symptom severity in ME/CFS.

Microbial and metabolic marker profiles differed by illness duration: shorter-duration ME/CFS showed distinct butyrate-producer depletion, while longer-term patients showed severe metabolic abnormalities without as evident dysbiosis.
Postmortem brain and spinal cord tissue from a small cohort of ME/CFS patients showed abundant HHV-6 viral miRNA compared with matched controls, where it was not detected.

In ME/CFS patients of shorter illness duration, butyrate-producing gut bacteria were distinctly depleted, whereas longer-duration patients showed less evident dysbiosis but more severe metabolic abnormalities.
Reduced abundance of health-promoting butyrate-producing bacteria was linked to greater symptom severity in ME/CFS.
Probiotic use by ME/CFS patients was reported to improve cognitive function, and rectal infusions of bacteria also improved ME/CFS symptoms.

Western blot of pEDS patient fibroblast lysates and supernatants revealed additional collagen I fragments (~72 kDa, 55 kDa, 43 kDa) that were absent in control fibroblasts, alongside intact ~150 kDa procollagen in all lines.

Immunofluorescence/confocal microscopy showed that pEDS patient fibroblasts formed a markedly reduced, thin and short extracellular collagen I fiber network compared to the strong, dense fibrous bundles seen in control fibroblasts.

siRNA-mediated knockdown of C1S in pEDS patient fibroblasts markedly reduced the 72 kDa and 55 kDa collagen I degradation fragments while leaving intact 150 kDa procollagen unchanged, and had no effect on procollagen in control fibroblasts, demonstrating that C1s causes the collagen I cleavage seen in patient cells.

Overnight incubation of purified collagen I from different sources with purified activated C1s (aC1s) in vitro produced additional smaller fragments on coomassie-stained gels, showing partial, source-independent cleavage of native collagen I by aC1s.

Thermal denaturation of collagen I (87°C, 10 min) prior to aC1s incubation resulted in near-complete degradation of the alpha, beta, and gamma collagen I chains, unlike partial degradation of native (non-denatured) collagen I, indicating aC1s preferentially cleaves unfolded collagen.

aC1s-mediated collagen I degradation was temperature-dependent: no degradation occurred at 33°C, partial degradation at 37°C, and almost complete degradation at 40°C, indicating that the degree of collagen denaturation determines susceptibility to aC1s cleavage.

The serine protease inhibitor PMSF at 10 mM abolished aC1s-mediated collagen I degradation in vitro, whereas lower PMSF concentrations had no inhibitory effect, indicating protease inhibition can prevent collagen breakdown.
In prior work by the authors, addition of C4 to pEDS fibroblast supernatant (but not control supernatant) resulted in highly significant complement C4 activation in vitro.

A population-based nested case-control study found duodenal eosinophil infiltration was positively correlated with early satiety, a defining symptom of PDS-type functional dyspepsia.
Prospective treatment with pantoprazole reduced duodenal eosinophil and mast cell counts, improved intestinal permeability, and reduced symptom severity in FD patients.
A case-control study found PPI-treated FD patients had lower descending duodenal eosinophil counts than untreated patients, with no difference in duodenal bulb or gastric eosinophils.

A randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial of steroids in FD patients with mucosal eosinophilia found no significant difference in symptomatic response versus placebo, though eosinophil count reduction correlated with improved postprandial fullness and early satiety.

Gastric fluid microbiota composition differed in FD patients versus healthy subjects, with decreased Prevotella and increased Bifidobacterium and Clostridium abundance, and Prevotella abundance negatively correlated with PDS symptom severity.
Gastric fluid samples from FD patients lacked Acidobacteria and showed a higher Bacteroidetes-to-Proteobacteria ratio compared to healthy individuals.

Luminal Streptococcus abundance was higher across the oral cavity, esophagus, stomach, and duodenum in FD patients than controls, and positively associated with upper GI symptoms in both PDS and EPS subtypes.

A systematic review and meta-analysis found FD patients were more likely to have SIBO detected by breath test than healthy controls, with no significant difference in SIBO prevalence between FD subtypes.
In an RCT of H. pylori-negative FD patients, continuous intake of the LG21 probiotic strain resulted in symptom resolution in PDS but not EPS.
Bacillus spore probiotics were more effective than placebo for FD, with responders showing decreased pro-inflammatory IL-17/Th17 cytokines and increased Faecalibacterium and Roseburia.

Stimulated lymphocytes from combined FD and IBS patients showed increased IL-5 and IL-13 and decreased IFN-γ production compared to controls, consistent with a Th2-type immune shift, alongside decreased IL-12 from monocytes.

FD patients showed increased circulating gut-homing T helper cells (CD4+α4β7+CCR9+) and increased serum TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, and IL-10, which were associated with abdominal pain, cramps, nausea, vomiting, and delayed gastric emptying.
In a 10-year Swedish follow-up study of 887 participants, baseline anxiety (but not depression) was associated with newly onset functional dyspepsia.

In FD patients (n=40) versus controls (n=20), resting-state glucose metabolism in the insula, anterior cerebral cortex, middle cingulate cortex, and middle frontal cortex was higher and positively correlated with anxiety and depression scores.

PET imaging showed FD patients had higher resting brain glucose metabolism in pain-modulation regions (anterior cingulate cortex, insula, thalamus) than healthy subjects, correlating with symptom severity rather than anxiety.
Occupational stress or burnout was found to be associated with functional dyspepsia among female employees.
FD patients showed higher subjective stress and salivary cortisol levels than controls, and preceding/concurrent stress correlated positively with fullness severity.

In healthy volunteers, psychological stress from public speaking increased intestinal mucosal permeability (lactulose-mannitol ratio), and CRH administration replicated this effect; the mast cell stabilizer cromoglycate blocked the permeability increase from both stress and CRH.

An updated meta-analysis of RCTs for FD drug therapy found antipsychotics, followed by pregabalin and tricyclic antidepressants, showed greater efficacy than placebo, while SNRIs, SSRIs, and serotonin-1A agonists provided no benefit.
A meta-analysis of 8 RCTs comparing acupuncture with sham therapy in FD patients found acupuncture significantly reduced symptoms and gastric emptying time, with few adverse effects.

In contrast to other meta-analyses, a Cochrane review found no evidence of benefit for acupuncture in FD, a discrepancy attributed to low evidence quality and lack of adequate sham controls in acupuncture trials.
An RCT of 86 FD patients without SIBO found rifaximin provided significantly more relief of postprandial fullness or bloating than placebo.

A 33-nation survey using Rome IV criteria found the prevalence of functional dyspepsia was 7.2% vs. 4.8%, and IBS prevalence was 4.1% vs. 1.5%, establishing FD as the most common gastroduodenal disorder.

Immunofluorescence showed that FBN1 and Cav1.2 were expressed at lower levels and unevenly distributed in MFS-HASMCs compared with control-HASMCs.

Plasma extracellular vesicle particle size was significantly larger in ME/CFS patients than in healthy controls.
Total concentration of plasma extracellular vesicles was significantly higher in ME/CFS patients than controls.

Cytokine-cytokine correlation networks (both in EVs and plasma) showed markedly more positive correlations in ME/CFS than in controls, suggesting altered inflammatory signaling architecture.

Plasma CSF2 (GM-CSF) was negatively correlated with male sex and positively with BMI in both groups, was higher in ME/CFS patients with comorbid IBS, and was negatively correlated with physical function and positively with fatigue specifically in ME/CFS.

Plasma leptin was negatively correlated with male sex and positively with BMI in both groups, was higher in ME/CFS with comorbid IBS, and was negatively correlated with physical function and positively with fatigue specifically in ME/CFS.
CCL2, CXCL10, and CCL11 plasma levels were positively correlated with age in the ME/CFS cohort but not in controls.
Plasma TNFα was positively correlated with BMI and negatively correlated with SF-36 physical function in ME/CFS subjects.
Plasma IL1RA was positively correlated with BMI and negatively correlated with SF-36 physical function in ME/CFS subjects.
Lower plasma IL13 was associated with greater reduced-activity scores in ME/CFS patients.
In controls, higher PROS1 was correlated with lower vitality and lower SF-36 physical component summary, and higher MFI-20 general fatigue, but no such correlation was seen in ME/CFS.
In controls, higher FCRL3 was correlated with lower vitality scores; no such correlation was found in ME/CFS.
In controls only, higher CETP was correlated with greater general and total fatigue on the MFI-20.
In controls only, lower HBA1 (hemoglobin subunit alpha 1) was correlated with greater general and total fatigue.
In ME/CFS subjects, higher SERPINA5 (a hemostasis-related serine protease inhibitor) was positively correlated with better SF-36 general health and social functioning scores.

IGHA2 showed a significant ME/CFS-by-IBS interaction: levels were lower in ME/CFS than controls among subjects without IBS, but higher in ME/CFS than controls among subjects with IBS.
LRG1 showed a significant ME/CFS-by-IBS interaction: levels were lower in ME/CFS than controls among subjects without IBS, but higher in ME/CFS than controls among subjects with IBS.

The authors' finding of larger and more numerous EVs in ME/CFS contrasts with a prior study using the same isolation method that reported reduced EV size, a discrepancy attributed to methodological differences (smaller sample size, no thrombin treatment, lower centrifugal force).

CAMP (Cathelicidin Antimicrobial Protein), a pro-inflammatory protein, was one of seven proteins identified by all three machine learning classifiers as top discriminators and was increased in ME/CFS cases compared to controls.
IGLV1-47 (Immunoglobulin Lambda Variable 1-47) was among the top 7 proteins common to all three ML classifiers and was reduced in ME/CFS cases relative to controls.
CRTAC1 (Cartilage Acidic Protein 1), an extracellular matrix protein linked to fibroblast growth, was reduced in ME/CFS cases and among the top 7 discriminating proteins.
LRG1 (Leucine Rich Alpha-2-Glycoprotein 1), secreted by hepatocytes and neutrophils, was overall reduced in ME/CFS cases and ranked among the top ML-selected proteins distinguishing groups.
IGF1 (Insulin Like Growth Factor 1) was reduced in ME/CFS cases and was among the top proteins distinguishing cases from controls, likely reflecting unfavorable effects on growth and metabolism.

Tubulin alpha (TUBA1A/B/C, cytoskeletal component) was among the top 7 discriminating proteins and reduced in ME/CFS, with authors noting tubulin signaling disruption has been linked to neurocognitive impairment in other contexts.
Plasma TNFα was elevated in ME/CFS cases compared to controls at an uncorrected p-value, though it did not survive correction for multiple comparisons in the plasma cytokine dataset.

Coagulation factor II (thrombin/F2) exhibited 31 positive correlations with other plasma proteins, of which 11 were unique to ME/CFS cases and not seen in controls, suggesting altered hemostasis-related protein networks.
A significant negative correlation between SERPINA1 and KNG1 protein levels was found only in the control group, not in ME/CFS cases.
Three of six protein pairs showing significant negative correlation uniquely in the ME/CFS group involved SERPINA7, indicating disease-specific alteration of its protein correlation network.
A single significant correlation was found between an EV cytokine (CXCL12) and a mass spectrometry-assayed plasma protein (PROZ) in the control group only.

EV-derived LIF levels correlated with a greater number of distinct plasma cytokines in ME/CFS (8 cytokines) compared to controls (5 cytokines), suggesting altered cross-compartment cytokine signaling networks.

The authors note that genetic variants in the SERPINA5 gene have previously been associated with ME/CFS, providing a genetic link consistent with their observed correlation of SERPINA5 protein levels with ME/CFS health status.

The authors linked their finding of a SERPINA5-health correlation to other recent reports of activated platelets, microclots, and altered platelet gene expression in ME/CFS, suggesting a broader hemostasis dysregulation.

Classical monocytes in ME/CFS exhibit a unique gene expression pattern compared to controls, and the authors speculate that elevated GM-CSF (CSF2) could be a signaling factor contributing to this altered monocyte profile.
The authors note that lower IL13 was previously reported to be lower specifically in females with ME/CFS versus controls, though other studies found conflicting associations with symptom severity.

A larger prior study (Hornig et al., 298 cases and 348 controls) did not find significant differences in several of the plasma cytokines that were top ML features in this study, highlighting inconsistency in the ME/CFS cytokine literature.

The study sample overlapped substantially with prior published cohorts, using 98 of 100 subjects previously analyzed for fecal metagenomics, plasma cytokines, and plasma proteomics by mass spectrometry.
Women with contested illnesses used vlogging as a strategy to resist epistemic smothering and to seek epistemic justice regarding their illness experiences.
Vlogging did not fully allow women to break with epistemic smothering practices, as the ableist design and gendered norms of YouTube were experienced as obstacles to attaining epistemic justice.
The review suggests whole-body cryotherapy might serve as an adjuvant therapy for ME/CFS due to its presumed pleiotropic and anti-inflammatory effects, though this is speculative and not yet studied.

Ionomycin treatment produced a significant increase in intracellular Ca2+-related fluorescence ratio (f[340/380]) in L6 skeletal muscle cells at the mid-measurement time point compared to pre-treatment baseline.
By the final 1-hour timepoint, the mean Ca2+-related fluorescence ratio had returned close to baseline, though the distribution shape remained significantly altered.

At 190 MHz, ionomycin-treated L6 cells showed a significantly higher differential reflection coefficient (ΔS11) signal than untreated cells, indicating electrical sensitivity to ionomycin-induced ionic changes.
Circuit-model-fitted cytoplasmic conductivity (σc) was significantly higher in ionomycin-treated cells compared to untreated cells.
Circuit-model-fitted cytoplasmic relative permittivity (εc) was significantly lower in ionomycin-treated cells compared to untreated cells.

Distinct frequency ranges of the broadband electrical spectra (10 MHz–1 GHz for ΔS11 and 1 MHz–10 MHz for ΔS21) distinguished untreated from ionomycin-treated L6 cells, consistent with β-scattering-dominated cytoplasmic sensitivity.

Single-shell circuit fitting showed only minimal differences in raw cytoplasmic resistance (Rc) and capacitance (Cc) between treated and untreated cells despite significant differences in derived dielectric parameters.
No signal drift was observed in electrical measurements between cells measured early versus late in the hour-long measurement window, indicating negligible leakage current after cell washing.

The spectral alteration pattern from Ca2+-elevated cells (ΔS11 increase in MHz range, GHz-range dip, and less negative ΔS21 in kHz range) resembles the electrical signature previously observed in L6 cells subjected to long-term oxidative stress, suggesting Ca2+ mismanagement contributes to the oxidative-stress electrical profile.

The updated guideline recommends using the simplified 2015 Institute of Medicine (IOM) criteria as a primary-care screening tool for suspected ME/CFS, requiring early assessment of post-exertional malaise, fatigue, unrefreshing sleep, cognitive impairment and orthostatic intolerance.
A definitive diagnosis of ME/CFS should only be made after at least 6 months of persistent symptoms, while a suspected diagnosis can be pursued once unexplained fatigue has lasted at least 3 months.

For secondary care and research settings, the Canadian Consensus Criteria (CCC) are commonly used, requiring pain and neurological/cognitive disturbances plus at least one further symptom from two of three categories: autonomic, neuroendocrine, and immunological manifestations.
The guideline recommends against offering ME/CFS patients graded physical activation based on the deconditioning concept with a predefined stepwise increase in exertion.

Individually adapted symptom-oriented therapy, stress reduction, and pacing (exertion only up to the tolerated threshold, avoiding extensive inactivity) can achieve stabilization and improvement in ME/CFS, though the course is usually chronic with frequent relapses.
Behavioral therapy may be offered to ME/CFS patients specifically to treat accompanying symptoms, rather than as a curative treatment.

Post-exertional malaise (PEM) is defined in the guideline as a symptom worsening lasting at least 24 hours triggered by physical or mental exertion, and its early identification is important because it implies a different therapeutic strategy than other causes of fatigue.

Because the etiology of ME/CFS is not sufficiently clarified, the guideline now prefers the term 'myalgic encephalopathy' over 'encephalomyelitis', explicitly without committing to a brain-organic cause.

For unexplained persistent fatigue in primary care, the guideline recommends a basic laboratory panel (blood glucose, differential blood count, CRP or ESR, transaminases or gamma-GT, TSH), with further targeted work-up only if history or exam findings warrant it.

Because of their frequency as treatable causes of fatigue in primary care, the guideline recommends screening for depression and anxiety disorders using core symptom questions and the PHQ-9 questionnaire.
CFS prevalence is estimated at approximately 0.3%, with women affected twice as often as men.

The Canadian Consensus Criteria (2003) require fatigue and post-exertional malaise, at least one of sleep disturbance or pain, two or more neurocognitive manifestations, and symptoms from further categories, with a minimum six-month duration, for CFS diagnosis.
The Bell Score (1995) is a scale used to measure the severity of functional impairment caused by CFS.
CFS shows high comorbidity with depression, anxiety disorders and other psychiatric conditions, as reported across numerous publications.
A relationship between CFS and fibromyalgia syndrome has been noted for years, along with numerous somatoform-like complaints.
Long-COVID refers to symptoms persisting more than four weeks after infection, while Post-COVID refers to symptoms persisting more than twelve weeks after infection.
The reported frequency of Post-COVID syndrome varies widely, ranging from 15% to 80% depending on the patient population studied.
Fatigue syndrome is by far the most common symptom of Post-COVID and poses a particular challenge for assessment and treatment.
The proportion of neuropsychiatric symptoms among Post-COVID patients is estimated at 25-56%.
Loss of smell and taste occurs in up to 80% of acute COVID-19 cases and is considered nearly pathognomonic for the infection.
Residual smell disorders resolve largely within six months in more than 85% of patients following COVID-19.
Mortality from acute COVID-19 infection is reported to be 1-2%.
Among COVID-19 cases, 80% show a mild course, 10-15% a severe course, and 5% a life-threatening course determined primarily by respiratory insufficiency from pulmonary involvement.
From a psychosomatic perspective, Henningsen considers the post-infectious etiology of CFS to be refuted.
In contrast to the psychosomatic view, numerous other publications propose an organic cause for CFS, possibly a multisystem disease with dysregulated immune regulation.
Elevated interleukin-6 has been discussed as a potential shared mechanism between Post-COVID fatigue and CFS.
Elevated interleukin-10 has been discussed as a potential shared mechanism between Post-COVID fatigue and CFS.
Treatment for both CFS and Long/Post-COVID remains symptomatic, following the "pacing" principle of maintaining an individualized activity level to avoid overexertion.
There is currently no specific diagnostic biomarker for CFS; various laboratory parameters may be abnormal but have not been validated in studies.
16S rDNA sequencing showed that APS altered the abundance of gut microbiota and increased levels of short chain fatty acid (SCFA)-producing and anti-inflammatory bacteria in a CFS mouse model.
The CFS model caused a reduction in SCFAs in the cecal content, which was alleviated by APS treatment.
CFS induced abnormal expression of Nrf2 and its downstream factors in the brain-gut axis, which was reversed by APS treatment.
CFS induced abnormal expression of NF-κB and its downstream factors in the brain-gut axis, which was reversed by APS treatment.
APS modulated serum metabolic pathway changes that were induced by the CFS model.
Butyrate was verified to exert antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects in neuronal cells in vitro.
Overall, APS increased SCFA content via gut microbiota regulation, and SCFAs (particularly butyrate) further regulated brain oxidative stress and inflammation, alleviating CFS in the mouse model.
The review notes that Sjögren's syndrome has been associated with fibromyalgia and chronic fatigue syndrome, among other conditions.
The review notes that Sjögren's syndrome has been associated with fibromyalgia as a comorbid condition.
Bamboo-based medicinal moxibustion reduced FS-14 (fatigue) scores more than routine acupuncture at 1 and 2 treatment courses and at 14-day follow-up.
Moxibustion group showed greater reduction in SPHERE (somatic and psychological health) scores compared with the acupuncture group after treatment and at follow-up.
Peripheral blood CD3+ T lymphocyte content increased after moxibustion treatment compared to before treatment, with no significant change in the acupuncture group.
Peripheral blood CD4+ T lymphocyte content increased after moxibustion treatment, and was higher than in the acupuncture group post-treatment.
CD4+/CD8+ ratio increased after moxibustion treatment compared to before treatment.

The overall clinical effective rate was higher in the moxibustion group (93.3%) than in the acupuncture group (73.3%).
In ME/CFS, suppression of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex reduces conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, leading to diminished mitochondrial ATP production from both OXPHOS and glycolysis.
The antiviral signaling protein MAVS is proposed to help protect ME/CFS patients against viral-related infections, relevant given the severe immune alterations seen in this progressive disease.

In ME/CFS patients, additional mitochondrial dysfunction mechanisms include altered AMPK-mediated protein recycling and fatty acid catabolism, mTORC1 signaling, and creatine kinase activity, affecting cell cycle stability across tissue and cell types.

ME/CFS patients show heightened lactate production in muscles, serum, and cerebrospinal fluid following exercise, reflecting an accelerated shift to aerobic glycolysis with increased lactate and suppressed ATP levels.

ME/CFS shares common pathophysiological mechanisms with other neuroinflammatory conditions such as depression, fibromyalgia, and migraine, including HPA axis alterations, cytokine-mediated inflammatory signaling, dysregulated monoamines, and excessive glutamatergic transmission with compromised GABAergic inhibition.

The ME/CFS-associated reduction in acetyl-CoA is proposed to impair melatonin-mediated cellular and mitochondrial protection, since acetyl-CoA is required for AANAT activity in the serotonin-to-melatonin synthesis pathway.
In an animal model of fibromyalgia, melatonin treatment improved PGC-1α, Mfn2, and other mitochondrial parameters.

In a cohort of 669 older adults (Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging, average age 67), participants with lower mitochondrial oxidative capacity had markedly higher IL-6, CRP, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate than those with better oxidative capacity, independent of age and sex.
CFS model rats showed higher general-condition impairment scores than normal rats, indicating fatigue-like phenotype induction.
CFS model rats had prolonged escape latency and fewer platform crossings in the Morris water maze compared with normal rats, indicating impaired learning and memory.
Hippocampal ERK mRNA and protein levels were decreased in CFS model rats compared with normal rats.
Hippocampal CREB mRNA and protein levels were decreased in CFS model rats compared with normal rats.
Hippocampal BDNF mRNA and protein levels were decreased in CFS model rats compared with normal rats.
TEAS treatment at ST36 and BL23 reduced the general-condition impairment score in CFS rats on days 42 and 49 compared with untreated model rats.
TEAS treatment shortened escape latency and increased platform crossings in the Morris water maze relative to untreated model rats, indicating improved learning and memory.
TEAS treatment increased hippocampal ERK, CREB, and BDNF mRNA and protein expression compared with the untreated CFS model group.

In the model group, CA1 hippocampal neurons showed reduced numbers, scattered arrangement, increased apoptosis, and ultrastructural damage (nuclear and mitochondrial changes) compared with normal rats.

TEAS treatment improved CA1 neuron morphology and ultrastructure compared with the model group, with more regular cell arrangement, fewer apoptotic cells, uniformly distributed chromatin/cytoplasm, and relatively intact mitochondrial cristae.

Among 733 patients assessed at an EDS Clinic, 56.5% were diagnosed with both hEDS/HSD and fibromyalgia, 23.8% with hEDS/HSD alone, 13.3% with fibromyalgia alone, and 7.4% had neither diagnosis (controls).
A family history of similar diagnosis was reported by significantly more hEDS/HSD&Fibro (66.7%), hEDS/HSD (56.3%), and Fibro (43.9%) patients than controls.
Joint pain was significantly increased in all three patient groups compared to controls, occurring in 97.3% of hEDS/HSD&Fibro, 96.9% of Fibro, and 83.2% of hEDS/HSD patients.
Joint subluxations were significantly increased in all three groups compared to controls, most notably in 81.2% of hEDS/HSD&Fibro patients.
Only hEDS/HSD&Fibro patients self-reported significantly more sprains and dislocations than controls, distinguishing this combined group from single-diagnosis groups.

All three patient groups reported significantly increased easy bruising and easy scarring compared to controls, and Fibro and hEDS/HSD&Fibro patients also reported significantly more poor wound healing.

Allergy/atopy occurred at a high rate (70-80%) across all patient groups but was similarly high in controls (66%), so only hEDS/HSD&Fibro patients had significantly more allergies than controls, while allergies/atopy showed no significant difference in women-only analysis.
Headache occurred significantly more often in all three groups compared to controls, with the highest rate (80.9%) in hEDS/HSD&Fibro patients.
Migraine was only significantly higher than controls in hEDS/HSD&Fibro patients (63.8% vs 37% in controls), suggesting the combination of both diagnoses is needed to significantly promote migraine.

Autonomic dysfunction, neuropathy, brain fog, vertigo, and tinnitus were self-reported in significantly more patients with Fibro or hEDS/HSD&Fibro compared to controls and hEDS/HSD-only patients, with brain fog occurring in ~90% of Fibro/hEDS/HSD&Fibro patients but only 49% of hEDS/HSD-only patients.

GI symptoms including nausea, heartburn/dyspepsia, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, and IBS were all reported significantly more often in patients with Fibro or hEDS/HSD&Fibro compared to controls or hEDS/HSD-only patients, with nausea being the most frequent symptom (70.4-76.6%).

Patients in this study did not self-report autism/autism spectrum disorder (ASD) more often than controls in any diagnostic group, despite prior literature reporting co-occurrence of hEDS/HSD and autism.

Anxiety was reported by a high percentage of all groups, but only hEDS/HSD&Fibro patients reported significantly more anxiety (75.1%) than controls (51.9%); depression was significantly elevated in both Fibro (59.2%) and hEDS/HSD&Fibro (60.1%) versus controls/hEDS/HSD (~30-35%).
PTSD and sexual abuse were reported significantly more often (around 22-33%) in Fibro and hEDS/HSD&Fibro patients compared to only 6-8% and 17% respectively in controls and hEDS/HSD-only patients.

In pairwise comparisons, 33 of the 40 examined symptoms/comorbidities did not significantly differ between Fibro-only and hEDS/HSD&Fibro patients, indicating that most overlapping symptoms are attributable to fibromyalgia rather than to hEDS/HSD.

Seven symptoms/comorbidities (subluxations, being clumsy, joint sprains, stopping sports due to injury, jaw clicks/TMJ, poor wound healing, and migraine) were significantly more common in hEDS/HSD&Fibro than in Fibro alone, with 5 of these uniquely distinguishing the combined diagnosis after excluding overlap with top fibromyalgia issues.

hEDS/HSD-only patients (without fibromyalgia) were significantly different from hEDS/HSD&Fibro patients across all 40 examined conditions, indicating symptoms/comorbidities occur far more often when fibromyalgia co-occurs with hEDS/HSD.
Patients with hEDS&Fibro (specifically hEDS rather than HSD) also reported significantly more dislocations as a distinguishing symptom, in addition to the other 5 top issues shared with HSD&Fibro.

In prior literature cited in this study, hypermobility based on Beighton scores co-occurred in 64% of fibromyalgia patients vs 22% of controls (Ofluoglu et al.), 46% vs 28% (Sendur et al.), and 81% hypermobile with only 18% meeting formal hEDS criteria in fibromyalgia patients (Eccles et al.), providing background evidence for the hEDS/fibromyalgia overlap examined in the present study.

A novel missense mutation in COL3A1 (c.2095G>T, p.Gly699Cys) was identified in a woman with recurrent intestinal perforations and concluded to be a likely pathogenic variant causing vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
The same COL3A1 missense mutation was detected in the patient's son, who had died suddenly from hepatic vessel rupture, supporting familial (autosomal dominant) transmission of vascular EDS.

Two related COL3A1 variants at the same codon (p.Gly699Arg and p.Gly699Asp) had previously been reported as pathogenic and registered in ClinVar, supporting pathogenicity of the novel variant found in this case.

The patient experienced repeated intestinal perforations (descending colon, transverse colon, and jejunum) requiring four separate surgical interventions over a two-month period, consistent with the digestive complications characteristic of vascular EDS.

Citing Byers et al., the paper states that 31% of vascular EDS cases experience repeated colonic perforation, and that protracted wound healing and anastomotic failure may occur due to connective tissue and vascular vulnerability from COL3A1 mutation.

Citing Pepin et al., the paper notes that the median life span of patients with vascular EDS is 48 years (range 6–73 years), mainly due to vascular rupture, and that prognosis after treatment remains poor.
