Multiple surgical interventions (colonic resection, Hartmann procedure, jejunal resection with FEEA, jejunostomy, and later stoma closures) successfully treated the repeated intestinal perforations, with the patient free of further perforation at 22 months follow-up.
Wearing compression garments immediately reduced sway velocity of the centre of pressure during dynamic balance conditions in hEDS patients.
After 4 weeks, sway velocity on a laterally oscillating platform with eyes closed improved more in the physiotherapy plus compression garment group than in the physiotherapy-alone group.
After 4 weeks, ellipse area on the laterally oscillating platform with eyes closed improved more in the physiotherapy plus compression garment group than in the physiotherapy-alone group.
The Romberg quotient measured on a foam cushion improved more in the physiotherapy plus compression garment group than in the physiotherapy-alone group after 4 weeks.
Pain decreased in both the physiotherapy-alone and physiotherapy plus compression garment groups after 4 weeks, with no significant difference between groups.

Molecular genetic testing identified a pathogenic loss-of-function splice-site mutation in COL3A1 (c.1662+1G<A) consistent with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS type IV) in a young child presenting with recurrent lower gastrointestinal bleeding.

Follow-up colonoscopy 6 weeks after initial clipping showed resolution of the previously noted angiodysplasia-like lesions but revealed new diffuse mucosal desquamation with superficial bleeding induced simply by endoscope contact, suggesting an underlying connective tissue fragility rather than true angiodysplasia.

Physical examination by an experienced neuropediatrician and syndromologist found no classic clinical features of connective tissue disorder except hypermobility of the toes, and further cardiovascular and ophthalmologic evaluation showed no abnormalities typical of vascular EDS type IV, despite confirmed pathogenic COL3A1 variant.

The authors note that gastrointestinal complications of vascular EDS type IV typically manifest later in life, making this pediatric case one of the earliest reported presentations of mucosal intestinal abnormalities in confirmed EDS type IV.
Patients with EDS had a significantly higher mean ISTH-BAT bleeding score than matched healthy controls.
A majority of EDS patients (62%) had an abnormal ISTH-BAT score compared to none of the healthy controls.
The most common bleeding symptoms identified among EDS patients were bruising, muscle hematomas, menorrhagia, epistaxis, oral cavity bleeding, and bleeding after tooth extraction.
A subset of EDS patients experienced severe, life-threatening or surgery-requiring menorrhagia.
Postmortem genetic testing of an antemortem blood sample revealed a likely pathogenic COL3A1 variant (c.1826G>A, p.Gly609Glu), confirming a diagnosis of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome after death.

During bilateral sequential lung transplantation, the patient's recipient tissues and vascular structures were noted intraoperatively to be extremely friable, with a thin-walled pulmonary artery causing profuse bleeding and requiring escalation to venoarterial ECMO and cardiopulmonary bypass.

The patient developed a large posterior membranous tracheal wall tear after an uncomplicated, single-attempt endotracheal intubation, attributed to underlying vEDS-related tissue fragility rather than technical intubation factors.

Postmortem examination revealed chronic dissections of the right and left renal arteries with severe left renal artery stenosis leading to left renal atrophy, consistent with the vascular complications typical of vEDS.

The patient exhibited classic vEDS phenotypic features on postmortem exam (bluish sclerae, thin nose, thin lips, gingival recession) and, per family history obtained afterward, had lifelong easy bruising, gingival fragility requiring dentures at age 34, severe varicose veins requiring stripping surgery, and hypermobile thumbs, despite having no history of joint hypermobility, poor wound healing, or spontaneous pneumothorax before the fatal event.

A cited case series of 136 vEDS patients undergoing chest CT found pulmonary abnormalities in 57.4% of patients, most commonly emphysema, along with linear opacities, clustered micronodules, and cavitating nodules.

In a previously reported case (Saez et al.), a 29-year-old female with known vEDS and emphysema underwent successful bilateral lung transplantation with good outcome after cardiopulmonary bypass was used from the start of surgery and coagulopathy was proactively managed, contrasting with the fatal outcome in the present case where vEDS was unknown preoperatively.

The patient ultimately died from profound hemorrhagic and cardiogenic shock due to massive hemoperitoneum, retroperitoneal bleeding, splenic capsular tear, right ventricular tear, and liver laceration, culminating in bowel ischemia and cardiac arrest.
The paper reports an imaging case of vascular complications occurring in a young patient diagnosed with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
Children with HCTD aged 8 years and older reported significantly higher somatization scores on the Children's Somatization Inventory compared to normative data.
Children with HCTD aged 8 years and older reported significantly higher pain intensity on the VAS compared to normative data.
Children with HCTD aged 8 years and older showed significantly greater functional disability on the CHAQ-30 compared to normative data.
Children with HCTD aged 8 years and older self-reported significantly lower pain catastrophizing (PCS-C) compared to normative data.
Parents of children with HCTD aged 8 years and older reported significantly lower proxy pain catastrophizing (PCS-P) compared to normative data.
Among children aged 8 years and older with HCTD, pain was present in 59% with a median of 4 (IQR 3-9) pain areas.
The combined intensity of nonspecific somatic symptoms and pain explained 45% of the variance in disability among children with HCTD aged 8 years and older.
Among children aged 7 years and younger with HCTD, pain was present in 35% with a median of 5 (IQR 1-13) pain areas, and mean VAS pain intensity was 1.5 (SD 2.9).
In children aged 7 years or younger with HCTD, mean pain intensity on the visual-analogue scale was 1.5 (SD 2.9).
In children ≤7 years, functional disability was moderately correlated with the number of pain areas.
In children ≤7 years, functional disability was moderately correlated with the intensity of nonspecific somatic symptoms.
In children ≤7 years, functional disability was strongly correlated with pain intensity.
The patient's underlying Ehlers-Danlos syndrome predisposed her to neuropathic syndromes and negatively affected her surgical outcomes and expectations for revision surgery success.
Impaired tissue quality associated with EDS led surgeons to defer allograft repair of a recurrent flexor carpi ulnaris fascial defect due to concern about graft failure risk.

Ulnar nerve peripheral nerve stimulator placement resulted in 100% improvement in the patient's left ulnar arm pain, reducing her pain score from 4/10 pre-procedure to 0/10 post-procedure, sustained at two months.
At two-month follow-up after PNS placement, the patient's DASH disability score improved from 82.5% to 38.3%.
The patient's LANSS score of 19/24 indicated significant neuropathic mechanisms contributing to her pain.
More than half of patients undergoing surgical decompression for ulnar nerve entrapment, regardless of technique, continue to experience pain and paresthesia.

PNS is believed to act on both peripheral and central nervous systems, modulating inflammatory pathways and the autonomic nervous system, and selectively activating large sensory fibers to inhibit A-delta and C fiber pain transmission.

A prior study of 26 patients with chronic refractory neuropathic pain of the upper limb from CRPS or nerve injury treated with brachial plexus or supra-scapular nerve PNS found it to be a safe, minimally invasive, and effective treatment for upper limb neuropathic pain.
A previously reported case documented 33% pain reduction and substantial functional improvement after ulnar peripheral nerve stimulation following a failed ulnar transposition surgery.
Vascular Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome (vEDS) is caused by mutations in COL3A1, which encodes collagen III and predisposes patients to aneurysm, arterial dissection, and rupture.
The overall protein content of ECM generated from vEDS donor fibroblasts differed significantly from ECM generated from healthy donor fibroblasts.
ECM from vEDS donor fibroblasts showed upregulation of collagen subtypes and other proteins related to ECM structural integrity compared to healthy donor ECM.
ECM generated from a vEDS donor with a glycine substitution mutation in COL3A1 was characterized by increased glycosaminoglycan content compared to healthy donor ECM.
ECM from the glycine-substitution vEDS donor exhibited unique viscoelastic mechanical properties, including an increased time constant for stress relaxation relative to healthy donor ECM.
Human aortic endothelial cells seeded on ECM from the glycine-substitution vEDS donor showed decreased migratory speed compared to cells on healthy donor ECM.
The authors propose that ECM mechanical properties could serve as a prognostic indicator for patients with vEDS and highlight the broader utility of cell-derived ECM in disease modeling.
The authors propose that mechanical properties of patient-derived ECM could be used as a prognostic indicator for vEDS disease severity.

The study identifies potential drug targets for vEDS by quantifying structural, biochemical, and mechanical properties of patient-derived ECM, and clarifies a broader role for collagen III in ECM mechanics relevant to fibrosis and cancer.

Proband 1 was found to carry compound heterozygous likely pathogenic variants in AEBP1 (c.821del and c.2248T>C) via panel-based whole genome sequencing in the UK 100,000 Genomes Project, classified as ACMG class 4.
Proband 2 was found to carry compound heterozygous pathogenic nonsense variants in AEBP1 via a UK EDS gene panel, classified as ACMG class 5.
Transmission electron microscopy of skin biopsies from both probands showed abundant abnormal 'collagen flowers,' a finding previously described in other AEBP1-related clEDS cases.
Hair loss resembling androgenetic alopecia was reported in 6 of 11 individuals with AEBP1-related clEDS type 2, a feature not consistently reported in other EDS types.

Proband 1 developed multiple vascular abnormalities including mild ascending aortic dilatation, chronic right vertebral artery dissection, splenic artery dilatation, an aberrant subclavian artery, and tortuous iliac arteries, despite having no cardiovascular risk factors.

Across the 11 reported AEBP1-related clEDS cases, cardiovascular complications included an aortic root aneurysm requiring surgery in 1/11, mitral valve prolapse in 4/11 (diagnosed at ages 33, 35, 39, 58), and peripheral arterial disease in 1/11 (age 53).
Osteopenia was identified in 6 of 11 individuals with AEBP1-related clEDS (including proband 2), three of whom had sustained fractures.
Among the 11 reported AEBP1-related clEDS type 2 cases, joint hypermobility (11/11) and skin hyperextensibility (11/11) were universal, with atrophic scarring in 9/11 and easy bruising in 10/11.

The AEBP1 gene encodes two isoforms: AEBP1, a nuclear transcriptional repressor of anti-inflammatory/apoptotic genes, and ACLP, a secreted extracellular matrix protein; disease-causing recessive variants disrupt ACLP function, and ACLP is implicated in TGFβ and WNT/β-catenin signalling pathways.
Nearly half of EDS patients' open-ended responses about unmet mental health needs spontaneously described experiences of institutional betrayal by healthcare providers or systems.

A substantial minority of EDS patients reported systemic omission-type institutional betrayal, such as healthcare systems' lack of knowledge about EDS or providers failing to educate themselves about the disease.

Gaslighting, a form of systemic commission institutional betrayal in which patients are told their EDS symptoms are not medically possible or are psychiatric, was the most commonly reported form of institutional betrayal.
Medical trauma was reported about three times more often than interpersonal trauma among EDS respondents, though spontaneous trauma reporting overall was low.
The large majority of EDS respondents' written comments contained content codeable as a PTSD-related or mental health symptom, most commonly stress/anxiety/fear.
Over half of EDS respondents' comments referenced feeling depressed, sad, or hopeless in relation to their EDS healthcare experiences.
A minority of EDS respondents self-reported increased anger, annoyance, or irritability in relation to their healthcare experiences.
EDS respondents reported a lack of trust in their current healthcare provider or team more than three times as often as they reported positive trust.

Almost universally negative expectations for future healthcare encounters were reported, including hopelessness, need for self-advocacy, expected provider incompetence, expected dismissal of symptoms, and fear of harm.
The majority of EDS respondents reported unmet mental health needs and about half reported unmet physical health needs, along with needs for HCP/insurer education about EDS and social support.
EDS patients reporting institutional betrayal were significantly more likely to also report a medical trauma than those without institutional betrayal.
There were no significant differences between EDS patients with and without institutional betrayal in reports of PTSD/anxiety, depression/sadness, or isolative symptoms.
EDS patients reporting institutional betrayal were significantly more likely to report anger and irritability compared with those without institutional betrayal.
EDS patients reporting institutional betrayal showed dramatically higher rates of lack of trust in their HCP compared with those without institutional betrayal.

EDS patients with institutional betrayal were significantly more likely than those without to expect provider incompetence, poor care/medical harm, being disbelieved (gaslit), and needing to self-advocate in future healthcare encounters.
EDS patients with and without institutional betrayal were equally likely to express the expectation that 'nothing will change' and they will simply have to cope with their disease.

EDS patients with institutional betrayal were significantly more likely than those without to desire better provider, healthcare system, and insurer education about EDS, though overall physical and mental health needs did not differ between groups.

EDS patients experienced a long diagnostic delay, with average age at EDS diagnosis (33.1 years) substantially later than the sample's mean current age minus onset, and most were diagnosed with the hypermobile subtype.
Patients with connective tissue disease undergoing valve-sparing root replacement were significantly younger than those without CTD.
Women were much more frequently represented in the CTD group than the non-CTD group.
Hypertension was less common in patients with CTD compared with those without CTD.
Bicuspid aortic valve was less frequent in the CTD group compared with the non-CTD group.
Operative mortality was nil overall and did not differ between CTD and non-CTD patients undergoing valve-sparing root replacement.
Major postoperative complications occurred at similarly low rates in CTD and non-CTD patients.
Residual mild aortic insufficiency after valve-sparing root replacement was more frequent in patients with CTD than without.
Ten-year overall survival after valve-sparing root replacement did not differ between CTD and non-CTD patients.
Ten-year freedom from moderate or greater aortic insufficiency was similar between CTD and non-CTD groups.
Ten-year freedom from valve reoperation did not differ between patients with and without connective tissue disease.
Among patients with residual aortic insufficiency followed longitudinally, most remained mild while a minority progressed to moderate or severe AI.

The connective tissue disease cohort undergoing valve-sparing root replacement was predominantly composed of Marfan syndrome patients, with smaller numbers of Loeys-Dietz syndrome and Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

The authors conclude that valve function and long-term durability after valve-sparing root replacement are not influenced by the presence of connective tissue disease, including in patients with Ehlers-Danlos related vascular pathology.
Reserpine-induced fibromyalgia model rats showed significantly decreased brain monoamine levels compared to controls.
GSH (reduced glutathione) levels were significantly decreased in the cerebral cortex of fibromyalgia model rats, indicating oxidative stress.
MDA levels, a marker of lipid peroxidation, were significantly increased in the cerebral cortex of fibromyalgia model rats.
NLRP3 and caspase-1 levels were significantly increased in the cerebral cortex of fibromyalgia model rats compared to controls, indicating inflammasome activation.
Cerebral cortex of fibromyalgia model rats showed an increase in mast cell number compared to controls, accompanied by increased IL-1β immuno-expression.
Beclin-1 immuno-expression was significantly decreased in the cerebral cortex of fibromyalgia model rats, suggesting impaired autophagy.
Fibromyalgia model rats exhibited blood brain barrier disruption in the cerebral cortex compared to controls.
Histological and ultrastructural assessment showed neuronal and neuroglial degeneration with microglia activation in the cerebral cortex of fibromyalgia model rats.
BMSC administration significantly improved behavioural alterations related to pain, fatigue, depression, and sleep disturbances in the fibromyalgia rat model.
BMSC treatment restored the reduced brain monoamines and GSH/oxidative stress markers that were decreased in the fibromyalgia model.
Fibromyalgia rats showed an increased number of mast cells in the cerebral cortex compared to controls.
IL-1β immunoexpression was significantly increased in the cerebral cortex of fibromyalgia rats.
Beclin-1 immunoexpression, an autophagy marker, was significantly decreased in the cerebral cortex of fibromyalgia rats.
Fibromyalgia rats exhibited disruption of the blood brain barrier in the cerebral cortex.
BMSC administration significantly improved behavioural alterations related to pain, fatigue, depression, and sleep disturbances in the reserpine-induced fibromyalgia rat model.
BMSC treatment restored the reduced brain monoamine and oxidative stress marker (GSH) levels seen in fibromyalgia rats.
BMSC treatment significantly reduced TNF-alpha, HMGB-1, NLRP3, and caspase-1 levels compared to untreated fibromyalgia rats.
BMSC-treated fibromyalgia rats showed improved histological structure of the cerebral cortex compared to untreated fibromyalgia rats.
BMSC treatment significantly decreased mast cell number and IL-1β immunoexpression in the cerebral cortex compared to untreated fibromyalgia rats.
The fibromyalgia rat model showed disruption of the blood-brain barrier in the cerebral cortex.
BMSCs treatment significantly increased DCX immune-expression in the cerebral cortex, indicating stimulation of neurogenesis.
BMSCs treatment significantly increased Beclin-1 immune-expression in the cerebral cortex, suggesting stimulation of autophagy.
BMSCs treatment significantly decreased mast cell number in the cerebral cortex compared to the fibromyalgia group.
BMSCs treatment significantly decreased IL-1β immune-expression in the cerebral cortex compared to the fibromyalgia group.
BMSCs treatment improved the histological and ultrastructural structure of the cerebral cortex compared to the fibromyalgia group.
The authors propose that dysregulated prolactin and prolactin receptor signaling may drive heightened pain in female-predominant pain conditions including migraine, fibromyalgia, and pelvic pain.
A systematic review of PubMed/EMBASE clinical studies found that serum prolactin levels are consistently increased in women with endometriosis compared to those without.

The authors suggest that pharmacologically targeting prolactin or its receptor could improve management of endometriosis-associated pain, presented as a proposed strategy rather than a tested treatment.

Alpha-gal syndrome is an IgE-mediated allergy to the mammalian sugar galactose-alpha-1,3-galactose acquired following tick bites, causing delayed urticaria, abdominal pain, nausea, and occasionally anaphylaxis after red meat consumption.
AGS can be clinically confused with other causes of urticaria and anaphylaxis such as chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU) and mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS) due to overlapping presentations.
Diagnosis of AGS relies on clinical history, positive alpha-gal IgE blood testing, and symptom improvement on a mammalian-restricted diet.

Management of AGS centers on avoidance of mammalian meats (and occasionally dairy/other products), acute allergic symptom management, and tick-avoidance counseling, with the condition often waning over time in many patients.
MAVS-deficient bone marrow-derived mast cells (BMMCs) developed, proliferated, and survived normally in vitro compared with WT cells.
IgE/antigen-induced degranulation (β-hexosaminidase release) was almost normal in MAVS-deficient BMMCs compared with WT.
Production of TNF, IL-6, and IL-13 was dramatically increased in IgE/Ag-stimulated MAVS-deficient BMMCs compared with WT cells.
Retroviral restoration of MAVS expression in MAVS-deficient mast cells reduced the elevated cytokine production back close to WT levels, confirming that the phenotype was due to MAVS loss.
Phosphorylation of Lyn at both the activating (Tyr-396) and inhibitory (Tyr-507) sites was comparable between WT and MAVS-deficient BMMCs.
Tyrosine phosphorylation of the FcεRI β and γ subunits after antigen stimulation was similar in MAVS-deficient and WT BMMCs.
Lyn protein expression was lower in MAVS-deficient BMMCs than in WT cells, although this did not affect FcεRI subunit phosphorylation.
Phosphorylation of Syk at its activation loop was dramatically increased in antigen-stimulated MAVS-deficient BMMCs, indicating much higher Syk activity in the absence of MAVS.
Known Syk phosphorylation targets Btk, PLC-γ2 and the p85 subunit of PI3K were more highly phosphorylated in MAVS-deficient than WT BMMCs after antigen stimulation.

Even before antigen stimulation, phosphorylation of Syk targets (Btk, PLC-γ2, p85 PI3K) and downstream molecules (PDK1, NF-κB p65, ERK1/2) was already increased in MAVS-deficient BMMCs, suggesting constitutively higher Syk activity.
IgE/antigen-stimulated MAVS-deficient mast cells showed enhanced intracellular Ca2+ responses compared with WT cells, consistent with increased PLC-γ2 phosphorylation.
Protein expression levels of Syk, Btk and PLC-γ2 were altered by MAVS deficiency in mast cells.

PDK1 phosphorylation was constitutively higher and antigen-induced Akt phosphorylation at both Thr-308 and Ser-473 was greater in MAVS-deficient than WT BMMCs, consistent with increased PI3K activity upstream.
Phosphorylation of ERK1, ERK2 and p38 MAPKs was increased in MAVS-deficient mast cells, whereas JNK1/JNK2 phosphorylation was comparable between genotypes.
NF-κB pathway activation, assessed by IκBα and p65 phosphorylation, was slightly increased in MAVS-deficient mast cells.
Early-phase passive cutaneous anaphylaxis (PCA) reactions, driven mainly by histamine, were similar between WT and MAVS-deficient mice in vivo.
Late-phase (4-6h) and chronic-phase (32-48h) passive cutaneous anaphylaxis responses, partly TNF-dependent, were greater in MAVS-deficient mice than WT mice.
Naïve MAVS-deficient mice had increased numbers of mast cells in the ear skin compared with WT mice, prompting engraftment experiments to control for mast cell numbers.

Mast cell-deficient KitW-sh/W-sh mice engrafted with MAVS-deficient BMMCs showed stronger late-phase and chronic-phase PCA responses than mice engrafted with WT BMMCs, despite comparable mast cell numbers, demonstrating a mast cell-intrinsic effect of MAVS loss.
RIG-I-deficient BMMCs degranulated normally but showed 20-40% reduced cytokine production upon FcεRI stimulation, opposite to the phenotype seen with MAVS deficiency.
Syk phosphorylation was slightly reduced in RIG-I-deficient BMMCs while Lyn Tyr-396 phosphorylation was comparable to WT, and PLC-γ2 phosphorylation was reduced at early stimulation time points.
In RIG-I-deficient BMMCs, Akt and ERK1/2 phosphorylation were similar to WT, but p38 phosphorylation was increased.

MDA5-deficient BMMCs showed normal degranulation, normal cytokine production, and indistinguishable phosphorylation of Lyn, Syk, LAT, PLC-γ2, Akt, ERK1/2 and p38 compared with WT, indicating MDA5 does not influence FcεRI signaling.
IRF3-deficient BMMCs degranulated normally and produced cytokines at WT levels upon FcεRI stimulation.
In IRF3-deficient BMMCs, early (10 min) phosphorylation of Lyn (pY396), Syk, LAT (pY191) and PLC-γ2 (pY1217) was increased compared with WT, while Akt, ERK1/2 and p38 phosphorylation were comparable.
Up to 90% of systemic mastocytosis cases carry a gain-of-function somatic KIT mutation, most commonly D816V, which causes ligand-independent constitutive receptor activation.
Genetic testing confirmed the KIT D816V mutation in this patient, establishing the diagnosis of systemic mastocytosis.
The patient's serum tryptase was markedly elevated at 220 mcg/L (normal range <11), prompting further work-up for mastocytosis.
Bone marrow biopsy showed 60% infiltration by abnormal mast cells expressing CD117, CD2, CD25 and tryptase, consistent with systemic mastocytosis.
Histamine, the most abundant mast cell mediator, stimulates osteoclasts and increases RANKL expression in osteoblasts, promoting osteoclast recruitment and bone resorption.
Mast cell mediators can either promote osteoclastic activity and inhibit osteoblastic activity, or conversely promote osteoblastic and inhibit osteoclastic activity, depending on context.
Increased osteoprotegerin and RANKL levels have been observed in systemic mastocytosis, implicating the RANKL/RANK/OPG pathway in disease-related bone changes.
Skeletal involvement occurs in around 50% of SM patients, and osteoporosis prevalence in SM ranges 18-37% with vertebral fractures in up to 20%.
There is no difference in osteoporosis prevalence between SM patients with or without skin lesions, so SM should not be excluded based on absence of cutaneous involvement.
Osteosclerosis and increased bone density are observed in 2-19% of SM patients, with lower rates of fragility fractures and coexistence with osteolytic lesions.
Serum tryptase and bone turnover markers are highest in SM patients with osteosclerosis and increased bone density, and tryptase correlates with markers of bone resorption and formation.

In a cohort of 32 advanced SM patients, 75% had increased bone density and 50% had osteosclerosis; these patients had higher mast cell burden, serum tryptase, alkaline phosphatase and KIT D816V allele burden than advanced SM patients without increased BMD, and this phenotype was associated with poorer prognosis.
Bone marrow mast cell infiltration and serum tryptase levels were significantly lower in SM patients with osteoporosis compared to those without osteoporosis.
In a study of 25 SM patients, a single dose of intravenous zoledronic acid increased BMD at the lumbar spine and total hip and reduced bone turnover markers at 12 months.
In 4 postmenopausal women with SM, subcutaneous denosumab for 6 months increased BMD at the lumbar spine and femoral neck, reduced bone turnover markers, and decreased tryptase in all patients.
The case patient tolerated a single intravenous zoledronic acid dose poorly, developing an acute phase reaction with a week of myalgias and malaise, so antiresorptive therapy was discontinued.

In the case patient, denosumab 60 mg every 6 months for 5.5 years led to a BMD increase of 18.7% at the lumbar spine and 10.3% at the total hip, without dose interruption or significant adverse events.

The FREEDOM extension trial reported BMD increases of up to 21.7% at the lumbar spine and 9.2% at the total hip after 10 years of denosumab treatment in the general osteoporosis population, against which the case patient's rate of gain was compared.
DKK1, a Wnt pathway inhibitor, was found elevated in SM patients compared to controls, whereas sclerostin was not, leaving the role of the Wnt/β-catenin pathway in SM bone disease unclear.
The PTH analogue teriparatide may promote further mast cell proliferation and is not recommended for treating bone loss in systemic mastocytosis.
Midostaurin initially reduced the patient's tryptase but she was never able to sustain normal tryptase levels, and levels later surged, suggesting emerging treatment resistance.
Osteoporosis in SM is more common at the lumbar spine than the hip, likely reflecting mast cell propensity to colonise metabolically active trabecular bone.

CT lumbar spine imaging in the case patient revealed multiple sclerotic foci with surrounding osteolysis in vertebral bodies, sacrum and ilium, without pathological fractures or vertebral height loss.

The mtDNA variant m.10191T>C in MT-ND3, previously associated with Leigh(-like) syndrome, was identified in this patient and attributed as the cause of small fiber neuropathy after secondary causes were excluded.
Tilt table testing confirmed Postural Tachycardia Syndrome (POTS) in the patient, who also had a history of orthostatic hypotension and recurrent syncope since childhood.
Skin biopsy showed reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber densities at the thigh, calf, and forearm relative to normative thresholds, confirming the diagnosis of small fiber neuropathy.
The patient's small fiber neuropathy-related pain and dysautonomia improved with gabapentin and a variety of dietary supplements, improving overall quality of life.
A cited study of 27 mitochondrial disorder patients found SFN detected via sudoscan testing, while large fiber neuropathy was detected by nerve conduction studies in 11 of the 27 patients.
Large fiber neuropathy was particularly common among mitochondrial disorder patients carrying POLG1 variants, the m.8344A>G variant, or the m.3243A>G variant, per cited literature.
In patients with a single mtDNA deletion, large fiber neuropathy was detected in only 11% of cases, per cited literature.

A previously reported 35-year-old male carrying the m.3243A>G mtDNA variant developed burning distal extremity pain and abnormal quantitative sensory thresholds with normal nerve conduction studies, and his SFN was attributed to the mtDNA mutation after excluding other causes.
Small fiber neuropathy can disturb all autonomic functions but most commonly presents as POTS, per the authors' general characterization.

The patient also presented with connective tissue manifestations, including joint hyperlaxity, easy bruising, scoliosis, and Chiari malformation, as part of the multisystem mitochondrial disease phenotype.
Across the full cohort, 17.2% of patients carried at least one potentially pathogenic sodium channel gene (SCG) variant.
In painful-DPN patients, smMIP-NGS revealed 36 different potentially pathogenic heterozygous SCG variants in 41 of 237 patients (17.3%).
In painless-DPN patients, 42 different potentially pathogenic heterozygous SCG variants were found in 46 of 309 patients (14.9%).
In painful-SFN patients, 71 different potentially pathogenic heterozygous SCG variants were found in 101 of 547 patients (18.5%).
In painless-SFN patients, ten different potentially pathogenic heterozygous SCG variants were detected in six of 32 patients (18.8%).
SCN9A and SCN11A variants were more frequent in painful-SFN than in painful- or painless-DPN, whereas SCN10A variants were less frequent in painful-DPN and painful-SFN than in painless-DPN.
Patients carrying any SCG variant more often reported a family history of neuropathy than those without a variant (33.3% vs 18.8%).
Among patients with painful neuropathy, coldness and hot flashes were significantly more common in those with SCG variants than those without.
In painful-DPN, the duration of neuropathy was shorter in patients with an SCG variant than in those without one.
Dry eyes were reported more often in painful-SFN patients with SCG variants than in those without.
Dry eyes were reported more often in painless-DPN patients with SCG variants than in those without.
Type I diabetes was more prevalent in painless-DPN than in painful-DPN patients.
Cell electrophysiology studies previously showed a gain-of-function effect for SCN9A variants c.2215A>G, c.2794A>C/c.2971G>T, and c.4612T>C, identified in this cohort.
The SCN11A variant c.3473T>C, found in this cohort, has previously been shown to cause a gain-of-function effect on Nav1.9 channels.
The SCN10A variant c.4568G>A, found in this cohort (including painful-DPN and painful-SFN patients), has previously been shown to cause DRG neuron hyperexcitability.
Of 16 painful-SFN-associated SCG variants tested by voltage/current-clamp electrophysiology, 13 showed a gain-of-function effect on Nav1.7, Nav1.8, or Nav1.9 channels.
In painful-SFN patients, SCN9A variants clustered predominantly in transmembrane domains I and II and the DI-DII intracellular linker.
In painful-SFN patients, SCN10A variants clustered predominantly in domains III and IV, the DIII-DIV linker, and the C-terminus of the protein.
Painful-SFN patients experienced more dullness, sensitivity, and intense deep/surface pain on the Neuropathic Pain Scale than painful-DPN patients.
12 of 13 SFN-related symptoms were reported more often by patients with painful neuropathy than those with painless neuropathy, with only diarrhea reported equally.

This study's finding of differing SCG variant frequencies between painful and painless neuropathy contrasts with Wadhawan et al. (2017), who found no significant difference in SCN9A, SCN10A, and SCN11A missense variant allele frequencies between painful and non-painful neuropathy in a cohort of 457 patients.

Unlike Blesneac et al. (2018), who found rare Nav1.7 (SCN9A) variants only in painful-DPN patients and none in painless-DPN, this study identified several rare SCN9A variants in both painful-DPN and painless-DPN.

This study's finding of differing SFN-SIQ scores by SCG variant status in painful-SFN contrasts with Eijkenboom et al. (2018), who reported comparable NPS and SFN-SIQ scores in 1139 pure-SFN patients regardless of SCN9A/SCN10A/SCN11A variant status.
Overall, a higher proportion of patients with painful neuropathy carried an SCG variant compared to patients with painless neuropathy (18.1% vs 15.2%).
In vitro preclinical studies show gadolinium compounds induce profibrotic responses in skin by activating and proliferating dermal fibroblasts and promoting their differentiation into myofibroblasts.
Gadolinium exposure increases matrix metalloproteinase-1 levels in skin, contributing to altered collagen production.
Gadolinium exposure increases tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinase-1 levels in skin, altering collagen homeostasis.
In animal studies, gadolinium deposits in the skin at higher concentrations when linear GBCAs are administered compared with macrocyclic agents.
Skin gadolinium deposits in animal studies decrease over time and are not linked to observable macroscopic or histological skin changes.

In clinical studies, gadolinium was detectable in the skin and hair of subjects with normal renal function at higher concentrations after intravenous linear GBCA compared with macrocyclic GBCA administration.
Clinically, gadolinium deposits detected in skin/hair decrease over time and are not associated with cutaneous or histological modifications.
Subclinical dermal involvement related to linear GBCA exposure may be detectable via brain MRI in exposed subjects.
The review concludes there is no conclusive evidence of a causal relationship between GBCA administration at clinical doses and cutaneous manifestations in patients with normal renal function.
At post-treatment, mindfulness- and acceptance-based therapies significantly reduced somatic symptom severity compared to inactive/non-specific control conditions.
Perceived health status (quality of life, illness impairment) improved significantly at post-treatment in the third-wave therapy groups versus controls.
Depressive symptoms were significantly reduced at post-treatment in third-wave therapy groups compared to controls.
Anxiety symptoms were significantly reduced at post-treatment in third-wave therapy groups compared to controls.
Trait/state mindfulness scores improved significantly at post-treatment in third-wave therapy groups compared to controls.
Psychological inflexibility was significantly reduced at post-treatment, supporting ACT's proposed mechanism of action.
Reduction in somatic symptom severity was maintained at short-term follow-up (up to 3 months) compared to controls.
At long-term follow-up (mean ~9.6 months), perceived health status improvement was no longer statistically significant.
At long-term follow-up, the reduction in depressive symptoms was no longer statistically significant.
Anxiety reduction was maintained and significant even at long-term follow-up (>3 months, mean ~9.6 months).
Acceptance-based therapy (ACT) and mindfulness-based therapies (MBCT/MBSR) did not differ significantly in efficacy for somatic symptom severity.
Subgroup analysis found no significant difference in treatment effect based on whether the control group was inactive (waitlist) or non-specific (TAU, enhanced care, placebo).
No significant subgroup difference in treatment effect was found between irritable bowel syndrome and fibromyalgia patient subgroups.
Neither total therapy duration (dosage) nor number of sessions significantly moderated treatment effects, and low- vs high-intensity treatment subgroups did not differ significantly.
Egger's test found no evidence of funnel plot asymmetry (publication bias) for any post-treatment outcome, and p-curve analysis indicated evidential value for all outcomes assessable.

Mastocytic enterocolitis is defined by increased mast cell aggregates (≥20/hpf) in the intestinal mucosal layer in patients with chronic diarrhea, with symptom improvement on antihistamine or steroidal treatment.
In a study of 47 patients with chronic intractable diarrhea of unknown etiology, 33 patients had increased mast cells (>20/hpf) on intestinal biopsy.
The patient's colon biopsy showed more than 20 CD117 (c-Kit)-positive mast cells per high-power field infiltrating the lamina propria of the left colon, confirming mastocytic enterocolitis.
Treatment with cetirizine 10 mg daily led to resolution of the patient's chronic diarrhea symptoms at three-month follow-up.
The patient's previous treatment with combined cetirizine and famotidine resolved symptoms, but discontinuation of these medications led to recurrence of diarrhea about one year later.
A mouse study showed that depleting mast cell numbers caused remission of existing colon polyps.
Retrospective studies found a significant inverse correlation between mast cell density and survival rate from colorectal cancer.

The patient, with a family history of colon cancer in his father and two uncles, developed new tubular adenomatous polyps in a colon segment that two years earlier showed only mastocytic enterocolitis without polyps.

Mastocytic enterocolitis and IBS-D patients typically both have normal routine laboratory findings (ESR, serum tryptase, chemistry panel), so distinguishing between them relies heavily on histological identification of mast cell infiltration.

The patient's random serum tryptase was normal, supporting that his mast cell disease was limited to the GI tract rather than systemic mastocytosis, so an exhaustive systemic mastocytosis work-up was not pursued.
Twelve weeks of progressive resistance training significantly improved cardiac autonomic control parameters in T2DM patients with cardiac autonomic neuropathy compared to usual care.
Serum interleukin-6 was significantly reduced after 12 weeks of resistance training in T2DM patients with cardiac autonomic neuropathy.
Serum interleukin-18 was significantly reduced after 12 weeks of resistance training in T2DM patients with cardiac autonomic neuropathy.
Endothelial nitric oxide synthase levels significantly increased after 12 weeks of resistance training, suggesting a role in vascular remodeling in T2DM patients with cardiac autonomic neuropathy.
Salusin-beta protein levels were increased in the paraventricular nucleus of rats with chronic heart failure compared with sham-operated rats.
Microinjection of salusin-beta into the PVN dose-dependently increased mean arterial pressure and renal sympathetic nerve activity and enhanced the cardiac sympathetic afferent reflex.
Neutralization of endogenous salusin-beta in the PVN with anti-salusin-beta IgG reduced sympathetic activity and CSAR, opposite to the effect of exogenous salusin-beta.

The excitatory effect of salusin-beta on sympathetic activity was blocked by a reactive oxygen species scavenger or NAD(P)H oxidase inhibitor but enhanced by a superoxide dismutase inhibitor, implicating a NAD(P)H oxidase-ROS pathway.
Blocking reactive oxygen species with a scavenger or inhibiting NAD(P)H oxidase abolished the pressor and sympathoexcitatory effects of salusin-beta microinjected into the PVN.
A superoxide dismutase inhibitor promoted (enhanced) the pressor and sympathoexcitatory effects of salusin-beta in the PVN, indicating superoxide-dependent action.
The sympathoinhibitory effect of anti-salusin-beta IgG was blocked by a nitric oxide synthase inhibitor, indicating that salusin-beta antagonism acts via increased NO release.
Chronic knockdown of salusin-beta in the PVN attenuated the cardiac sympathetic afferent reflex and reduced sympathetic output in rats with chronic heart failure.
Chronic salusin-beta knockdown in the PVN improved myocardial remodeling and cardiac function in CHF rats.
Chronic salusin-beta knockdown in the PVN decreased NAD(P)H oxidase activity and ROS levels while increasing NO levels in CHF rats, supporting a redox-based mechanism.
Ovariectomy combined with MCT further shortened median survival of PAH rats to 4 weeks, with all rats in this group dead by 8 weeks, compared to MCT alone.

Intragastric TMP administration extended median survival of ovariectomized PAH rats from ~4 weeks to 8 weeks in a dose-dependent manner and reduced RVSP, mPAP, Fulton index, pulmonary artery wall thickness, and fibrosis.

Myocardin protein expression was significantly reduced in pulmonary artery smooth muscle of MCT-induced PAH model rats compared to normal rats, alongside reduced α-SMA, smoothelin, ERα and increased OPN/SM22-α.
TMP treatment significantly upregulated myocardin, α-SMA and smoothelin protein expression in pulmonary artery smooth muscle of PAH rats while downregulating OPN and SM22-α, without affecting ERα.
ERα protein expression was reduced in pulmonary artery smooth muscle of ovariectomized MCT-PAH rats compared to normal rats and was not restored by TMP treatment.
TMP at concentrations up to 100 μM did not significantly affect PSMC viability, so subsequent experiments used TMP ≤100 μM.

CoCl2-induced PSMC proliferation model showed significantly reduced α-SMA and significantly increased OPN protein expression by immunofluorescence, confirming successful induction of a proliferative phenotype.
TMP reduced CoCl2-induced PSMC numbers in a dose-dependent manner (0, 25, 50, 100 μM) and induced a contracted cell morphology.
TMP significantly reduced proliferation-promoting cytokines TGF-β and CTGF and increased anti-proliferative NO levels in CoCl2-induced PSMCs.

Myocardin siRNA knockdown in CoCl2-induced PSMCs aggravated abnormal proliferation and cell morphology changes, and reduced myocardin, α-SMA and smoothelin protein/mRNA while increasing OPN and SM22-α.

Myocardin siRNA knockdown had no significant effect on ERα protein and mRNA expression in PSMCs, and TMP-mediated regulation of α-SMA and OPN was significantly blocked when myocardin was knocked down.
The ERα-specific inhibitor MPP aggravated CoCl2-induced PSMC proliferation and significantly downregulated protein and mRNA expression of myocardin, α-SMA and smoothelin.

TMP significantly reduced PSMC proliferation and restored α-SMA and myocardin protein/mRNA expression even when ERα activity was inhibited by MPP, indicating TMP's effect does not strictly require ERα.
Co-immunoprecipitation showed TMP promoted nuclear translocation of MRTF-A and its combination with myocardin to form a transcription complex.

Protein expression trends of ERα and myocardin were synchronized across in vivo and in vitro models, supporting positive regulation of myocardin by ERα, though the direct regulatory mechanism remains unclear.
Higher serum IL-8 concentrations were associated with prolonged gastric emptying time in individuals with diabetes.
Higher serum IL-10 concentrations were associated with prolonged colonic transit time in individuals with diabetes.
No significant associations were found between IL-6, TNF-α, or IFN-γ and gastric emptying, colonic transit, or small bowel transit time.
Higher IL-6 levels were inversely correlated with nausea/vomiting symptom severity in the diabetes cohort.
Higher IL-6 levels were inversely correlated with bloating symptom severity in the diabetes cohort.
Serum TNF-α was the only cytokine differing between healthy controls and diabetes, being elevated relative to type 1 diabetes but reduced relative to type 2 diabetes.
Four of five pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-8, TNF-α, IFN-γ) were significantly higher in type 2 diabetes compared to type 1 diabetes.
In type 1 diabetes, males had higher IL-6 and TNF-α levels than females.
Colonic transit times were significantly longer in both diabetes cohorts compared to healthy controls.
A cited meta-analysis found IL-6 plasma levels were significantly higher in diarrhoea-predominant IBS patients compared to healthy controls, but not in constipation-predominant IBS.
Bleomycin injection decreased body weight and increased the lung weight ratio in mice, indicating induction of pulmonary fibrosis.
Baricitinib treatment reversed bleomycin-induced body weight loss and increased lung weight ratio in the SSc-ILD mouse model.
Baricitinib decreased plasma pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1β and IL-6 and increased anti-inflammatory cytokines IL-4 and IL-10 compared with bleomycin-treated mice.

Bleomycin caused disruption of alveolar structure, alveolar septal and dermal thickening, inflammatory cell infiltration, and increased collagen deposition in lung and skin as measured by HE and Masson's trichrome staining and modified Ashcroft score.
Baricitinib significantly attenuated bleomycin-induced fibrosis, reducing modified Ashcroft fibrosis score, dermal thickness, and collagen content in lung and skin.
Collagen mRNA expression was significantly downregulated in both skin and lung tissue of baricitinib-treated mice relative to bleomycin-only mice.
Bleomycin significantly increased JAK2 and phospho-JAK2 protein expression in lung and skin tissue, and this was reduced by baricitinib treatment.
TGF-β1 protein expression was significantly increased in lung and skin tissue of bleomycin-induced SSc-ILD mice and reduced by baricitinib.
TGF-β receptor type I and II protein expression was significantly increased in lung and skin of bleomycin-induced SSc-ILD mice and reduced by baricitinib treatment.
Immunofluorescence staining confirmed increased numbers of p-JAK2+ and TGF-β1+ cells in lung tissue of bleomycin-treated mice, which were suppressed by baricitinib.
TGF-β1 stimulation of human fetal lung fibroblasts (HFLs) dose-dependently increased collagen 4, fibronectin, and SMA (myofibroblast marker), indicating fibroblast-to-myofibroblast transformation.

TGF-β1 stimulation increased JAK2 and TGF-β receptor protein expression in HFLs in a concentration-dependent manner, suggesting the JAK2 and TGF-β1 pathways jointly facilitate fibroblast transformation and collagen deposition.
Baricitinib treatment of TGF-β1-stimulated HFLs reduced SMA expression and collagen deposition and significantly decreased TGF-β receptor protein expression in a dose-dependent manner.

siRNA-mediated knockdown of JAK2 in HFLs produced similar reductions in SMA and TGF-β receptor expression as pharmacological JAK2 inhibition by baricitinib, confirming JAK2's role in fibroblast transformation.

Pharmacological JAK2 inhibition decreased protein expression and activation (phosphorylation) of collagen, STAT3, and Smad3 in TGF-β1-stimulated HFLs, indicating JAK2/STAT3 pathway crosstalk with TGF-β1/Smad3 signaling.
Pharmacological STAT3 inhibition (stattic) and STAT3 siRNA knockdown both decreased Smad3 protein expression and activation, indicating STAT3 regulates Smad3 signaling downstream of JAK2.

The TGF-β receptor I/II inhibitor LY2109761 reduced TGF-β1-induced collagen accumulation, inhibited fibroblast-to-myofibroblast transformation, and reduced JAK2 expression, showing that the TGF-β1 pathway also regulates JAK2 (bidirectional crosstalk).

The non-neuropathic comparison group in this pain registry cohort included 794 patients with Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome/Hypermobility Spectrum Disorder alongside low back pain, fibromyalgia, and whiplash-associated disorder.
Fibromyalgia patients (n=5,640) made up the largest single diagnostic subgroup within the non-neuropathic comparison cohort in this registry study.
The proportion of men was significantly higher in the chronic neuropathic pain group than in the chronic non-neuropathic pain group.

At baseline, the neuropathic pain group reported significantly more physician visits, higher age, shorter pain duration, and less spatial spreading of pain (Pain Region Index) than the non-neuropathic group, though effect sizes for these differences were mostly small.
Roughly equal proportions of neuropathic (43%) and non-neuropathic (44%) chronic pain patients went on to participate in interdisciplinary pain rehabilitation (IPRP) after baseline assessment.
Immediately after IPRP, overall multivariate improvement (MIS) did not differ significantly between neuropathic and non-neuropathic pain groups.

At 12-month follow-up, the neuropathic pain group showed statistically significantly better overall multivariate improvement (MIS) than the non-neuropathic group, though the effect size was clinically insignificant.

A significantly higher proportion of neuropathic pain patients reported diminished pain (Change-pain) after IPRP compared to non-neuropathic patients, both immediately post-treatment and at 12 months.

There was no significant difference between neuropathic and non-neuropathic groups in self-reported improvement in ability to cope with life situations after IPRP, with over 75% of both groups reporting improvement.

Comparing baseline to immediately post-IPRP, both neuropathic and non-neuropathic groups showed significant within-group improvement in nearly all 22 mandatory outcome variables, with moderate effect sizes for pain severity, bodily pain, and vitality.

At 12-month follow-up, 21 of 22 mandatory outcome variables showed significant within-group improvement in both groups relative to baseline, with moderate effect sizes for pain severity, pain interference, and bodily pain, and additionally NRS pain and EQ-5D in the neuropathic group.
Perceived punishing responses from significant others (MPI-punish) did not change significantly after IPRP in either the neuropathic or non-neuropathic pain group, at either follow-up point.
The already female-skewed proportion of patients further increased among those who actually participated in IPRP compared to those merely assessed at baseline, in both diagnostic groups.

Non-neuropathic pain patients reported a longer latency (~2 years) from pain onset to development of persistent pain compared to neuropathic pain patients (~1 year), suggesting a different trajectory toward chronicity.
Patients with chronic neuropathic pain reported significantly less spatial spreading of pain (Pain Region Index) than patients with chronic non-neuropathic pain, with a moderate effect size.
Long COVID (≥1 residual symptom >1 month post-onset) occurred in 29.6% of the SARS-CoV-2 positive group compared to only 6% of the symptomatic SARS-CoV-2 negative control group.
Age over 50 years was associated with more than twice the odds of developing long COVID compared to individuals aged 15-30.
Having more than five symptoms during the acute phase of COVID-19 was associated with a substantially higher likelihood of developing long COVID.
Female sex showed a trend toward higher odds of long COVID, though the confidence interval crossed unity.
The most frequently reported residual symptoms among long COVID cases were fatigue, olfactory disorder, myalgia, gustatory disorder, and headache, all of which had started during the acute phase.
Among long COVID patients assessed with EQ-5D-3L, over half reported alteration in at least one quality-of-life dimension, with pain and depression the most commonly affected domains.

Long COVID symptoms showed strong co-occurrence patterns, with fatigue frequently co-reported alongside gustatory dysfunction, anorexia, dysphonia, chest pain, headache, breathlessness, or myalgia, and gustatory dysfunction strongly linked to olfactory dysfunction.

Hospitalisation rates were similar between patients who developed long COVID and those who recovered, suggesting hospitalisation was not a major driver of long COVID in this mostly mild-disease cohort.
Using the WHO's stricter three-month case definition, long COVID prevalence was estimated at 31.5% among COVID-19 cases followed to that timepoint versus 7.4% in non-COVID-19 controls.
Personal history of any cancer was not significantly different between MSA patients and matched controls.
Family history of cancer in parents did not differ significantly between MSA cases and controls.
Family history of cancer in siblings did not differ significantly between MSA cases and controls.
Personal history of breast cancer among female MSA cases was not significantly different from female controls.
Age-adjusted breast cancer incidence rates in MSA and controls were both lower than, and not significantly different from, US population incidence data.

In male ME/CFS patients, 118 genes were differentially expressed between maximal exertion and baseline (36 overexpressed, 72 underexpressed), whereas neither male healthy controls nor previously-reported female ME/CFS patients showed DEGs meeting significance criteria at this comparison.

Functional pathway analysis showed that the IL-12 signaling pathway was significantly affected in male ME/CFS patients between maximal exertion and baseline, a change also seen in female healthy controls but not in female ME/CFS patients.
Male ME/CFS patients showed significant activation of pathways related to positive regulation of response to external stimulus after exercise, a change not seen in female ME/CFS patients.

NK-cell-mediated cytotoxicity pathways and KIR3DL1 expression changes were significantly affected in male ME/CFS patients after exercise, suggesting dysfunction of granule-dependent and -independent NK cytotoxic pathways.

Male ME/CFS patients had a significant decrease in naive CD4+ T cells and a significant increase in NK cells (by CIBERSORTx-estimated abundance) between baseline and maximal exertion, mirroring the pattern previously seen in female healthy controls.
Male healthy controls showed no differentially expressed genes meeting significance criteria between maximal exertion and baseline, unlike male ME/CFS patients.

Genes encoding immunoglobulin/chemokine receptors and immune signaling molecules, including KIR3DL1 (referred to in text as KRI3DL2), CD160 and CCL4, were upregulated in male ME/CFS patients in response to exertion.
Genes involved in DNA transcription into RNA, including LINC00342, POLR2J4 and PRR12, were downregulated in male ME/CFS patients between baseline and maximal exertion.

Transcriptional regulation of granulopoiesis was the most significantly different pathway between male and female healthy controls during recovery from exercise, consistent with a greater increase in eosinophil abundance seen only in male HCs.

Regulation of IL-1β production was significantly more affected in male ME/CFS patients than female ME/CFS patients during recovery from exercise (T2 vs T1), a cytokine previously reported as elevated and discriminatory for PEM in ME/CFS.

Female ME/CFS patients showed significantly more alteration in herpes simplex virus 1 infection-related gene pathways than male ME/CFS patients during recovery from exercise (T2 vs T1), suggesting a sex-specific interaction with herpesviruses.

Female ME/CFS patients showed significant transcriptomic alterations in NF-κB signaling compared with male ME/CFS patients during recovery from exercise, consistent with prior reports of elevated NF-κB protein in ME/CFS PBMCs.

Females with ME/CFS had significantly altered cellular response to stress pathways compared with males with ME/CFS during recovery from exercise, potentially reflecting impaired antioxidant/redox defenses previously reported in ME/CFS.

Male ME/CFS patients had the most significant enrichment of the PDGFRB pathway when comparing baseline to 4-hours-post-exercise gene expression, a pathway implicated in NK cell inhibition and pro-inflammatory macrophage/lymphocyte phenotypes.

Female ME/CFS patients showed distinct enrichment of IL-10 signaling pathways when comparing baseline to 4-hours-post-exercise, which the authors interpret as possible resistance to IL-10's anti-inflammatory action.

Female ME/CFS patients showed unique enrichment of ferroptosis-related pathways when comparing baseline to 4-hours-post-exercise gene expression, which the authors link to mitochondrial dysfunction and lipid peroxidation reported in ME/CFS.

During recovery from exercise (T2 vs T1), male ME/CFS patients downregulated genes involved in metabolic reprogramming of immune cells (SLC7A5, CREM) while upregulating genes related to immune cell infiltration and survival (GIMAP8, GIMAP5, GIMAP4).

Unlike females with ME/CFS (who had significantly worse bodily pain than female HCs), male ME/CFS patients showed no significant difference from male HCs on the SF-36 bodily pain domain, paralleling the shared IL-12 pathway regulation seen in male ME/CFS and female HCs.

Immune cell-type abundance shifts during recovery from exercise (T2 vs T1) differed markedly by sex and disease status: female HCs decreased memory B cells, CD8+ T cells, NK cells and eosinophils while increasing naive/memory CD4+ T cells and activated mast cells; male HCs increased CD8+ T cells, NK cells, dendritic cells and eosinophils while decreasing naive CD4+ T cells; male ME/CFS patients decreased NK cells, dendritic cells and eosinophils while increasing naive CD4+ T cells, similar to female ME/CFS patients.
Approximately 90 percent of DEGs identified by RNA-Seq across all comparisons were validated using an orthogonal Nanostring nCounter panel, supporting the reliability of the transcriptomic findings.

Adolescents with ME/CFS reported greater fatigue and pain and poorer sleep quality, and performed worse on cognitive measures of processing speed and sustained attention, compared with healthy controls.
White matter fiber cross section of the left inferior longitudinal fasciculus was greater in ME/CFS adolescents than controls, but this difference did not survive correction for intracranial volume.

No significant group differences were found between ME/CFS adolescents and controls across a broad range of white and gray matter macrostructural and microstructural measures (volume, cortical thickness, fractional anisotropy, diffusivity metrics, neurite dispersion/density, fiber density and cross section).
The proinflammatory cytokine IL-8 is overexpressed in people with both CFS and MS.
Global immunologic activation patterns in CFS patients differed from those seen in MS patients and healthy controls when comparing stimulated and unstimulated peripheral blood mononuclear cells.
A study found that 71% of ME/CFS patients consulted more than four doctors before an accurate diagnosis, and 63% searched for a diagnosis for more than two years.
95% of women who sought medical help for CFS reported feeling lonely, and CFS patients experienced 66% more physician-caused illness than a general medical patient group.

A study on the impact of ME/CFS on life found a mean health status score of 33.8 on a 0-100 Visual Analogue Scale, with standard activity performance, pain, mobility, and self-care most impacted, and anxiety least affected.

Parasympathetic and sympathetic nervous system activity measures are abnormal in ME/CFS patients, with common cardiovascular problems including neurally mediated hypotension, orthostatic intolerance, and POTS.
Replicable findings in ME/CFS include increased sympathetic activity at rest and decreased vagal modulation.

Attenuated cardiac sympathetic reactivity, shown by diminished heart rate responses, was observed in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy individuals and could not be explained by deconditioning or inactivity.
An activity-pacing self-management (APSM) intervention improved the ability of women with CFS to engage in preferred activities of daily living.
Multiple investigations on ME/CFS have found elevated levels of the key proinflammatory cytokines TNF and IL-1.

The long-held belief that people with ME/CFS have an overactive Th2 immune system has been called into question, as only some patients show a balance of proinflammatory and anti-inflammatory cytokines, unlike the majority.

CFS patients have decreased cerebral perfusion throughout the brain, especially in the brainstem, as measured by SPECT, and SPECT abnormalities are more frequently detected than MRI abnormalities in ME/CFS.

A significant reduction in brainstem hypoperfusion and a positive correlation between neurocognitive impairments and reduced frontal blood flow was observed in ME/CFS patients compared with healthy counterparts.
FDG-PET imaging has shown widespread hypometabolism of glucose in the brain of CFS patients.

Voxel-based morphometry MRI has found gray matter volume loss in individuals with ME/CFS, with minimal connection to disease severity or patient age; subcortical white matter hyperintensities have also been repeatedly documented.

Proton MRS found considerably lower N-acetyl aspartate levels in the hippocampus of ME/CFS patients, along with higher choline signaling in the basal ganglia and a significant choline/creatine signal in the occipital brain.
Blood levels of proinflammatory cytokines IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-alpha were elevated in CFS patients, indicating an inflammatory role in disease pathophysiology.
Oxidative stress markers malondialdehyde (MDA) and protein carbonyls were found to be elevated in CFS patients compared to healthy counterparts.

Graded exercise therapy (GET) can improve fatigue and physical function in CFS individuals per a recent review, but it is controversial with reports of adverse effects, and careful monitoring/individualized plans are emphasized.
Fatigue is frequent in both MS and ME/CFS but differs in onset pattern, severity, and treatment response; fatigue was reported as a significant problem in 80% of MS individuals in one study.
Pooled analysis of nine datasets from seven studies found significantly lower serum acylcarnitine levels in ME/CFS/SEID patients compared with healthy controls.
Across the nine collected datasets, the majority of studies showed no significant difference in serum total carnitine levels between ME/CFS/SEID patients and healthy controls.
Similarly, the majority of studies showed no significant difference in serum free carnitine levels between ME/CFS/SEID patients and healthy controls.
The authors hypothesize that low serum acylcarnitine levels in ME/CFS/SEID may result from an impaired mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation cascade caused by viral infections, including COVID-19.
A cited prior study by Kuratsune et al. found lower acylcarnitine levels in ME/CFS/SEID patients that may correlate with fatigue severity.
Funnel plot analysis of the studies comparing serum acylcarnitine levels showed no visually apparent publication bias.
A meta-analysis of 57 studies covering over 250,000 people found that 43% of people had ongoing symptoms impairing functional mobility at least 6 months after acute COVID-19.
A study of nearly 100,000 COVID cases vs matched never-infected controls found over 40% of cases had persistent symptoms and impairment across daily activities at 18 months.

A study of ~6,000 hospitalized COVID patients vs uninfected matched controls found persistent symptoms in approximately 30% of cases at least 2 years after acute infection, much more often than in uninfected controls.
Among people with persistent debilitating symptoms following acute COVID-19, an estimated 13-45% meet the National Academy of Medicine case definition for ME/CFS.

In a community outbreak, 6% of 2,500 people developed a sudden infectious-like illness followed by at least 5 months of a cyclic debilitating illness with fatigue, objectively confirmed cognitive impairment, and pain.
Functional impairment in ME/CFS may be greater than in congestive heart failure and major depression, and greater than in Long COVID.
Post-exertional malaise, the cardinal symptom of ME/CFS, is reported by the vast majority of people with Long COVID.

A meta-analysis-informed symptom comparison found decreased smell/taste, rash and hair loss are frequent in Long COVID but rare in ME/CFS, while painful lymph nodes, chemical sensitivities and tinnitus are frequent in ME/CFS but rare in Long COVID.
Multi-organ MRI in Long COVID patients and non-symptomatic post-COVID subjects showed abnormalities in many organs up to 1 year post-infection, but correlation with persistent symptoms was poor.
In both illnesses there is initial activation of neuroendocrine axes and cytokine production, followed after several years by an apparent exhaustion of neuroendocrine and immunologic activity.
Impaired attention and information processing speed are the most consistently observed cognitive abnormalities in both ME/CFS and Long COVID.
One study estimated that the objective cognitive deficit measured in Long COVID was equivalent to 10 years of aging.

A population-based longitudinal study with pre- and post-pandemic MRI and cognitive testing found that people who developed COVID-19 (even without hospitalization) had greater reduction in gray matter thickness, global brain size, and greater cognitive decline than matched uninfected controls.
Both ME/CFS and Long COVID show reduced cerebral blood flow, likely related to autonomic dysfunction and possibly reduced blood volume.
There appears to be down-regulation of activity in several hypothalamic-pituitary axes in ME/CFS, with some similar reports in Long COVID.
Both illnesses show autonomic 'dyshomeostasis' with poor sympathetic-parasympathetic balance, favoring sympathetic dominance.
Objective autonomic dysfunction is common in the first 6-12 months following acute COVID-19 but becomes less common by 24 months, compared with matched controls without COVID-19.
Autonomic dysfunction in both illnesses could be caused by antibodies directed at autonomic receptors and biopsy-documented small-fiber neuropathy.
The ability to generate energy (ATP) from fatty acids, amino acids, glucose and oxygen is impaired in ME/CFS, with similar evidence emerging in Long COVID.
Beyond energy metabolic deficits, both illnesses show evidence of a systemic hypometabolic state, redox balance abnormalities, and kynurenine pathway abnormalities.

Diminished exercise capacity (especially on repeat exercise testing 24h after the first), reduced ventilatory efficiency, and endothelial dysfunction (more prominent in Long COVID but also present in ME/CFS) are the best-documented cardiopulmonary abnormalities.
Differences in frequency of several reactivated herpesviruses and in the gut microbiome distinguish ME/CFS and Long COVID patients from comparison/control groups.
A meta-analysis estimated the prevalence of chronic fatigue syndrome at 0.68% (95% CI 0.48-0.97).
Electron microscopy showed hippocampal neurons in CFS model rats had shrinkage, membrane invagination, and apoptosome formation.
Neuropathological autopsy of a CFS patient revealed focal white matter loss, bead-like axonal changes, atypical neurons, and neurofibrillary tangles in frontal cortex, thalamus, and basal ganglia.
Acupuncture at GV20, ST36, SP6 significantly improved hippocampal neuron morphology and nuclear structure clarity in CFS model rats compared to untreated model rats.
Electroacupuncture targeting head acupoints improved hippocampal/hypothalamic neuron morphology and reduced inflammatory infiltration in CFS model rats.
Acupuncture at GV20, HT7, houssanli, BL20, BL18, BL23 significantly decreased previously elevated hippocampal neuron apoptosis in CFS rats.
Lloyd et al. (1991) found increased levels of IFN-α in the cerebrospinal fluid of patients with CFS.

Natelson et al. found decreased CSF GM-CSF and increased IL-10 in CFS patients, but a subsequent study found an opposite result of significantly reduced IL-10, illustrating inconsistent findings across studies.
Hornig et al. described increased CSF CCL11 and CXCL10 levels along with dysregulation of IL-1 signaling in CFS patients.

Electroacupuncture at GV20, emotional area I, and bilateral sensory areas significantly reduced NF-κB p65 and COX-2 protein levels in the hippocampus and hypothalamus of CFS rats compared to the model group.

Mongolian warm acupuncture on dǐnghuì and xīnxué markedly reduced IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α levels in the hippocampus and hypothalamus of CFS rats, likely through inhibiting hippocampal Caspase-3 activation.
Electroacupuncture using head acupoints selected by brain structural zones reduced mRNA expression and protein levels of TGF-β1 and Smad4 in the hippocampus and hypothalamus of CFS model rats.
Oxidative and nitrosative stress-induced injuries to lipid, protein, and DNA were accelerated, and antioxidative defense was reduced in CFS patients.
Acupuncture at GV20, ST36, SP6 increased brain superoxide dismutase (SOD) activity and lowered maleic dialdehyde (MDA) concentration in CFS model rats relative to the model group.
CFS model rats showed significantly increased iNOS and MDA and significantly decreased SOD and GSH-Px activities in the hippocampus, which Mongolian warm acupuncture obviously regulated.
Electroacupuncture combinations (GV20+ST36+LR3 or ST36+BL23/back-shu points) regulated hypothalamic CRH mRNA and β-endorphin levels, and reduced CRH, GnRH, and TRH levels in CFS rats.

Acupuncture altered neurotransmitter levels including 5-HT, norepinephrine, dopamine, and neuropeptide Y in CFS model rats, though results varied across studies due to differing modeling, acupoint selection, and manipulation methods.

Acupuncture at GV20, HT7, houssanli, BL20, BL18, BL23 regulated CFS-related sleep disorder by stimulating basal forebrain adenosine release acting on A1 receptors in the striatum/ventrolateral preoptic hypothalamus and A2A receptors in striatum/nucleus accumbens.

Acupuncture activated the 5-HT/Gnai1/PLC pathway by upregulating hippocampal miR-184 expression and inhibited Caspase-3 protein expression, reducing neuronal apoptosis and improving cognitive dysfunction in CFS rats.

Acupuncture at BL18, BL20, BL23 given during the Mao period upregulated Per1 and Per2 mRNA/protein expression in the suprachiasmatic nucleus of male Syrian hamsters with CFS, delaying locomotor activity onset and regulating circadian rhythm.

MRI studies (voxel/surface-based morphometry, arterial spin labeling, BOLD-fMRI, MRS) found gray and white matter reduction, decreased cerebral blood flow, abnormal functional connectivity, and metabolite disorders in the brains of CFS patients.

PET imaging studies showed significantly decreased glucose metabolism in specific brain areas along with neuroinflammatory response and disordered serotonergic, cholinergic, glutamatergic, and GABAergic neurotransmitter metabolism in CFS patients.

In a BOLD-fMRI/MRS study, CFS patients showed significantly worse CIS, SPHERE, and SF-36 scores than healthy subjects, along with reduced activity in visual/occipital brain regions and altered activity in temporal/parietal/frontal regions during a cognitive task, plus lower GPC+PCh levels in the right occipital lobe.

After 4 weeks (16 sessions) of acupuncture at GV20, BL18, BL23, HT7, ST36, CFS patients showed lower CIS (total, fatigue, concentration, motivation, activity) and SPHERE scores, higher SF-36 physical/psychological/pain/vitality/emotional scores, enhanced activation in cognitive-related brain regions during PVSAT, and increased right occipital GPC+PCh and NAA+NAAG levels.
A follow-up study by Li with an increased sample size, applying only MRS after the same acupuncture protocol, reached similar conclusions to the earlier Tang study.

A survey found 90% of CFS patients in Scotland tried complementary/alternative therapies, with acupuncture the most common treatment for CFS-related pain and a reported effective rate of 60%, differing from Chinese studies possibly due to sample size and selection bias.
A scoping review of 16 studies and 12 guidelines found that most did not include any psychiatric involvement in the diagnosis or treatment of paediatric chronic fatigue syndrome.

When psychiatry was mentioned in the reviewed literature, it was used interchangeably with psychological interventions or discussed only in the context of treating distinct psychiatric comorbidities and suicidal ideation.

The authors concluded that the role of psychiatry in the diagnosis and treatment of pCFS is poorly defined and that future research is needed to clarify how psychiatrists can contribute to patient care.

The Hindi-translated version of the International Consensus Criteria (ICC-H) showed no significant difference in individual component and global scores compared to the original English version (ICC-E) administered 4 weeks later.
Individual item scores and global scores of the Hindi and English questionnaires were highly correlated with each other.

The paper notes significant symptom overlap between long COVID and myalgic encephalomyelitis, with fatigue as a major shared component, suggesting a shared pathophysiology potentially involving neuroimmune exhaustion.

A single latent factor (principal component) was extracted from pure depression, pure anxiety, and physiosomatic symptom scores, indicating these domains are interrelated expressions of a shared physio-affective phenome of Long COVID.
Duration of the acute infectious phase was significantly longer in severe Long COVID than in mild Long COVID, which in turn was longer than in controls.
Peak body temperature (PBT) during acute infection was significantly higher, and SpO2 significantly lower, in the severe Long COVID group compared with mild Long COVID and controls.
Serum CRP and composite inflammation/IR scores were significantly higher in severe Long COVID compared with mild Long COVID and controls, with the lowest values in controls.
Fasting blood glucose was significantly higher in severe Long COVID compared with controls.
Serum insulin levels were higher in Long COVID patients than in controls.
Serum tryptophan was significantly lower in the severe Long COVID group compared with the mild Long COVID group.
The kynurenine/tryptophan (KYN/TRY) ratio composite was higher in severe Long COVID than in both mild Long COVID and controls, suggesting mildly increased IDO activity.
Individual TRYCATs (KYN, KA, QA, 3-HK) and their composite score did not significantly differ between severe Long COVID, mild Long COVID, and control groups.
Tryptophan was inversely, and the KYN/TRY ratio positively, associated with Fibro-Fatigue, pure anxiety, and physiosomatic symptoms, but not with pure depression.
The severity of acute-phase infection (z PBT − z SpO2) was significantly correlated with all four physio-affective symptom domains as well as with z KYN/TRY and inflammation/IR composites.
Duration of the acute infectious phase correlated significantly with Fibro-Fatigue, pure anxiety, physiosomatic symptoms, and acute-phase severity (z PBT − z SpO2).

Regression analyses showed that CRP, insulin resistance (IR), and the KYN/TRY ratio jointly predicted 25.0% of the variance in Fibro-Fatigue symptoms, and when acute-phase biomarkers (PBT, SpO2, duration) were added, this rose to 32.1%.
CRP and insulin resistance predicted 20.6% of the variance in cognitive deficit scores; adding PBT raised this to 27.0%.
CRP, KYN/TRY, and IR predicted 23.9% of the variance in insomnia scores; adding acute-phase PBT-SpO2 explained a similar 23.9% via CRP and z PBT-SpO2.
KYN/TRY ratio and CRP predicted 23.9% of variance in pure anxiety; with acute/chronic biomarkers combined (KYN/TRY, CRP, duration, BMI) this rose to 36.5%.
CRP, IR, KYN/TRY, and sex predicted 41.2% of the variance in pure depression scores; with acute-phase biomarkers, CRP and z PBT-SpO2 explained 37.0%.
CRP, KYN/TRY, IR, and age explained 33.6% of variance in physiosomatic symptoms; with acute-phase biomarkers added (CRP, PBT+duration-SpO2, KYN/TRY) this rose to 41.1%.

Age and a composite of CRP+KYN/TRY+IR explained 41.0% of variance in the physio-affective phenome; combining acute-phase biomarkers (CRP, PBT+duration-SpO2, KYN/TRY) increased explained variance to 42.8%.

Two-step cluster analysis identified a distinct endophenotypic subgroup of severe Long COVID characterized by very low acute-phase SpO2, high kynurenine, very low tryptophan (high KYN/TRY ratio), very high CRP, moderate IR increases, and the highest ratings on all symptom domains.
Approximately 31.1% of COVID-19 patients showed moderate-to-severe depressive symptoms consistent with major depression using a BDI-II cutoff of 23.
Mean HAMD, HAMA, and Fibro-Fatigue scores in the severe Long COVID group indicated moderate-to-severe anxiety and mild chronic fatigue syndrome persisting 3-12 months after acute infection.
The vast majority (98%) of survey respondents with hEDS/G-HSD reported experiencing pain.
Pain most commonly localized to the neck, lower back, upper back, knees, shoulders, and hips.

About 80% of participants reported fatigue, joint hypermobility, joint instability, interference with daily activities, gastrointestinal problems, orthostatic hypotension, muscle weakness, and emotional distress.
About 60% of respondents reported walking issues, balance issues, and reduced joint proprioception.
Nearly 40% of participants reported pelvic floor dysfunction and cardiovascular problems.
Participants with hEDS reported slightly more pain days per week on average than those with G-HSD.
Participants reported low exercise frequency (none to less than three times per week) and no physical therapy treatment.
Joint hypermobility is more prevalent in females than males and is also more common in children and adolescents.
Rates of joint hypermobility vary by ethnicity, being higher in Inuit, African and Asian populations and lower in Europe and Australasia.
