The 2017 International Classification defines 13 distinct clinical EDS subtypes caused by deleterious variants in 19 different genes.
Hypermobile EDS (hEDS) is the only EDS subtype that remains without a known molecular basis or causative gene, and is diagnosed purely clinically.
A fourteenth EDS type resembling classic EDS but with autosomal recessive inheritance was described in association with biallelic AEBP1 variants.
Specific variants in COL1A1 and COL1A2 are associated with an osteogenesis imperfecta/EDS overlap phenotype, proposed as a possible fifteenth EDS type (COL1-related overlap disorder).
A prior review found that nociceptive, neuropathic, and nociplastic pain all contribute to reduced quality of life in people with EDS (mainly hEDS) and HSD.

Neuropathic pain in hEDS/HSD may progressively superimpose on nociceptive pain via mechanisms including nerve entrapment, compression, peripheral neuropathies, and small fibre neuropathy, though none fully explain the observed neuropathic features.
In more advanced JHM-related pain phenotypes, pain becomes widespread and chronic with allodynia and hyperalgesia, showing clear overlap with fibromyalgia.

Advanced JHM-related dysfunctional phenotypes are complicated by non-MSK pain (headache, abdominal pain, dyspareunia) and comorbidities including depression, anxiety, and gastrointestinal functional disorders.
Preliminary data indicate that the separation between HSD and hEDS is not simply a matter of severity of the phenotype.

Extra-musculoskeletal functional symptoms including psychological distress, psychiatric comorbidities, developmental coordination disorders, functional gastrointestinal symptoms, and orthostatic intolerance likely determine patient needs in HSD/hEDS more than pain severity alone.
Spontaneous arterial ruptures are a major feature of vascular EDS but can also occur, at lower rates, in other EDS clinical subtypes.
Preliminary genotype-phenotype correlations suggest that the severity of cardiovascular involvement in vascular EDS varies according to the specific mutation type.
Serum immunoassay for tenascin X is a useful investigation supporting molecular testing in TNXB-related classic-like EDS.

The Beighton score has reliability concerns for recognizing generalized joint hypermobility in real-world practice because it does not account for laterality, acquired limitations, ethnicity, or sex differences.
Joint hypermobility is common in the general population and is usually a benign trait without significant health-related manifestations.
Seminal work by Voermans and colleagues identified a high rate of chronic musculoskeletal and systemic symptoms in individuals with EDS, significantly impacting quality of life.
The patient was genetically diagnosed with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome based on a heterozygous mutation in the COL3A1 gene, which encodes type III collagen.
Administration of 400 mg celiprolol hydrochloride improved the patient's easy bruising symptoms and resolved her iron deficiency anemia, allowing discontinuation of iron supplementation.
Serum hemoglobin, iron, and ferritin levels improved more with celiprolol hydrochloride administration than with prior iron supplementation alone.

Over a 7-year follow-up period following transcatheter arterial embolization and celiprolol initiation, the patient experienced no cardiac or vascular events, with stable arterial morphology and normal ankle-brachial index.

Emergent transcatheter arterial embolization using a liquid embolic agent (NBCA and iodized oil) successfully resolved a ruptured iliolumbar artery aneurysm causing retroperitoneal hemorrhage in this vEDS patient, without complications.

The patient's clinical presentation included nonspecific minor features of vEDS (scoliosis, clubfoot, easy bruising, iron deficiency anemia) alongside major vascular criteria (arterial dissection and aneurysm rupture), and a family history of vascular events (carotid cavernous fistula, myocardial infarction, aortic dissection) despite no prior family diagnosis of vEDS.

Loss-of-function mutation in CHST14, encoding dermatan 4-O-sulfotransferase 1, causes musculocontractural EDS via defective collagen fiber assembly through decorin, resulting from dermatan sulfate deficiency.

Among 58 patients with classical (typical, mild), hypermobile, or vascular EDS, 52% had clinical/radiographic scoliosis, with the highest rate in classical (typical) EDS (54%), followed by vascular (33%), hypermobile (30%), and classical (mild) (11%) types.
Vertebral fractures were significantly more common in a large EDS cohort (predominantly hypermobile and classical types) compared with control subjects.
T1 (chondroitin sulfate N-acetylgalactosaminyltransferase-1) knockout mice exhibiting EDS-like connective tissue defects all developed severe scoliosis.
Nell1-deficient mouse models showed narrowing of the disc space and spinal curve alterations, implicating Nell1 in spinal deformity development.

In a series of 12 mcEDS patients, characteristic spinal abnormalities included cervical vertebral body deformity (83%), scoliosis (67%), cervical kyphosis (50%), advanced kyphosis at the thoracolumbar transition (42%), and atlantoaxial subluxation (17%); three patients (25%) had severe thoracolumbar kyphosis (>50°).
Bone tissue observation and morphometry in mcEDS patients revealed no calcification disorder but reduced bone metabolic turnover.

Two serious vascular complications (segmental artery avulsion with iliac artery/vein rupture; superior gluteal artery avulsion) occurred among 5 kyphoscoliotic (type VI) EDS patients undergoing spinal deformity surgery.
Vogel et al. reported three neurological complications (two resulting in permanent paraplegia) and one vascular complication during spinal deformity surgery in EDS type VI patients.
In a study by Yang et al., all three EDS patients undergoing spinal deformity surgery displayed massive intraoperative bleeding, ranging from 600 mL to 6 L.

Case 1 (16-year-old female with mcEDS and severe scoliosis/kyphosis) underwent posterior spinal corrective fusion (T10-L4), achieving 76% coronal curve correction (33° to 8°) and 19% kyphosis correction (57° to 46°), with 1550 g blood loss and no acute neurovascular complications, but later developed a chronic infected screw fistula and progressive kyphosis recurrence over 8.8 years.

Case 2 (12-year-old male with mcEDS) underwent staged posterior spinal corrective fusion (T4-L3) with preoperative desmopressin to prevent hematoma, achieving 53% coronal curve correction and 79% kyphosis correction, with improved back pain (VAS 0/100) and walking ability sustained at 2.6-year follow-up.

Case 3 (19-year-old female with mcEDS) underwent posterior spinal corrective fusion (T4-L4) with preoperative desmopressin, achieving 69% coronal curve correction and 78% kyphosis correction, with resolved back pain (VAS 0/100) and improved walking tolerance (from 50 m with crutches preoperatively to 30 minutes unaided at 1-year follow-up).
Mean total intraoperative blood loss in the three reported mcEDS surgical cases (2433 g) was substantially higher than reported blood loss for corrective surgery in idiopathic scoliosis patients.
Preoperative intranasal 1-desamino-8-D-arginine vasopressin (desmopressin) was administered in mcEDS surgical cases to help prevent large subcutaneous hematomas.

No reports of successful orthotic (bracing) therapy for spinal deformity in EDS patients were identified, in contrast to more established bracing evidence in idiopathic scoliosis and other syndromic scolioses.
In spondylodysplastic EDS, scoliosis or kyphoscoliosis was much more common in B3GALT6-deficient patients (68%) than in B4GALT7-deficient patients (14%).

A 41-year-old woman with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome developed over 100 dermatomyofibromas over several years, representing a uniquely widespread presentation compared to only six prior reports of multiple dermatomyofibromas.

In vitro and transcriptomic studies show fibroblasts from hypermobile EDS patients have a significantly increased propensity for fibroblast-to-myofibroblast transition, which the authors propose could predispose to dermatomyofibroma formation.
The increased fibroblast-to-myofibroblast transition seen in hypermobile EDS fibroblasts is not observed in classical or vascular EDS.

Immunohistochemistry of biopsied lesions showed weak smooth muscle actin positivity and focal factor XIIIa positivity in lesional cells, with negative staining for Sox-10 and desmin, confirming the diagnosis of dermatomyofibroma.

Topical corticosteroid and calcineurin inhibitor treatments (triamcinolone, clobetasol, pimecrolimus, intralesional triamcinolone) provided only modest success in managing the patient's dermatomyofibroma lesions.

Literature indicates simple excision is highly effective at preventing recurrence of solitary dermatomyofibroma lesions, even without clear margins, but this approach was impractical for this patient due to the size and widespread distribution of lesions.

A 3-year-old male with clinical features of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome developed a growing skull fracture in the frontal bone following a crib fall, reported as the first such association in the literature.
Intraoperative findings revealed marked fragility of the dura mater, which the authors attribute to the patient's underlying Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
The growing skull fracture was surgically treated with duraplasty and cranioplasty using an autologous graft, complicated by the fragility of the EDS-affected dura mater.
A novel homozygous splice acceptor site variant in COL12A1 (c.395-1G>A) at exon 6 causes in-frame skipping of exon 6 and results in autosomal recessive myopathic Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

The patient's milder clinical manifestations compared with previously reported mEDS patients may be explained by the variant's location within the region encoding the first von Willebrand factor A (VWA) domain, which affects only the long isoform of collagen XII, unlike prior variants that disrupted both long and short isoforms.

This is the second reported family with autosomal recessive inheritance of myopathic EDS due to COL12A1 variants, among 15 families (24 patients) previously reported, most of which were autosomal dominant.
Among over 1.15 million patients hospitalized with acute myocardial infarction, spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) was identified in 0.75% of cases.
Fibromuscular dysplasia was the strongest independent predictor of SCAD among AMI patients, with a markedly elevated odds ratio.
A diagnosis of Marfan syndrome or Ehlers-Danlos syndrome was an independent predictor of SCAD in patients presenting with AMI.
Polycystic ovarian syndrome was an independent predictor of SCAD in AMI patients.
Female gender was an independent predictor of SCAD among patients with AMI.
Aortic aneurysm was an independent, though weaker, predictor of SCAD in AMI patients.
The derived SCAD risk score, combining fibromuscular dysplasia, Marfan/EDS, PCOS, female gender, and aortic aneurysm, showed only modest discrimination in both derivation and validation cohorts.
Nearly a third of individuals with classical EDS reported clinically relevant average pain intensity (VAS ≥5/10) over the past month.
Individuals with cEDS reported worse health-related quality of life compared with controls.
The cEDS group showed higher detection thresholds for vibration stimuli at the lower limb, indicating hypoesthesia (reduced vibration sensitivity).
cEDS patients had reduced thermal sensitivity with significantly more paradoxical thermal sensations compared with controls.
cEDS patients showed hyperalgesia with lower pain thresholds to mechanical (pressure) stimuli at both the upper and lower limbs compared with controls.
cEDS patients showed lower pain thresholds to cold stimulation at the lower limb compared with controls, indicating cold hyperalgesia.
Using a parallel conditioned pain modulation paradigm, the cEDS group showed significantly smaller antinociceptive responses than controls, suggestive of impaired endogenous pain modulation.
Approximately 27% of toddlers born preterm met criteria for joint hypermobility using a Beighton score cut-off of 4 or more.
Among the five Beighton items, passive dorsiflexion of the ankle was the most frequently positive item in toddlers born preterm.
Proprioception cooperation rate and success rate did not differ between toddlers born preterm with and without joint hypermobility.
Cognitive developmental composite scores did not differ between toddlers born preterm with versus without joint hypermobility.
Language developmental composite scores did not differ significantly between toddlers born preterm with versus without joint hypermobility, though the p-value approached significance.
Motor developmental composite scores did not differ between toddlers born preterm with versus without joint hypermobility, contrasting with a prior study reporting an association.
No significant correlations were found among joint hypermobility, proprioception, and developmental functioning measures when examined pairwise in preterm toddlers.
Patients who expected complete recovery had increased odds of reporting an important improvement in physical shoulder symptoms after 16 weeks of exercise-based treatment.
Higher baseline self-efficacy appeared to be associated with greater improvement in shoulder function, shoulder pain, and quality of life following the exercise-based treatment.
Greater fear of movement appeared to be associated with increased shoulder pain and decreased quality of life after exercise-based treatment.
Longer symptom duration prior to treatment was associated with decreased quality of life after the 16-week exercise-based treatment.

The Arabic version of the Bristol Impact of Hypermobility (BIoH) questionnaire showed a very good, statistically significant negative correlation with the SF-12 total score, supporting its concurrent validity.

The Arabic BIoH showed a very good, statistically significant negative correlation with the SF-12 Physical Component Score (PCS), similar to the correlation found for the original English BIoH with SF-36 PCS.
The Arabic BIoH showed a good, statistically significant negative correlation with the SF-12 Mental Component Score (MCS), somewhat lower than its correlation with the physical component.
The Arabic BIoH demonstrated excellent test-retest reliability over a one-week interval in patients with stable health status.
The Arabic BIoH showed high internal consistency among its items.
The smallest detectable change (SDC) for the Arabic BIoH was calculated, representing the minimum change needed to indicate a real clinical difference beyond measurement error.

Among the 55 patients with hypermobility spectrum disorder recruited from orthopedic/physiotherapy clinics, the majority had generalized HSD, with smaller proportions having localized or peripheral HSD.

The study sample was predominantly female, consistent with the higher reported prevalence of HSD in women, and the reliability sub-sample was exclusively female, which the authors note may limit generalizability to men.
Meta-analysis of two studies estimated the pooled prevalence of dysphagia in adults with fibromyalgia to be 51.9%.
Meta-analysis of two studies estimated the pooled prevalence of GERD in adults with fibromyalgia to be 25.9%.
In a case-control study of 67 fibromyalgia patients, xerostomia was reported by the Xerostomia Questionnaire in 70.9% of participants.
Glossodynia (burning mouth/tongue pain) was reported in 32.83% of participants in a case-control study of fibromyalgia patients, and in the single participant of a separate case study.
Dysgeusia (taste disturbance) was reported in 34.32% of participants in a case-control study, and in the single participant of a separate case study.
Odynophagia (painful swallowing) was reported in the single participant of a fibromyalgia case study, the only study reporting this outcome.
A sensation of choking or bolus sticking in the pharyngeal region was reported by 48% of fibromyalgia/IBS patients in a retrospective cohort study examining GERD outcomes post-Nissen fundoplication.

No included studies reported data on aspiration/penetration on food, liquids, or secretions, impaired mastication, pain on chewing, fatigue on chewing, or unintentional weight loss in fibromyalgia patients.

The authors hypothesize that altered heart rate variability and autonomic dysfunction (sympathetic hyperactivation with decreased parasympathetic function), previously observed in fibromyalgia, GERD, and IBS, may amplify normally-occurring autonomic changes during swallowing and contribute to fibromyalgia-associated dysphagia.
Significant improvements in physical fitness tests were found in the majority of the included studies following combined training programs.
Combined training programs decreased the overall symptoms and impact of FM in most of the studies reviewed.
Lower limb muscle strength improved in three of the studies following combined training.
Among exercise modalities, aerobic and combined interventions produced the greatest reduction in FIQ scores, whereas flexibility-only interventions were not significant.
Exercise programs lasting 13-24 weeks with sessions of no more than 60 minutes were associated with greater improvements in pain relief.
Training protocols lasting up to 6 weeks did not generate greater benefits for pain threshold, FIQ, functional capacity, or muscle strength gains compared to longer programs.
Aerobic exercise combined with Tai Chi improved FIQ, pain threshold, anxiety/depression, and sleep quality more than aerobic exercise alone.
A 24-week Tai Chi plus aerobic exercise program improved FIQ impact more than a 12-week program of the same combination.
Combined aerobic and strength training produced greater improvements in concentric leg extension strength than aerobic or strength training alone.

In one study, high-intensity interval training (HIIT) plus strengthening/stretching and moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT) plus strengthening/stretching both improved FM effect, pain, functional capacity and QoL versus control, but HIIT was not superior to MICT and body composition improved only with MICT.
Combining muscle strengthening exercises with flexibility exercises improved pain threshold and quality of life.

Bidonde et al. found low-quality evidence for improvements in pain intensity, fatigue, stiffness and physical function with exercise, and moderate-quality evidence for withdrawals and health-related quality of life at intervention completion (6-24 weeks).
Aquatic exercise in warm water was reported to positively affect FM symptoms such as pain, anxiety and depression.
Exercise is proposed to increase serotonin and norepinephrine concentrations, improving mood and physical well-being and reducing pain via endogenous inhibitory pathways in FM patients.

Risk of bias assessment (PEDro scale) showed that all 13 included studies had weaknesses in blinding of participants and therapists, though none were classified as poor methodological quality overall.

In a mouse model of nociplastic pain, females were more easily induced into a nociplastic pain state than males, and pain mediation mechanisms differed by sex, with spinal microglia implicated in male mechanical hypersensitivity and afferent silencing reducing hypersensitivity in females.
A study in fibromyalgia patients reported a correlation between serum C-reactive protein level and pain severity.
Lower serum tryptophan and altered tryptophan-kynurenine metabolic pathway activity have been linked to neuroinflammation in nociplastic pain.
Serum BDNF concentration was reported to be lower in fibromyalgia patients, but the difference between nociplastic and nociceptive pain subgroups was not statistically significant.
An MRI-based study reported that treatment reversed brain changes previously caused by chronic low back pain.
Children and adolescents with nociplastic pain more often present with panic disorder and social phobia and report worse sleep quality compared to patients with other pain types.
In pediatric rheumatic disease, nociplastic pain is reported to have a stronger genetic component than in older individuals.
Type 1 complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS) is described as caused by nociplastic pain, with some sources terming it a 'nociplastic pain syndrome.'
In patients infected with HTLV-1, the virus was associated with greater intensity and distinct characteristics of nociplastic pain.
A Cochrane review concluded that NSAIDs cannot be regarded as useful for treating fibromyalgia.
A Cochrane review found no significant difference between selective and non-selective NSAIDs for low back pain.

In fibromyalgia, a weak opioid analgesic effect is proposed to result from disorganized endogenous opiate receptor signaling, high opioidergic tone, and MOR downregulation, so opioids may fail to modulate pain and can even exacerbate it.
TCAs were reported to be more effective at pain reduction than SNRIs in nociplastic pain, but carried a higher risk of adverse effects in older patients.
SNRIs were reported to have a positive effect on nociplastic pain, greater than NSAIDs, though clinical research findings have been contradictory and adverse effects should be considered.
Reports on gabapentinoids for nociplastic pain are mixed, with some studies showing relief and others showing no benefit.
Pregabalin is FDA-recommended for treating fibromyalgia.
Benzodiazepines and codeine were reported to increase the risk of prescription opioid misuse when used to treat nociplastic pain.
Ketamine has been reported to be effective for pain reduction in CRPS type 1, but its use is limited to CRPS and fibromyalgia and requires further research.
Vitamin B12 may provide pain-relief benefits as an auxiliary treatment for nociplastic pain.
Some studies have reported that naltrexone may relieve nociplastic pain.
Cannabis-based medicine has been reported to reduce pain severity in nociplastic pain but carries risks of adverse effects and addiction.
Pain catastrophizing, believed to contribute to nociplastic pain, has been shown to be a barrier to achieving remission in rheumatoid arthritis.
In a study of Achilles tendinopathy, the presence of nociplastic pain was not confirmed in the examined group.
A validated screening tool identified painful cold within 2 weeks after surgery as a strong predictor of the development of chronic postsurgical pain.
TLR4-mediated cytokine/chemokine release has been evaluated as an immunological mechanism contributing to nociplastic pain pathophysiology.

The rat grimace scale was reported to be able to predict the presence of nociplastic pain in reserpine-induced fibromyalgia-like rats, suggesting utility for translating intervention effects between animals and humans.
A study by McDonough et al. showed that spinal microglia can transmit nociplastic pain, with a sex-dependent mechanism emphasized.
In a mouse model (RIM6/ASI), the σ1R antagonist BD1063 provided longer-lasting pain relief than pregabalin.
SR 57227A was reported as a potential therapeutic agent for chronic pain conditions such as fibromyalgia in an animal model, without addictive potential.
A meta-analysis evaluating exercise treatments for chronic pain along the nociplastic pain continuum found exercise interventions to be a useful component of a tailored treatment approach.
Cannabis-based medicine has been evaluated for nociplastic pain, with some reports showing reduced pain severity but carrying risks of adverse effects and addiction.
Acetyl-L-carnitine has been reported as potentially beneficial in some diseases associated with nociplastic pain.
The role of polyunsaturated fatty acids in regulating pain has also been assessed in the context of nociplastic pain.
Pain catastrophizing, believed to contribute to nociplastic pain, has been shown to be a barrier to achieving disease remission in patients with rheumatoid arthritis.
In a study of Achilles tendinopathy, the presence of nociplastic pain was not confirmed in the examined patient group.
A validated screening tool identified painful cold sensation within 2 weeks after surgery as a strong predictor of chronic postsurgical pain development.
Toll-like receptor 4-mediated cytokine/chemokine release has been evaluated as part of an immunological mechanism contributing to nociplastic pain.
The rat grimace scale was reported to predict the presence of nociplastic pain in reserpine-induced fibromyalgia-like rats and may help translate therapeutic effects between animals and humans.
Postinjury stimulation of the wounded area was reported to cause conversion of pain into a nociplastic phenotype, with sex-dependent mechanisms implicated.
A study by McDonough et al. showed that spinal microglia can transmit nociplastic pain, with a sex-dependent mechanism emphasized.
In a mouse model, the sigma-1 receptor antagonist BD1063 provided longer-lasting pain relief in acidified saline injection-induced pain than pregabalin did in the reserpine-induced myalgia model.
SR 57227A, tested in an animal model, was reported as a potential therapeutic agent for chronic pain conditions such as fibromyalgia without addictive potential.
The efficacy of pregabalin, acetaminophen, and duloxetine for nociplastic pain has been evaluated in animal models.
PEA's mechanism of action involves mast cells and basophils and has demonstrated a neuroprotective effect on cerebellar granule cells, suggesting potential relevance to nociplastic pain treatment.
PEA has been shown to suppress inflammation, supporting its potential relevance to nociplastic pain conditions.
Vitamin B12 may provide pain relief effects useful as an auxiliary treatment for nociplastic pain.
The placebo effect is reported to play an important role in nociplastic pain outcomes.

Procedural treatments such as steroid injections for temporomandibular disorders, normal saline injections, transcranial direct current stimulation, and repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation have shown potential benefit but are reported as less effective than in other pain types.
Obesity has been identified as a risk factor for fibromyalgia.
The Central Sensitization Inventory (CSI) can indicate central sensitization as well as comorbidities per IASP criteria.
Some diagnostic scales and questionnaires used to assess nociplastic pain have been reported to have low accuracy.
Magnetic resonance imaging studies showed that treatment reversed brain changes caused by low back pain.
During incongruently cued high-pain anticipation, fibromyalgia patients showed reduced left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex activation compared to healthy controls.

Despite the actual pressure being lowered during incongruent high-pain cued trials, fibromyalgia patients continued to rate the subsequent painful stimuli as high, indicating a failure to update pain expectation.
During congruently cued low pain anticipation, fibromyalgia patients showed decreased right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex activation compared to healthy controls.

Fibromyalgia patients exhibited decreased functional connectivity between the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and primary somatosensory cortex/postcentral gyrus and supplementary motor area/midcingulate cortex during low pain anticipation, compared to healthy controls.
Fibromyalgia patients exhibited a stronger conditioned pain response for high-pain associations compared to healthy controls, associated with reduced dlPFC activation during incongruent trials.
During both congruent and incongruent low-pain associations, fibromyalgia dlPFC brain activation remained indifferent, i.e., did not significantly differ across these conditions.
The review reports long COVID incidence estimates of ~30% after mild acute infection, ~70% after moderate-to-severe infection, and ~12% in vaccinated individuals.

Female sex, type 2 diabetes, prior EBV infection, presence of autoantibodies, prior autoimmune/connective tissue disorders, hyperactivity, and allergic disorders are cited as risk factors for developing long COVID.
Long COVID is associated with depleted T cells and a lack of naive T and B cells, reflecting prolonged immune dysfunction.
Long COVID is associated with elevated type I and type III interferons alongside highly activated innate immune cells.

Mast cells are proposed as major cytokine producers in COVID-19 due to their abundant expression of ACE2 receptors and toll-like receptor-driven autoantibody formation that activates mast cell immunoglobulin receptors.
SARS-CoV-2 infection increases substance P secretion by immune cells and activates the neurokinin receptor via protein cross-linking with PSD-95/Dlg/ZO-1, contributing to mast cell activation.

An observational study by Weinstock et al. found that long COVID patients have virtually identical mast cell activation symptom profiles and severity as previously diagnosed MCAS patients without long COVID, including physical weakness, brain fog, tachycardia, insomnia, and shortness of breath among many others.
Serum tryptase is recommended as the marker of choice for diagnosing MCAS, with elevation above baseline (or persistent baseline >15 ng) during symptomatic periods used as diagnostic criteria.
H1 antihistamines (nonsedating and sedating), often combined with H2 antihistamines, are described as the cornerstone treatment for MCAS, sometimes titrated up to four times the standard dose.
Sodium-cromoglycate, and to a lesser extent ketotifen, have been shown to improve skin, gastrointestinal, and neuropsychiatric symptoms in MCAS by inhibiting mast cell mediator release.
Histamine-dependent mechanisms are reported to mediate T-cell disorders in long COVID, suggesting antihistamine-based treatments could also address hyperinflammatory states.
MCAS increases the risk of anaphylaxis, which the authors note could threaten patient survival, particularly when comorbid with long COVID.
People with HIV who report chronic widespread pain have significantly higher plasma cell-free heme levels than HIV-negative individuals with or without pain and HIV-positive individuals without pain.
HIV-positive individuals with chronic widespread pain have significantly higher plasma histamine than HIV-negative individuals with or without pain and HIV-positive individuals without pain.
HIV-positive individuals with chronic widespread pain have significantly higher plasma bradykinin than HIV-negative individuals with or without pain and HIV-positive individuals without pain.

Hemin treatment caused RBL-2H3 mast cells to change from elongated/spindle-shaped to round/irregular morphology with extracellular release of granules, indicating degranulation, and this was blocked by co-treatment with the CO donor CORM-A1.
Hemin challenge increased histamine release from RBL-2H3 cells, an effect significantly reduced by co-treatment with CORM-A1.
Hemin challenge increased β-hexosaminidase release (an index of mast cell degranulation) from RBL-2H3 cells, an effect significantly reduced by CORM-A1 co-treatment.
HO-1 siRNA significantly reduced HO-1 protein levels in RBL-2H3 cells compared to scrambled siRNA-treated control cells, validating the knockdown model.

HO-1-silenced RBL-2H3 cells released more histamine, with or without hemin treatment, compared to scrambled-siRNA control cells, and CORM-A1 significantly reduced this hemin-induced histamine release in HO-1-deficient cells.

HO-1-silenced RBL-2H3 cells released more β-hexosaminidase, with or without hemin treatment, compared to scrambled-siRNA control cells, and CORM-A1 significantly reduced this hemin-induced release in HO-1-deficient cells.
HO-1 knockout (HO-1−/−) mice had significantly higher plasma histamine levels compared to wildtype mice.
HO-1 knockout (HO-1−/−) mice had significantly higher plasma bradykinin levels compared to wildtype mice.
HO-1−/− mice showed a significantly greater number of mast cells in the dermal skin layer compared to wildtype mice, indicating HO-1 depletion activates/recruits mast cells.
HO-1−/− mice exhibited a higher thermal (cold) allodynia score on the acetone evaporation test compared to wildtype mice.
The hot plate test showed no significant difference in latency to heat-evoked response between HO-1−/− and wildtype mice, indicating HO-1 deletion does not affect heat sensation.
In a phenylhydrazine (PHZ)-induced hemolysis mouse model, plasma cell-free heme was elevated, and hemopexin (but not CORM-A1) treatment reduced this PHZ-induced increase in plasma heme.
Both hemopexin and CORM-A1 significantly reduced the PHZ-induced increase in dermal mast cell numbers in mice.
Plasma histamine was elevated in PHZ-exposed mice, and this increase was significantly attenuated by treatment with either hemopexin or CORM-A1.
Plasma bradykinin was elevated in PHZ-exposed mice, and this increase was significantly attenuated by treatment with either hemopexin or CORM-A1.
CORM-A1 treatment attenuated PHZ-induced mechanical allodynia in mice, as measured by the Von Frey filament test.
CORM-A1 treatment attenuated PHZ-induced thermal (cold) allodynia in mice, as measured by the acetone evaporation test.
CORM-A1 treatment did not alter PHZ-dependent thermal (heat) hyperalgesia measured by the hot plate test.

Pretreatment with 10 μM ethyl caffeate significantly inhibited FICZ- or DHNA-induced SEAP reporter activity in the AhR-responsive HeXS34 reporter cell line, while EC alone showed no AhR agonistic activity.
EC at 1 or 10 μM consistently inhibited FICZ- or DHNA-induced Cyp1A1 mRNA expression in mouse bone marrow-derived mast cells, similar to the effect of the AhR antagonist CH-223191.
EC at concentrations of 1–25 μM did not affect cell viability in HeXS34 reporter cells or BMMCs, based on cell counts, WST, and annexin V assays.
EC at 1 and 10 μM inhibited the FICZ-induced downregulation of AhR protein levels in BMMCs, though no clear concentration-dependent rescue effect was observed.
DHNA induced IL-6 production by BMMCs, and this induction was inhibited by EC at 10 μM.
Pretreatment of mice with oral EC (10 mg/kg) or CH-223191 inhibited DHNA-induced CYP1A1, CYP1B1, and AhRR expression in the small intestine in vivo.
BMMCs cultured for 2 weeks in AhR-ligand-rich IMDM showed enhanced IgE-mediated degranulation compared to those cultured in RPMI 1640 medium, as measured by β-hexosaminidase release.
Both EC (10 μM) and CH-223191 significantly inhibited IgE-mediated degranulation in BMMCs cultured in either RPMI 1640 or IMDM medium, as measured by β-hexosaminidase release and CD63 expression.
Combining EC with CH-223191 did not enhance the suppressive effect on degranulation seen with either agent alone, suggesting EC and CH-223191 act via the same target.
Both EC and CH-223191 inhibited degranulation in mucosal-type mast cells (MMCs) differentiated via co-culture of BMMCs with Notch ligand-expressing CHO cells.

Oral administration of EC or CH-223191 prior to passive cutaneous anaphylaxis (PCA) induction significantly decreased ear swelling, Evans blue dye extravasation, and serum MCP-1 levels compared to vehicle treatment.
The reduction in PCA reaction severity by EC or CH-223191 was associated with suppression of constitutively expressed CYP1A1 and AhRR in the skin.
HeXS34 reporter cells cultured in IMDM secreted more SEAP at baseline than cells cultured in RPMI 1640 medium, and this baseline secretion was inhibited by 10 μM EC or CH-223191.
Serum tryptase level interpretation as a marker of mast cell activation in drug hypersensitivity has been complicated by recent discoveries in tryptase genetics.
New pathophysiological insight into non-mast cell-dependent immediate hypersensitivity mechanisms has been reported, indicating alternative pathways beyond classic mast cell activation.
Oral norisoboldine reduced serum OVA-specific IgE levels in a mouse model of allergic asthma.
Norisoboldine treatment reduced airway hyperresponsiveness in OVA-induced allergic asthma mice.
Norisoboldine reduced eosinophilia in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid of allergic asthma mice.
Norisoboldine treatment increased CD4+Foxp3+ regulatory T cells in the spleen of allergic asthma mice.
Norisoboldine decreased histamine levels in BALF of allergic asthma mice.
Norisoboldine decreased PGD2 levels in BALF of allergic asthma mice.
Norisoboldine decreased levels of IL-4, IL-5, IL-6 and IL-13 in BALF of allergic asthma mice.
NOR treatment decreased levels of the Th2 cytokines IL-4, IL-5, IL-6, and IL-13 in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid of OVA-challenged mice.
Histological analysis showed that NOR treatment reduced airway inflammatory cell recruitment and mucus production in OVA-induced allergic asthma mice.
NOR dose-dependently reduced expression of the high-affinity IgE receptor FcεRI in IgE/OVA-activated bone marrow-derived mast cells (BMMCs).
NOR dose-dependently reduced production of PGD2 and the inflammatory cytokines IL-4, IL-6, IL-13, and TNF-α in IgE/OVA-activated BMMCs.
NOR decreased degranulation of BMMCs activated by IgE/OVA.

Inhibition of the FcεRI-mediated JNK signaling pathway using the selective JNK inhibitor SP600125 produced a similar suppressive effect on BMMC activation as NOR, implicating JNK signaling as a mechanism underlying NOR's antiallergic action.
The number of mast cells in connective tissue disease and tumor tissue specimens correlates with the degree of pathological fibrosis.
Mast cells specifically express the chemokines CCL19 and CCL21, with CCL19 being especially prominent.
CCR7-positive fibroblasts are highly expressed within mast cell clusters in fibrotic tissue.
The HMC-1 mast cell line regulates CD14+ monocyte-derived fibroblasts via CCL19 signaling in vitro.
Mast cell activation may increase CCL19 expression in diseased tissue, thereby inducing CCR7-positive fibroblast migration to the tissue and driving fibrosis.
A significantly higher proportion of FMF patients reported symptoms of mast cell activation compared with healthy controls.
Whole blood histamine was elevated in a substantial subset of FMF patients relative to healthy controls.
Urinary histamine was elevated in a notable subset of FMF patients compared with healthy controls.
Digestive mucosal mast cell infiltration in FMF patients was similar to that in Crohn disease and normal biopsies, but lower than in systemic mastocytosis biopsies.
Serum TSH levels differed significantly between chronic spontaneous urticaria cases and controls.
Anti-TPO antibody levels differed significantly between chronic spontaneous urticaria cases and controls, supporting an association with thyroid autoimmunity.
Serum T3 levels did not differ significantly between chronic spontaneous urticaria cases and controls.
Serum T4 levels did not differ significantly between chronic spontaneous urticaria cases and controls.
Chronic spontaneous urticaria severity scores in the case group were distributed as 40% score one, 35% score two, and 25% score three.
The mean duration of chronic spontaneous urticaria symptoms among cases was 6.90 ± 0.78 weeks, ranging from 6 to over 8 weeks.
Pruritus intensity in the case group was distributed as 40% mild, 35% moderate, and 25% severe.
Wheal counts in the case group were distributed as 40% with fewer than 20 wheals, 35% with 20-50 wheals, and 25% with more than 50 wheals, with a mean of 28.45 ± 23.19 wheals.

The study concludes there is a strong correlation between chronic spontaneous urticaria and thyroid autoimmune disease, with CSU patients more likely to test positive for anti-TPO antibodies, supporting screening for thyroid autoimmunity in CSU regardless of cause.

Mitral valve prolapse frequently occurs as a cardiac feature of inherited connective tissue disorders, including Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, with dysregulated TGF-β signaling proposed as a central shared mechanism.

Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is a heterogeneous group of inherited connective tissue disorders caused by mutations in collagen I, III, V, or XI genes, with an overall population prevalence of about 1 in 3,500 to 1 in 5,000.

Among EDS subtypes, the hypermobile variant (hEDS) is most common, but the rarer cardiac-valvular EDS (cvEDS) subtype is more specifically associated with mitral valve prolapse, skin abnormalities, and joint hypermobility.
Cardiac-valvular EDS (cvEDS) is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner and is caused by mutations in the COL1A2 gene, which encodes the collagen type I α2 chain.

In EDS, collagen structural and processing defects are hypothesized to reduce connective tissue stiffness and increase flexibility, producing excessive biomechanical tension within the mitral valve tissue during systole, though the exact mechanism linking EDS to MVP remains unclear.

The excessive biomechanical tension hypothesized in EDS-affected valve tissue is proposed to stimulate valvular interstitial cell signaling, increasing production of glycosaminoglycans and other ECM components implicated in MVP development.
Acute sacral nerve stimulation with parameter P1 significantly increased colon transit (phenol red recovery) at 90 minutes compared to sham stimulation in normal rats.
SNS with parameter P1 also significantly increased colon transit at 100 minutes compared to sham stimulation in normal rats.
Sacral nerve stimulation with parameter P2 (previously effective for intestinal inflammation) did not alter colon transit compared to sham stimulation.

One week of Loperamide administration reduced the number of fecal pellets by approximately 50% compared to baseline in both treatment groups, confirming successful induction of opioid-induced constipation.
Chronic SNS treatment increased fecal pellet number compared to sham-SNS, with the 7-day average significantly higher in the SNS group.
Chronic SNS increased the wet weight of fecal pellets compared to sham-SNS over the 7-day treatment average.
Chronic SNS increased the water content of fecal pellets compared to sham-SNS over the treatment period.
Six days of chronic SNS treatment significantly shortened whole gut transit time compared to sham-SNS in Loperamide-treated rats.
Chronic SNS decreased sympathetic activity (LF power) compared to sham-SNS after 1 week of treatment.
Chronic SNS increased vagal activity (HF power) compared to sham-SNS after 1 week of treatment.
One week of Loperamide administration markedly increased the sympathovagal (LF/HF) ratio compared to baseline, indicating autonomic imbalance associated with opioid-induced constipation.
SNS significantly reversed the Loperamide-induced increase in sympathovagal (LF/HF) ratio compared to sham-SNS.
Loperamide-induced constipation increased colonic nNOS protein expression in the sham-SNS group compared to normal control rats.
SNS treatment normalized (reduced) the elevated nNOS protein expression in colon tissue compared to sham-SNS.
Loperamide-induced constipation reduced colonic ChAT protein expression in the sham-SNS group.
SNS treatment significantly increased ChAT protein expression in colon tissue compared to sham-SNS.
Immunohistochemistry showed SNS markedly increased the number of ChAT- and PGP9.5-positive cells in colonic muscularis propria compared to sham-SNS.
Immunohistochemistry showed SNS reduced the number of nNOS-positive cells in colonic muscularis propria compared to sham-SNS.

The number of PGP9.5-positive enteric neurons was markedly reduced in colon tissue after Loperamide administration in the sham-SNS group, indicating neuronal loss/degeneration in opioid-induced constipation.
Loperamide treatment significantly decreased colonic GDNF protein expression compared to normal control rats.
SNS treatment markedly increased colonic GDNF protein expression compared to sham-SNS, restoring levels toward normal.

Phosphorylated AKT (p-AKT) was dramatically upregulated in colon tissue of both sham-SNS and SNS treated rats compared to normal controls, suggesting an endogenous neuroprotective response to Loperamide.
SNS further increased p-AKT expression by more than 25% compared to sham-SNS, consistent with enhanced enteric neuronal survival.
The Fit-Fat Index calculated using waist-to-height ratio (FFI_WHR) was significantly associated with heart rate variability parameters in sedentary adults.
The Fit-Fat Index calculated using visceral adipose tissue (FFI_VAT) was the index most consistently associated with heart rate variability parameters among the three FFIs tested.
Isolated cardiorespiratory fitness or fatness indicators (VO2max, WHR, FM%, VAT) were also associated with HRV parameters, but the association was weaker than for the composite Fit-Fat Indices.

Overall, compound Fit-Fat Indices combining fitness and fatness were better predictors of HRV parameters than either cardiorespiratory fitness or fatness indicators alone, with the VAT-based FFI performing best.
Older women with IBS showed reduced indices of vagal activity compared to younger women with IBS.
In older women with IBS, nausea was inversely correlated with Ln RMSSD, a vagally-mediated HRV index.
In older women with IBS, nausea was inversely correlated with Ln pNN50, a vagally-mediated HRV index.
Heartburn in older women with IBS was positively associated with sleepiness.
Heartburn in older women with IBS was positively associated with anger.
Nausea was significantly correlated with anger in the younger group of women with IBS.
No significant relationships were found between HRV indicators and nausea or heartburn in younger women with IBS.
ERBIN mutations enhance TGFb signaling and impair the ability of STAT3 to negatively regulate TGFb signaling.
Impaired STAT3-mediated negative regulation of TGFb signaling due to ERBIN mutations may explain overlap between STAT3 and TGFb signaling disorders.
Excessive TGFb signaling in ERBIN deficiency leads to increased IL-4 receptor expression, contributing to atopic disease.
Blocking the IL-4 receptor is proposed as a precision-based therapy for the atopic disease seen in ERBIN deficiency.
The mechanism by which PGM3 deficiency causes atopic phenotypes remains poorly understood, with preliminary evidence suggesting overlap with IL-6 receptor signaling defects.
The prevalence of IBS among fibromyalgia patients was estimated at approximately 50-70% in the original 1981 report by Yunus et al.
Gut microbiota of fibromyalgia patients showed lower abundance of Lachnospiraceae, Ruminococcaceae, Eubacterium and Bifidobacterium.
Rikenellaceae family and multiple Clostridia class species were overrepresented in fibromyalgia patients' gut microbiota.
Serum and urine concentrations of butyric acid were increased in fibromyalgia patients, suggesting dysregulated rather than deficient SCFA production.
Peripheral glutamate levels were found to be increased in fibromyalgia patients, consistent with a shift in the GABA/glutamate balance toward excitatory nociceptive signaling.
Bacterial species belonging to the Clostridia class were associated with disease severity symptoms in fibromyalgia, including widespread pain index, pain intensity, fatigue and sleep alterations.
In fibromyalgia patients, serum α-muricholic acid was reduced and negatively correlated with symptom severity, supporting a pathogenic role for Clostridium scindens-mediated bile acid alterations.
Ruminococcaceae family, including Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, and Bifidobacterium genus were reduced in IBS patients.
F. prausnitzii abundance negatively correlated with symptom severity in IBS patients.
Bifidobacterium genus abundance was negatively associated with depression in IBS patients.
Lachnospiraceae was enriched specifically in IBS patients with diarrhoea.
Low levels of Lachnospiraceae were reported in IBS patients showing anxiety and depression.
In contrast to fibromyalgia, Eubacterium genus abundance was found to be increased in IBS patients and correlated with symptom severity.
Rikenellaceae, which is expanded in fibromyalgia, is usually depleted in IBS patients.
SIBO incidence, measured by lactulose hydrogen breath test, was higher in fibromyalgia patients than in IBS patients and correlated with pain severity.
Antibiotic therapy was reported to be useful in counteracting intestinal distress in fibromyalgia patients, but this finding has not been further tested in clinical trials.
Probiotic administration with Lactobacillus, Enterococcus and Bifidobacterium bifidum improved symptom severity in IBS patients.
Bifidobacterium longum treatment reduced depression and improved quality of life in IBS patients, but caused no change in IBS symptom severity or faecal microbiota profile.
A probiotic mixture of B. infantis and B. longum improved abdominal pain and quality of life in children with IBS.

L. casei and B. infantis probiotic supplementation improved cognition (impulsive choice and decision-making) in fibromyalgia patients, but showed no effect on pain, quality of life, depression or anxiety.

A probiotic combination (L. rhamnosus, L. paracasei, L. acidophilus and B. bifidus) produced a beneficial effect on cognitive and emotional symptoms in fibromyalgia patients, though this benefit was not confirmed, possibly due to short treatment duration.
Faecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) in IBS patients improved abdominal pain, associated with relative abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila.
In rat models, transplantation of faecal microbiota from constipation-predominant IBS patients induced visceral hypersensitivity.

A fibromyalgia patient achieved full recovery after faecal microbiota transplantation, accompanied by an increase in faecal Bifidobacterium (0% to 5.23%) and a decrease in Streptococcus (26.39% to 0.15%).
Transplantation of intestinal microbes from IBS patients into germ-free mice induced IBS-like symptoms, supporting a causal role for gut microbiota in IBS.
Faecal microbiota transplantation from healthy donors to IBS patients relieved psychological symptoms.
Faecal microbiota transplantation using depression-patient microbiota induced neurobehavioral changes in rats, supporting a causal gut-brain link.
Nitrite is vasodilator-inactive at resting plasma concentrations but acts as a potent, fast vasodilator at near-physiological concentrations of 1.0–2.0 µM.
High-intensity dynamic exercise substantially elevates plasma nitrite/nitrate by up to 20 µM, attributed to iNOS activation from oxidative stress during maximal arousal.

The paper's own CFD model of 20-orders of bifurcating arteries shows that during exercise, but not at rest, cumulative near-wall nitrite concentration reaches vasodilator-active levels (>1000 nM) in arterioles smaller than 0.2 mm in diameter.
Bifurcation-induced mixing of flowing blood with core stream reduces near-wall nitrite concentration by 10-38% at rest and 20-50% during exercise in arteries larger than 0.20 mm.
In L-NAME-inhibited rats, nitrite infusion decreased mean arterial pressure by 96% and increased cerebral blood flow by 13%.
Inhalation of NO raises arterial nitrite levels by 11%, while eNOS inhibition during exercise reduces local blood flow by approximately 25%.

Intra-brachial NO infusion raised plasma nitrite 30-fold but produced no intrinsic vasodilator effect, because the resulting nitrite level (0.5 µM) remained below the 1.0 µM first-pass vasoactive threshold.

Local suppression of NO production in large arterioles (500-1000 µm diameter) reduced NO concentration by nearly 40%, and up to 60% of wall NO in small arteries was estimated to originate from blood-borne transport rather than local synthesis.

Nitrite reductase activity of hemoglobin is maximized at 50% oxygen saturation, while compartmentalization of hemoglobin within red blood cells reduces the rate of NO inactivation by approximately 1,000-fold compared to free hemoglobin.

Plasma nitrite inhibits hemolysis-derived vasoconstriction and potentiates vasodilation when cell-free plasma hemoglobin concentrations are below 25 µM, relevant to exercise-induced hemolysis (e.g., footstrike hemolysis during running).
In peripheral artery disease patients, L-arginine infusion restoring NO formation improved pain-free walking distance by 230% and absolute walking distance by 155%.
Improved plasma nitrite flux in peripheral artery disease patients was associated with improved exercise performance, peak walking time, and maximal oxygen uptake.

A complete circle of Willis augments vertebrobasilar blood velocity acceleration by 82-134% relative to variants lacking full anastomotic connections, based on the authors' prior reduced-order pulse-wave modeling.

Cardiolocomotor synchrony (periodic acceleration) during running reduces run-time by an average of 35 seconds over three miles and is associated with more than a 5.7-fold increase in plasma nitrite levels.
NOS inhibition was accompanied by an 80% decrease in plasma nitrite concentration, leading to the conclusion that approximately 70% of plasma nitrite is derived from eNOS activity.
Peripheral artery occlusive disease due to atherosclerosis causes intermittent claudication with symptomatic leg pain affecting 5% of the population over age 50.
Increases in oscillatory shear index and wall shear stress magnitude associated with exercise are linked to a 14-fold increase in endothelial NO release.
Serum from ME/CFS patients caused a significant loss of circadian rhythm robustness (decreased goodness of fit) in NIH3T3 Per2-luc fibroblasts compared to serum from matched healthy controls.
ME/CFS serum nominally increased the rate of damping of cellular circadian rhythms compared to control serum.
The rate of damping of cellular rhythms induced by patient serum was associated with insomnia severity, as measured by the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, in ME/CFS patients.
Applying recombinant TGFB1 peptide directly to NIH3T3 Per2-luc cells reduced circadian rhythm amplitude, caused a phase delay, and decreased rhythm robustness.
Serum TGFB1 levels did not differ significantly between ME/CFS patients and matched controls, indicating that TGFB1 levels alone do not explain the serum effect on cellular circadian rhythms.
ME/CFS patients had significantly higher plasma levels of IgG, IgA, and IgM anti-endotoxin (EndoCAb) antibodies than healthy controls.
IgG, IgA, and IgM antibodies to bacterial flagellin were significantly elevated in ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls.
Within the ME/CFS cohort, increased antibody responses to flagellin correlated significantly with elevated EndoCAb levels for each antibody isotype.
ME/CFS patients had significantly higher IgG, IgA, and IgM antibodies to wheat gliadin than healthy controls, indicating enhanced systemic reactivity to translocated dietary antigens.
ME/CFS patients showed significantly elevated IgG, IgA, and IgM antibodies to milk casein compared with healthy controls.
Significant correlations were observed between corresponding isotypes of anti-gliadin and anti-casein antibodies in the ME/CFS cohort.

IgM antibody responses to microbial antigens (LPS, flagellin) correlated significantly with IgM responses to dietary antigens (gliadin, casein) in the ME/CFS cohort, suggesting a shared innate-like B cell response.
Plasma FABP2, a marker of intestinal epithelial cell damage and turnover, was significantly elevated in ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls.

Despite elevated antibody responses to microbial antigens, plasma levels of the acute-phase markers LBP and sCD14 were not significantly different between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls at rest.

Maximal exercise significantly increased LBP and sCD14 acute-phase markers in healthy controls, but ME/CFS patients showed no significant LBP increase and only a modest sCD14 rise, indicating a suppressed acute-phase innate immune response to exercise-induced microbial translocation.
Circulating LPS levels increased significantly after maximal exercise in ME/CFS patients but not in healthy controls, consistent with insufficient neutralization of translocated microbial products.
In contrast to the dampened LBP/sCD14 response, ME/CFS patients showed a significantly increased IgM antibody response to LPS and gliadin after maximal exercise.

IL-10 levels increased significantly in response to maximal exercise only in the ME/CFS group, not in healthy controls, suggesting an immunoregulatory response accompanying the suppressed acute-phase response.
No significant change in IFN-γ or TNF-α cytokine concentrations in response to exercise was observed in either the ME/CFS or healthy control group.
Fewer metabolites showed a significant fold change after exercise in the ME/CFS group than in healthy controls, with distinct sets of exercise-responsive metabolites unique to each group.

Plasma glucose levels rose significantly after exercise in healthy controls but not in ME/CFS patients, suggesting an impaired metabolic substrate response needed for optimal innate immune activation.
Citrate levels rose significantly after exercise only in healthy controls, not in ME/CFS patients, potentially limiting macrophage inflammatory activation and M1 polarization in ME/CFS.
The exercise-induced citrate response correlated negatively with the IL-10 response and positively with the LBP response, linking metabolic, immunoregulatory, and acute-phase pathways.
A meta-analysis of seven studies found a significant difference in urinary free cortisol (UFC) between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls, though heterogeneity was very high.
Four of eight studies reported reduced urinary free cortisol in ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls, while three found no significant difference.

Jerjes et al. found significantly lower urinary cortisol and cortisone levels at all measured timepoints across a 15-hour period except between 1800-2100h in ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls.
Three studies reported no significant differences in urinary free cortisol excretion between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls.
Maloney et al. found that allostatic load, of which urinary cortisol was a key component, was higher in ME/CFS patients and accurately discriminated ME/CFS from healthy controls.
Urinary cortisol metabolites measured in three studies showed no significant differences between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls.
Cleare et al. found no significant difference in 24-hour urinary growth hormone output between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls.
Ruiz-Núñez et al. reported significantly lower 24-hour urinary iodine output in ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls.
Casado et al. found significantly lower urine creatinine concentration in ME/CFS patients with comorbid fibromyalgia compared with healthy controls.
Casado et al. found significant differences in electrophoretic peak patterns representing creatinine and uric acid, including amplitude and prevalence, between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls.

Lidbury et al. found significantly lower 24-hour urinary creatinine clearance in ME/CFS patients, which combined with serum urea and serum activin showed strong predictive capability for identifying ME/CFS from healthy controls.
Armstrong et al. found creatinine levels significantly higher in ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls, contrasting with other studies reporting reduced creatinine.
Maes et al. found associations between variance in urinary 8-hydroxydeoxyguanosine and urinary excretion of creatinine in ME/CFS, although absolute creatinine levels were not reported.
Two studies by Jones et al. reported no significant differences in creatinine, free creatinine, or total carnitine excretion rates between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls.
One study using NMR spectroscopy found significantly lower urinary pyruvate levels in ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls.
Two studies described significantly lower urine acetate levels in ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls, regardless of post-exertional malaise experience.
Armstrong et al. conducted correlation analysis between urine, faecal, and blood serum metabolites in ME/CFS and healthy controls, but significant associations were only observed in healthy controls.
Jones et al. reported significantly lower excreted β-alanine in ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls, while Hannestad et al. found no significant difference.
Hannestad et al. reported no significant difference in urinary GABA excretion levels between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls.
Significantly lower urinary levels of hydroxyproline, histidine, valine, methionine, cystine, alanine, serine, and phenylalanine were described in ME/CFS patients across two studies.
McGregor et al. reported an association between higher urine volume and increased pain distribution in ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls.
Three studies reported no significant difference in average urine volumes between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls.
McGregor et al. found that post-exertional malaise was significantly associated with lower serum levels of the purine metabolite hypoxanthine.
Prior evidence cited in this review shows reduced plasmalogen content, biosynthesis, and metabolism in ME/CFS and acute COVID-19, correlating with symptom severity and clinical outcomes.

The authors propose that chronic systemic and central nervous system inflammation together with dysfunctional glial reactivity are shared pathobiological hallmarks underlying both post-COVID-19 syndrome and ME/CFS.

The authors propose plasmalogen replacement therapy (PRT) as a potentially simple, effective, and safe strategy to relieve debilitating symptoms of ME/CFS and post-COVID-19 syndrome, based on promising outcomes of PRT in other neurodegenerative/neuropsychiatric disorders.
Approximately 10% of adults with a positive SARS-CoV-2 PCR test develop persistent symptoms beyond 3 months, defined as post-COVID-19 syndrome.
Vaccination against SARS-CoV-2 provides partial protection against developing post-COVID-19 syndrome.
In most adult PCS patients, symptom severity persists or worsens after 12 months.
PCS predominantly affects previously healthy young and middle-aged adults, with a female preponderance, while children/adolescents show lower prevalence and severity.
Most younger PCS patients show no evidence of organ damage but present a symptom cluster of fatigue, exertion intolerance, cognitive impairment, orthostatic intolerance and autonomic dysfunction.
ME/CFS had an estimated prevalence of 0.3–0.8% (including children/adolescents) prior to the COVID-19 pandemic.
German health insurance data from nearly 30 million individuals showed the 2020 annual incidence of an ME/CFS-like condition was 6/1000 in adults with prior COVID-19 versus 2/1000 in those without.
Reactivation of EBV frequently occurs during COVID-19 and constitutes a risk factor for developing post-COVID-19 syndrome.
A subset of PCS patients show evidence of viral persistence, with SARS-CoV-2 spike and nucleoprotein detectable in serum.
Soluble inflammatory markers and autoantibodies including ANA and GPCR antibodies correlate with symptom severity in PCS, though biomarker profiles could not yet delineate clinical phenotypes.
Endothelitis is common in acute COVID-19 and can persist in PCS, manifesting as endothelial dysfunction, biomarkers of endothelial inflammation, microclots, and hypoperfusion.

Immune dysregulation and autoantibodies are implicated in ME/CFS, supported by high rates of autoimmune disease among first-degree relatives, associations with autoimmunity-related gene variants and MHC alleles, skewed B cell receptor genes, and GPCR antibody association with symptom severity.
ME/CFS patients show endothelial dysfunction in both medium arteries (flow-mediated dilation) and capillaries (post-occlusive reactive hyperemia).
Multiple reports find altered cytokine levels correlating with severity in ME/CFS, but findings are frequently inconsistent between studies.
Rituximab was tested in several phase II trials and one phase III trial in ME/CFS but produced inconclusive results.
A small trial of the PDE5 inhibitor sildenafil showed a significant improvement in fatigue in 5 treated ME/CFS patients compared to 6 receiving placebo.
Rintatolimod, a TLR-3 agonist, showed evidence of efficacy in a phase III ME/CFS trial among patients with shorter disease duration, though the trial used Fukuda criteria not requiring PEM.
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy improved neurocognitive function in a phase II sham-controlled RCT in long COVID patients.
The aptamer BC007 demonstrated safety and GPCR autoantibody-neutralizing capacity in a phase I trial.
Efgartigimod, a neonatal Fc receptor inhibitor that enhances IgG degradation and is licensed for myasthenia gravis, is being tested in a clinical trial for PCS/ME-CFS.

A phase II RCT with the guanylate cyclase stimulator vericiguat, already licensed for heart failure, has been initiated to target endothelial dysfunction and hypoperfusion in PCS and post-COVID ME/CFS.
Low dose naltrexone has shown evidence of efficacy in ME/CFS case reports and in an open trial in PCS, prompting a planned phase 2 RCT.
Guanfacine was described in a case series to ameliorate symptoms in PCS.
Case series have suggested positive effects of prednisolone treatment in PCS patients with neurological symptoms.
Diastolic blood pressure was significantly higher at the end of the 10-minute NASA Lean Test in both the <4-year ME/CFS and PASC cohorts compared with healthy controls.
The PASC cohort had significantly higher heart rate than healthy controls at both 5.5 minutes and the end of the 10-minute orthostatic challenge.

Pulse pressure narrowed to below 25% of systolic blood pressure by 4-5 minutes into the orthostatic challenge in PASC and <4-year ME/CFS cohorts, dropping to 20 mmHg by the end of the test in PASC, whereas the >10-year ME/CFS and healthy control cohorts did not narrow below this threshold.

The orthostatic challenge caused significantly greater worsening of cognitive efficiency across all three DANA Brain Vital tests in PASC, short-duration ME/CFS, and long-duration ME/CFS cohorts compared with healthy controls.

The >10-year ME/CFS cohort had significantly lower cognitive efficiency scores than healthy controls at all time points (baseline, immediately post-NLT, day 2, and day 7) across all three DANA Brain Vital measures.
On day 7 after the orthostatic challenge, Go/No-Go cognitive efficiency remained significantly lower in PASC and >10-year ME/CFS cohorts compared with <4-year ME/CFS and healthy controls.
Change in pulse pressure during the orthostatic challenge significantly mediated slowed Go/No-Go information processing in the PASC cohort, partially explaining disease effects on cognition.
There was a significant direct effect of PASC disease status versus healthy controls on decreased cognitive performance after the orthostatic challenge, independent of the pulse pressure mediator.
Elevated heart rate during the orthostatic challenge was not a significant mediator of slowed cognitive efficiency for any of the disease cohorts in the first mediation model.
In participants aged 40 years or older, change in heart rate during the orthostatic challenge significantly mediated slowed procedural reaction time in both the PASC and <4-year ME/CFS cohorts.
There was a significant direct effect of PASC disease status on slowed procedural reaction time cognitive efficiency.
The direct effect of short-duration (<4 year) ME/CFS disease status on procedural reaction time cognitive efficiency did not reach statistical significance.
Change in pulse pressure was not a significant mediator of the relationship between disease state and cognitive efficiency in either the <40 or >=40 age-stratified models.

The >10-year ME/CFS cohort experienced no significant hemodynamic changes during the orthostatic challenge, which the authors hypothesize reflects long-term compensatory cardiovascular adaptation despite ongoing abnormal cerebral perfusion.
No significant direct or indirect mediation effects linking hemodynamic change to cognitive efficiency were found for the >10-year ME/CFS cohort in any mediation model.
The 2021 NICE guideline reversed prior recommendations and stated that graded exercise therapy should not be used to treat CFS/ME.
The 2021 NICE guideline restricted cognitive-behavioural therapy to symptom management and distress reduction, no longer endorsing it as a treatment aimed at recovery.
The authors argue the NICE committee created a new case definition of CFS/ME that had the effect of downgrading the certainty rating of existing trial evidence.
The authors state the NICE committee omitted data from standard trial endpoints normally used to assess treatment efficacy.
The authors argue the committee discounted trial evidence when assessing treatment harms, instead favouring lower-quality surveys and qualitative studies.
The authors state the committee minimised the importance of fatigue as an outcome measure in its evidence assessment.
The authors state the committee did not use accepted GRADE practices to adequately synthesise the trial evidence.
The NICE committee recommended an energy management approach for CFS/ME despite the absence of supportive research evidence for this strategy.

The authors conclude that the 2021 NICE guideline deviated from usual scientific standards of evidence review, with the consequence that patients with CFS/ME may be denied helpful treatments and risk persistent ill health and disability.

A placebo-controlled trial of the antiviral immune modulator rintatolimod in 92 ME/CFS patients showed statistically significant improvements in performance status, exercise capacity, daily function, and cognition, plus reduced use of symptom-relieving medication.

A second multicenter placebo-controlled trial of rintatolimod in 234 ME/CFS patients found improved exercise tolerance and reduced dependence on symptom-alleviating medication at 40 weeks compared to baseline.

In a small placebo-controlled trial of 30 CFS patients with elevated HHV-6 and EBV titers, valganciclovir improved mental fatigue, fatigue severity, and cognition scores, but the trial was underpowered and reported no pain-specific outcomes.
A placebo-controlled trial of intravenous immunoglobulin G given monthly for six months in 30 CFS patients found no significant benefit in symptoms or functional status among the 28 completers.

Older studies of acyclovir (1988 RCT, 27 CFS patients) and valganciclovir (2012 retrospective chart review, 61 CFS patients) reported improvements in mood, cognition, or physical function, but these improvements did not correlate with antibody titers to suspected causative pathogens, raising the possibility of a placebo effect.

Gut microbial dysbiosis is proposed as a mechanism in ME/CFS development, and antimicrobial regimens may act as either a risk factor or a potential treatment depending on their net effect on gut microbiota composition.

Multiple pathogens (EBV, enterovirus, hepatitis C, cytomegalovirus, West Nile virus, Borrelia burgdorferi, HHV-6, parvovirus B-19, Chlamydia pneumoniae, Coxiella burnetii) have been implicated in ME/CFS etiology, with pathophysiologic similarities noted between ME/CFS and long COVID.

In a VA database retrospective study, non-hospitalized patients treated with oral nirmatrelvir within 5 days of a positive COVID-19 test had a lower risk of post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 than untreated patients, independent of vaccination or prior infection status.

A case series of four COVID-19 patients receiving nirmatrelvir found that three with prior long COVID diagnoses reported improvement, while one patient treated within 24 hours of acute symptom onset experienced overall symptom worsening.
A prospective cohort study of 669 test-confirmed COVID-19 patients found that non-vaccination status was strongly associated with increased odds of developing long COVID symptoms.

A large retrospective cohort study of 9,479 vaccinated individuals matched to unvaccinated controls found vaccination was not associated with a decreased overall risk of long COVID, though it was associated with reduced incidence of myalgia and pain.

A systematic review of 16 observational studies (>614,000 patients) on vaccination and long COVID incidence found widely varying odds ratios with no clear dose-response pattern, and heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis.

Among five studies in the Byambasuren systematic review examining vaccination administered after COVID-19 infection, odds ratios for subsequent long COVID ranged from 0.38 to 0.91, suggesting a possible but variable protective effect.

A small open-label study of 42 long COVID patients found a single post-diagnosis vaccine dose improved symptoms in 16.7% but worsened symptoms in 21.4%, with worsening associated with significantly higher serum antibody titers, suggesting an excessive immune response as a possible mechanism.
A meta-analysis of 9 RCTs in over 2,800 IBS patients found rifaximin had a modest benefit over placebo for IBS symptoms, and single trials of neomycin and norfloxacin were also positive.

A larger meta-analysis of 18 RCTs in over 9,800 patients with diarrhea-predominant or mixed-pattern IBS found rifaximin did not demonstrate greater efficacy than placebo for global IBS symptoms or abdominal pain, despite a lower adverse-effect risk than other pharmacologic classes studied.
After 4 weeks, the 60-minute Long-snake-like moxibustion group showed significantly greater reduction in physical fatigue score than the 30-minute group.
Total FS-14 fatigue score decreased significantly more in the 60-min moxibustion group compared to the 30-min group after 4 weeks of treatment.
Mental fatigue scores did not differ significantly between the 60-min and 30-min moxibustion groups after treatment.
Total Spleen-Kidney Yang Deficiency symptom score was significantly lower in the 60-min moxibustion group than in the 30-min group after treatment.
Fear of cold and cold extremities score was significantly lower in the 60-min group than the 30-min group after treatment.
Shortness of breath and laziness to speak score was significantly lower in the 60-min group compared to the 30-min group.
Soreness and weakness of the waist and knees was significantly reduced more in the 60-min group compared to the 30-min group.
Lumbar cold pain score improved significantly more in the 60-min group than the 30-min group.
Loose stool score was significantly lower in the 60-min group compared with the 30-min group.
Nighttime urinary frequency/coldness score was significantly lower in the 60-min group than the 30-min group.
Lassitude and lack of strength score did not differ significantly between the 60-min and 30-min moxibustion groups.
Depression scores (SDS) decreased in both groups after treatment but did not differ significantly between the 60-min and 30-min moxibustion groups.
Anxiety scores (SAS) decreased in both groups after treatment but showed no significant between-group difference.

At baseline, CFS patients showed significantly lower thermal radiation values (ΔT) than healthy controls in Middle Jiao, Lower Jiao, Shenque (CV8), neck, upper arm, and thoracic segments, indicating low energy metabolism.

After 4 weeks, ΔT values in the 60-min moxibustion group no longer differed significantly from healthy controls at previously abnormal sites, whereas the 30-min group still showed significant differences from controls in the neck and upper arm.

In the 60-min moxibustion group, reductions in Yang deficiency symptom scores (e.g., fear of cold, lassitude, shortness of breath, lumbar cold pain, abdominal fullness) were significantly negatively correlated with increases in ΔT at multiple sites including upper arm, thoracic/lumbar segments, renal region, Upper Jiao, Danzhong, Zhiyang, Dazhui, Zhongwan and Shenque.
In the 30-min moxibustion group, only a single significant correlation was found, between fear of cold/cold extremities improvement and ΔT change at Zhiyang (GV9), far fewer than in the 60-min group.

Overall, 60-minute Long-snake-like moxibustion was more effective than 30-minute moxibustion in relieving fatigue, improving Spleen-Kidney Yang Deficiency symptoms, and normalizing low thermal/energy metabolism toward healthy control levels.
SELENOP autoantibodies were roughly ten times more prevalent in CFS patients than in healthy controls using two different positivity thresholds.
Severe selenium deficiency (<45.7 μg/L) was more common in CFS patients than in controls, occurring in 9% of Dutch and 2% of Spanish CFS patients versus essentially none of controls.
None of the severely selenium-deficient subjects were positive for SELENOP autoantibodies, indicating severe Se deficiency and SELENOP-aAb represent distinct subgroups.

In SELENOP-aAb positive samples, serum selenium no longer correlated with plasma GPx3 activity, unlike the expected linear relationship seen in SELENOP-aAb negative samples, suggesting impaired selenium delivery to GPx3-expressing kidney tissue.
Inflammatory biomarkers hsCRP, white blood cell count, and the tryptophan/kynurenine ratio showed no significant differences between controls and SELENOP-aAb positive or negative CFS patients.
Urinary isoprostane concentrations were elevated in SELENOP-aAb positive CFS patients compared with negative patients, indicating increased oxidative stress in the kidney.
Serum isoprostane concentrations were particularly low in SELENOP-aAb negative CFS patients compared with controls and SELENOP-aAb positive patients.

The ratio of urinary to serum isoprostanes increased progressively from controls to SELENOP-aAb negative to SELENOP-aAb positive CFS patients, consistent with a shift toward renal-specific oxidative stress.
SELENOP-aAb positive CFS patients had elevated free T4 along with elevated rT3/TT4 and rT3/TT3 ratios compared to controls and SELENOP-aAb negative patients.
Total T4 and total T3 concentrations were significantly reduced in CFS patients overall compared with controls.

Multiple indices reflecting T4-to-T3 activation were suppressed in CFS patients, with the lowest values found in SELENOP-aAb positive patients, indicating reduced peripheral thyroid hormone activation.
The calculated total deiodinase activity index (SPINA GD) was reduced in CFS patients and lowest in SELENOP-aAb positive patients, compatible with reduced peripheral thyroid hormone activation.

The calculated thyroid secretory capacity index (SPINA GT) was reduced in CFS overall but was not significantly different between SELENOP-aAb positive CFS patients and controls, suggesting the thyroid gland itself is not primarily impaired.

24-hour urinary iodine concentrations were about half as high in CFS patients as in controls and were lowest and least variable in SELENOP-aAb positive patients, all of whom fell into the iodine-insufficient range.

The product of the SPINA GD deiodinase activity index and urinary iodine concentration emerged as the most sensitive combined marker for identifying CFS patients with reduced thyroid hormone metabolism.
Functional connectivity between the left rostral medulla and right midbrain cuneiform nucleus was significantly stronger in Long-COVID subjects than healthy controls during the Stroop cognitive task.
Connectivity between the left rostral medulla and a right default mode network hub (DM.LP_R) was stronger in Long-COVID than healthy controls.

Seed-to-voxel analysis showed that connectivity between the left anterior insula salience network hub and clusters in the left inferior temporal and left middle frontal/pre-central regions was weaker in Long-COVID than healthy controls.
A cluster in the right operculum showed stronger connectivity with the left anterior insula salience hub in Long-COVID compared to healthy controls.
