In Long-COVID, but not healthy controls, connectivity involving brainstem (medulla, PAG) and salience network hubs correlated significantly with disability severity scores, suggesting abnormal RAS function linked to disability.

Right medulla to right rostral prefrontal cortex connectivity was positively correlated with respiration rate variability in Long-COVID, while left DMN inferior parietal to right salience supramarginal gyrus connectivity was negatively correlated with respiration rate variability.
Long-COVID subjects had significantly lower accuracy than healthy controls on the neutral condition of the Stroop cognitive task.
Long-COVID subjects had slower reaction times than healthy controls across Stroop task conditions, but this difference did not reach statistical significance.

During the same Stroop task, brainstem medulla-to-midbrain connectivity was stronger in Long-COVID relative to controls, whereas a prior ME/CFS study reported weaker medulla-midbrain connectivity relative to controls, indicating opposite directionality between the two conditions despite shared brainstem involvement.

The authors cite prior work reporting impaired cell membrane calcium transport and TRPM3 ion channel dysfunction in both ME/CFS and Long-COVID, potentially relevant to microglial recruitment and medullary involvement.

A companion structural MRI study of the same subject cohort found larger brainstem volumes in Long-COVID than healthy controls, consistent with the increased brainstem functional connectivity reported here.
The review states that emerging data link both CFS and fibromyalgia to deficiencies in CoQ10 and NADH, cofactors important for mitochondrial ATP production.
Mitochondrial failure reduces ATP synthesis in CFS, while CoQ10 and NADH are proposed to enhance ATP production via oxidative phosphorylation.
Castro-Marrero et al. reported clinical improvement in fatigue symptoms after initiating oral NADH or CoQ10 supplementation in CFS patients.
Combined CoQ10 (200 mg/day) plus NADH (20 mg/day) is proposed as a potentially safe way to reduce cognitive fatigue and improve health-related quality of life in ME/CFS.
In a pilot study, 10 mg/day of NADH for 4 weeks was suggested as a valuable adjunctive therapy for CFS.
An RCT of 150 mg/day CoQ10 for two months in CFS patients found no significant improvement in fatigue symptoms.
Serum oxidative stress markers are associated with symptoms of CFS, suggesting oxidative stress underlies fatigue.
Severe fatigue is reported by essentially all fibromyalgia patients, with up to 80% also meeting criteria for chronic fatigue syndrome.
Antioxidant proteins catalase and SOD are diminished in fibromyalgia, and FM has been linked to CoQ10 deficiency.
Ubiquinol-10 treatment in juvenile fibromyalgia patients with CoQ10 deficiency improved chronic fatigue scores measured by CFQ 11.
Forty days of CoQ10 administration (300 mg/day) in fibromyalgia patients significantly reduced pain, fatigue, and morning tiredness subscales of the FIQ.
CoQ10 administration in fibromyalgia patients significantly reduced gene expression of IL-6, IL-8, and TNF.
Higher-dose CoQ10 (200 mg twice daily) for three months relieved fatigue symptoms by approximately 22% in fibromyalgia patients.
Oral SAMe (800 mg/day) for six weeks versus placebo significantly improved fatigue, disease activity, morning stiffness, pain, and mood in fibromyalgia patients.
Intramuscular SAMe (200 mg plus oral tablets) for 7 days significantly reduced pain and fatigue in fibromyalgia patients, unlike TENS.

A modified Myers' intravenous nutrient formula (IVNT) in treatment-resistant fibromyalgia patients reduced pain by 60% and fatigue by 80%, with no reported side effects, though no participant achieved complete resolution.

In CFS, acetylcarnitine had a significant effect on mental fatigue and propionylcarnitine on general fatigue, both improved attention/concentration, but the combined treatment showed less improvement.
In the stability evaluation test, hEDS patients showed significantly greater postural sway velocity in the double-leg stance on foam versus firm surface.
hEDS patients showed significantly greater postural sway in the single-leg stance on foam versus firm surface.
hEDS patients showed significantly greater postural sway in the tandem stance on foam versus firm surface.
On the Modified CTSIB, hEDS patients had significantly greater postural sway with eyes closed compared to eyes open on the firm surface, indicating visual dependence for balance.
On the foam surface of the Modified CTSIB, hEDS patients had significantly greater postural sway with eyes closed than eyes open.
In the unilateral stance test, hEDS patients showed significantly greater sway when standing on the left leg with eyes closed compared to eyes open.
hEDS patients showed significantly greater sway when standing on the right leg with eyes closed compared to eyes open.
Decreased proprioceptive acuity has long been associated with EDS, with deficits demonstrated in both hand and knee joints, believed to underlie balance and gait alterations.
Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome is a prevalent comorbidity in hEDS and can impair balance through episodes of dizziness or nausea.
Hyper-elasticity of ligaments and tendons in hEDS reduces their ability to mediate force transmission and provide structural support, contributing to greater postural instability.
Muscle weakness and hypotonia in hEDS make effective coordination of motor responses difficult, contributing to instability during upright tasks.
In a separate large survey of hEDS patients (N=503), 33% reported a PTSD diagnosis, making it the 14th most common comorbidity among 64 queried diagnoses.
Among hEDS patients with a PTSD diagnosis, 81% believed the diagnosis was an appropriate construct to explain their symptoms.
85% of interviewed hEDS patients could immediately identify one or a small number of specific clinical encounters they recalled as particularly stressful/traumatic.
89% of participants felt that clinicians had been disrespectful or unprofessional toward them, and 92% reported feeling invalidated by clinicians.
46% of participants believed their clinician had acted punitively toward them, such as blocking access to needed care or services.
Only 14% of participants felt clinicians understood their emotions most of the time or always, and only a quarter felt their feedback was heeded, reflecting low perceived clinician empathy.
73% of participants experienced feelings of abandonment when clinicians terminated the relationship via referral or more abruptly.
96% of participants described the healthcare system itself as an antagonistic force, and 87% said interacting with medical bureaucracy interfered with raising children and maintaining employment.

81% of participants reported experiencing negative health outcomes resulting from inappropriate care, including medication reactions, scarring, and complications from procedures, often attributed to clinicians' lack of hEDS knowledge.

85% of participants reported avoiding specific clinicians with whom they had negative experiences, and another 85% reported avoiding clinical care in general as a result of clinician-associated traumatization.
68% of participants avoided disclosing their EDS diagnosis to clinicians for fear of stigma and bias, and even when disclosed, many downplayed their symptoms.
Eight of 26 participants unprompted reported having previously been suicidal as a result of unmanaged pain and hopelessness about treatment, compounded by fear of seeking further care.
A separate survey study found that only 26.9% of hEDS patients expressed trust in their healthcare providers.

The authors report a novel construct, 'clinician-associated traumatization,' whereby cumulative negative healthcare encounters (rather than a single life-threatening medical event, as required by the DSM-5 definition of medical trauma) produce PTSD-like symptoms including intrusive thoughts, avoidance, hypervigilance, and exaggerated negative self-beliefs.

Cited literature indicates women may be more likely than men to develop persistent trauma symptoms even when exposed to the same traumatic event, relevant to the predominantly female hEDS study population.

The EDS ECHO clinician education program has been shown to reduce clinicians' feelings of being overwhelmed or frustrated when caring for hEDS patients, suggesting a potential means to improve empathy and reduce clinician-associated traumatization.

Two participants (mothers) in the authors' prior study described clinicians threatening to report them to Child Protective Services for seeking hEDS-related care for their children, exemplifying institutional betrayal and traumatization.
During a 9-week control period without intervention prior to the rehabilitation program, no significant changes in outcome measures were observed among hEDS patients.
Immediately after the 9-week rehabilitation program, hEDS patients showed significant improvements in functional exercise capacity, balance with eyes closed, fatigue, and quality of life.
Six weeks after completion of the rehabilitation program, further improvements beyond the immediate post-RP gains were observed in hEDS patients.
At 6-month follow-up, sustained improvement was maintained in functional exercise capacity, kinesiophobia, depression, hyperventilation, and some quality of life components among hEDS patients.

A 33-year-old woman with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and severe joint contractures/scoliosis underwent transurethral lithotripsy (TUL) to successfully crush and remove an 8 mm ureteral calculus without mucosal damage to the ureteral orifice.

Extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy (ESWL) was considered but rejected due to the patient's severe joint contractures preventing supine positioning, difficulty with ventilator management, and a calculated major diameter index of 13,257 (HU >12,000) predicting >50% likelihood of needing multiple treatments.

Post-void residual urine volume exceeded 200 mL in this EDS patient, consistent with prior reports that EDS patients may have residual urine volumes of 100-200 mL, thought to be due to non-neurogenic bladder sphincter dysfunction.

The urinary calculi in this EDS patient were compositionally mixed: the ureteral calculus was equally calcium oxalate and calcium phosphate, while sandy bladder calculi consisted of acidic ammonium urate, calcium oxalate, and calcium phosphate, with formation potentially accelerated by low fluid intake and chronic bacteriuria.
The authors note there are no reports indicating urinary tract calculi occur more frequently in EDS patients than in the general population.

Genetic testing identified a novel heterozygous de novo missense variant c.1889G>A (p.Gly630Glu) in COL3A1, classified as likely pathogenic and causative of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome in this patient.
The variant was confirmed to have arisen de novo, as it was absent in both unaffected parents' samples.

The patient exhibited recurrent spontaneous pneumothoraces (at ages 14 and 17) and recurrent hemoptysis/pulmonary hemorrhage as atypical presenting features of vEDS, in the absence of classic facial, skin, or joint hypermobility signs.

Extensive vascular imaging revealed multiple aneurysms, ectasia, dissection, and arteriovenous shunts including a hypertrophic diaphragmatic artery with two aneurysms (one thrombosed), a dissection flap in the right external iliac artery, and arterio-venous shunts between the 12th intercostal artery and the pulmonary vein.

Hematologic screening for coagulation disorders (CBC, PT, aPTT, PFA-100, coagulation factor assay, vWF dosage) performed after severe hemoptysis showed no abnormalities, ruling out a bleeding disorder as the cause.
Following diagnosis, the patient was started on celiprolol 200mg daily, a treatment previously shown to improve outcomes and cardiovascular events in vEDS.

Heart-lung transplantation, the only potentially resolutive treatment for the patient's recurrent pulmonary hemorrhages, was deemed unfeasible by the surgical team due to prior chemical pleurodesis and tissue fragility.
Population-level literature indicates the median age for the first major vascular event in vEDS is 24.6 years and median survival is 48 years due to high complication rates.

Literature indicates approximately 65% of pathogenic COL3A1 variants are missense variants substituting a glycine residue in the triple helical domain, 25% are aberrant splicing variants, and 5% are nonsense/frameshift variants causing haploinsufficiency.

Cited literature reports that splicing variants in COL3A1 are associated with the most severe vEDS disease course, followed by glycine-substitution missense variants, while haploinsufficient variants are associated with a milder course and increased life expectancy.

Literature indicates that for 70% of vEDS patients the presenting sign is vascular or organ rupture, and 12% present atypically with spontaneous pneumothorax due to lung bleb rupture as their first manifestation.
Approximately 50% of COL3A1 pathogenic variants occur de novo, contributing to diagnostic difficulty especially without family history.
A de novo COL3A1 variant was identified as the genetic cause of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome in a young woman.
The patient presented clinically with a spontaneous direct carotid-cavernous fistula as a vascular complication of her connective tissue disorder.

Exome sequencing identified a homozygous pathogenic FKBP14 variant (c.362dupC, p.Glu122fs) as the cause of the patient's connective tissue disorder, establishing a diagnosis of FKBP14 kyphoscoliotic Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

The patient's FKBP14-related kyphoscoliotic EDS was misdiagnosed as Larsen syndrome for 42 years because no confirmatory molecular testing for FLNB (the Larsen syndrome gene) had been performed, and the phenotypes overlap.

Despite FKBP14-kEDS being classified as a nonvascular type of EDS, a cited study found that arterial dissections are the most frequently reported vascular complication among nonvascular EDS types specifically in FKBP14-kEDS.

The patient with FKBP14-kEDS experienced bilateral carotid artery dissections (ages 27 and 32, the second postpartum) and ischemic strokes (ages 27 and 40), later managed with long-term anticoagulation.
Following molecular diagnosis, the patient was started on bisoprolol (beta-blocker) and continued anticoagulation, and has had no additional vascular episodes or complications since diagnosis.

Physical examination of the patient revealed craniofacial and skeletal features consistent with kyphoscoliotic EDS, including hypertelorism, low-set ears, high-arched palate, pectus excavatum, and hypermobile wrists and lumbar joints.

The authors recommend that patients with a clinical (non-molecularly confirmed) diagnosis of Larsen syndrome, and those with connective tissue disorder features plus significant vascular events, undergo broad-based genetic sequencing for multiple hereditary connective tissue disorders.
The paper states that connective tissue disorders such as hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome can cause bleeding symptoms via impaired hemostasis due to defective collagen.

The paper notes there is a significant diagnostic gap between symptom onset and diagnosis of bleeding disorders in adolescent and young adult women despite longstanding ACOG screening recommendations for heavy menstrual bleeding.
Fatigue is reported in a large proportion of functional neurological disorder patients, ranging from 47% to 93%.
Cognitive symptoms are reported in 80-85% of FND patients, making them the second most common comorbid symptom after fatigue.
Psychiatric disorders, particularly anxiety and mood disorders followed by neurodevelopmental disorders, are reported in 40-100% of FND patients depending on FND subtype.
Childhood trauma exposure, predominantly emotional neglect and physical abuse, along with maladaptive coping strategies, has been identified in up to 75% of FND patients.
Epilepsy is reported as a comorbidity in about 20% of patients with functional dissociative seizures (FDS).
Functional motor disorder (FMD) is reported to co-occur with Parkinson's Disease in about 7% of cases.
Somatic symptom disorders, including chronic pain syndromes, are frequently associated with FND, occurring in about 50% of patients.
Recent data suggest a high comorbidity between functional neurological disorder and hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome, occurring in about 55% of cases.
Marfan syndrome is caused by heterozygous mutations in FBN1, a large 230 kb gene with 65 exons on chromosome 15q21.1, which encodes the ECM protein fibrillin-1.
Aortic root (sinus of Valsalva) dilation, creating a characteristic pear-shaped aortic root, occurs in approximately 80% of adult MFS patients.
Ectopia lentis, a cardinal MFS feature caused by weakness of the ciliary zonulae, is found in about 60% of patients.
Myopia, the most common ocular minor feature, is found in 34-44% of MFS patients and often progresses rapidly in childhood.
